options.text: A gradient is a record of which neurons fire to each test input, and recording single neurons was possible long before representations were discussed.
options.why: A generalization gradient is not a record of neurons. It is measured from what the animal does, which is why it needs no claim about what goes on inside.

options.text: A gradient is a measure of the physical differences between test inputs, which instruments could record well before any theory of the mind existed.
options.why: The physical differences are not the gradient, and closeness in physical units turns out to predict generalization poorly. A gradient is measured from the animal’s responses.

options.text: A gradient is a count of the inputs an animal fails to tell apart, and counting such failures needs no theory of how inputs are told apart.
options.why: A gradient is not a count of failures. Generalizing can be a bet that two things share a consequence, made by an animal that tells them apart perfectly well.

items.stem: An animal is trained to respond to one tone. In tests it responds more strongly to the tone an octave above the trained one than to a tone only slightly below it, although the lower tone is physically much closer. What does this result show?

options.text: The differences that govern generalization are not simply the physical ones, so which tones count as alike has to be measured from behavior.
options.why: Correct. A tone can be treated as more like the tone an octave above it than like physically closer tones below. Which differences matter has to be found by watching what the animal does.

options.text: The animal cannot hear the slightly lower tone well, so the weaker response to it reflects a limit of its ears rather than how it generalizes.
options.why: Nothing in the result points to poor hearing. A tone treated as more like its octave than like a closer tone is a known pattern of generalization, not a hearing defect.

options.text: The animal has failed to discriminate the octave from the trained tone, so the stronger response to the octave shows it cannot tell them apart.
options.why: Generalizing is not the same as failing to discriminate. The animal may tell the octave apart perfectly well; the result is about which differences govern its responding.

options.text: The result is not a generalization gradient at all, since a real gradient has to fall off steadily with the physical difference between tones.
options.why: A gradient is a description of behavior plotted against how the test input differs. The result shows that physical difference is not always the difference that governs it.

items.stem: An engineer proposes to predict how an animal will generalize from a trained input by measuring, in physical units, how much each test input differs from it. What is wrong with the proposal?

options.text: Closeness in physical units predicts generalization poorly, since the same physical difference can matter a great deal on one dimension and hardly at all on another.
options.why: Correct. The physical measure of a difference and the difference that governs generalization come apart, and they come apart differently on different dimensions.

options.text: Physical units cannot be measured precisely enough, so the small differences between nearby test inputs would be lost in the error of the instruments.
options.why: Precision is not the problem. Even measured perfectly, physical closeness is a poor predictor of how animals generalize.

options.text: Physical difference is the right measure, but it has to be taken inside the animal, as differences in receptor activity, rather than from the inputs themselves.
options.why: The point is not where a physical difference is measured. Which differences govern generalization has to be measured by watching what the animal does.

options.text: Physical difference works for sounds and lights but not for smells and tastes, since chemical inputs have no physical units in which they could be measured at all.
options.why: Chemicals can be measured physically too. The trouble is the same on every dimension: physical closeness does not predict well how animals generalize.

items.stem: Researchers have measured in detail how pigeons generalize across colors of light. They now want to know how goldfish generalize across the same colors. What should they do?

options.text: Measure the goldfish’s own generalization, since the pattern of generalization differs from one species to another.
options.why: Correct. The pattern of generalization differs from species to species, so a gradient measured in pigeons cannot simply stand in for a goldfish.

options.text: Use the pigeons’ generalization gradient for the goldfish, since a gradient depends on the lights and not on the animal.
options.why: A gradient is a description of an animal’s behavior, and that behavior differs between species. The pigeons’ gradient says nothing certain about goldfish.

options.text: Measure the physical differences between the colors, since those differences set the gradient for any animal tested on them.
options.why: Physical closeness is a poor predictor of how animals generalize, and the pattern differs between species, so the colors alone cannot settle the question.

options.text: Use the pigeons’ gradient with its slope halved, since fish respond to differences in color less strongly than birds do.
options.why: Nothing licenses a fixed correction from one species to another. The goldfish’s gradient has to be measured in goldfish.

items.stem: A student wants to know which stream smells the small fish treats as more or less like an eel. She plans to analyze each smell chemically and rank the smells by how much their chemistry differs from an eel’s. Why would that ranking fall short?

options.text: The differences that make a smell more or less like an eel to the fish are not simply the physical ones, so they have to be measured by watching what the fish does.
options.why: Correct. Which differences govern generalization is not given by physical measurement. For the small fish it has to be measured from the fish’s own behavior.

options.text: The fish’s receptors respond to chemicals the analysis cannot detect, so a finer chemical analysis of each smell would give the ranking the student wants.
options.why: A finer analysis would still be a physical measure. The differences that govern generalization are not simply the physical ones, however finely those are measured.

options.text: The fish generalizes only to smells it cannot tell apart from an eel’s, so the ranking should instead list the smells by how often the fish confuses each of them with an eel’s.
options.why: Generalizing is not the same as failing to tell inputs apart. It can be a bet that two things share a consequence, made by an animal that tells them apart perfectly well.

options.text: The fish’s responses change from one sniff to the next because of noise, so no single ranking of the smells could describe how the fish treats them at all.
options.why: Noise makes each decision variable, but responding can still be measured across many trials. The trouble with the plan is that it measures chemistry rather than the fish.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how a researcher would measure a generalization gradient in an animal, why the measurement needs no claim about what goes on inside the animal, and why the physical differences between the test inputs cannot simply be assumed to be the ones that matter.
items.answer: The researcher trains the animal to give a response to one input, then tests it on inputs that differ from the trained one by different amounts, and records how strongly it gives the trained response to each. Responding falls off smoothly, and often steeply, as the input differs more, and that fall-off is the generalization gradient. It is a description of behavior, response strength against how the test input differs, so it needs no claim about representations, which is why it was measured long before anyone spoke of them. But closeness in physical units predicts generalization poorly. The same physical difference can matter a great deal on one dimension and hardly at all on another, and the pattern differs between species. So which differences count has to be measured by watching what the animal does.
rubric: Describes training a response to one input and testing on inputs that differ from it by different amounts.
Says responding falls off as the test input differs more from the trained one.
States that the gradient is a description of behavior and needs no claim about what goes on inside the animal.
States that physical closeness is a poor predictor, or that the same physical difference can matter on one dimension and not on another.
Concludes that which differences matter has to be measured from the animal’s behavior.

items.stem: What is signal detection theory?

options.text: A framework for decisions about whether something is present, which separates how well the evidence tells the two cases apart from where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn.
options.why: Correct. It was developed for faint signals on radar, and it is now used wherever a decision is about whether something is there.

options.text: A framework for decisions about which of several categories an input belongs to, which assigns the input to whichever category has stored examples it resembles most.
options.why: Sorting an input among categories by comparing it with stored examples is the job of a categorization model, such as an exemplar model. Signal detection theory is about deciding whether one thing is present.

options.text: A framework for measuring how an animal generalizes from one trained input, which records how its responding falls off as the test inputs differ from it more and more.
options.why: That describes measuring a generalization gradient. Signal detection theory separates how well evidence distinguishes present from absent from where the line is drawn.

options.text: A framework for building a separate detector for each thing in the world, which links one receptor to one response so that the receptor’s firing is itself the detection.
options.why: That describes a labeled line, the way the worm recognizes copper. Signal detection theory is a framework for deciding under noisy, overlapping evidence.

items.stem: What is the name of the framework for decisions about whether something is present, which separates how well the evidence distinguishes “present” from “absent” from where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn?

options.text: Signal detection theory
options.why: Correct. Signal detection theory pulls apart the two quantities, sensitivity and criterion, that percent correct mixes together.

options.text: Decision-bound model
options.why: A decision-bound model divides a space of inputs into regions, one for each response. It grew out of signal detection theory, but the framework named here is signal detection theory itself.

options.text: Pattern recognition
options.why: Pattern recognition is identifying something from a combination of activity across many inputs. The framework for yes-or-no decisions under noise is signal detection theory.

options.text: k-nearest-neighbor classification
options.why: That method assigns a new input to whichever category is most common among the stored examples most similar to it. The framework for deciding whether something is present is signal detection theory.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is a hit?

options.text: Judging a target present when it is present.
options.why: Correct. A hit is one of the two correct outcomes: the target is there, and it is judged to be there.

options.text: Judging a target present when it is absent.
options.why: That is a false alarm, one of the two errors: something is judged to be there that is not.

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is present.
options.why: That is a miss, the other error: a target that is there goes undetected.

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is absent.
options.why: That is a correct rejection, the other correct outcome: nothing is there, and nothing is judged to be there.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is the outcome called when a target is present and is judged to be present?

options.text: Hit
options.why: Correct. A target present and judged present is a hit.

options.text: False alarm
options.why: A false alarm is judging a target present when it is absent. Here the target really is there, so the outcome is a hit.

options.text: Correct rejection
options.why: A correct rejection is also a correct outcome, but it is judging a target absent when it is absent.

options.text: Sensitivity
options.why: Sensitivity is not an outcome of a single decision. It is how far apart the evidence for “present” and for “absent” lie.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is a miss?

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is present.
options.why: Correct. A miss is the error in which a target that is there goes undetected.

options.text: Judging a target present when it is absent.
options.why: That is a false alarm, the other kind of error. A miss is failing to detect a target that is really there.

options.text: Failing to respond at all, because the evidence was too weak to register.
options.why: In signal detection theory every decision has an outcome, and “no” is a response. A miss is a “no” given when the target is present.

options.text: Setting the criterion in the wrong place, so that percent correct falls.
options.why: The criterion is where the line is drawn, not an outcome. A miss is one outcome of a single decision: a target present and judged absent.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is the outcome called when a target is present but is judged to be absent?

options.text: Miss
options.why: Correct. A target present and judged absent is a miss.

options.text: Correct rejection
options.why: A correct rejection is judging a target absent when it really is absent. Here the target is present, so the “no” is an error, a miss.

options.text: False alarm
options.why: A false alarm is the other error, judging a target present when it is absent. Here a present target was judged absent.

options.text: Criterion
options.why: The criterion is where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn. It is not the outcome of a single decision.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is a false alarm?

options.text: Judging a target present when it is absent.
options.why: Correct. A false alarm is the error in which something is judged to be there that is not.

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is present.
options.why: That is a miss, the other kind of error. A false alarm is a “yes” given when no target is there.

options.text: Responding to a real target, but too late to be of use.
options.why: Timing plays no part in the four outcomes. A false alarm is defined by a “yes” when there is no target at all.

options.text: Any decision made with a criterion set lower than the best one.
options.why: A low criterion produces more false alarms, but the criterion is not an outcome. A false alarm is a single decision: target absent, judged present.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is the outcome called when no target is present but one is judged to be there?

options.text: False alarm
options.why: Correct. No target present but one judged to be there is a false alarm.

options.text: Hit
options.why: A hit is a “yes” when the target really is present. Here nothing was there, so the “yes” is a false alarm.

options.text: Miss
options.why: A miss is the other error, judging a target absent when it is present. Here an absent target was judged present.

options.text: Correct rejection
options.why: A correct rejection is a “no” when no target is present. Here something absent was judged present, which is a false alarm.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is a correct rejection?

options.text: Judging a target absent when it is absent.
options.why: Correct. A correct rejection is the correct outcome in which nothing is there and nothing is judged to be there.

options.text: Judging a target present when it is present.
options.why: That is a hit, the other correct outcome. A correct rejection is a correct “no”.

options.text: Rejecting an input as the wrong kind of target.
options.why: The four outcomes concern whether a target is there, not which kind of target it is. A correct rejection is a “no” when nothing is there.

options.text: Changing a “yes” to “no” after a second look.
options.why: A correct rejection is not a revised decision. It is a single “no” given when no target is present.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is the outcome called when no target is present and none is judged to be there?

options.text: Correct rejection
options.why: Correct. No target present and none judged to be there is a correct rejection.

options.text: Miss
options.why: A miss is also a “no”, but it is given when a target is present. A “no” when nothing is there is a correct rejection.

options.text: Hit
options.why: A hit is the other correct outcome, judging a target present when it is present.

options.text: Discrimination
options.why: Discrimination is the demand that inputs calling for different responses be told apart. It is not one of the four outcomes of a decision.

items.stem: The evidence for “eel” that reaches the small fish is plotted twice, once for encounters with an eel and once for encounters without one. The two distributions overlap. Why do they overlap?

options.text: The evidence varies from one encounter to the next in both cases, since no two sniffs are the same and the receptors and neurons are noisy.
options.why: Correct. Even with an eel present the evidence varies, and without one it varies too, so some encounters without an eel give more evidence than some encounters with one.

options.text: The fish has not yet learned which smell belongs to the eel, so the evidence it receives stays random from one encounter to the next until that learning is complete.
options.why: Learning is not what makes the distributions overlap. Sniffs differ and receptors and neurons are noisy, so the evidence varies whatever the fish has learned.

options.text: The eel gives off no smell of its own, so all of the evidence for “eel” comes from other things carried in the water around it.
options.why: An eel does give off a mixture of chemicals. The overlap comes from that evidence varying from one encounter to the next, with and without an eel.

options.text: The fish’s criterion is set too low, so it counts as evidence for “eel” many smells that have nothing to do with eels.
options.why: The criterion is a line drawn across the distributions, and moving it does not move them. The overlap is in the evidence itself.

items.stem: A deer at dusk hears rustling in the brush. A rustle sometimes comes from a wolf and sometimes only from the wind, and the amount of wolf-like evidence in a rustle varies widely in both cases, with much overlap. What does any rule for when to flee have to amount to?

options.text: A line drawn somewhere along the evidence, with flight for rustles above it and grazing for rustles below it.
options.why: Correct. With overlapping evidence, a line has to be drawn somewhere along the evidence axis: flee above it, keep grazing below it.

options.text: A rule that waits until a rustle is certain to be a wolf, since only certainty rules out ever fleeing from the wind.
options.why: With overlapping evidence, certainty never arrives. Any workable rule draws a line somewhere along the amount of evidence.

options.text: A separate detector for each wolf the deer has met, since each wolf makes a rustle that differs from the wind.
options.why: No single rustle settles the question, and no two encounters are the same. What the deer needs is a line along the evidence, not a detector for each wolf.

options.text: A rule that flees whenever a rustle is louder than the last one, since rising evidence means a wolf is coming nearer.
options.why: Comparing each rustle with the last ignores how the evidence varies with and without a wolf. The rule has to be a line along the amount of evidence.

items.stem: Signal detection theory was developed for operators looking for faint signals on radar. Why does the same framework apply to a doctor deciding whether a scan shows a tumor?

options.text: Both are decisions about whether something is there, made on evidence that varies whether or not it is there.
options.why: Correct. Signal detection theory applies wherever a decision is about whether something is there: a faint tone, a disease, a remembered face, a junk message.

options.text: Both are read from electronic screens, and the framework describes how a viewer judges whether a faint mark on a screen is real.
options.why: The screen is incidental. The framework applies to a remembered face or a junk message just as well, because each is a decision about whether something is there.

options.text: Both concern rare targets, and the framework applies only when targets are rare and when every error is costly.
options.why: How common targets are affects where the best criterion lies, but it does not decide whether the framework applies. Any decision about presence fits it.

options.text: Both are decisions about which of many categories an input belongs to, made by comparing it with stored cases.
options.why: Sorting among many categories by stored cases is what an exemplar model does. Signal detection theory concerns a yes-or-no decision about presence.

items.stem: A spam filter lets a junk message through to the inbox. In signal detection terms, which outcome is that?

options.text: A miss
options.why: Correct. The target here is a junk message. It was present and was treated as absent, so the outcome is a miss.

options.text: A false alarm
options.why: A false alarm would be a real message sent to the junk folder, a target treated as present when it is absent.

options.text: A correct rejection
options.why: A correct rejection would be a real message left in the inbox, no target present and none treated as there.

options.text: A hit
options.why: A hit would be a junk message caught and filtered out, a target present and treated as present.

items.stem: A witness is shown a single person and asked whether this is the man she saw at the scene. The person is innocent, but she says “that’s him”. In signal detection terms, which outcome is that?

options.text: A false alarm
options.why: Correct. The target, the man she saw, is not present, and she judges him present. That is a false alarm.

options.text: A hit
options.why: A hit would be naming the man she actually saw when he is shown to her. Here the person shown is someone else.

options.text: A miss
options.why: A miss would be failing to recognize the man she saw when he is shown to her, a target present and judged absent.

options.text: A correct rejection
options.why: A correct rejection would be saying “that’s not him” about an innocent person. She said “yes” instead.

items.stem: A hit and a correct rejection are both correct decisions. What is the difference between them?

options.text: A hit is judging a target present when it is present; a correct rejection is judging it absent when it is absent.
options.why: Correct. The two correct outcomes differ in whether the target is there, and in whether the answer given is “yes” or “no”.

options.text: A hit is a correct decision made at once; a correct rejection is a correct decision reached only after a second look.
options.why: Speed and second looks play no part in the four outcomes. A hit is a correct “yes”, and a correct rejection is a correct “no”.

options.text: A hit is a correct decision about a strong signal; a correct rejection is a correct decision about a faint signal.
options.why: A faint signal that is really there and is detected is still a hit. A correct rejection is a “no” when no target is there at all.

options.text: A hit is a correct decision with a low criterion; a correct rejection is a correct decision with a high criterion.
options.why: Either correct outcome can happen at any criterion. Lowering the criterion gives more hits, but what defines a hit is a target present and judged present.

items.stem: Each time the small fish catches a whiff of something, it either flees or stays. Which pair of behaviors are the fish’s two kinds of error?

options.text: Staying put while an eel is near, and bolting when no eel is near.
options.why: Correct. Staying put beside an eel is a miss, and bolting from nothing is a false alarm.

options.text: Bolting from an eel that is near, and staying put when no eel is near.
options.why: Those are the two correct outcomes. Fleeing from an eel is a hit, and feeding calmly with no eel near is a correct rejection.

options.text: Staying put while an eel is near, and bolting from an eel that is near.
options.why: Staying beside an eel is a miss, an error, but fleeing from an eel is a hit, a correct outcome.

options.text: Bolting when no eel is near, and feeding calmly when no eel is near.
options.why: Bolting from nothing is a false alarm, an error, but feeding calmly when no eel is near is a correct rejection.

items.stem: Signal detection theory separates two quantities that are sometimes confused. What is the difference between sensitivity and the criterion?

options.text: Sensitivity is how far apart the two distributions of evidence lie; the criterion is where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn.
options.why: Correct. Sensitivity, usually measured as d′, is the separation of the distributions. The criterion is a separate choice of where to draw the line across them.

options.text: Sensitivity is how little evidence is needed before saying “yes”; the criterion is how far apart the two distributions of evidence lie.
options.why: That swaps the two. How little evidence is needed for a “yes” is set by the criterion; how far apart the distributions lie is sensitivity.

options.text: Sensitivity is the proportion of targets that are detected; the criterion is the proportion of all decisions that turn out correct.
options.why: Both of those proportions shift when the line moves, so neither is sensitivity. Percent correct mixes sensitivity and criterion together.

options.text: Sensitivity is set by the difference between what a miss and a false alarm cost; the criterion is set by how noisy the receptors and neurons are.
options.why: That reverses where each comes from. Costs bear on where the criterion should go; noise in the evidence bears on how far apart the distributions lie.

items.stem: A car’s lane-departure warning is reset so that it sounds at smaller drifts toward the edge of the lane than before. Nothing else about the car changes. What should the driver expect?

options.text: More warnings when the car really is leaving its lane and fewer real departures missed, but also more warnings when it is not leaving at all.
options.why: Correct. The warning now has a lower criterion. A lower criterion produces more hits and fewer misses, but also more false alarms.

options.text: More warnings when the car really is leaving its lane, and fewer warnings when it is not, since the system is now better at its task.
options.why: Resetting the line does not make the system better at telling drifts apart. Moving the criterion trades one kind of error for the other.

options.text: Fewer warnings of every kind, since a warning that needs less evidence is a weaker warning and so is set off less often.
options.why: Needing less evidence means the warning goes off more readily, not less. Both real departures and harmless drifts set it off more often.

options.text: The same warnings as before when the car is leaving its lane, but more when it is not, since only false alarms depend on the setting.
options.why: The setting moves both rates at once. A lower criterion adds false alarms and also adds hits, catching departures that used to be missed.

items.stem: Lowering the criterion produces more hits, but also more false alarms. Why does it leave sensitivity exactly where it was?

options.text: Sensitivity is how far apart the two distributions lie, and moving the line along the evidence axis moves neither of the distributions.
options.why: Correct. The criterion is drawn across the distributions, so sliding it changes which outcomes occur but leaves the separation between them exactly as it was.

options.text: The extra hits and the extra false alarms always come in equal numbers, so the gain and the loss cancel each other out exactly.
options.why: The two need not be equal; on the face memory test a more liberal criterion added a few hits and many more false alarms. Sensitivity is unchanged because the distributions have not moved.

options.text: Sensitivity is fixed by the receptors an animal is born with, so nothing a decider does can raise or lower it at any time.
options.why: Sensitivity can change, through a better representation of the input. Moving the criterion simply is not one of the things that changes it.

options.text: Sensitivity counts only hits and misses, and a lower criterion turns some misses into hits without changing how many there are in total.
options.why: Sensitivity is not a count of outcomes. It is how far apart the two distributions of evidence lie, which a moving line cannot change.

items.stem: On a face memory test, each of two people sees 50 studied faces and 50 new ones. One is right 84% of the time and the other only 74%, yet both have a d′ of about 2.0. What explains the difference in percent correct?

options.text: The second person says “yes” more often, a more liberal criterion, which adds a few hits but many more false alarms.
options.why: Correct. The second person says “yes” to 49 studied faces rather than 42, but to 25 new faces rather than 8. Sensitivity is the same; only the criterion differs.

options.text: The second person remembers the studied faces less well, so fewer of them are recognized and more are wrongly rejected.
options.why: Remembering less well would lower d′, and the two d′ values match. The second person in fact says “yes” to more studied faces, not fewer.

options.text: The second person has lower sensitivity, which the matching values of d′ conceal because d′ leaves out the false alarms.
options.why: d′ is the distance between the centers of two distributions, one for studied faces and one for new faces, so false alarms on new faces are part of it. Matching d′ means matching sensitivity.

options.text: The second person says “yes” less often, a more conservative criterion, which avoids false alarms but misses studied faces.
options.why: That reverses the case. The second person says “yes” more often, to 74 faces in all against the first person’s 50.

items.stem: Two trainee radiologists read the same set of scans. Trainee A is right more often overall than Trainee B, but B calls “tumor” far more often than A. A supervisor concludes that A is better at telling tumors from healthy tissue. What should signal detection theory make the supervisor check first?

options.text: Whether the gap in percent correct comes from a difference in criterion, by comparing the two trainees’ sensitivity directly.
options.why: Correct. Percent correct mixes sensitivity and criterion together. B’s frequent “tumor” calls suggest a lower criterion, which can lower percent correct with no difference in sensitivity.

options.text: Whether B’s extra calls of “tumor” were mostly hits, since a higher hit rate on its own shows which trainee is the better reader.
options.why: A lower criterion raises the hit rate by itself, without any better reading. Hits alone cannot show sensitivity.

options.text: Whether A’s percent correct is high enough to pass, since percent correct already captures how well each trainee reads scans.
options.why: Percent correct is exactly the measure that mixes sensitivity with criterion, so it cannot settle which trainee reads scans better.

options.text: Whether A makes fewer false alarms, since the reader with fewer false alarms always has the better sensitivity of the two.
options.why: Fewer false alarms can come from a higher criterion alone. False alarms on their own no more measure sensitivity than hits do.

items.stem: On a face memory test, one person is right 84% of the time and another only 74%, yet both have a d′ of about 2.0. In a few sentences, explain how both can be true, and what this shows about percent correct as a measure.
items.answer: Sensitivity, measured as d′, is how far apart the evidence for studied faces and the evidence for new faces lie. The criterion is where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn. The two people tell studied faces from new ones about equally well, so their sensitivity is the same. The second simply says “yes” more often. That gains a few hits, 49 instead of 42, but adds many more false alarms, 25 instead of 8, so percent correct falls. Percent correct mixes sensitivity and criterion together, and signal detection theory pulls them apart.
rubric: Treats d′ as sensitivity, how well the evidence separates studied from new faces, and says it is the same for both people.
Identifies the difference as one of criterion: the second person says “yes” more often.
Notes that saying “yes” more often here adds more false alarms than hits, which lowers percent correct.
Concludes that percent correct mixes sensitivity and criterion together.

items.stem: In everyday speech, a smoke alarm that goes off whenever toast burns is called “sensitive”. In signal detection terms, what does that alarm actually have?

options.text: A low criterion, so that it goes off on little evidence, catching fires but also sounding for burnt toast.
options.why: Correct. The everyday word builds in the confusion signal detection theory removes. Going off on little evidence is a fact about where the line is drawn.

options.text: A high sensitivity, so that the evidence from smoke and from no smoke lies far apart and it seldom errs.
options.why: An alarm that sounds for burnt toast is erring often, in false alarms. Going off readily is a matter of criterion, not of how far apart the distributions lie.

options.text: A high criterion, so that it needs a great deal of evidence before it sounds and goes off only for fires.
options.why: That reverses the case. An alarm set off by toast needs little evidence, which is a low criterion.

options.text: A low sensitivity, so that the evidence from fires and from toast overlaps too much for any setting to work.
options.why: Sounding for toast does not by itself show poor sensitivity. It shows that the line is drawn at a low amount of evidence.

items.stem: A clinic replaces its blood test with a new one. The new test comes back positive for more of the patients who have the disease, and also for more of the patients who do not. The maker advertises it as “more sensitive”. In signal detection terms, what does this pattern by itself show?

options.text: It fits a lower criterion, with more hits bought at the price of more false alarms, and on its own does not show any gain in sensitivity.
options.why: Correct. More hits together with more false alarms is exactly what moving the criterion does, and moving the criterion leaves sensitivity where it was.

options.text: It shows a gain in sensitivity, since detecting more of the patients who have the disease is what sensitivity means.
options.why: Detecting more patients who have the disease is a rise in hits, which a lower criterion produces on its own. Sensitivity is how far apart the two distributions lie.

options.text: It shows a loss of sensitivity, since a test that flags more of the healthy patients must be telling the two groups apart less well.
options.why: More false alarms come with a lower criterion even when sensitivity is unchanged. The pattern alone does not show the distributions moving closer.

options.text: It shows a higher criterion, since the new test needs more evidence than the old one before it comes back positive.
options.why: A test that comes back positive more often, for patients with and without the disease, needs less evidence, not more. That is a lower criterion.

items.stem: A town must decide how much evidence of a tornado its warning siren should need before it sounds. According to signal detection theory, which two things should set that criterion?

options.text: What each outcome gains or loses, and how common tornadoes are.
options.why: Correct. Which criterion is best depends on what each outcome gains or loses, and on how common targets are.

options.text: How often the siren was right about tornadoes before, and how often it has sounded.
options.why: A past record of being right mixes sensitivity and criterion. The best criterion depends on the costs of each outcome and on how common targets are.

options.text: How loud the sirens are, and how many people live near each one.
options.why: Loudness and reach affect who hears a warning, not where the line between sounding and staying silent should be drawn.

options.text: Whatever setting makes the siren right most often, whatever errors cost.
options.why: Accuracy is the wrong measure when the two errors lose different amounts. A missed tornado and a needless alarm do not cost the same.

items.stem: A lifeguard watches a crowded beach for swimmers in trouble. Missing one could cost a life, while swimming out to someone who turns out to be fine costs a few minutes. Where does the lifeguard’s best criterion lie?

options.text: Toward the liberal end, going out on fairly weak evidence and accepting many false alarms in order to avoid misses.
options.why: Correct. When misses lose a great deal, the best criterion is liberal. Many cheap false alarms are better than one costly miss.

options.text: Toward the conservative end, going out only on strong evidence, since every false alarm leaves the rest of the beach unwatched.
options.why: A false alarm here costs a few minutes, while a miss may cost a life. When misses lose a great deal, the best criterion is liberal.

options.text: At the neutral point, since that is where the lifeguard is right most often, and being right most often is the goal of the job.
options.why: Accuracy is the wrong measure when the two errors lose different amounts. The point that maximizes accuracy ignores how costly a miss is.

options.text: Wherever the lifeguard’s sensitivity is highest, since the criterion should be placed so the two distributions lie farthest apart.
options.why: Moving the criterion never changes sensitivity, because the distributions do not move. The criterion is placed according to costs and how common targets are.

items.stem: A screening test is used for a disease that is very rare, and every positive result sends the patient straight to a risky operation. Where does the best criterion for calling a result positive lie?

options.text: Toward the conservative end, since the targets are rare and each false alarm loses a great deal.
options.why: Correct. When targets are rare and false alarms lose a great deal, the best criterion is conservative.

options.text: Toward the liberal end, since any test for a disease should catch every case, whatever the cost of a false alarm.
options.why: A liberal criterion fits when misses are what lose a great deal. Here the disease is rare and a false alarm sends a healthy person to a risky operation.

options.text: At the neutral point, since accuracy is highest there, and accuracy is what a medical test should be judged by.
options.why: Accuracy is the wrong measure when the two errors lose different amounts. Here a false alarm is far costlier than the neutral point allows for.

options.text: Wherever the test’s sensitivity is greatest, since moving the criterion is how a test gets better at telling sick from healthy.
options.why: Moving the criterion leaves sensitivity exactly where it was. The criterion is chosen from costs and from how common targets are.

items.stem: In one worked example, a false alarm loses 15 points and a miss loses only 1. How does the criterion that gives the highest accuracy compare with the criterion that earns the most points?

options.text: Accuracy is highest with a neutral criterion, but the points earned are highest with a conservative one.
options.why: Correct. Because false alarms cost far more than misses, the criterion that earns the most points is conservative, even though accuracy peaks elsewhere.

options.text: Accuracy and points are both highest with a conservative criterion, since avoiding false alarms raises both together.
options.why: Points peak with a conservative criterion, but accuracy peaks with a neutral one. The two measures part ways when errors lose different amounts.

options.text: Accuracy is highest with a conservative criterion, but the points earned are highest with a liberal one instead.
options.why: That reverses the costs. With false alarms losing 15 points and misses 1, points favor a conservative criterion, not a liberal one.

options.text: Accuracy and points are both highest with a neutral criterion, since the two measures always agree with each other.
options.why: The two measures disagree whenever the two errors lose different amounts, which is exactly why accuracy is the wrong measure here.

items.stem: A factory inspector checks parts for cracks, and about one part in ten comes off the line cracked. Rejecting a sound part wastes one dollar, while shipping a cracked part can cost five hundred. The manager scores inspectors only by their percent correct. What is wrong with that score?

options.text: Accuracy is the wrong measure when the two errors lose different amounts, and here a miss costs far more, so the best criterion is liberal.
options.why: Correct. A miss, shipping a cracked part, loses far more than a false alarm, and cracked parts are not especially rare. So the best criterion is liberal, even if that lowers percent correct.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since an inspector who is right most often will also be the one who costs the factory the least money overall.
options.why: Being right most often and costing least come apart whenever the two errors lose different amounts. Here a miss costs five hundred times a false alarm.

options.text: Accuracy is the wrong measure because it ignores sensitivity; scoring inspectors by d′ alone would show which of them ships the fewest cracked parts.
options.why: d′ says how well an inspector tells cracked from sound parts, but how many cracked parts get shipped also depends on the criterion. The problem with accuracy is unequal costs.

options.text: Percent correct rewards inspectors who reject too many parts, since every rejection is counted as correct whenever the part turns out to be cracked.
options.why: Rejecting a cracked part is a hit and counts as correct, but rejecting a sound part is a false alarm and counts as an error. The real problem is that percent correct weighs a costly miss the same as a cheap false alarm.

items.stem: Why do people walk more carefully in a dim room than in a bright one?

options.text: In the dim room sensitivity is poorer, and the poorer the sensitivity, the more extreme the best criterion becomes.
options.why: Correct. In the dark it is harder to tell an obstacle from empty floor, and with poorer sensitivity the best criterion moves further toward caution.

options.text: In the dim room the criterion is lower, and a lower criterion raises sensitivity enough to make up for the poor light.
options.why: Moving the criterion never changes sensitivity. The poor light lowers sensitivity, and the best criterion becomes more extreme as a result.

options.text: In the dim room sensitivity is higher, because the eyes adjust to the dark and pick up every faint shape more readily.
options.why: The dim room makes it harder, not easier, to tell obstacles from empty floor. Poorer sensitivity is what pushes the best criterion further out.

options.text: In the dim room accuracy matters most, and walking carefully is how a person is right most often in the dark.
options.why: The best criterion is set by what each outcome gains or loses, not by accuracy. Walking carefully means accepting many false alarms to avoid a costly miss.

items.stem: Hitting an obstacle on the road costs a driver far more than braking for nothing. On a clear day a driver ignores small dark shapes on the road ahead, but in heavy fog she brakes for shapes she would ignore in clear weather. Why is that change sensible?

options.text: Fog lowers her sensitivity, and the poorer the sensitivity, the more extreme the best criterion, here further toward braking.
options.why: Correct. In fog the evidence for “obstacle” and for “nothing there” overlaps more. With costly misses her best criterion already leans liberal, and poorer sensitivity pushes it further out on that same side, toward braking.

options.text: Fog raises her sensitivity, since she watches the road far more closely, and a higher sensitivity calls for braking at fainter and fainter shapes.
options.why: Fog makes obstacles harder to tell from empty road, which lowers sensitivity. It is the poorer sensitivity that makes the best criterion more extreme.

options.text: Fog moves her criterion, and moving the criterion lowers her sensitivity, so braking more often is the only way she can keep her sensitivity up.
options.why: Moving the criterion never changes sensitivity. Fog lowers sensitivity directly, and her criterion moves in response to that.

options.text: Fog makes accuracy the right measure, since in fog being right most often matters more than what each kind of error happens to cost.
options.why: Accuracy is the wrong measure whenever errors lose different amounts, in fog or out of it. Hitting an obstacle still costs far more than an unneeded stop.

items.stem: Of two small fish, a jumpy one flees at the faintest hint of eel and a cautious one waits for strong evidence. The jumpy fish is wrong more often. Why can its policy still be the better one?

options.text: A miss may end a fish’s life while a false alarm costs a few minutes of feeding, so many cheap errors beat a fatal one.
options.why: Correct. The best criterion for the small fish is liberal. The jumpy fish is wrong more often, but the cautious fish is eventually eaten.

options.text: The jumpy fish has the higher sensitivity, since fleeing so often gives it more practice at telling eels from other fish.
options.why: Fleeing readily is a matter of criterion, not sensitivity. The jumpy policy is better because a miss costs so much more than a false alarm.

options.text: The jumpy fish is right more often about eels, and being right about eels is the only thing percent correct measures.
options.why: Percent correct counts every decision, including the many false alarms the jumpy fish makes. The case for jumpiness rests on unequal costs.

options.text: The jumpy fish has a higher criterion, so it needs more evidence before it flees and wastes less of its feeding time.
options.why: Fleeing at the faintest hint is a low, liberal criterion. It wastes feeding time on false alarms, and pays that price to avoid a fatal miss.

items.stem: The argument about the small fish concludes that its best criterion is liberal. Does that argument show that real fish in streams use liberal criteria?

options.text: No, since it shows only where the best criterion lies, and whether a real fish sits near that point can be answered only by measuring real fish.
options.why: Correct. The argument says where the best criterion lies. Whether any real fish is near it is an empirical question.

options.text: Yes, since any fish far from its best criterion would long since have been eaten, so the fish alive in streams today must all sit at or near it.
options.why: The argument establishes the optimum, not where real fish are. Whether any real fish sits near its best criterion can be answered only by measuring real fish.

options.text: Yes, since a fish’s criterion is fixed by its receptors, so every member of a species shares the same liberal criterion from birth.
options.why: A criterion can move with no change in how the fish represents its input, so it is not fixed by receptors. And the argument concerns the optimum, not real fish.

options.text: No, since real fish cannot have a criterion at all, a criterion being a feature only of radar operators and of human judgment in a laboratory.
options.why: Any animal deciding under noise draws a line somewhere along the evidence. The argument does apply to fish; it just does not say where real fish sit.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why the best criterion for the small fish is liberal, even though a jumpy fish is wrong more often than a cautious one, and say what question about real fish the argument leaves open.
items.answer: Missing an eel may end the fish’s life, while a false alarm costs only a few minutes of feeding. The best criterion depends on what each outcome gains or loses, so the fish does best to flee on fairly weak evidence and accept many false alarms in order to avoid misses. The jumpy fish makes more errors in total, but they are cheap ones, while the cautious fish, though right more often, is eventually eaten. The argument says where the best criterion lies. Whether any real fish sits near it can be answered only by measuring real fish.
rubric: Contrasts the cost of a miss, possibly death, with the cost of a false alarm, lost feeding time.
Concludes that the best criterion is liberal.
Explains why being wrong more often can still be better: the jumpy fish’s errors are cheap, and the cautious fish is eventually eaten.
States that the argument concerns the best criterion, and that whether real fish sit near it has to be measured.

items.stem: Suppose the small fish’s decisions about eels change. How does a change in its criterion differ from a change in its sensitivity in what each requires?

options.text: The criterion can move with no change in how the fish represents its input; sensitivity can improve only through a better representation.
options.why: Correct. The two quantities are different kinds of thing to change. Only sensitivity depends on how the input is represented.

options.text: The criterion can move only through a better representation of the input; sensitivity can change with no change in how the fish represents its input.
options.why: That swaps the two. Where the line is drawn can change with the representation untouched; how far apart the distributions lie cannot.

options.text: Both require a better representation of the input, since neither one can change unless the fish’s smell receptors are first replaced.
options.why: The criterion can move with no change in representation at all. Only sensitivity depends on a better representation of the input.

options.text: Neither requires any change in representation, since both are set entirely by the costs of misses and of false alarms.
options.why: Costs bear on where the best criterion lies, but they cannot move the distributions apart. Sensitivity improves only through a better representation.

items.stem: A baggage screener’s performance changes twice. First she is told that missing a weapon will cost her the job. Later, after months of practice, she can tell knives from hairbrushes on the screen in shapes that used to blur together. Which change is which?

options.text: The warning can move her criterion without altering her representation; the practice can raise her sensitivity through a better representation.
options.why: Correct. A new cost for misses moves where the line is drawn. Learning to pull apart shapes that used to blur together is a better representation, which is the only route to better sensitivity.

options.text: The warning raises her sensitivity by making her look harder at every bag; the practice moves her criterion by making her more willing to call a weapon.
options.why: That swaps the two. The warning changes what a miss costs, which bears on the criterion. The practice changes how well she tells the shapes apart.

options.text: Both changes raise her sensitivity, since each one leaves her catching more of the weapons that pass through the scanner.
options.why: Catching more weapons can come from a lower criterion alone. Only the practice changes how well she tells weapons from harmless objects.

options.text: Both changes move only her criterion, since sensitivity is fixed by the scanner and cannot be changed by practice.
options.why: Sensitivity can improve through a better representation of the input, and practice that pulls apart shapes that used to blur together provides one.

items.stem: Two detectors have the same distance between the centers of their two distributions of evidence, but in the second detector each distribution is much more spread out. How do their sensitivities compare?

options.text: The second detector has lower sensitivity, since d′ measures the distance between the centers in units of their spread.
options.why: Correct. d′ is the distance between the centers in units of the spread, so the same distance counts for less when the distributions are wider and overlap more.

options.text: The two detectors have equal sensitivity, since d′ is the distance between the centers, which has not changed, whatever the spread.
options.why: The distance alone is not d′. It is measured in units of the spread, so wider, more spread-out distributions give a smaller d′.

options.text: The second detector has higher sensitivity, since wider distributions cover more of the evidence and so catch more targets.
options.why: Wider distributions overlap more, which makes the two cases harder to tell apart. That is lower sensitivity, not higher.

options.text: Their sensitivities cannot be compared until a criterion is set, since sensitivity depends on where the line is drawn.
options.why: Sensitivity is how far apart the distributions lie, whatever the criterion. It can be compared without drawing any line.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is sensitivity?

options.text: How far apart the evidence for “present” and the evidence for “absent” lie, whatever the criterion happens to be.
options.why: Correct. Sensitivity, usually measured as d′, is the separation between the two distributions of evidence, and moving the criterion leaves it unchanged.

options.text: How little evidence is needed before a decision changes from “no” to “yes”, so that targets are seldom missed.
options.why: That describes a low criterion, which is what the everyday word “sensitive” often means. Sensitivity is the separation between the two distributions.

options.text: How often decisions turn out correct overall, counting the hits and correct rejections together against all decisions.
options.why: That is percent correct, which mixes sensitivity and criterion together. Sensitivity is how far apart the two distributions lie.

options.text: How strongly a receptor responds to a weak input, so that faint targets produce a large signal at the very first stage.
options.why: A strong receptor response is not what signal detection theory means. Sensitivity is how far apart the evidence for “present” and for “absent” lie.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is the name for how far apart the evidence for “present” and the evidence for “absent” lie, usually measured as d′?

options.text: Sensitivity
options.why: Correct. Sensitivity is the separation between the two distributions of evidence, and it stays the same wherever the line is drawn.

options.text: Criterion
options.why: The criterion is where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn. How far apart the two distributions lie is sensitivity.

options.text: Discrimination
options.why: Discrimination is the demand that inputs calling for different responses be told apart. The measured separation of the two distributions is sensitivity.

options.text: Tolerance
options.why: Tolerance is a cell’s keeping its preferred response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus. The separation of the distributions is sensitivity.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is the criterion?

options.text: The amount of evidence at which a decision changes from “no” to “yes”, so that moving it trades misses for false alarms.
options.why: Correct. The criterion is where the line is drawn, and moving it leaves sensitivity unchanged.

options.text: The separation between the evidence for “present” and for “absent”, so that raising it reduces misses and false alarms alike.
options.why: That describes sensitivity. Moving the criterion cannot reduce both kinds of error at once; it trades one for the other.

options.text: The proportion of decisions that turn out correct, so that raising it means fewer errors of either kind on the same task.
options.why: That describes percent correct, which mixes sensitivity and criterion together. The criterion is where the line is drawn.

options.text: The smallest difference between two inputs that an animal can tell apart, so that a lower one means finer discrimination.
options.why: A smallest detectable difference is a measure of discrimination. The criterion is the amount of evidence at which “no” turns to “yes”.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, what is the name for the amount of evidence at which a decision changes from “no” to “yes”?

options.text: Criterion
options.why: Correct. The criterion is where the line is drawn along the evidence. Moving it trades misses for false alarms and leaves sensitivity unchanged.

options.text: Sensitivity
options.why: Sensitivity is how far apart the evidence for “present” and for “absent” lie. The point where “no” turns to “yes” is the criterion.

options.text: Decision boundary
options.why: A decision boundary is a line through a space of possible inputs, the kind a single unit draws. The criterion is a point along one axis of evidence.

options.text: Hit
options.why: A hit is one outcome of a single decision, a target present and judged present. The point where “no” turns to “yes” is the criterion.

items.stem: A bedside monitor in a hospital sounds an alarm when its readings suggest that a patient’s heart has stopped. In a short paragraph, name the four possible outcomes for this monitor, say which error costs more, and argue where its best criterion lies. Then say why percent correct would be the wrong way to judge the monitor.
items.answer: A hit is sounding the alarm when the heart has stopped, and a miss is staying silent when it has. A false alarm is sounding when the heart is beating normally, and a correct rejection is staying silent when it is. A miss may let a patient die unattended, while a false alarm costs a nurse a trip to the bedside. The best criterion depends on what each outcome gains or loses, and when misses lose a great deal it is liberal, so the monitor should sound on fairly weak evidence and accept many false alarms. Percent correct counts every error the same, but accuracy is the wrong measure when the two errors lose different amounts, so a monitor tuned for the highest accuracy would accept misses that are far too costly.
rubric: Names all four outcomes correctly for the monitor: hit, miss, false alarm, and correct rejection.
Identifies the miss as the far costlier error.
Places the best criterion toward the liberal end because misses lose much more than false alarms.
Explains that percent correct is the wrong measure because it treats two errors that lose different amounts as equal.

items.stem: A trainer wants a sniffer dog to find more of the hidden explosives it is searching for. In a short paragraph, contrast two ways the dog’s performance could change, one through its criterion and one through its sensitivity. Say what each would require, and what moving the criterion would do to the dog’s false alarms.
items.answer: The dog’s criterion could be lowered, so that it signals on weaker evidence than before. That gives more hits and fewer misses, but also more false alarms, and it leaves sensitivity exactly where it was, because the distributions of evidence with and without explosives have not moved. Moving the criterion requires no change in how the dog represents what reaches its nose. Alternatively, the dog’s sensitivity could improve, so that the evidence from explosives and the evidence from everything else lie further apart. That can happen only through a better representation of the input, for example through training that pulls apart smells that used to blur together.
rubric: Describes lowering the criterion as signaling on weaker evidence, with more hits and fewer misses.
States that lowering the criterion also brings more false alarms.
States that moving the criterion leaves sensitivity unchanged and needs no change in representation.
States that sensitivity can improve only through a better representation of the input.

items.stem: When the lab’s first scenario loads, its fish has no hidden units and no weights set yet. Over the first ten encounters, watched live, which of the four outcomes did it produce?

options.text: Only hits and false alarms, because it darted to cover at every encounter, whether an eel was there or a sucker.
options.why: Correct. With every weight at zero the evidence is 0 against a criterion of 0, and the fish darts when the evidence is at or above the criterion. So every eel was a hit and every sucker a false alarm, and a miss or a correct rejection never occurred.

options.text: Only misses and correct rejections, because it stayed to feed at every encounter, whether an eel was there or a sucker.
options.why: Staying at every encounter is what would happen if the evidence fell below the criterion. Here the two were equal, and the fish darts at equality, so it fled every time.

options.text: All four outcomes in roughly equal numbers, because a fish with no weights responds to each smell more or less at random.
options.why: Nothing in the fish is random: zero evidence against a zero criterion gives the same verdict every time. The fish fled at every encounter, so only two outcomes occurred.

options.text: Mostly hits and correct rejections, because an eel’s smell and a sucker’s smell differ enough to be sorted from the start.
options.why: The smells do differ, but a fish whose weights are all zero gives both the same evidence, 0 against a criterion of 0, so the difference never reaches the verdict. It fled every time.

items.stem: In the Jumpy or blind? scenario, under The fish’s stakes (a miss costs 20, a correct rejection earns 1, and the other outcomes earn nothing), the healthy fish’s criterion is moved from 0 down to the liberal setting that earns the most energy. How do percent correct and Energy per 100 encounters at that setting compare with their values at 0?

options.text: Percent correct is lower than at 0, and energy goes from a clear loss at 0 to a small gain.
options.why: Correct. At 0 the healthy fish is right about 86 percent of the time and still loses energy, because each miss costs 20. Lowered to about −0.6 or −0.7 it is right noticeably less often, but it almost never misses, so it earns a little. Accuracy is the wrong measure when the two errors lose different amounts.

options.text: Percent correct is lower than at 0, and energy goes from a small gain at 0 to a much larger gain.
options.why: Percent correct does fall, but at 0 the healthy fish was not gaining energy. It misses enough eels at 0, at 20 apiece, to run at a clear loss, and the best setting only just turns that into a small gain.

options.text: Percent correct is lower than at 0, and energy rises from a heavy loss at 0 to a smaller loss that is still below zero.
options.why: Percent correct does fall and energy does rise, but at the best setting energy crosses into a small gain. With misses nearly gone, the correct rejections that remain earn more than the few misses cost.

options.text: Percent correct is higher than at 0, and energy goes from a clear loss at 0 to a small gain.
options.why: Energy does go from a loss to a small gain, but percent correct falls. Lowering the criterion trades misses for false alarms, and here the false alarms grew far faster than the misses fell.

items.stem: In the Jumpy or blind? scenario, keeping The fish’s stakes, How often an eel is upstream is set to 20 percent, so eels are now rare. Where did the criterion that earns the most energy end up, compared with where it sat when eels were half the stream?

options.text: Closer to zero than before, but still below it, so the best criterion stayed liberal.
options.why: Correct. Rarer eels pulled the best criterion toward zero, from about −0.6 or −0.7 to somewhere around −0.3 to −0.5, but a miss still costs twenty times what a correct rejection earns, so the best setting stayed liberal. A conservative best criterion needs rare targets and costly false alarms together.

options.text: Above zero, so the best criterion became conservative once eels were rare.
options.why: Rare targets push toward a conservative criterion only when false alarms are also costly. Under these stakes a false alarm costs only a missed meal, and the best criterion stayed below zero.

options.text: Further below zero than before, so the best criterion became more liberal as eels grew rare.
options.why: That is the direction the best criterion moved when eels became common, at 80 percent. With eels rare it moved toward zero.

options.text: At about zero, so the best criterion became neutral once eels were rare.
options.why: The best criterion did move toward zero, but it stopped short. A miss still costs twenty times what a correct rejection earns, so the best setting stayed below zero, on the liberal side.

items.stem: On the lab’s Fish tab, two of the diagnosed fish missed many eels and had nearly the same percent correct, yet a meal could put one of them right and no change of criterion could put the other right. In a few sentences, say what in their counts and the By hand box told the two apart, roughly how large that difference was, what was wrong with each, and what the second one would need.
items.answer: Their false alarms and their d′ told them apart. The fish a meal could fix had only about a dozen false alarms, and a d′ about as large as the healthy fish’s. It was hungry, its criterion to dart was high, and so it stayed even for many eels. The other had about as many false alarms as misses, and a d′ only about half the healthy fish’s, so its two evidence distributions overlapped far more. Its sensitivity was poor, and moving its criterion would only trade misses for false alarms. It would need a better representation, with weights that rely on what actually separates eels from suckers.
rubric: Points to the false-alarm counts, or to d′, as what tells the two apart, and not to percent correct.

Reports the sizes seen in the run: the fixable fish had only a handful of false alarms and a near-normal d′, while the other had about as many false alarms as misses and a d′ roughly half the healthy fish’s.
Says the fixable fish’s criterion is high (it is hungry), so a meal would put it right.
Says the other fish’s sensitivity is poor, so moving its criterion would only trade one kind of error for the other.
Says the second fish needs a better representation (different weights), not different chemistry.

items.stem: On the lab’s Fish tab, two diagnosed fish gave nearly the same counts, with almost no misses and many false alarms, and Reveal said one of them was “not broken”. That fish comes with a switch for its own stream, where eels make up 80 percent of encounters. In a few sentences, say whether that fish’s Energy per 100 encounters in its own stream came out as a clear gain, about break-even, or a loss, how that compared with the healthy fish’s at the same base rate, and what that says about calling an animal “too jumpy” from its behavior alone.
items.answer: In the stream with 80 percent eels, the low-criterion fish came out near break-even, a little below zero rather than a clear gain, while the healthy fish, with its criterion at 0, lost heavily, about two hundred per hundred encounters. So the low criterion was not a fault: which criterion is best depends on the stakes and on how common targets are, and with eels this common a liberal criterion pays. Its counts looked just like those of the fish whose chemistry was at fault, so behavior alone cannot say whether a criterion is wrong. That depends on the world the animal lives in, which has to be measured too.
rubric: Reports that the low-criterion fish came out near break-even (slightly below zero, not a clear gain) in its own stream.
Reports that the healthy fish, at the same 80 percent base rate, lost heavily, so the low-criterion fish did far better.
Says the best criterion depends on how common targets are (and on the stakes), so a liberal criterion suits a stream with many eels.
Says the two fish with the same counts had different causes (one a fault in chemistry, one suited to its stream).
Concludes that counts alone cannot show a criterion is a fault without knowing the animal’s world.

items.stem: What is a category?

options.text: A set of things treated as the same kind, for some purpose, even when its members differ from one another.
options.why: Correct. The definition turns on use. Things form a category because they are treated as the same kind for some purpose, which is why a goal can hold a category together even when its members have almost nothing in common.

options.text: A set of things that all share a list of defining features, each one necessary and all of them together sufficient.
options.why: That is the classical view of what holds a category together, and it fits few everyday categories. A category is simply a set of things treated as the same kind, for some purpose.

options.text: A pattern of activity that stands for something in the world, so that what an animal does next depends on it.
options.why: That is a representation. A category is the set of things in the world treated as the same kind, not the activity that stands for one of them.

options.text: A summary of a group of things, such as its average member, against which a new thing can be compared.
options.why: That is a prototype, a summary of a category rather than the category itself. A category is the set of things treated as the same kind.

items.stem: What is the term for a set of things treated as the same kind, for some purpose?

options.text: Category.
options.why: Correct. A category is defined by use: its members are treated as the same kind for some purpose, though some are better examples than others.

options.text: Generalization.
options.why: Generalization is the demand that inputs calling for the same response be treated alike. It names a demand on responding, not the set of things that end up treated alike.

options.text: Prototype.
options.why: A prototype is a summary of a category, such as its average member. It stands in for a category, and is not the set of things itself.

options.text: Typicality.
options.why: Typicality is how good an example of a category a member is. It describes the members of a set, not the set.

items.stem: Deciding whether an eel is present is a question about one target. According to the lecture, what does most recognition involve instead?

options.text: Sorting things into categories, sets treated as the same kind for some purpose, whose members are not all equally good examples.
options.why: Correct. The lecture turns from a fish detecting one target to the more common case. Most recognition is sorting into categories, and categories have structure of their own.

options.text: Detecting one target after another, with the criterion moved for each new target according to what its outcomes gain or lose.
options.why: Moving a criterion is part of detecting a single target. The lecture’s point is that most recognition is sorting things into categories, which have structure of their own.

options.text: Responding through labeled lines, each one firing for a single kind of thing in the world and staying silent for everything else.
options.why: Labeled lines suit cases like the worm and copper, where one receptor is enough. Most of what matters arrives as patterns, and most recognition is sorting into categories.

options.text: Learning one new pairing at a time, between a single cue and the particular outcome that has followed that cue in the past.
options.why: Pairing single cues with outcomes is one kind of learning, and some categories defeat it. Most recognition, the lecture says, is sorting things into categories.

items.stem: What is typicality?

options.text: How good an example of a category a member is, as when a robin is a better example of a bird than a penguin.
options.why: Correct. Typicality is graded goodness of membership. A penguin is a bird, but a poorer example of one than a robin.

options.text: How many members a category has, as when there are many more kinds of bird in the world than kinds of penguin.
options.why: The size of a category is not its typicality. Typicality grades the members themselves: a robin is a better example of a bird than a penguin, although both are birds.

options.text: How strongly a trained response is given to a new input, as the new input differs more and more from the trained one.
options.why: That is a generalization gradient, a measure of behavior after training. Typicality is how good an example of its category a member is.

options.text: How far apart the evidence for a target and the evidence for no target lie, as when a fish with keen receptors tells eel from no eel well.
options.why: That is sensitivity, from signal detection theory. Typicality is about how good an example of a category each member is.

items.stem: What is the term for graded goodness of membership in a category, the fact that some members are better examples of it than others?

options.text: Typicality.
options.why: Correct. Typicality is how good an example of a category a member is, as when a robin is a better example of a bird than a penguin.

options.text: Prototype.
options.why: A prototype is a summary of a category, such as its average member. Typicality is the graded goodness of the members, which several accounts, one built on prototypes among them, try to explain.

options.text: Generalization gradient.
options.why: A generalization gradient is graded too, but it is the fall-off in responding to a new input as it differs from a trained one. Typicality is about how good an example of a category a member is.

options.text: Category.
options.why: A category is the set of things treated as the same kind. Typicality describes how good an example of that set each member is.

items.stem: How did the classic rating study of typicality measure how good an example of a category each member was?

options.text: Students rated members of everyday categories on a seven-point scale, from a very good example to a very poor one.
options.why: Correct. The ratings came from 209 students across ten everyday categories, with 1 the best possible score and 7 the worst.

options.text: Students listed every attribute of each member, and a member’s typicality was the number of attributes they could list for it.
options.why: Listing attributes was a later study, which asked what makes one member more typical than another. The typicality ratings came from asking students to rate each member on a seven-point scale.

options.text: Students sorted each member into the category or out of it, and typicality was the share of students who sorted it in.
options.why: Sorting in or out treats membership as all or none. The students instead rated how good an example each member was, on a seven-point scale.

options.text: Students were timed while deciding whether each member belonged, and typicality was how quickly each decision was made.
options.why: Timing membership decisions is a reasonable way to probe categories, but it is not how these ratings were collected. The students rated each member directly, on a seven-point scale.

items.stem: Students rated members of the category bird from 1, a very good example, to 7, a very poor one. How did a robin, a penguin, and a bat compare?

options.text: A robin was rated close to 1, a penguin near the middle of the scale, and a bat, which is not a bird at all, close to 7.
options.why: Correct. The robin scored 1.02, the penguin 4.53, and the bat 6.15. Membership is graded: a penguin is a bird, but a poorer example of one than a robin.

options.text: A robin and a penguin were both rated close to 1, since both are birds, and a bat close to 7, since it is not a bird.
options.why: That is what we would expect if membership were all or none, with every member equally good. Students rated the penguin a much poorer example than the robin, though both are birds.

options.text: A robin was rated close to 1, a bat near the middle of the scale since it flies, and a penguin close to 7 since it cannot fly.
options.why: Flying might seem to decide it, but the bat, which is not a bird at all, was rated close to the worst possible example. The penguin sat near the middle.

options.text: A robin and a penguin were rated close to 1, and the bat was left off the scale, since students rated only animals that are birds.
options.why: The bat was rated, and its rating shows the scale at work: an animal that is not a bird at all scored close to the worst possible example.

items.stem: Suppose people asked to rate members of the category fish call a trout an excellent example and a seahorse a poor one, while all agreeing that a seahorse is a fish. What does this pattern of ratings show?

options.text: The members of the category are not all equally good examples of it; goodness of membership is graded, which is typicality.
options.why: Correct. Both animals belong, and one is a better example than the other. That graded goodness of membership is typicality.

options.text: The seahorse has been placed outside the category, since a member rated a poor example has in effect been judged a non-member.
options.why: A poor rating does not put a member outside its category. A penguin is a bird, though a poorer example than a robin, and here the raters agree the seahorse is a fish.

options.text: The raters have trouble telling a seahorse from a trout, since a poor rating shows that two members are being confused with one another.
options.why: A seahorse is easy to tell from a trout, and a poor rating says nothing about confusion. It grades how good an example of a fish each one is.

options.text: The category has a definition that a trout meets in full and a seahorse meets only in part, and the ratings measure how much of it each meets.
options.why: A definition is met or not met, and under a definition every member belongs equally. The ratings measure something else: how good an example each member is.

items.stem: Different groups of students rated how good an example each member of a category was. What did comparing the groups show?

options.text: They agreed closely, so the graded ratings were not the quirk of one particular group of raters.
options.why: Correct. Close agreement across groups is part of what makes typicality a robust finding, one that any account of categories has to explain.

options.text: They disagreed widely, so each group of students turned out to have its own idea of a good example of a bird.
