options.why: Had the groups disagreed, typicality would be a weak finding. In fact different groups agreed closely on the ratings.

options.text: They agreed about members that plainly belong, and disagreed about members such as the bat that do not belong at all.
options.why: The chapter reports close agreement on the ratings, with no exception for the bat, which was rated close to the worst possible example of a bird.

options.text: They agreed only after each group was given a definition of the category to rate the members against.
options.why: No definition was supplied. Students rated each member against their own idea of the category, and different groups still agreed closely.

items.stem: When people listed the attributes of twenty members of each of several categories, few or no attributes were listed for all twenty. How did the members of a category overlap instead?

options.text: Like faces in a family: one shares some features with a second, the second others with a third, and nothing runs through all.
options.why: Correct. That pattern is called family resemblance. Features are shared in overlapping pieces, and no single attribute runs through every member.

options.text: Like the terms of a definition: every member has a few core attributes in common with all the others, and they differ only in the rest.
options.why: That is what a definition would need, and it is what the attribute lists failed to find. Few or no attributes were listed for all twenty members.

options.text: Like the rungs of a ladder: each member has every attribute of the member below it, and then adds one more attribute of its own.
options.why: Nested attributes would give every member the attributes of the lowest rung, so some attributes would run through the whole set. Almost none did.

options.text: Like a crowd of strangers: members share no attributes with one another at all, and are grouped only by the name they are given.
options.why: Members did share features, just not the same features throughout. One shares some with a second, and the second shares others with a third.

items.stem: Suppose we counted, for each member of the category fruit, how many features it shares with other fruits and how many it shares with vegetables. Which member would the family-resemblance finding predict to be rated most typical?

options.text: The fruit that shares the most features with other fruits and the fewest with vegetables.
options.why: Correct. The most typical members were the ones sharing the most features with other members of their own category, and the fewest with members of neighboring categories.

options.text: The fruit that shares the most features with other fruits and the most with vegetables as well.
options.why: Sharing features with a neighboring category counts against typicality. The most typical members shared the most with their own category and the fewest with neighboring ones.

options.text: The fruit with a striking feature no other fruit has, which makes it the easiest one of all to remember.
options.why: A feature no other member has adds nothing to what a member shares with its category. Typicality went with sharing many features with members of one’s own category.

options.text: The fruit that shares the fewest features with anything at all, since it stands out most clearly from the rest.
options.why: Standing apart from everything makes a member atypical, not typical. The most typical members shared the most with their own category.

items.stem: A student reads that people rate a robin a far better example of a bird than a penguin, and concludes that people must sort things by comparing them with a summary of each category. What is wrong with the conclusion?

options.text: Several quite different accounts explain graded ratings equally well, so typicality alone cannot settle which is right.
options.why: Correct. Typicality is a fact any account of categories has to explain, but because several accounts explain it equally well, it cannot decide between them.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since only a summary of each category could make some members better examples than others.
options.why: A summary is one way to get graded examples, but not the only one. Several quite different accounts explain typicality equally well.

options.text: The ratings point the other way, since graded examples arise only when people compare things with every example they remember.
options.why: That swaps one unwarranted conclusion for another. Typicality is explained equally well by several accounts, so it favors none of them.

options.text: The ratings tell us little about categories, since they reflect how familiar each kind of animal happened to be to the students.
options.why: The ratings are a robust fact about human categories that any account has to explain. Their limit is that they cannot choose among the accounts.

items.stem: A magazine article reports that people agree on which birds are good examples of a bird, and concludes that the finding reveals how every animal sorts its world and which theory of categories is correct. What two cautions does the lecture attach to evidence of this kind?

options.text: The evidence comes from human beings, and since several quite different accounts explain it, it cannot decide between accounts on its own.
options.why: Correct. The lecture names both. Any account of categories has to explain typicality, but the evidence is human, and it does not favor one account over another.

options.text: The evidence comes from a single small group of students, and since the scale had only seven points, the grades are too coarse to use.
options.why: The ratings came from 209 students, and different groups agreed closely, so the finding is robust. The cautions concern whose categories it describes and what it can decide.

options.text: The evidence comes from birds alone, and since a bat was included by mistake, the ratings for other categories cannot be trusted either.
options.why: The ratings covered ten everyday categories, and the bat’s rating, close to the worst, is part of the finding rather than an error. The cautions are that the evidence is human and that it cannot choose among accounts.

options.text: The evidence comes from human beings, and since the ratings are graded, it shows that no bird belongs to the category fully.
options.why: The first half is right. But graded goodness of membership is not partial membership: a penguin is a bird, only a poorer example of one. The second caution is that several accounts explain typicality equally well, so it cannot decide between them.

items.stem: A researcher wants to claim that, for the small fish, some eel smells are better examples of “eel” than others, and cites the typicality ratings as support. What is the main weakness of that support?

options.text: The typicality evidence comes from human beings, so on its own it does not show how a fish’s categories are structured.
options.why: Correct. Typicality is a robust fact about human categories. Whether a fish’s categories have the same graded structure is a separate question, and the human ratings do not answer it.

options.text: The typicality ratings were unreliable, since different groups of students disagreed about which members were good examples.
options.why: The ratings were robust: different groups of students agreed closely. The weakness lies elsewhere. The evidence comes from human beings, not from fish.

options.text: Graded membership requires rating things on a scale, so a fish, which cannot rate anything, cannot have graded categories at all.
options.why: Rating is how typicality was measured in people, not a condition for a category to have graded structure. The weakness is that the evidence comes from human beings, so it does not settle the question for fish either way.

options.text: Typicality was found only in categories built around a goal, and the eels that hunt in a stream do not form a category of that kind.
options.why: Typicality was found in everyday categories such as birds, which are not built around a goal. The weakness is that the evidence comes from human beings, not from fish.

items.stem: Typicality is a robust finding about human categories. In a few sentences, explain why every account of categories has to explain typicality, and why typicality still cannot show on its own which account is right.
items.answer: Typicality is graded goodness of membership: people rate a robin a far better example of a bird than a penguin, though both are birds, and different groups of raters agree closely. Because the finding is so robust, any account of how human categories work has to produce it, or that account is wrong about human categories. But several quite different accounts explain typicality equally well. A finding that all of them predict cannot favor one of them over the others, so deciding between the accounts needs evidence on which they disagree.
rubric: Defines typicality as graded goodness of membership, with an example such as the robin and the penguin.
Notes that the finding is robust, for instance that different groups of raters agree closely.
States that any account of categories must therefore explain it.
States that several quite different accounts explain it equally well.
Concludes that typicality alone cannot decide between those accounts.

items.stem: A tent, a box of matches, a first-aid kit, and a can opener have almost nothing in common, yet a person packing for a camping trip treats them as one kind of thing. What holds this category together?

options.text: A goal: all four are things the trip needs, treated as one kind for that purpose rather than for any resemblance.
options.why: Correct. Not every category is held together by resemblance among its members. Some are built around a goal, like things to take out of a burning house, and their members can have almost nothing in common.

options.text: A hidden defining feature, shared by all four, which a careful enough listing of their attributes would eventually reveal.
options.why: Nothing about the four objects has to be shared. The category is built around a goal, and its members are united by the purpose they serve.

options.text: A family resemblance, in which each item shares some features with the next, though no one feature runs through all four.
options.why: Family resemblance holds many categories together, but these four items have almost nothing in common, even in overlapping pieces. They are united by a purpose.

options.text: Nothing holds it together, since a set of things whose members do not resemble one another cannot be a category at all.
options.why: A category is a set of things treated as the same kind for some purpose, and resemblance is not required. Some categories are built around a goal.

items.stem: A heron, a pike, and a jumping spider look nothing alike, yet each is rightly called a predator. What makes an animal a member of the category predator?

options.text: What it does to other animals, since the category is defined by a relation and not by the animal’s own appearance.
options.why: Correct. Nothing about an animal’s own appearance makes it a predator. What makes it a predator is what it does to other animals.

options.text: A set of visible features, such as sharp teeth or grasping limbs, that every predator has to at least some degree.
options.why: Predators differ widely in how they look. The category is defined by a relation, what the animal does to other animals, not by its appearance.

options.text: How good an example of the category it is rated, since an animal rated a poor example of a predator is not really one.
options.why: Typicality grades the members of a category, and a poor example can still be a member, as a penguin is a bird. Ratings do not decide membership.

options.text: Its size compared with the animals around it, since the larger animal in any encounter belongs to the category.
options.why: Size is a fact about the animal itself, and nothing about the animal on its own makes it a predator. What makes it one is what it does to other animals.

items.stem: How does a category built around a goal differ from a category defined by a relation?

options.text: A goal-built category gathers things that serve one purpose; a relation-defined one gathers things by how they stand toward something else.
options.why: Correct. Things to take out of a burning house share a purpose; predators share what they do to other animals. In neither case does resemblance among the members hold the category together.

options.text: A goal-built category is held together by resemblance among its members; a relation-defined category is held together by a definition.
options.why: Neither kind is held together by resemblance, which is why both are examples of categories that resemblance does not explain. A goal unites one kind, a relation the other.

options.text: A goal-built category gathers things with almost nothing in common; a relation-defined one gathers things alike in appearance, as predators are.
options.why: The first half is right. But nothing about an animal’s own appearance makes it a predator, and predators can look nothing alike. A relation-defined category gathers things by how they stand toward something else.

options.text: A goal-built category is used only for sorting things; a relation-defined category is used only for inferring what cannot be seen.
options.why: Sorting and inferring unseen properties are both uses of categories in general, not marks of one kind. What separates the two kinds is what holds the members together: a purpose in one case, a relation in the other.

items.stem: Sorting things is only one use for categories. What else do categories let an animal, or a person, do?

options.text: Infer properties of a thing that cannot be seen, and, for people, explain what happens and communicate.
options.why: Correct. Knowing what kind a thing is tells an animal about properties it cannot see, and people also use categories to explain and to communicate.

options.text: Detect whether one target is present under noise, by placing a criterion somewhere along a single axis of evidence.
options.why: That is signal detection, deciding whether a single target is there. Categories also let an animal infer what it cannot see, and let people explain and communicate.

options.text: Treat each new thing as a new kind, so that nothing learned about one member has to carry over to the next.
options.why: That describes the fish that only discriminates, which learns nothing that carries over. Categories do the reverse: what is known about the kind extends to a new member.

options.text: Respond to a thing through a single receptor’s firing, so that no pattern across many inputs ever has to be read.
options.why: That is a labeled line, the worm’s way of recognizing copper. Categories serve inference, explanation, and communication.

items.stem: A forager finds a mushroom, recognizes it as a kind known to be poisonous, and leaves it alone, though nothing about the poison can be seen or smelled. Which use of categories does this show?

options.text: Inferring a property that cannot be seen from the mushroom’s membership in a category the forager has learned.
options.why: Correct. Categories let an animal infer properties it cannot see. Recognizing the kind supplies the poison, which no sense could detect.

options.text: Explaining what happens, by giving a reason why the mushroom grew in that particular spot in the woods.
options.why: Explaining what happens is another use of categories, but nothing is explained here. The forager uses the mushroom’s kind to infer a hidden property.

options.text: Communicating with others, by giving the mushroom a name that other foragers in the area will understand.
options.why: Communicating is another use of categories, but the forager says nothing to anyone. The category supplies a property that cannot be seen.

options.text: Sorting the mushroom from its surroundings by its pattern alone, with no further consequence for what the forager does.
options.why: Sorting happens, but the point here is what follows from it. The poison cannot be seen, and membership in the category supplies it.

items.stem: Two berries smell almost exactly alike, but one kind makes an animal sick and the other does not. On the chapter’s view of recognition, what should decide whether the animal treats the two smells as one kind of thing?

options.text: Whether they share a consequence, since what matters is which inputs share a consequence, not only how alike they are.
options.why: Correct. Recognition is not only a matter of how alike inputs are. Two very alike smells with different consequences call for different treatment.

options.text: How alike the two smells are, since the more alike two inputs are, the more readily they must be treated as one kind.
options.why: That is the natural first answer, and resemblance does matter. But recognition is not only a matter of how alike inputs are; it turns on which inputs share a consequence.

options.text: Whether the two contain one defining chemical, since membership in a category is fixed by what all of its members contain.
options.why: That would make every category a definition, and many are not, such as categories built around a goal. Recognition turns on which inputs share a consequence.

options.text: Whether the two are equally typical, since only inputs that are equally good examples can belong to the same category.
options.why: Members of one category differ in typicality, as a robin and a penguin do. Typicality does not decide membership.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how categories built around a goal and categories defined by a relation show that recognition turns on more than how alike inputs are. Use one example of each other than those the chapter uses.
items.answer: Some categories are held together by a goal. Presents suitable for a young child’s birthday, such as a ball, a picture book, and a kite, have little in common, yet they are treated as one kind because they serve one purpose. Other categories are defined by a relation. Nothing about an animal’s own appearance makes it prey; what makes it prey is what other animals do to it. In both cases the members need not resemble one another at all. What unites them is a shared purpose or role, so recognizing a member is a matter of which inputs share a consequence, not only of how alike they are.
rubric: Gives a goal-built category not in the chapter, whose members have little in common.
Gives a relation-defined category not in the chapter, defined by how its members stand toward something else.
States that the members of such categories need not resemble one another.
Concludes that recognition turns on which inputs share a consequence, not only on how alike they are.

items.stem: For some categories, each input carries information on its own; for others, only combinations of inputs do. What separates the two kinds?

options.text: In the first, more of one input makes the category more likely whatever else is present; in the second, no input says anything alone.
options.why: Correct. A little more eel smell makes an eel a little more likely, whatever else is present. In the fruit case, neither smell alone says anything about food, and the right response depends only on the combination.

options.text: In the first, one input decides the answer alone, as a labeled line does; in the second, every one of the inputs has to be present at once.
options.why: Needing every input at once is still a case where each input helps on its own, since each one present makes the category more likely. In the second kind, no input says anything by itself.

options.text: In the first, the inputs are noisy and have to be weighed; in the second, the inputs arrive without noise, so combinations can be read exactly.
options.why: Noise affects both kinds of category alike. What separates them is whether a single input carries any information on its own.

options.text: In the first, the animal has to generalize across inputs; in the second, it has to discriminate, since combinations demand finer distinctions.
options.why: Both demands apply to both kinds of category. What separates them is whether any input on its own says anything about the answer.

items.stem: For the chapter’s hypothetical fruit-eating animal, what does each combination of two smells, A and B, mean?

options.text: Either smell alone means ripe fruit, both together mean rotting fruit, and neither means there is no fruit at all.
options.why: Correct. That pattern is exclusive or: one smell or the other, but not both. Because of it, each smell is present as often when there is food as when there is not.

options.text: Either smell alone means unripe fruit, both together mean ripe fruit, and neither means there is no fruit at all.
options.why: That is a rule in which both smells are needed for food. In the fruit case, either smell alone means ripe fruit, and both together mean the fruit is rotting.

options.text: Either smell alone means ripe fruit, both together mean riper fruit still, and neither means the fruit is unripe.
options.why: That rule would let each smell point toward food. In the fruit case, both smells together mean rotting fruit, and neither means no fruit at all, not unripe fruit.

options.text: Smell A alone means ripe fruit, smell B alone means rotting fruit, and both together mean there is no fruit at all.
options.why: That would give each smell a meaning of its own. In the fruit case the two smells play the same part: either one alone means ripe fruit.

items.stem: The hypothetical fruit-eating animal detects smell A, and has no information yet about smell B. What does smell A, on its own, tell the animal about whether there is food?

options.text: Nothing, since smell A is present in half of the cases that mean food and in half of the cases that do not.
options.why: Correct. Smell A turns up with ripe fruit when smell B is absent, and with rotting fruit when smell B is present. On its own it points neither way; only the combination does.

options.text: That food is likely, since smell A is present in one of the two cases that mean ripe fruit, and so it points toward food.
options.why: Smell A is present in one food case, but it is also present in the rotting case, which does not mean food. Taken alone, it tells the animal nothing.

options.text: That food is unlikely, since smell A is present whenever the fruit is rotting, and so it points away from food.
options.why: Smell A is present when the fruit is rotting, but it is also present in a ripe case. Half of its cases mean food and half do not.

options.text: That food is certain, since either of the two smells alone is enough to mean ripe fruit for this animal.
options.why: Either smell alone means ripe fruit, but the animal does not yet know whether smell B is absent. With smell B present as well, the fruit is rotting.

items.stem: What is the rule called in which one input is true, or the other, but not both?

options.text: Exclusive or.
options.why: Correct. It is often written XOR. The fruit-eating animal’s rule has this form: either smell alone means ripe fruit, and both together do not.

options.text: AND.
options.why: AND is true only when both inputs are true, which is exactly the case this rule excludes.

options.text: OR.
options.why: OR is true when one input is true or both are. The rule here is the same except that it is false when both are true.

options.text: NOT.
options.why: NOT reverses a single input. The rule here concerns two inputs, and it is true when exactly one of them is.

items.stem: Suppose a songbird learns that a seed pod is ready to eat when it is either soft or brown, but not both: a pod that is soft and brown has gone moldy, and one that is neither is unripe. Taken on its own, what does a pod’s being brown tell the bird?

options.text: Nothing, since brown pods are moldy as often as they are ready, and only whether the pod is also soft settles the matter.
options.why: Correct. The bird’s rule is exclusive or. Brownness turns up in half the pods worth eating and half the pods that are not, so it says nothing alone; only the combination of the two cues does.

options.text: That the pod is ready, since brown is one of the two signs of a ready pod that the bird has learned to use.
options.why: Brown alone means ready, but brown together with soft means moldy. Brownness is present in as many pods to avoid as pods to eat.

options.text: That the pod should be avoided, since every pod that has gone moldy is brown, so brown is the sign of mold.
options.why: Every moldy pod is brown, but so is every pod that is brown and not soft, and those are ready. Brownness alone points neither way.

options.text: A little in favor of eating, since brown turns up in more of the pods that are ready than of the pods that are not.
options.why: Count the cases: brown turns up in one kind of pod to eat and one kind to avoid. It is no more common among the ready pods than among the others.

items.stem: Suppose a fruit smells right only when one chemical is at just the right strength: too little means unripe, and too much means rotten. Why does the chemical’s strength, on its own, fail to settle the answer?

options.text: More of the chemical is good news up to a point and bad news after it, so a stronger smell can mean better fruit or worse.
options.why: Correct. Below the right strength more of the chemical is welcome, and past it more is unwelcome, so a change in strength points in no consistent direction.

options.text: The chemical varies from sniff to sniff, so its strength is too noisy to separate ripe fruit from rotten fruit reliably.
options.why: Noise is a real problem for any detection, but it is not the problem here. Even measured perfectly, the strength is good news up to a point and bad news after it.

options.text: The chemical is present at the same strength in every fruit, so its strength cannot differ between ripe fruit and rotten.
options.why: The strength does differ, from too little to too much. The trouble is that more is good news up to a point and bad news after it.

options.text: The chemical carries information only together with a second smell, as in exclusive or, so its strength alone cannot matter.
options.why: The chapter says this case has the same character as exclusive or, not that it is exclusive or. One chemical is involved, and its strength alone does not point consistently either way.

items.stem: Suppose a plant-eating animal can safely eat a leaf only when its salt content is moderate: too little and the leaf lacks what the animal needs, too much and the leaf harms it. A student proposes the rule “the saltier, the better”. What is wrong with that rule?

options.text: Salt is good news only up to a point and bad news after it, so a rule that runs in one direction cannot be right.
options.why: Correct. This is a just-right-strength case. Salt carries the information, but its effect reverses past the ideal, so no rule that runs in one direction works throughout.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since salt is the one input here that carries all the information about whether the leaf is safe to eat.
options.why: Salt does carry the information, but not in one direction. More salt helps up to a point and harms after it, so “the saltier, the better” fails past that point.

options.text: The rule should be reversed, since a leaf with less salt in it is always safer for the animal to eat than a leaf with more.
options.why: Reversing the rule fails at the other end, since too little salt leaves the animal short of what it needs. Neither direction is right throughout.

options.text: The rule needs a second cue, since salt can carry information only in exclusive or with some other chemical in the leaf.
options.why: The case is like exclusive or in character, but it involves a single input. The problem is that the effect of salt reverses, not that a second cue is missing.

items.stem: What do the fruit exclusive-or case and the just-right-strength case have in common?

options.text: In each, no single input, taken on its own, points consistently toward one answer.
options.why: Correct. In the fruit case each smell is present as often without food as with it; in the second case more of the chemical is good news up to a point and bad news after it. Either way, no input on its own settles the answer.

options.text: Each is an instance of exclusive or, with too little and too much playing the parts of the two smells.
options.why: The chapter says the second case has the same character as exclusive or, not that it is exclusive or. One involves two smells, the other a single chemical.

options.text: Each involves two smells, one of which means ripe fruit and the other of which means rotten fruit.
options.why: In the fruit case either smell alone means ripe fruit, and the second case has only one chemical. Neither case gives each input a meaning of its own.

options.text: Each can be solved by adding up the evidence one input at a time, given enough experience with the fruit.
options.why: Adding up evidence one input at a time is exactly what fails in both, since no input on its own points toward the answer.

items.stem: In a few sentences, contrast a category in which each input carries information on its own with one in which only combinations of inputs do. Give a hypothetical example of each, other than the eel and the fallen fruit.
items.answer: In the first kind, a little more of one input makes the category a little more likely, whatever else is present. For a hypothetical bird, a little more of a sweet smell might make a berry a little more likely to be ripe, whatever its color. In the second kind, no input says anything on its own, and only the combination does. Suppose a hypothetical animal finds a nut good to eat when it is either heavy or dark, but not both: heavy and dark means rotten inside, and neither means empty. Heaviness is present in as many bad nuts as good ones, and so is darkness, so only the combination tells the animal what to do.
rubric: States that in the first kind, each input on its own makes the category more or less likely, whatever else is present.
States that in the second kind, no input on its own carries information, and only the combination does.
Gives a fresh example of the first kind.
Gives a fresh example of the second kind in which each input alone turns up as often with one outcome as with the other.

items.stem: Where was the problem of categories that depend only on combinations of inputs first discovered?

options.text: In animal learning, before anyone studied exclusive or in neural circuits or had built an artificial neural network.
options.why: Correct. Animal-learning researchers met the problem in discrimination tasks where only a combination of cues predicted the outcome, before neural circuits or artificial networks entered the story.

options.text: In artificial neural networks, and it was later found to apply to animals learning tasks in the laboratory.
options.why: The order ran the other way. Animal-learning researchers found the problem before anyone built an artificial neural network.

options.text: In recordings from neural circuits, when it was found that individual neurons could not respond to such a combination.
options.why: The problem was discovered in behavior, not in recordings. Animal-learning researchers found it before anyone studied exclusive or in circuits.

options.text: In animal learning and in artificial neural networks at about the same time, as both fields took up the same tasks.
options.why: The two did not arrive together. Animal-learning researchers met the problem before anyone had built an artificial neural network.

items.stem: Animal-learning researchers trained animals on discrimination tasks in which every single cue was rewarded half the time. What did that arrangement mean for an animal trying to learn which choice would pay?

options.text: No cue on its own predicted reward, so only a combination of cues could tell the animal which choice would pay.
options.why: Correct. A cue rewarded half the time, whatever else is present, says nothing about which choice will pay. Only a combination of cues predicts the outcome, which is what makes such a task a problem of combinations.

options.text: Any cue predicted reward as well as any other, so the animal could learn from whichever cue it happened to notice first.
options.why: It is true that no cue did better than any other. But that is because none of them predicted reward at all, so learning from any one cue leaves the animal no better off.

options.text: The animal was rewarded on half its trials whatever it chose, so no choice it learned to make could raise its rate of reward.
options.why: This confuses how often each cue is followed by reward with how often the animal is rewarded. An animal that learned the combinations could choose correctly every time.

options.text: Each cue was shown on only half of the trials, so the animal had too little experience with any one cue to learn it.
options.why: The half describes how often a cue is followed by reward, not how often it appears. The difficulty is that no single cue predicts reward, so only a combination can.

items.stem: Suppose an animal could learn only how often each single cue is followed by reward. Faced with a task in which every single cue is rewarded half the time, what should it be able to learn, and what did real animals do on such a task?

options.text: It should learn nothing useful from any one cue, and so fail the task; real animals learned the task anyway.
options.why: Correct. The single-cue account predicted that no animal could learn the task, and animals learned it anyway. Whatever they learned, it was not only about single cues.

options.text: It should learn the task quickly, since a reward on half of all trials is plenty to learn from; real animals were slower.
options.why: A cue rewarded half the time, whatever else is present, says nothing about which choice will pay. The single-cue account predicted failure, and animals succeeded.

options.text: It should learn the task only after very long training; real animals never learned it, however long they were trained.
options.why: The account predicted that no animal could learn the task at all, and the animals did learn it.

options.text: It should learn to choose at random, which is the best anything can do on such a task; real animals did the same.
options.why: Choosing at random is all the single-cue account leaves an animal, but real animals did better. They learned the task.

items.stem: Beyond the early discrimination tasks in which only a combination of cues predicted reward, what did a number of later studies show about tasks of that kind?

options.text: That a range of animals, from rats to monkeys, are capable of learning them, not only one or two species.
options.why: Correct. Learning from combinations of cues is not confined to one kind of animal; studies since have found it from rats to monkeys.

options.text: That only monkeys and apes can learn them, since such tasks call for the large brain of a primate.
options.why: Rats learn them too. A range of animals, from rats to monkeys, can learn tasks in which only combinations of cues predict the outcome.

options.text: That only animals trained on them from birth can learn them, since combinations take a lifetime to learn.
options.why: Nothing in the studies requires training from birth. A range of animals, from rats to monkeys, can learn such tasks.

options.text: That no animal learns them reliably, and the early successes came from single cues the researchers had missed.
options.why: The later studies extended the early result rather than overturning it. Animals from rats to monkeys learn such tasks.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, describe the evidence that animals and people can learn categories in which only combinations of cues predict the outcome, and say what account of learning that evidence counted against.
items.answer: Animal-learning researchers trained animals on discrimination tasks in which every single cue was rewarded half the time, so that only a combination of cues predicted the outcome. An account in which animals learn only about single cues predicted that no animal could learn such a task, since no single cue predicts the reward. Animals learned it anyway, and later studies found the same in a range of animals, from rats to monkeys. People can learn such categories too. In controlled experiments, categories that could be sorted by adding up evidence one feature at a time were no easier to learn than categories that could not. The animal results counted directly against the account in which learning is only about single cues, which had predicted failure.
rubric: Describes a task in which every single cue is rewarded half the time, so that only a combination of cues predicts the outcome.
States the single-cue account’s prediction that no animal could learn such a task.
Reports that animals learned it anyway, across a range from rats to monkeys.
Gives evidence from people, such as additive categories being no easier to learn than the others.

items.stem: In controlled experiments, how did people learn categories that could be sorted by adding up evidence one feature at a time, compared with categories that could not?

options.text: The additive categories were no easier to learn than the categories that could not be sorted that way.
options.why: Correct. People can learn categories that depend only on combinations, and in these experiments such categories were no harder than additive ones.

options.text: The additive categories were far easier, and people mostly failed to learn the ones that could not be sorted that way.
options.why: That is what an account built on single features would predict, and it is not what was found. Categories that depend on combinations were no harder.

options.text: The additive categories were harder, since people attend to combinations of features before they attend to single ones.
options.why: The finding was only that additive categories were no easier, not that they were harder. Nothing here says people attend to combinations first.

options.text: The additive categories could be learned by people, while the others could be learned only by trained animals.
options.why: People can learn categories that depend only on combinations too. In these experiments such categories were no harder than additive ones.

items.stem: Two practiced observers learned a category with the shape of exclusive or. What does that result show?

options.text: That people can learn a category of that shape, though two observers cannot show that most people learn one easily.
options.why: Correct. Two observers are enough to show that such a category can be learned by people. They cannot show how easily people in general would learn one.

options.text: That every person learns a category of that shape easily, since two observers who agree make the result fully general.
options.why: Two observers show that such a category can be learned, not that everyone learns it easily. A result from two people should not be stretched to people at large.

options.text: That only practiced observers can learn such categories, since people without practice have been shown to fail at them.
options.why: No failure of that kind is reported. In controlled experiments more broadly, categories that depend only on combinations were no harder to learn than categories that could be sorted one feature at a time.

options.text: That people learn such categories faster than animals do, since animals needed far longer training on tasks of that kind.
options.why: A result from two people says nothing about how fast animals learn. Animals and people can both learn tasks in which only combinations of cues predict the outcome, and no comparison of speed is made.

items.stem: In the lab’s fruit scenario, either of two smells alone marks ripe fruit, and both together mark rotting fruit. A fish with no hidden units learns whether to eat over two runs of 1,000 encounters, with the feature space checked after each run. What did the white line and the test set’s percent wrong do, and why?

options.text: The white line kept swinging from place to place and never came to rest, and percent wrong stayed high, because each smell comes with nourishing fruit half the time.
options.why: Correct. Neither smell says anything about food by itself: each is present in half the cases that nourish and half the cases that do not. With no hidden units, each run of encounters pushes the weights one way and then another, and nothing the fish learns from one smell at a time makes the errors go away.

options.text: The white line came to rest across the middle after the first run and stayed put, with about half the fruit wrong, because one line can do no better than chance here.
options.why: It is true that no single line sorts this fruit. But the line did not settle anywhere; it kept moving from run to run, and percent wrong did not hold steady at one value.

options.text: The white line settled between the ripe and the rotting fruit after a slow start, and percent wrong fell close to zero, because the evidence from the two smells was added together.
options.why: More encounters did not help. Added up, the two smells give rotting fruit the most evidence of all, so adding the evidence from each smell cannot single out the rotting fruit.

options.text: The white line came to rest pointing the wrong way, and the fish ate only the rotting fruit and the twigs, because the rule pushed each weight backward.
options.why: The fish did not learn the problem backward; it could not learn it at all. Its errors come from the fact that neither smell alone carries any information about food.

items.stem: What is invariance?

options.text: Recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as changes of distance, position, or viewpoint.
options.why: Correct. An eel near and far, or a face seen from the front and from the side, produce inputs that barely overlap. Invariance is recognizing the one thing across changes like these.

options.text: A cell’s keeping its preferred response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus, such as changes of position or size.
options.why: That is tolerance, which single cells in the visual pathway show. Invariance is what the animal has to achieve: recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal.

options.text: Combining the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood, so that a small shift in the input no longer changes the result.
options.why: That is pooling, one way a network builds in a little tolerance to shifts. Invariance is the demand itself, recognizing a thing across large changes in its input.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, so that a faint or partial input produces the response the whole would.
options.why: That is pattern completion, proposed for circuits whose cells excite one another. Invariance is recognizing a thing across changes of distance, position, or viewpoint.

items.stem: What is the term for recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as changes of distance, position, or viewpoint?

options.text: Invariance.
options.why: Correct. The near eel and the far eel, or the face seen from the front and turned to one side, are the cases the term names.

options.text: Tolerance.
options.why: Tolerance is a single cell’s keeping its preferred response over a limited range of changes. Recognizing a thing across large changes, whatever does it, is invariance.

options.text: Pooling.
options.why: Pooling combines the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood, so that a small shift no longer changes the result. It is one partial way of meeting invariance, not invariance itself.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. Recognizing one thing across changes of distance, position, or viewpoint is invariance.

items.stem: Which of these is a case of one thing producing inputs that barely overlap?

options.text: A face seen from the front, and the same face turned to one side, which share little of their image.
options.why: Correct. One face, two views, and very little of the image in common. Recognizing the face across both views is the demand called invariance.

options.text: An eel’s smell and a sucker’s smell, which share much of their chemistry although they come from different fish.
options.why: That is two things producing inputs that overlap a great deal, the case that calls for discrimination. The question asks about one thing whose inputs barely overlap.

options.text: Many different scenes that cast exactly the same image, so that the image alone cannot say which scene is there.
options.why: That is the reverse side of the difficulty, many things producing one input. Invariance is one thing producing many different inputs.

options.text: Two smells that are each present in half the cases that mean food, and in half the cases that do not.
options.why: That describes the fruit-eater’s exclusive-or problem, where only a combination of smells is informative. It is not about one thing producing different inputs.

items.stem: How can two smells of the same eel compare with the smell of a harmless sucker?

options.text: The two eel smells can differ from each other more than either differs from the sucker’s, and still have to be treated as one thing.
options.why: Correct. One eel, close by and far away, gives off smells at very different strengths, and either smell can be more like the sucker’s than like the other.

options.text: The two eel smells always differ from each other less than either differs from the sucker’s, which is what lets them be treated as one thing.
options.why: That is the easy case, and it does not always hold. One eel’s smells can differ from each other more than either differs from the sucker’s.

options.text: The two eel smells share nothing with the sucker’s, so telling the eel from the sucker is easy and only treating the eel smells alike is hard.
options.why: The sucker’s smell shares much of its chemistry with the eel’s. Both demands are hard here: telling the two fish apart, and treating the eel smells alike.

options.text: The two eel smells can differ from each other more than either differs from the sucker’s, and so they have to be treated as two different things.
options.why: The smells do differ that much, but they still come from one eel and call for one response, flight. Treating them as two things would be a failure of invariance.

items.stem: Why is invariance described as discrimination and generalization at their hardest?

options.text: The smells that must be treated alike can differ more than those that must be told apart, so both demands bear down on the same inputs.
options.why: Correct. Generalization has to stretch across eel smells that barely overlap, while discrimination has to hold the sucker apart even when its smell is more like one eel smell than the eel smells are like each other.

options.text: The smells that must be told apart are so faint that a very low criterion is needed to pick them up, so a great many false alarms cannot be avoided.
options.why: That mixes in signal detection, where moving the criterion trades one error for the other. Invariance is about which inputs must be treated alike and which apart.

options.text: The smells of one eel change from moment to moment, so the fish has to start over each time and treat every new smell as a new thing.
options.why: Treating every eel smell as a new thing is the failure of a fish that only discriminates. Invariance is the demand that the changing smells be treated as one eel.

options.text: The smells that must be treated alike always overlap a great deal, so generalization is easy here and the discrimination is the hard part.
options.why: That reverses the difficulty. In invariance the inputs to be treated alike barely overlap, so generalization is hard as well.

items.stem: A crow on a fence sees a hawk circling high overhead as a small speck, and a minute later sees the same hawk gliding low, filling much of its view. The two images on its eyes have little in common. If the crow treats both as the same danger, which of these describes what it is achieving?

options.text: Invariance, because one hawk has produced two inputs that barely overlap and both call for the same response.
options.why: Correct. A change in distance changes the image a great deal, and recognizing the hawk across that change is invariance.

options.text: Discrimination, because the two images are so different that the crow has to tell them apart before it can respond.
options.why: Discrimination is telling apart inputs that call for different responses. These two images call for the same response, so treating them alike is what is needed.

options.text: Learning in sequence, because the crow saw the high hawk first and the low hawk later, with time between them.
options.why: The images arrive at different times, but nothing new is being learned here. The crow is recognizing one thing across a large change in its input.

options.text: Pattern completion, because the speck is a partial view of the hawk that the crow fills out into the whole bird.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. The speck is not part of the hawk’s image but a very different image of the whole hawk, and recognizing it is invariance.

items.stem: A familiar tune is played in a new key, a half step higher than usual. Its melody is unchanged, but every note is now a different pitch, and the new version shares few notes with the original. A different tune, played in the original key, shares many notes with the original. What does recognizing the familiar tune in its new key require?

options.text: Treating the two versions of the tune as one thing, though the original shares more notes with the different tune than the two versions share with each other.
options.why: Correct. This is the eel and the sucker in sound. One tune produces inputs that barely overlap, while a different tune shares more with the original than the two versions of the one tune share with each other.

options.text: Treating whichever tune shares the most notes with the original as the same tune, since shared notes are what make two inputs one thing.
options.why: That would pick the wrong tune. Invariance is hard precisely because what comes from one thing can share less than what comes from different things.

options.text: Treating the two versions of the tune as different tunes, since inputs that share almost nothing always call for different responses.
options.why: Inputs that barely overlap can still come from one thing and call for one response. That is the generalization side of invariance.

options.text: Treating all three as the same tune, since all of them are built from notes of the same kind and played on the same instrument.
options.why: That generalizes too far and gives up discrimination. The different tune must still be told apart, even though it shares many notes with the original.

items.stem: In Module 1, we saw a difficulty in vision: many different scenes can cast exactly the same image. How does invariance relate to that difficulty?

options.text: It is the other side of the same difficulty, since one object can cast many different images that must all be recognized.
options.why: Correct. In the problem we saw in Module 1, many scenes lead to one image. In invariance, one object leads to many images, and all of them must be recognized as that object.

options.text: It is the same difficulty under a new name, since many different scenes cast one image and the animal must work out which.
options.why: That is the problem from Module 1 itself. Invariance runs the other way, from one object to many images.

options.text: It is the easier side of that difficulty, since one object casting many images gives more evidence than one image.
options.why: Invariance is the other side of the difficulty, but not the easier one. Recognizing one thing across inputs that barely overlap is discrimination and generalization at their hardest.

options.text: It is unrelated to that difficulty, since invariance concerns smell and the many-scenes problem concerns vision alone.
options.why: A face seen from the front and from the side is a visual case of invariance. Invariance applies to any sense, and it is the other side of the problem from Module 1.

items.stem: Invariance is one side of a difficulty in vision. The other side is that many different scenes can cast exactly the same image. A large ball far away and a small ball close by can cast exactly the same image on the eye. Which side of the difficulty does this ball case show, and why?

options.text: The side in which many scenes cast one image, since two different scenes, a large ball far off and a small one close by, produce the same image.
options.why: Correct. Two different scenes produce one image, so the image alone cannot say which scene is there. Invariance is the other side, one object casting many images.

options.text: The invariance side, since a ball far away and a ball close by are one kind of object, seen at two quite different distances from the eye.
options.why: Distance is a change that invariance often involves, which makes this tempting. But here two different balls produce one image, and invariance is one object producing many different images.

options.text: The side in which many scenes cast one image, since one ball moved from far away to close by casts many different images on the eye.
options.why: The side is right, but the reason describes invariance, one object casting many images. The ball case is two different scenes casting one image.

options.text: Neither side, since the large ball and the small ball are different objects, and nothing has to be recognized across a change in either one.
options.why: The ball case is exactly one side of the difficulty. Two different scenes cast one image, so the image alone cannot say which scene produced it.

items.stem: For the small fish’s nervous system, what does invariance mean?

options.text: Some neuron downstream has to fire for every eel smell, faint or strong, and stay quiet for the sucker’s smell.
options.why: Correct. The neuron’s firing has to follow the eel, not the strength or the particular mixture of the smell, and it has to stay quiet even when the sucker’s smell is more like one eel smell than the eel smells are like each other.

options.text: Some receptor in the nostrils has to respond to eels and only to eels, whether the eel’s smell is faint or strong.
options.why: No receptor stands for an eel; an eel is a pattern of activity across many receptors. The demand falls on a neuron downstream of them.

options.text: Some neuron downstream has to fire more strongly the stronger the smell is, so that faint smells from far away are ignored.
options.why: Firing that follows strength would miss the faint eel far away. Invariance asks for firing that follows the eel, faint or strong.

options.text: Some neuron downstream has to fire for whichever smell is most like the last eel smell, even when that smell is the sucker’s.
options.why: That neuron would send the fish fleeing from the sucker whenever its smell happened to be most like the last eel smell. The neuron has to stay quiet for the sucker even then.

items.stem: Suppose a neuron downstream of the fish’s smell receptors fires whenever the smell in the water is strong, and stays quiet whenever it is faint. Why does this neuron fail the demand that invariance makes?

options.text: It would not fire for an eel far away and could fire for a sucker close by, so its firing would not follow whether an eel is there.
options.why: Correct. An eel near and an eel far produce smells at very different strengths. A neuron that follows strength follows distance, not the eel.

options.text: It would meet generalization but fail discrimination, since it would treat strong smells alike, whether they come from an eel or from a sucker.
options.why: It does fail discrimination, but it fails generalization too. It would treat a faint eel and a strong eel differently, though both call for flight.

options.text: It is a single neuron, and invariance requires that no one neuron fire for every eel smell, only a pattern of activity across many.
options.why: Invariance is stated in exactly those terms: some neuron downstream has to fire for every eel smell. The trouble is what this particular neuron fires for.

options.text: It would meet the demand, since a strong smell usually means a nearby eel, and a nearby eel is the danger most worth fleeing from.
options.why: A distant eel still calls for flight while there is time to get away. And a strong smell could just as well come from a sucker close by.

items.stem: How does the small fish learn what an eel smells like?

options.text: Across many encounters, and it learns about other things in the time between those encounters.
options.why: Correct. Learning about eels is spread over many encounters, and the fish learns about other things in between them.

options.text: All at once, in a single encounter that settles what an eel smells like for good.
options.why: One encounter cannot settle it, since no two eel smells are the same. The fish learns across many encounters.

options.text: Across many encounters, with nothing else learned until the eel’s smell is settled.
options.why: The fish learns about other things in between, and that is part of what makes learning in sequence a problem.

options.text: Across many encounters with one eel, since that eel’s smell stays the same over time.
options.why: One eel’s smell changes from moment to moment, and the fish encounters many eels. Learning is spread over many encounters with other learning in between.

items.stem: A young songbird has learned that a hawk’s outline overhead means danger. Later it learns about an owl, whose outline shares much with the hawk’s and with the outlines of harmless pigeons. Why does learning about the owl bear on what the bird already knows?

options.text: The owl has much in common with things learned earlier, so learning about it touches what is known about those things.
options.why: Correct. Things learned at different times often overlap, and when they do, learning about one bears on what is already known about the others.

options.text: Learning about the owl leaves old learning untouched, since each thing an animal learns about is kept apart from the rest.
options.why: Learning in sequence would be easy if that were so. Because the owl’s outline shares so much with the others, learning about it cannot be kept apart from them.

options.text: The owl was learned about later, and later learning replaces earlier learning whatever the two things have in common.
options.why: Order alone is not the problem; overlap is. And the requirement is that new learning add to old learning rather than replace it.

options.text: The owl is a predator like the hawk, so the bird simply treats the owl as a hawk and has nothing new to learn about it.
options.why: Treating the owl like the hawk would be generalization, but the bird is learning about the owl. Its overlap with the hawk and the pigeons is what makes that learning bear on the old.

items.stem: When an animal learns about one thing after another, what has to be true of the new learning?

options.text: It has to add to the old learning without overwriting it, so that what was learned before is kept.
options.why: Correct. That is the requirement learning in sequence states. Learning a new predator must not erase what the fish knows about eels.

options.text: It has to replace the old learning, so that the most recent encounter decides what the animal does.
options.why: Replacing old learning is exactly what must not happen. The fish that learns a new predator still needs what it knows about eels.

options.text: It has to wait until the old learning is complete, so that the two never go on at the same time.
options.why: The fish learns about other things in between its encounters with eels. The requirement is that new learning add to old, not wait for it.

options.text: It has to use receptors the old learning never used, so that the two cannot affect each other.
options.why: The new predator’s smell and the eel’s are carried by many of the same receptors. The requirement has to be met despite that overlap.

items.stem: A bee finds nectar in yellow flowers with stripes and in blue flowers without stripes, and none in yellow flowers without stripes or in blue flowers with stripes. What can the bee rely on to predict nectar?

options.text: Only the combination of color and stripes, since each color and each marking brings nectar on some visits and nothing on others.
options.why: Correct. When the same features turn up in rewarded and unrewarded flowers, no single feature reliably predicts the outcome, and only combinations do.

options.text: The color yellow, since nectar turns up in half of the yellow flowers, and a cue rewarded half the time is better than none.
options.why: Nectar turns up in half of the blue flowers too. A feature followed by reward half the time, whichever way the other feature goes, says nothing about which flower holds nectar.

options.text: The stripes, since the striped yellow flowers hold nectar on every visit, and stripes are easier to see from a distance than color.
options.why: Striped yellow flowers do hold nectar, but striped blue flowers do not. Stripes come with nectar on some visits and with nothing on others, so no single feature is reliable in this patch.

options.text: Nothing at all, since a cue that is rewarded only some of the time is one that no animal is able to learn anything from.
options.why: Animals, from rats to monkeys, learn tasks in which only combinations predict the outcome. The bee can rely on the combination.

items.stem: Two foraging birds learn which berries to eat. Where the first lives, the edible and the bitter berries share almost none of their colors, sizes, and smells. Where the second lives, edible and bitter berries share most of their colors, sizes, and smells, in different combinations. For which bird does more of the reliable information lie in combinations of features?

options.text: The second, since the more the berries share features, the more of the reliable information lies in combinations of them.
options.why: Correct. When features are shared across edible and bitter berries, each single feature is followed by a good meal some of the time and not at others, and the combinations carry what is reliable.

options.text: The first, since features that the two kinds of berry do not share have to be combined before they can say anything about which to eat.
options.why: Where features are not shared, each one predicts the outcome on its own. A single color or smell is enough for the first bird.

options.text: Both equally, since how many features the berries share does not change where the reliable information about which to eat lies.
options.why: How much objects share is exactly what moves the reliable information. The more they share, the more of it lies in combinations.

options.text: Neither, since a bird learns only about single features, so even the second bird could not learn about combinations at all.
options.why: Animals do learn tasks in which only combinations predict the outcome. And the question is where the information lies, which the second bird’s berries put in combinations.

items.stem: Learning in sequence sets stability against plasticity, and recognizing an eel sets discrimination against generalization. How do these two tensions differ?

options.text: Stability against plasticity concerns how much to change when learning; discrimination against generalization concerns which inputs to treat alike and which apart.
options.why: Correct. Stability versus plasticity is changing enough to learn something new while changing little enough to keep the old. Discrimination and generalization are two demands on a single mapping from inputs to responses.

options.text: They do not really differ, since plasticity is another name for generalization, and stability is another name for discrimination, applied to learning.
options.why: Each is a pull between two demands, but the two tensions are not the same. One concerns how learning changes what came before; the other concerns how inputs are mapped to responses.

options.text: Stability against plasticity is about where to draw the line between “yes” and “no”; discrimination against generalization is about how far apart the evidence lies.
options.why: That describes criterion and sensitivity from signal detection theory, and those two do not pull against each other, since moving the criterion leaves sensitivity unchanged.

options.text: Stability against plasticity is a demand on animals with a neocortex; discrimination against generalization is a demand on animals without one.
options.why: The small fish has no neocortex, and it faces both. It must tell the eel from the sucker, and it must learn a new predator without losing the eel.

items.stem: One fish’s responses are reshaped completely by each new smell it learns about. Another fish’s responses hardly change, whatever it experiences. How does each fish fall short on the stability–plasticity trade-off?

options.text: The first changes too much to keep what it learned before, and the second changes too little to learn anything new.
options.why: Correct. The trade-off is changing enough to learn something new, while changing little enough to keep what was learned before. Each fish has given up one side of it.

options.text: The first changes too little to learn anything new, and the second changes too much to keep what it learned before.
options.why: That swaps the two fish. Being reshaped by every new smell is too much change, and hardly changing at all is too little.

options.text: The first fails discrimination as new smells blur into old ones, and the second fails generalization as nothing carries over.
options.why: Those are failures of the mapping from inputs to responses. The trade-off asked about here concerns how much new learning changes what came before.

options.text: Neither falls short, since the trade-off concerns only how fast an animal learns, and not whether old learning is kept.
options.why: Keeping old learning is half of the trade-off. Stability is changing little enough to keep what was learned before.

items.stem: Why can the small fish not simply keep what it learns about a new predator’s smell apart from what it knows about eels?

options.text: The two smells are carried by many of the same receptors, so learning about one bears on what is known of the other.
options.why: Correct. The new predator’s smell may share much of its chemistry with the eel’s, and learning the new smell must not erase what the fish knows about eels.

options.text: The two smells are the same mixture of chemicals, so the fish has no way to tell the new predator from the eel by smell.
options.why: The smells may overlap a great deal, but they are not identical. The problem is the overlap, which makes learning about one bear on the other.

options.text: The fish has a single receptor for predators, so the smell of each new predator is carried by that one receptor.
options.why: No receptor stands for a predator, just as none stands for an eel. The overlap comes from many receptors that the two smells share.

options.text: The fish learns about eels once, early in life, so the later learning about predators has to be fitted into that record.
options.why: The fish learns about eels across many encounters. The difficulty is that two smells learned at different times share many receptors.

items.stem: In the lecture, invariance is stated as a demand on the animal, with nothing said about how the demand is met. Which of these statements describes the demand itself, rather than a way of meeting it?

options.text: Some neuron downstream has to fire for an eel’s smell, faint or strong, and stay quiet for the sucker’s smell.
options.why: Correct. That is what invariance requires of a nervous system, stated without any procedure or tissue for achieving it.

options.text: The same small detector is copied to every position in an input, so that a feature is found wherever in the input it falls.
options.why: That is convolution, an architecture that builds in part of what invariance needs, and only for shifts in position. It is a way of meeting the demand.

options.text: A network is trained on copies of each example that have been shifted, rotated, and rescaled, so it sees those changes in training.
options.why: That is how many networks come to recognize objects across such changes, and whether it explains animals is a live dispute. Either way it is a way of meeting the demand.

options.text: Cells further along the visual pathway keep their preferences over wider changes in an object’s position and size than earlier cells.
options.why: That describes tolerance in real cells, evidence about how a brain partly meets the demand. A statement of the demand is about what must happen, not how.

items.stem: In the lecture, the requirement that new learning add to old without overwriting it is stated, and the stability–plasticity trade-off is named, with nothing said about how either is achieved. At which of Marr’s levels is that statement made, and what does it leave out?

options.text: The computational level, since it is a statement of what the fish has to manage, with the procedure and the tissue left out.
options.why: Correct. The requirement and the trade-off describe the problem. How a procedure meets it, and what physical machinery runs that procedure, are left for the other two levels.

options.text: The algorithmic level, since it is a statement of the procedure that keeps old learning, with only the tissue left out.
options.why: No procedure is named. What has to happen is stated, which is the computational level, and the procedure is left open.

options.text: The implementational level, since it is a statement about the fish’s receptors, with the problem being solved left out.
options.why: The receptors come up only to explain why the smells overlap. The statement is about what the fish has to manage, which is the problem itself.

options.text: The computational level, since it is a statement of the procedure the fish uses, with only the reason the fish needs it left out.
options.why: The level is right, but the reasoning is reversed. A computational statement is about what and why, and it is the procedure that is left out.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why invariance is discrimination and generalization at their hardest, using the small fish, the eel, and the sucker.
items.answer: An eel close by and the same eel far away produce smells at very different strengths, so one eel’s smells can differ from each other more than either differs from the sucker’s. Generalization has to treat those barely overlapping eel smells as one thing, since all of them call for flight. Discrimination has to keep the sucker’s smell apart, even when it is more like one of the eel smells than the eel smells are like each other. So both demands bear down hardest on the same smells at once. For the fish’s nervous system, this means some neuron downstream has to fire for every eel smell, faint or strong, and stay quiet for the sucker.
rubric: Says one eel can produce smells that barely overlap, for example when it is near and when it is far.
Says the eel smells can differ from each other more than either differs from the sucker’s.
Identifies treating the eel smells alike as generalization, and keeping the sucker apart as discrimination.
States the demand on a downstream neuron: fire for every eel smell, faint or strong, and stay quiet for the sucker.

items.stem: In Module 1, we saw a difficulty in vision: many different scenes can cast exactly the same image. In a few sentences, explain how invariance and that difficulty are two sides of one problem, and give a fresh example of each side, different from the chapter’s.
items.answer: In the difficulty from Module 1, many different scenes can cast exactly the same image, so the image alone does not say which scene produced it. A round plate tilted away from the eye and an oval plate held upright can cast the same oval image. Invariance runs the other way: one object can cast many different images. A bicycle seen from the side shows two round wheels, and the same bicycle seen head-on is a narrow upright shape, and the two images share little. In both cases the image and the thing come apart. In one, many things lead to one input, and in the other, one thing leads to many inputs that still have to be recognized as that thing.
rubric: States the side from Module 1: many different scenes can cast one image.
States invariance’s side: one object can cast many different images.
Says the two are inverses of each other, not the same problem.
Gives a valid new example of different scenes casting the same image.
Gives a valid new example of one object casting images that barely overlap.

items.stem: A young bird has learned which butterflies are good to eat. It then learns about a new, bad-tasting kind, every one of whose colors and markings is also found on the good kinds, in different combinations. In a short paragraph, explain why learning about the new kind bears on what the bird already knows, why none of those colors or markings, taken alone, can now be relied on to predict a good meal, what the new learning has to do, and what trade-off that learning faces.
items.answer: The new butterfly’s colors and markings overlap with those of the kinds the bird already knows, so learning about it bears on what was learned about them. Each of those colors and markings now comes with a bad taste on some occasions and a good meal on others, so none of them alone predicts the outcome reliably, and only combinations do. The new learning has to add to the old without overwriting it: the bird must learn to avoid the new kind and still eat the good ones. This is the trade-off we called stability versus plasticity in Module 5, changing enough to learn something new while changing little enough to keep what was learned before.
rubric: Says the overlap in colors and markings makes learning about the new kind bear on old learning.
Says each shared color or marking is followed by a good meal on some occasions and a bad taste on others, so no single one is reliable and only combinations are.
States that new learning has to add to old learning without overwriting it.
Names stability versus plasticity and describes both sides of it.

items.stem: A fish with no hidden units learns only from eels and suckers that pass close by, so every smell it learns from is strong. Then it is taken downstream, where every smell arrives diluted to three tenths of its strength, and learning is switched off. Over a dozen encounters there, what did it do, and which demand does that show it failing?

options.text: It stayed to feed at every encounter and was struck by every eel, failing invariance, which asks it to treat faint and strong eel smells as one thing.
options.why: Correct. Far off, every smell is weak, and the fish treated every far smell the way it had treated a near sucker, so it stayed. Recognizing one thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as distance, is invariance.

options.text: It fled at every encounter and never fed, failing discrimination: it treated every faint smell, a sucker’s as well as an eel’s, as an eel.
options.why: A fish that fled every faint smell would at least survive, and its failure would be one of discrimination. The downstream fish did the opposite: it stayed for everything, eels included.

options.text: It told the far eels from the far suckers about as well as near ones, showing that what it learned from strong smells carries over to faint ones.
options.why: The far smells were not told apart at all. Every one reached the fish weak, the fish stayed for every one, and every eel struck it.

options.text: It stayed for every sucker and fled from every eel, but late, failing the demand to reach a verdict while there is still time to get away.
options.why: The fish never fled a far eel at all, early or late. The failure lies in treating a faint eel smell as an eel, not in timing.

items.stem: In the lab’s new-predator scenario, a fish with six hidden units learns eels and suckers for 1,000 encounters, then spends 1,000 encounters with a pike and a chub alone. Then an eel comes back. What happened at that encounter, and what does it show?

options.text: The fish stayed and was struck, showing that learning the pike and the chub overwrote what it had learned about eels instead of adding to it.
options.why: Correct. After learning the pike and the chub alone, the fish stayed for the returning eel and the eel lunged: a miss. New learning has to add to old learning without overwriting it, and here it did not.

options.text: The fish darted to cover in time, showing that learning the pike and the chub added to what it had learned about eels without overwriting it.
options.why: That is what the requirement asks for, but not what happened. The fish stayed for the eel and was struck: learning the new pair alone cost it what it knew about eels.

options.text: The fish darted to cover in time, since the pike’s and the chub’s smells differ from the eel’s, so learning about them left the old learning alone.
options.why: Different smells are still carried by the same two receptors, so learning about one thing bears on what was learned about others. The fish stayed for the eel and was struck.

options.text: The fish stayed and was struck, showing that it had never learned eels well in its first 1,000 encounters, before the pike and the chub arrived.
options.why: The fish did stay and was struck, but not for that reason. After its first 1,000 encounters it was nearly always right about eels and suckers; what it knew was lost while it learned the pike and the chub alone.

pools.title: Definitions, Rules, and a Space of Inputs
pools.covers: reading §7.2.1, §7.2.2 · lecture 7.2 slides title, definitions_and_rules, a_space_of_inputs, three_families

items.stem: Knowing which smells should send a fish fleeing is not the same thing as having a way to sort them. In the chapter’s sense, what is an algorithm for that sorting?

options.text: A procedure that sorts the smells, using what the fish has learned from the smells it has already experienced.
options.why: Correct. Knowing which smells call for flight states the problem. An algorithm is the procedure that actually does the sorting, drawing on past experience.

options.text: A statement of which smells call for flight and which do not, and of why getting that right matters to the fish.
options.why: That is the problem itself, at the computational level: what has to be done and why. An algorithm is a procedure for doing it.

options.text: The neurons and connections in the fish’s brain that physically carry out the sorting of each new smell.
