options.why: That is the implementational level, the physical means. An algorithm is the procedure those means might carry out, described apart from the tissue.

options.text: A record of every smell the fish has experienced, each one paired with the response that it called for.
options.why: A record of past cases is something an algorithm might store and consult. On its own, it says nothing about how a new smell gets sorted.

items.stem: What is the classical view of categories?

options.text: The view that a category is defined by features that are individually necessary and jointly sufficient.
options.why: Correct. Everything with all of the defining features belongs to the category, and nothing without them does.

options.text: The view that a category is represented by one summary of its members, such as the average member.
options.why: That describes a prototype model, which stores a central tendency and sorts a new input by closeness to it. The classical view stores a definition.

options.text: The view that a category is represented by every member a person has stored, with new items compared to all of them.
options.why: That describes an exemplar model, which keeps the members themselves. The classical view lists defining features instead.

options.text: The view that members overlap the way faces in a family do, with no single feature running through the whole set.
options.why: That is family resemblance, the pattern found in everyday categories and part of the evidence against the classical view, not the view itself.

items.stem: What is the name for the account under which a category is defined by features that are individually necessary and jointly sufficient for membership, so that everything with all of them belongs and nothing without them does?

options.text: Classical view.
options.why: Correct. It is the oldest answer to how categories might be formed, and for a long time it was the default account.

options.text: Prototype.
options.why: A prototype is a summary of a category, such as its average member. A prototype model sorts by closeness to that summary, not by a list of defining features.

options.text: Exemplar.
options.why: An exemplar is a stored example of a category. An exemplar model sorts by summed similarity to stored members, with no defining features at all.

options.text: Decision-bound model.
options.why: A decision-bound model divides the feature space into regions and responds by region. A definition can be read that way, but the name for the account built on defining features is the classical view.

items.stem: A hiking club defines a “full member” as someone who has paid this year’s dues and has completed the safety course. Read as a classical definition, which statement follows?

options.text: Anyone who has done both is a full member, whatever else is true of them, and anyone who has done only one is not.
options.why: Correct. Each feature is individually necessary, so lacking either one excludes a person, and the two together are jointly sufficient, so nothing else is needed.

options.text: Someone who has done only one of the two is a partial member, closer to full membership than someone who has done neither.
options.why: That treats membership as graded. Under the classical view membership is all or none, so missing one necessary feature leaves a person out entirely.

options.text: Someone who has done both may still fall short if they are an unusual sort of member, since typical members count for most.
options.why: Typicality plays no part in a classical definition. The two features are jointly sufficient, so having both is enough, however unusual the member.

options.text: Someone who has done neither can still qualify if they share enough other features with the club’s most typical members.
options.why: That is family resemblance, which is how everyday categories often look. A classical definition makes each defining feature necessary.

items.stem: Suppose a triangle is defined as a closed figure with three straight sides. Compare a neat triangle with three equal sides and a long, thin triangle with one very sharp corner. What does the classical view say about the two?

options.text: Both are triangles, and both belong to the category equally, since each one has every defining feature.
options.why: Correct. Under the classical view membership is all or none, and every member belongs equally. An odd shape with all the defining features is no less a member.

options.text: The neat triangle belongs more fully than the thin one, since it is closer to the average of all triangles.
options.why: Closeness to an average is how a prototype model sorts. The classical view gives membership no degrees.

options.text: The thin triangle belongs only in part, since one of its corners lies far from the usual shape of a triangle.
options.why: Partial membership is exactly what the classical view rules out. A figure with all the defining features belongs, and belongs fully.

options.text: Neither one belongs until it has been compared with the stored triangles that a person has already seen.
options.why: Comparison with stored examples is how an exemplar model sorts. A classical definition needs only a check of the defining features.

items.stem: Which category comes closest to what the classical view expects of every category?

options.text: Odd number, a whole number that leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 2.
options.why: Correct. Odd number is one of the chapter’s examples of a classical definition: every member has the defining feature, and nothing without it belongs.

options.text: Bird, an animal that has feathers and is able to fly through the air.
options.why: A penguin has feathers and cannot fly. For everyday categories such as bird, it may be very hard to find a definition that reaches all the way down.

options.text: Chair, a piece of furniture made for one person to sit upon.
options.why: Chair is one of the chapter’s own examples of an everyday category for which a chain of definitions may be very hard to find.

options.text: Things to take out of a burning house, such as children, pets, and photographs.
options.why: A goal-built category like this one has members with almost nothing in common, so there is no feature list for a definition to give.

items.stem: How has the standing of the classical view changed over time?

options.text: It was long the default in psychology and philosophy; most cognitive scientists now think it is not the best general account.
options.why: Correct. The classical view was the default for a long time. Most cognitive scientists now think it is not the best explanation of how animals, especially humans, form categories.

options.text: It was a minority view in psychology for most of its history, and it gained ground once artificial networks came to compute rules.
options.why: The classical view was not a minority view. For a long time it was the default account of categories in both psychology and philosophy.

options.text: It was long the default, and it has since been shown to be false for categories of all kinds, numbers included.
options.why: That overstates the case. Odd numbers show that graded ratings can sit alongside a definition, and some categories are probably learned as rules.

options.text: It was the default in philosophy but not in psychology, where categories were studied through typicality from the start.
options.why: The classical view was the default in both psychology and philosophy. The typicality evidence came later and counted against it.

items.stem: The lecture calls a classical definition “a more complex labeled line”. In what sense is a definition more complex than a labeled line such as the worm’s copper-sensing neuron?

options.text: A labeled line is a single test, while a definition is a set of such tests combined by a rule.
options.why: Correct. One kind of receptor responds and a response follows: that is a single test. A definition gathers several tests and combines them by a rule.

options.text: A labeled line answers to one receptor, while a definition answers to a pattern across many receptors that no rule can state.
options.why: A pattern that no single input identifies is what pattern recognition deals with. A definition is exactly a pattern that a rule does state.

options.text: A labeled line carries its label on the line itself, while a definition carries its label at the far end, in what it connects to.
options.why: That reverses the point about labeled lines. The label of a labeled line is at the far end, in what the line connects to, not on the line itself.

options.text: A labeled line is learned from experience, while a definition is fixed before any learning starts and never changes.
options.why: The chapter does not contrast labeled lines and definitions by how they arise. The contrast it draws is between one test and several tests combined by a rule.

items.stem: Suppose “kitten” is defined as “a cat that is young”. In Module 4’s terms, which arrangement would compute this definition?

options.text: A labeled line for each defining feature, one for being a cat and one for being young, feeding a unit that computes AND.
options.why: Correct. Each defining feature is detected by its own labeled line, and the AND unit fires only when every test is passed.

options.text: A labeled line for each defining feature, one for being a cat and one for being young, feeding a unit that computes OR.
options.why: An OR unit fires when either test is passed, so it would accept any cat and any young animal. A definition needs every feature, which is AND.

options.text: A single labeled line for kittens, running from a kind of receptor that responds to kittens and to nothing else.
options.why: A single labeled line is one test. A definition is a set of tests, one for each defining feature, combined by a rule.

options.text: A layer with one unit for each kitten already seen, each unit responding to inputs that are close to its own stored example.
options.why: One unit per stored example is how an exemplar model can be read in network terms. A definition stores tests, not examples.

items.stem: In a hypothetical bird, a call counts as an alarm when it has a high note or a rapid trill, but not both. Could a definition in the classical sense capture this category?

options.text: Yes, since a definition combines its tests by a rule, and “one or the other, but not both” is a perfectly good rule.
options.why: Correct. Rules are not limited to AND. The chapter makes the same point about the fruit, where either smell alone means ripe fruit and both mean rot.

options.text: No, since a definition combines its tests by AND, which would require each defining feature to be present.
options.why: AND is the simplest rule, not the only one. A definition can combine its tests by exclusive or as well.

options.text: No, since no single straight line divides these cases, and a definition must sort every input with a single straight cut.
options.why: The single straight line is the limit of one unit, not of a rule. A definition can state exclusive or, though one unit cannot compute it.

options.text: Yes, but just by listing each alarm call the bird has heard, one by one, as the members of the category.
options.why: Listing every heard example is closer to an exemplar model. A definition captures the category with two tests and a rule.

items.stem: “Smell A or smell B, but not both” is a perfectly good rule for a definition, yet no single unit of the kind in Module 4 can compute it. How can both be true?

options.text: Stating a rule is one question and computing it with one straight boundary is another; from the two smells alone, it takes more than one unit.
options.why: Correct. Rules are not limited to AND, so this one can serve in a definition. A single unit draws one straight line, and in the space of the two smells exclusive or is not linearly separable, so computing it from those smells takes more than one unit.

options.text: They cannot both be true, since a definition combines its tests by AND, so the fruit’s rule is not really a definition.
options.why: Rules are not limited to AND, and exclusive or is a perfectly good rule. The tension dissolves once we separate stating a rule from computing it with one unit.

options.text: A single unit can compute the rule once its weights are learned from experience rather than set by hand.
options.why: No setting of a single unit’s weights or threshold computes exclusive or, however the setting is reached. Its limit is the single straight line.

options.text: A definition captures the rule roughly, sorting most cases correctly and a few wrongly, as one line does with overlapping clouds.
options.why: A definition sorts by its rule exactly, with no cases left over. Sorting most cases correctly is what one line does when two categories overlap.

items.stem: A rectangle is a closed figure with four straight sides and four right angles. If definitions are stacked, how is “right angle” handled?

options.text: It has a definition of its own in terms of simpler properties of lines, which rest in turn on tests a receptor can perform.
options.why: Correct. A defining feature need not be detected directly. Built this way, a definition is a hierarchy of tests, with receptor-level tests at the bottom.

options.text: It is detected directly by one kind of receptor that responds to right angles, so the rectangle needs no further levels below it.
options.why: Some tests at the very bottom are simple enough for a receptor. A right angle is not one of them; it is defined in terms of simpler properties.

options.text: It is left undefined, since only the category at the top of a definition needs a list of defining features.
options.why: Stacking means the reverse: each defining feature can have a definition of its own, level after level.

options.text: It is learned as the average of the right angles experienced so far, and each new corner is compared with that average.
options.why: Comparing with an average is what a prototype model does. In a stacked definition, each feature is itself defined by tests and a rule.

items.stem: In Module 4’s terms, what is a stacked definition?

options.text: A hierarchy of units, each computing a truth table over the units beneath it.
options.why: Correct. Each level combines the results of the level below by a rule, and in Module 4’s terms that is a unit computing a truth table.

options.text: A single unit computing AND over every receptor at once, with no levels in between.
options.why: A single AND unit is the plain, unstacked definition. Stacking adds levels, each defined in terms of the level below.

options.text: A large middle layer wired at random and never trained, with learning only at the output.
options.why: That describes the original perceptron, one answer to where useful features come from. A stacked definition is a hierarchy of rules.

options.text: A layer with one unit for each stored example, each responding to inputs close to it.
options.why: That is how an exemplar model can be read in network terms. A stacked definition holds tests and rules, not examples.

items.stem: A student tries to build a stacked definition of “tool”, working downward through simpler and simpler tests. What is most likely to make the attempt hard?

options.text: Each level must be definable from the one below, down to receptor tests, and for an everyday category that chain may be very hard to find.
options.why: Correct. For a square the chain reaches all the way down. For everyday categories such as bird or chair, it may be much harder to identify one.

options.text: Stacked definitions can combine their tests only by AND, and a category like “tool” would need other rules, such as exclusive or, at some level.
options.why: Rules are not limited to AND; exclusive or is a perfectly good rule. The difficulty lies in finding definitions at every level.

options.text: A hierarchy of tests would need a separate receptor for every kind of tool, and no animal has nearly that many kinds of receptor.
options.why: In a stacked definition only the bottom tests are done by receptors, and they are simple ones. The problem is defining each level from the one below.

options.text: A stacked definition can sort only the inputs it has already experienced, so any new kind of tool would fall outside it.
options.why: A definition sorts anything that passes its tests, new or not. The trouble is in building the chain of definitions in the first place.

items.stem: A critic argues that the classical view fails because definitions are too weak to compute anything complicated. How does the chapter answer the critic?

options.text: Definitions can use any rule and can be stacked, so the case against them rests on what people’s categories turn out to be like.
options.why: Correct. The case against the classical view does not rest on what definitions can compute. It rests on typicality and on how people’s categories are structured.

options.text: The critic is right, since definitions can combine tests only by AND, which is why they cannot capture categories that have exceptions.
options.why: Rules are not limited to AND, and definitions can be stacked into hierarchies. The weakness of definitions is not the case against them.

options.text: The critic is right, since a definition cannot capture a category with the shape of exclusive or, like the fruit that rots.
options.why: A definition can capture the fruit, since “smell A or smell B, but not both” is a perfectly good rule.

options.text: The critic is wrong, since people never use definitions at all, which leaves the computing power of definitions beside the point.
options.why: The chapter says some categories are probably learned as rules. The real reply is that the case against definitions concerns what categories are like.

items.stem: Suppose people list the attributes of twenty kinds of furniture, and no attribute is listed for all twenty. Why would that finding count against the classical view of furniture?

options.text: A definition lists features that every member has, and if no feature is true of all twenty there is nothing for a definition to list.
options.why: Correct. This is the shape of the chapter’s evidence: for most everyday categories, few or no attributes were true of all twenty members listed.

options.text: A definition can hold only a handful of features, and twenty kinds of furniture would need far more attributes than that.
options.why: A definition can hold as many tests as it needs, and can be stacked. The problem is that no feature is shared by every member.

options.text: A definition makes every member equally good, and listing attributes is a way of rating how good each member is.
options.why: Equal membership is a separate part of the case, tested by typicality ratings. Attribute listing shows there is nothing shared to list.

options.text: A finding like this shows that furniture is a goal-built category, like things to take out of a burning house, which no account explains.
options.why: The finding says nothing about a goal. It says that no feature runs through all twenty members, which counts against definitions specifically; other accounts can explain categories without a shared feature.

items.stem: People rated a robin a far better example of a bird than a penguin, and a bat worse still. Which part of the classical view sits poorly with these ratings?

options.text: That every member belongs equally, so no bird should be a better example of a bird than any other.
options.why: Correct. A definition makes every member equally good, while people’s ratings were sharply graded.

options.text: That membership depends on a rule, so birds should be sorted by an AND unit over their features.
options.why: Sorting by a rule is not what the ratings challenge, since a rule could sort robins and penguins alike. What they challenge is equal membership.

options.text: That definitions can be stacked, so every bird feature should be defined right down to receptor tests.
options.why: Stacking is about how definitions are built. The ratings bear on whether every member is equally good.

options.text: That categories come from experience, so a bird seen more often should be rated a better example than a rare one.
options.why: The classical view makes no claim about which birds people see. Its trouble with the ratings is that it makes all members equal.

items.stem: Suppose people rate 4 as a better example of an even number than 1,006, while agreeing that both are even and that every even number is equally even. By the chapter’s reasoning, what does this result show?

options.text: Graded ratings can exist alongside a definition, so typicality alone does not show that a category lacks one.
options.why: Correct. This mirrors the odd-number finding. People can know an exact definition and still rate some members as better examples.

options.text: Even number has no real definition, since graded ratings are the main evidence against the classical view.
options.why: Typicality is the main evidence against the classical view as a general account, but it cannot refute a definition alone, as numbers show.

options.text: People do not really understand what an even number is, since anyone who did would rate every member the same.
options.why: The people in such a study know the definition perfectly well. Graded ratings and an exact definition can coexist in one mind.

options.text: Numbers form a family resemblance, since small even numbers share more features with one another than large ones do.
options.why: Family resemblance describes categories with no feature running through every member. Every even number shares the defining feature.

items.stem: Why does one study’s finding about odd numbers matter to the case against the classical view?

options.text: People rated 3 a better odd number than 447 while knowing all odd numbers belong equally, so typicality alone cannot refute definitions.
options.why: Correct. Graded ratings can exist alongside a definition. Some categories are probably learned as rules, and others are not.

options.text: People rated 3 and 447 as equally good odd numbers, which confirmed that typicality disappears wherever a definition exists.
options.why: The finding was the reverse: people did rate some odd numbers as better examples than others.

options.text: People could not reliably say whether 447 was odd, which showed that even exact definitions are learned through family resemblance in the end.
options.why: The people knew the definition perfectly well. The finding was about graded ratings, not about uncertainty over membership.

options.text: People rated 3 a better odd number than 447, which showed that odd number has no exact definition after all.
options.why: Odd number plainly has an exact definition. The point of the finding is that graded ratings can coexist with one.

items.stem: Anyone who can think of “purple” and of “elephant” can think of a purple elephant, though no such animal has ever been seen. Which sense of the word concept does this illustrate?

options.text: A concept as a part of thought, which combines with other concepts to form new thoughts.
options.why: Correct. This is the sense the chapter illustrates with a pet and a fish making a pet fish. A concept in this sense is more than a category.

options.text: A concept as a summary of a category’s members, such as the average member of the category.
options.why: A summary such as an average member is a prototype. The purple elephant is about combining concepts into a new thought.

options.text: A concept as a single unit that fires for one thing and for nothing else, wherever it appears.
options.why: One unit per thing is a localist representation, a kind of code. The sense at issue is a part of thought that combines with others.

options.text: A concept as a region of a feature space, holding all the inputs that should get one response.
options.why: A region of a feature space is how a category can be pictured for sorting. Nobody has sorted a purple elephant; it was formed by combining.

items.stem: A student argues: “The typicality findings count against the classical view, so they also show that definitions cannot be the parts of thought that combine into new thoughts, the way pet and fish make pet fish”. What is wrong with the argument?

options.text: Typicality bears on how categories are structured; whether definitions can serve as parts of thought is a separate question, and one argued for a very long time.
options.why: Correct. A concept in that sense is a part of thought that combines with others. Whether definitions, or the accounts that follow them, can play that part has been argued for decades, or even millennia, and the chapter leaves it for Module 14 rather than settling it with the typicality findings.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since definitions that fail as an account of categories must also fail as parts of thought, which are categories under another name.
options.why: That treats a concept in thought as another word for a category. The word concept is also used for something more than a category, and whether definitions can play that part is a separate, long-argued question.

options.text: The typicality findings support the classical view rather than counting against it, since people rate members by how many defining features they have.
options.why: Typicality is the main evidence against the classical view as a general account. A definition makes every member equally good, while people’s ratings are graded.

options.text: The typicality findings were overturned by the odd-number study, which showed that people do not really rate some members as better examples than others.
options.why: The odd-number study found graded ratings too: people rated 3 a better odd number than 447. It showed that graded ratings can sit alongside a definition, not that they are absent.

items.stem: A moth has two kinds of sound receptor. In a feature space built from them, what is the sound reaching the moth at one moment?

options.text: A single point, placed on each axis by how strongly that kind of receptor responds.
options.why: Correct. Each kind of receptor gets an axis, and the input at each moment is one point in that space.

options.text: A cloud of points, one for each receptor cell, spread out across the whole of the space.
options.why: A cloud appears when many inputs are plotted, such as many sounds of one kind. A single moment’s input is one point.

options.text: A straight line through the space, dividing sounds to flee from sounds to ignore.
options.why: A straight line is a boundary between regions. The input itself is a point that falls on one side of such a line.

options.text: A region of the space, holding every sound that the moth treats in the same way.
options.why: A region holds all the inputs that get one response. One moment’s sound is a single point within some region.

items.stem: In the chapter’s smell space with two axes, how do many sniffs of many eels and many sniffs of the harmless sucker look?

options.text: Two scattered clouds of points, one for each kind of fish, overlapping at their edges.
options.why: Correct. One sniff is a point, many sniffs make a scattered cloud, and the eel and sucker clouds overlap at the edge.

options.text: Two single points, one for each kind of fish, since each kind of fish gives off one smell.
options.why: No two sniffs of an eel are the same, so many sniffs make a scattered cloud rather than a single point.

options.text: Two compact clouds far apart, since eel and sucker smells share none of their chemistry.
options.why: The sucker’s smell shares much of its chemistry with the eel’s, which is why the two clouds overlap.

options.text: One shapeless cloud, since a fish cannot tell eel sniffs from sucker sniffs at all.
options.why: The two kinds of sniff make two clouds that overlap only at the edge. Most eel sniffs and most sucker sniffs lie apart.

items.stem: What is a feature space?

options.text: A space with one axis for each feature of an input, in which each input is a single point.
options.why: Correct. In a feature space, inputs that are alike land close together and inputs that are different land far apart.

options.text: An arrangement in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells of the tissue.
options.why: That is a topographic map, a layout of tissue. A feature space is a picture of inputs, with one axis per feature.

options.text: The region of the sensory world where a stimulus changes one cell’s activity.
options.why: That is a receptive field, a property of a single cell. A feature space places every input as a point.

options.text: The list of features that every member of a category has in common.
options.why: A list of shared features is what a classical definition would give. A feature space is a space, with an axis for each feature.

items.stem: What do we call a picture of inputs with one axis for each feature of an input, in which each input is a single point?

options.text: Feature space.
options.why: Correct. A feature space turns sorting inputs into dividing a space into regions.

options.text: Feature engineering.
options.why: Feature engineering is deciding, before learning begins, what the inputs to a learning system will be. It chooses the axes; it is not the space.

options.text: Topographic map.
options.why: A topographic map is an arrangement in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells.

options.text: Decision boundary.
options.why: A decision boundary is a line through the space of inputs, separating what a unit fires to from what it does not.

items.stem: Two sniffs land close together in the small fish’s smell space. What can be concluded from their closeness alone?

options.text: The two sniffs are alike in how the receptors respond, though they may still call for different responses.
options.why: Correct. Closeness means alike inputs. Because the eel and sucker clouds overlap at the edge, a sucker sniff can sit right beside an eel sniff.

options.text: The two sniffs come from the same kind of fish, since sniffs from one kind of fish always land together.
options.why: Sniffs of one kind of fish form a scattered cloud, and the eel and sucker clouds overlap, so nearby sniffs can come from different fish.

options.text: The two sniffs call for the same response, since closeness in the space is what sets which response a sniff calls for.
options.why: Closeness says how alike the inputs are. Which response each calls for depends on which fish it came from, and near the overlap neighbors can differ.

options.text: The two sniffs arrived close together in time, since the axes of the space record when each sniff arrived.
options.why: The axes record how strongly each kind of receptor responds, not when the sniff arrived.

items.stem: The lecture says a feature space gives a picture to the mapping from inputs to responses that the fish’s world calls for. In that picture, what does the mapping become?

options.text: A division of the space into regions, one for each response, with a boundary between them.
options.why: Correct. The inputs that should get one response form a region, and the mapping divides the space with a boundary.

options.text: A single point for each response, placed at the average of the inputs that get that response.
options.why: One point per category at the average is a prototype. The mapping itself is a division of the whole space.

options.text: A threshold along each axis of the space, marking the strength at which each kind of receptor begins to fire.
options.why: A threshold on each axis would treat receptors one at a time. The mapping divides the space as a whole into regions.

options.text: A list of every input already experienced, each stored together with the response it received.
options.why: Storing every input is what an exemplar model does. The picture the feature space gives is a division into regions.

items.stem: A second harmless fish moves into the stream, and its smell overlaps the eel’s far more than the sucker’s does. What happens to where the small fish’s boundary between fleeing and feeding should run?

options.text: The right boundary changes, since where it should run is set by which smells come from which fish and how much they overlap.
options.why: Correct. Where the boundary should run is set by the inputs themselves, so a new source of smells changes where it ought to be.

options.text: The right boundary stays put, since it is fixed by which kinds of receptor the fish has rather than by the smells around it.
options.why: The receptors set which axes the space has. Where the boundary should run within that space depends on the smells.

options.text: The right boundary stays put, since a boundary always runs halfway between the two most common kinds of smell.
options.why: Halfway between two averages is where a single-prototype model would put it. Where the boundary should run depends on all the smells and their overlap.

options.text: The boundary disappears, since smells that overlap this much cannot be divided by any boundary at all.
options.why: Overlapping clouds can still be divided, with a few inputs on the wrong side. The overlap changes where the boundary should go.

items.stem: Suppose a fish has forty kinds of smell receptor. What is a straight boundary in its feature space?

options.text: A hyperplane, which cannot be pictured but still divides the space into two parts.
options.why: Correct. With three axes a straight boundary is a flat plane, and with more it is a hyperplane, the many-dimensional version of a flat plane.

options.text: Nothing at all, since a straight boundary is defined only for spaces of two or three axes.
options.why: We lose the ability to picture the space beyond three axes, but the geometry extends, and a single hyperplane still divides it.

options.text: A set of forty separate lines, one on each axis, each marking one receptor’s threshold.
options.why: A straight boundary is a single flat surface through the whole space, not a separate cut on each axis.

options.text: A flat plane, exactly as in a space of three axes, since the extra axes add nothing to it.
options.why: A flat plane is the straight boundary in three dimensions. With more axes the boundary is a hyperplane.

items.stem: What does it mean for two categories to be linearly separable?

options.text: One straight line or flat surface through the feature space puts all of one category on one side and all of the other on the other.
options.why: Correct. That property is linear separability, and it settles whether one straight cut is enough.

options.text: A single straight line through the feature space puts most of one category on one side and most of the other category on the other side.
options.why: Most is not enough. Two overlapping clouds can be mostly divided by one line and still not be linearly separable.

options.text: The points of the two categories do not overlap anywhere in the feature space.
options.why: Not overlapping is needed but not enough. The just-right fruit’s acceptable smells overlap none of the others, yet no straight line can wrap around that island.

options.text: Each category can be picked out by a single feature on its own, without any regard to the other features.
options.why: AND depends on two features together, and it is still linearly separable. One straight line may run across several axes at once.

items.stem: What is the name for the property of two categories that can be divided by a single straight line, or a single flat surface, through the feature space, with all of one category on one side and all of the other on the other?

options.text: Linear separability.
options.why: Correct. AND and OR have this property, which is why one unit could compute each of them; exclusive or does not.

options.text: Discrimination.
options.why: Discrimination is treating differently the inputs that call for different responses. It is a demand on the mapping, not a property of a division.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units, which makes it more likely that a straight boundary will work.

options.text: Invariance.
options.why: Invariance is recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as distance or viewpoint.

items.stem: In the two-receptor smell space, a diagonal line leaves most eel sniffs on one side and most sucker sniffs on the other, with a few of each on the wrong side. Are the eel and sucker clouds linearly separable?

options.text: No, since the clouds overlap; they would be linearly separable only if they did not overlap.
options.why: Correct. Linear separability requires all of each category on its own side. With the overlap, a few points always land on the wrong side.

options.text: Yes, since a single straight line sorts most of the points correctly, and that is what separability requires.
options.why: Separability requires every point on its own side, not most of them. The overlap leaves a few on the wrong side.

options.text: Yes, since any two clouds of points become linearly separable once a curved boundary is allowed.
options.why: A curved boundary is not a straight one. Linear separability is about whether a single straight line or flat surface is enough.

options.text: No, since two clouds in a smell space can never be divided by a straight line, overlapping or not.
options.why: If the eel and sucker clouds did not overlap, the same diagonal line would put every eel on one side and every sucker on the other.

items.stem: A single unit of the kind in Module 4 could compute AND and could compute OR, but not exclusive or. What property did AND and OR have that made a single unit enough?

options.text: Both are linearly separable, so one straight line through the input space divides all of their cases correctly.
options.why: Correct. A single unit draws one straight line, so it can compute exactly those functions whose cases one line can divide.

options.text: Both take only two inputs, and a single unit can compute any function that takes just two inputs.
options.why: Exclusive or also takes only two inputs, and no single unit computes it. The number of inputs is not what matters.

options.text: Both were learned by the delta rule, which can set a single unit’s weights for any function at all.
options.why: No weight setting, however it is reached, lets one unit compute exclusive or. Its single straight line is the limit.

options.text: Both give an output that is all or none, which is exactly the kind of output that a single unit with a threshold produces.
options.why: Exclusive or is all or none too. What sets AND and OR apart is that a straight line divides their cases.

items.stem: For a hypothetical bee, a flower is worth visiting when it has a sweet scent or a blue color, but not both. With one axis for the scent and one for the color, where do the four combinations fall, and can one straight line sort them?

options.text: The two cases worth visiting sit at opposite corners, as do the other two, so no straight line puts both of those corners on one side.
options.why: Correct. This is exclusive or. Any straight line that is tried leaves at least one case on the wrong side.

options.text: The two cases worth visiting sit side by side along one edge of the space, so one straight line can cut them off from the other two.
options.why: The two cases worth visiting are scent alone and color alone, which sit at opposite corners, not along one edge.

options.text: The cases worth visiting form an island in the middle of the space, so a straight line can cut off only one side of it.
options.why: An island in the middle is the just-right strength case. Here the four cases sit at the four corners of the space.

options.text: The four cases fall on a single straight line, so one threshold placed along that line sorts them correctly.
options.why: Two features that can each be present or absent give four corners of a square, not four points on a line.

items.stem: A hypothetical seed sprouts only when the soil is neither too dry nor too wet, and neither too cold nor too hot. With one axis for moisture and one for temperature, why can no single straight line sort sprouting from not sprouting?

options.text: The sprouting conditions form an island in the middle, and a straight line can cut off one side of it but cannot wrap around it.
options.why: Correct. This has the shape of the fruit whose chemical must be at just the right strength: unacceptable conditions lie on every side.

options.text: The sprouting conditions sit at opposite corners of the space, so any straight line leaves one corner on the wrong side.
options.why: Opposite corners is the shape of exclusive or. Here the acceptable conditions sit in the middle, surrounded on every side.

options.text: The sprouting and non-sprouting conditions overlap, so the same soil sprouts a seed on one day and not on another.
options.why: Nothing in the case makes the outcome vary for the same soil. The problem is the shape of the acceptable region, not overlap.

options.text: The two axes measure different kinds of thing, and a straight line can divide only a space whose axes measure the same kind of thing.
options.why: Axes in a feature space can measure quite different things. A straight line fails here because of where the acceptable region lies.

items.stem: For the fruit where either smell alone means ripe fruit and both together mean rot, which added third input lets a single flat plane separate the ripe cases from the rest?

options.text: An input that is active only when both smells are present, the product of the two smells.
options.why: Correct. The product moves the rotting corner away from the other three, and then a single flat plane separates the ripe cases from the rest.

options.text: An input that reports the sum of the two smells, so that a stronger combined smell gets a larger value.
options.why: A sum is largest when both smells are present, which is why it can look like a fix. But on the sum the ripe cases fall between no fruit and rot. The input that moves the rotting corner away from the other three is one active only when both smells are present.

options.text: A second copy of smell A’s input, so that smell A is reported twice and counts for more than smell B.
options.why: A copy of smell A carries nothing that smell A did not already carry. The ripe cases still sit at opposite corners; what moves the rotting corner away is an input active only when both smells are present.

options.text: An input that reports smell B at a higher gain, so that small amounts of smell B register strongly.
options.why: Reporting smell B more strongly changes how far apart the cases sit along one axis, not which cases sit at opposite corners. What moves the rotting corner away is an input active only when both smells are present.

items.stem: A hypothetical lizard basks only when a rock is about the right temperature, and moves off when it is too cool or too hot. One threshold on rock temperature cannot mark off the right range. Which added input would let a single threshold do it?

options.text: An input reporting the temperature’s squared distance from the ideal, so that low values mean close to it.
options.why: Correct. This is how the chapter handles the island. On squared distance from the ideal, one threshold marks off everything close enough.

options.text: An input reporting the rock temperature a second time, so that the threshold has two copies of it to work with.
options.why: A second copy of rock temperature carries nothing the first did not. The acceptable range still sits in the middle, with a bad side above and below.

options.text: An input reporting the product of rock temperature and the time of day, as in the fruit with two smells.
options.why: A product is the added input for exclusive or, where both smells together meant rot. The just-right case is an island, and the added input that marks off an island with one threshold is its distance from the ideal.

options.text: An input reporting how warm the rock was the day before, so that recent history can set the threshold.
options.why: Yesterday’s temperature does not tell how far today’s is from the ideal. The range would still need cutting on both sides.

items.stem: A student says: “Exclusive or can never be solved by one straight boundary, whatever inputs we start from”. What is wrong with the student’s claim?

options.text: Separability depends on which features the space is built from; with the right added feature, one flat surface separates the cases.
options.why: Correct. Exclusive or is not linearly separable in the space of the two smells. Add the product of the two, and a single flat plane does the job.

options.text: Nothing is wrong; exclusive or can be solved only by a network with a hidden layer, never by any single straight boundary.
options.why: A hidden layer is one way of supplying new features. Once the inputs are re-represented, a single straight boundary can do the rest.

options.text: Exclusive or can be solved by one straight line in the original two-smell space, once a unit’s weights have been trained for long enough.
options.why: No amount of training gives one unit a line that puts both food corners on one side in the original space. What changes things is new features.

options.text: Exclusive or is linearly separable in the original two-smell space, as long as the straight line is drawn diagonally.
options.why: Every straight line in the two-smell space, diagonal or not, leaves at least one case on the wrong side.

items.stem: With the right features, the hard combination problems become easy to sort with one straight cut. What question does that leave open, and what answers are named?

options.text: Where such features come from: they can be learned, wired at random, or built in.
options.why: Correct. With the right features the hard problems are easy, so the open question becomes where the features come from.

options.text: Whether such features are real: they may be inputs no receptor reports, so the space is only a convenience.
options.why: The features can be real inputs, whether supplied by receptors or by later units. The open question is where useful ones come from.

options.text: Which family of algorithm to use: a decision bound, a prototype, or a set of stored exemplars.
options.why: The three families are a separate topic, about what is stored and consulted. The open question here is the source of useful features.

options.text: How many axes such features need: two can be pictured, three need a plane, and more cannot be divided.
options.why: A space with many axes can still be divided by a hyperplane. The open question is where useful features come from.

items.stem: Psychologists have proposed three broad families of algorithm that treat an input as a point in a feature space. What chiefly distinguishes the families from one another?

options.text: What has to be stored, and consulted, before a response can be made.
options.why: Correct. One family stores the boundary itself, and the others store something about the members of each category.

options.text: Whether they place inputs in a feature space at all, or work from definitions instead.
options.why: All three families treat an input as a point in a feature space. That is what they have in common.

options.text: Whether they end up drawing a boundary between categories, or manage to avoid drawing one.
options.why: Every family ends up drawing a boundary, whether it stores that boundary or not.

options.text: Whether they learn from experience, or have every category built in from the very start.
options.why: The families are not divided by learned versus built in. They differ in what is stored and consulted.

items.stem: Two models of how people sort shapes work very differently inside: one stores a boundary, and the other stores every example it was trained on. On every shape, both draw the same boundary. What follows?

options.text: The two models will be very hard to tell apart from sorting data, whatever their inner workings.
options.why: Correct. Every family ends up drawing a boundary, and two models that draw the same boundary make the same choices, so data can barely separate them.

options.text: The model storing the boundary is the correct one, since it reaches the same answers while storing much less.
options.why: Storing less does not make a model the right description of people. Models that draw the same boundary cannot be told apart this way.

options.text: The model storing examples draws no boundary at all, so the two models cannot be compared with each other.
options.why: A model that stores examples still ends up drawing a boundary, wherever summed similarity is equal. That is what makes comparison possible.

options.text: Testing a few more shapes will reveal the difference, since models that differ inside must differ in how they sort.
options.why: Models can differ inside and still sort every input alike. If the boundary is the same everywhere, more shapes will not separate them.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why most cognitive scientists do not take the classical view as the general account of categories, and why graded typicality alone does not settle the matter.
items.answer: The case against the classical view does not rest on what definitions can compute, since a definition can combine tests by any rule and can be stacked. It rests on what people’s categories are like. When people listed the attributes of twenty members of an everyday category, few or none were true of all twenty, so there is nothing for a definition to list. And a definition makes every member equally good, while people rated a robin a far better bird than a penguin. But typicality alone does not refute definitions. People rate 3 a better odd number than 447 while knowing that every odd number belongs equally. So graded ratings can exist alongside a definition, and some categories are probably learned as rules.
rubric: Says the case rests on what people’s categories are like, not on what definitions can compute.
Gives the attribute-listing finding: few or no attributes are shared by every member, so there is nothing to list.
Gives graded typicality (robin against penguin, or similar) as conflicting with every member belonging equally.
Gives the odd-number finding: graded ratings alongside an exact definition.
Concludes that typicality alone does not refute definitions, and that some categories may be learned as rules.

items.stem: For the fruit where either smell alone means ripe fruit and both together mean rot, explain in a few sentences why no single straight line can sort the four cases in a space with one axis per smell, and how adding a third input changes that.
items.answer: With one axis for each smell, the two ripe cases, smell A alone and smell B alone, sit at opposite corners, and so do no fruit and rot. No straight line can put both ripe corners on one side and both other corners on the other, so the problem is not linearly separable in that space. If we add a third input that is active only when both smells are present, the product of the two, the rotting corner moves away from the other three. Then a single flat plane separates the ripe cases from the rest. Whether one straight boundary is enough depends on which features the space is built from.
rubric: Places the two ripe cases at opposite corners, and the other two cases at the remaining corners.
States that no straight line puts both ripe corners on one side.
Names the added input as the product, active only when both smells are present.
Says the added input moves the rotting corner away so a single flat plane separates the cases.
Draws the general point that separability depends on the features the space is built from.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, use a square to explain how a definition can be built as a hierarchy of tests, and explain why the same construction may be much harder for an everyday category such as bird.
items.answer: A square is a closed figure with four straight sides of equal length and four right angles. None of those features is a single test. A right angle is itself defined in terms of simpler properties of lines, and those in terms of simpler properties still. So a stacked definition is a hierarchy of tests, with tests simple enough for a receptor to perform at the bottom, and each level combining the results of the level below by a rule. In Module 4’s terms, it is a hierarchy of units, each computing a truth table over the units beneath it. The hierarchy works only if every level can be defined in terms of the one below, all the way down to receptor tests. For a square that can be done. For bird it may be much harder to find a chain of definitions that reaches all the way down.
rubric: Gives the square’s defining features and notes that each can have a definition of its own.
Describes the result as a hierarchy, with receptor-level tests at the bottom.
Says each level combines the level below by a rule, or equivalently that each unit computes a truth table.
States the condition: every level must be definable down to tests a receptor can perform.
Says that for bird such a chain may be much harder to find, keeping the hedge rather than declaring it impossible.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the difference between two sniffs being close together in the small fish’s smell space and two sniffs calling for the same response. Use the eel and the sucker.
items.answer: Closeness in a feature space means the inputs are alike: the receptors respond to them in much the same way. Which response a sniff calls for depends on where it came from, an eel or a sucker. The eel and sucker clouds overlap at the edge, so a sucker sniff can sit right beside an eel sniff and still call for feeding rather than flight. The mapping divides the space into regions, one for each response, and where the boundary should run is set by which smells come from which fish and how much the two overlap. Because of the overlap, no single straight line puts every eel sniff on one side and every sucker sniff on the other; the clouds would be linearly separable only if they did not overlap.
rubric: Says closeness means the inputs are alike in how the receptors respond.
Says the response a sniff calls for depends on which fish produced it.
Uses the overlap of the eel and sucker clouds to show that neighbors can call for different responses.
Describes the mapping as regions with a boundary set by the smells and their overlap.
Notes that, with the overlap, the clouds are not linearly separable.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain how three families of categorization algorithm that store different things can still be compared with one another, and why two models that draw the same boundary are hard to tell apart.
items.answer: The three families differ in what has to be stored, and consulted, before a response can be made. One stores the boundary itself, and the others store something about the members of each category. But every one of them ends up drawing a boundary between categories, whether it stores that boundary or not, so the boundaries give a common ground for comparing them. Two models that draw the same boundary sort every input the same way, so they are very hard to tell apart in data, even when they work very differently inside.
rubric: Says the families differ in what is stored and consulted before a response.
Says every family ends up drawing a boundary, whether or not it stores one.
Says the boundaries are what allow the families to be compared.
Explains that the same boundary means the same sorting, so data can barely separate the models.
Does not declare any family the winner.

items.stem: In the lab’s One line will do scenario, where smells vary only a little, the encounters land on the feature space, receptor A across and receptor B up, in two clouds. How do the two clouds sit relative to each other?

options.text: The eel cloud lies further along receptor A and lower on receptor B than the sucker cloud, with a clear gap between them.
options.why: Correct. An eel’s smell is around A 0.75 and B 0.45, and a sucker’s around A 0.45 and B 0.60. Each sniff is one point, and at this small spread the two clouds do not overlap.

options.text: The eel cloud lies higher on both receptors than the sucker cloud, since an eel’s smell is stronger at every receptor than a sucker’s.
options.why: An eel’s smell has more A than a sucker’s, but less B. The eel cloud sits to the right of the sucker cloud and lower, not higher on both.

options.text: The two clouds lie on top of each other in the middle, since eels and suckers smell alike and only the outcome tells them apart.
options.why: Two averages landing on top of each other in the middle happens in the fruit problem, not here. Eels and suckers smell different, and their clouds are apart.

options.text: The eel cloud lies lower on receptor A and higher on receptor B than the sucker cloud, overlapping it heavily at its edge.
options.why: That reverses the two kinds. And at this small spread the clouds do not overlap; overlap comes when smells are made to vary more.

items.stem: In the lab’s One line will do scenario, How much smells vary is raised from 0.06 to 0.20, and the fish learns for 1,000 encounters, with the rule working exactly as before. What did the test set show, and why?

options.text: Most answers were right, but a sizeable share stayed wrong, because the clouds now overlap and no straight line puts every eel on one side and every sucker on the other.
options.why: Correct. At 0.06 the test set ends almost perfect; at 0.20 something like a fifth to two fifths stay wrong, so the fish still does far better than guessing. Overlapping clouds are no longer linearly separable, and more training cannot remove errors that no line can avoid.

options.text: About half stayed wrong, no better than guessing, because once the two clouds overlap a single straight line carries no information about which fish is there.
options.why: Overlap leaves errors only where the clouds meet. Most eel sniffs and most sucker sniffs still lie on their own sides of the line, so the fish ends well short of half wrong, though well above none.

options.text: Nearly every answer came out right, because the rule kept moving the line until it found one that put every eel on its own side of the space.
options.why: No such line exists once the clouds overlap. However the rule moves the line, some eels and some suckers sit on the wrong side.

options.text: A sizeable share stayed wrong, because 1,000 encounters were too few, and a few thousand more would bring the test set back to nearly perfect.
options.why: More training would not help. The errors come from the overlap of the two clouds, not from the rule running out of time.

items.stem: In the lab’s Ripe or rotting scenario, with no hidden units, the fish was given the built-in receptor Both together, which responds to the product of the two smells, and then learned for a few hundred encounters. In a few sentences, say what happened, and explain in terms of the feature space why.
items.answer: The fish solved the fruit within a few hundred encounters, with no hidden layer at all. The product is large only when both smells are present, so it adds a third axis along which the rotting corner moves away from the other three. In that three-axis space a single flat plane separates the two ripe corners from the twig and the rotting fruit, so one unit can now draw a boundary that sorts them. With only the two smells, the ripe cases sat at opposite corners, and no single line could put both on one side.
rubric: Reports that the fish solved the problem (nearly every test answer right) within a few hundred encounters.
Says the product is active only when both smells are present.
Says the new input moves the rotting corner away from the other three, along a third axis.
Says a single flat plane (one boundary) now separates ripe from not ripe, which no line could do with the two smells alone.

items.stem: In the lab’s island scenario, fruit nourishes only when both receptors respond at about the right strength, so the nourishing smells form a disk in the middle of the feature space. A fish with no hidden units is given the built-in receptor Distance from the ideal strength. Once it succeeds, what does its decision boundary look like on the feature space?

options.text: A circle around the disk, since one threshold on the new input marks off every smell within a fixed reach of the center.
options.why: Correct. The receptor reports how far each smell is from the ideal, so one threshold on that one input marks off the island. Drawn on the two original axes, the smells at that threshold form a circle, and the fish reached 5 percent wrong within a few hundred encounters.

options.text: A single straight line across the disk, since one unit can only ever draw one straight boundary, whatever distance its inputs report.
options.why: On the two original axes the boundary here is not straight. A straight cut can take off one side of the island but cannot wrap around it, and this fish succeeded.

options.text: Two parallel lines with a band between them through the middle, since a band is the shape a single unit draws when it combines two smells.
options.why: A band is what two hidden units and an output draw for exclusive or. This fish has no hidden units, and its boundary wraps all the way round.

options.text: A rounded triangle around the disk, since one built-in receptor gives the unit three straight sides to work with.
options.why: A rounded triangle is what three learned hidden units draw. The distance receptor gives one threshold on distance, which wraps the disk in a circle.

items.stem: What is a decision-bound model of categorization?

options.text: A model that divides the feature space into regions, one for each response, and responds according to the region an input falls in.
options.why: Correct. A decision-bound model learns the boundary itself, and the side of the boundary an input lands on settles the response.

options.text: A model that stores one summary of each category, such as its average member, and assigns a new input to whichever summary is nearest.
options.why: That is a prototype model. It stores something about the members, and its boundary follows from what it stores rather than being learned directly.

options.text: A model that stores every member of each category, and assigns a new input to the category with the largest summed similarity to it.
options.why: That is an exemplar model. It stores the members themselves, while a decision-bound model stores the boundary instead.

options.text: A framework for deciding whether something is present, which separates how well the evidence tells the cases apart from where the line is drawn.
options.why: That is signal detection theory, the framework decision-bound theory grew out of. Its line is a criterion on one axis of evidence; a decision-bound model divides a whole feature space into regions, one for each response.

items.stem: What is the name for a model of categorization that learns the boundary itself, dividing the feature space into one region for each response and responding according to the region an input falls in?

options.text: Decision-bound model.
options.why: Correct. Of the three families, the decision-bound model is the one that stores the boundary rather than anything about the members.

options.text: Prototype model.
options.why: A prototype model stores one summary of each category and assigns an input to the closest one. Its boundary follows from those summaries; it is not stored.

options.text: Exemplar model.
options.why: An exemplar model stores every member and sums an input’s similarity to them. Its boundary follows from what it stores; it is not learned directly.

options.text: Signal detection theory.
options.why: Signal detection theory is the framework decision-bound theory grew out of, for deciding whether a target is present. The family that learns a boundary in a feature space is the decision-bound model.

items.stem: How is a decision bound related to the criterion of signal detection theory?

options.text: The criterion is a boundary drawn on a single axis of evidence, and a decision bound is that same idea extended to a feature space with many axes.
options.why: Correct. The criterion splits one evidence axis into “yes” and “no”. A decision bound splits a feature space with many axes into one region per response.

options.text: The criterion is a boundary in a space with many axes, and a decision bound is the simpler case of that same idea on a single axis of evidence.
options.why: This reverses the two. The criterion is the one-axis case, drawn along a single axis of evidence; the decision bound generalizes it to many axes.

options.text: The criterion measures how far apart the two distributions of evidence lie, and a decision bound measures that same distance across many axes.
options.why: How far apart the distributions lie is sensitivity, not the criterion. The criterion is where the line between “yes” and “no” is drawn, and a decision bound is that line in many dimensions.

options.text: The criterion and a decision bound are rival accounts, one for detecting a target and one for sorting categories, so neither is a case of the other.
options.why: They are not rivals. Decision-bound theory grew out of signal detection theory, and a decision bound is the criterion’s idea carried into a space with many axes.

items.stem: One bird learns to eat beetles that are both green and longer than a centimeter, and to leave the rest. A second bird learns to sort beetles by a boundary through many features of color and shape that no one has managed to put into words. How do the two birds fit the decision-bound family?

options.text: Both have learned decision bounds; the first bound has a simple verbal form, which makes it a rule, and the second has no simple verbal form.
options.why: Correct. Some decision bounds can be stated in words, such as “large squares belong to category A”, and those are rules. Many decision bounds cannot be stated that way.

options.text: Only the first bird has learned a decision bound, because a decision bound has to be a rule that can be stated in words before it can sort anything.
options.why: A rule is one kind of decision bound, not a requirement for one. Many decision bounds have no simple verbal form, and the second bird’s is one of them.

options.text: Only the second bird has learned a decision bound, because a rule stated in words is a classical definition, and a definition is a rival to a boundary.
options.why: A classical definition is not a rival to a decision bound. In a feature space it is a decision bound made of straight cuts along the feature axes.

options.text: Neither bird has learned a decision bound, because both are sorting by similarity to the beetles they have already eaten and stored.
options.why: Sorting by similarity to stored members is what an exemplar model does. Nothing in either case says the birds stored beetles; each learned a boundary.

items.stem: A library lends rare books only to people who are over 18 and have held a library card for at least a year. Picture every applicant as a point in a space with one axis for age and one for years holding a card. What does that lending rule look like in the space?

options.text: Two straight cuts, one along each axis, with the lending region in the corner where both conditions are met.
options.why: Correct. A classical definition, pictured in a feature space, is a decision bound built from one straight cut per defining feature, with the category where every condition holds.

options.text: One diagonal straight line, tilted so that more years holding a card can make up for an applicant being younger.
options.why: A tilted line is what a single unit adding up weighted evidence would draw. Under a definition the conditions do not trade off; each must be met on its own.

options.text: A curved boundary that wraps around the most typical applicant, so that unusual applicants fall outside the lending region.
options.why: That would make membership graded by closeness to a typical case. A definition makes membership all or none, so its boundary is made of straight cuts.

options.text: A scatter of stored points, one for each past borrower, with a new applicant accepted when closest to an accepted past borrower.
options.why: That is how an exemplar or nearest-neighbor model would sort applicants. A definition stores no members, only a cut for each defining feature.

items.stem: What is a unit’s decision boundary?

options.text: The line through the space of possible inputs that separates the combinations the unit fires to from the combinations it does not.
options.why: Correct. For a single unit the decision boundary is a straight line, with firing on one side and silence on the other.

options.text: The amount of evidence at which the unit’s response changes from “no” to “yes”, marked as one point on a single axis of evidence.
options.why: That is the criterion, a point on one evidence axis. The decision boundary is the set of inputs in the whole input space whose evidence sits at that criterion.

options.text: The distance between the unit’s responses to two categories, measured in units of how much those responses vary from trial to trial.
options.why: That describes sensitivity, measured as d′. The decision boundary is a line through the input space, not a distance between distributions.

options.text: The fall-off in the unit’s response as an input differs more and more from the input on which the unit was originally trained.
options.why: That describes a generalization gradient. The decision boundary is a sharp dividing line in the input space, with firing on one side only.

items.stem: A single unit of the kind in Module 4 fires to some combinations of its inputs and stays silent for the rest. What is the name for the straight line through the space of possible inputs that separates those two sets of combinations?

options.text: Decision boundary.
options.why: Correct. The decision boundary is the line that separates the combinations a unit fires to from the ones it does not.

options.text: Criterion.
options.why: The criterion is the amount of evidence at which a response changes, a point on one axis. The line through the input space is the decision boundary.

options.text: Linear separability.
options.why: Linear separability is a property of two categories, that one straight line can divide them. The line itself is the decision boundary.

options.text: Generalization gradient.
options.why: A generalization gradient is a smooth fall-off in responding with distance from a trained input, not a line separating firing from silence.

items.stem: Which change to a unit turns its decision boundary to a new angle, and which change slides the boundary without turning it?

options.text: Changing the weights turns the line, and changing the threshold or the baseline firing rate slides it.
options.why: Correct. The weights set the line’s angle; the threshold or baseline sets where along that angle the line sits.

options.text: Changing the threshold turns the line, and changing the weights or the baseline firing rate slides it.
options.why: This swaps the two. The weights set the balance among the inputs, which is the angle; the threshold sets how much evidence is needed, which is the position.

options.text: Changing the weights slides the line, and changing the threshold bends it into a curve around the inputs.
options.why: A single unit’s boundary never bends; it stays a straight line whatever its settings. The weights turn it and the threshold slides it.

options.text: Changing the baseline firing rate turns the line, and changing the weights leaves the line where it was.
options.why: The baseline firing rate works like the threshold and slides the line. The weights are what turn it.

items.stem: A unit with two inputs, each weighted 1, computes AND when its threshold is 1.5 and OR when its threshold is 0.5. Why can one unit compute both with no change at all to its weights?

options.text: The two computations’ lines are parallel, so going from one to the other only slides the line, which is what a change of threshold does.
options.why: Correct. AND and OR need lines at the same angle in different places, and the threshold is what slides a line from one place to another.

options.text: The two computations need lines at different angles, and a change of threshold is enough to turn a unit’s line to whatever angle is needed.
options.why: A change of threshold does not turn the line; changing the weights does. AND and OR need no turning, because their lines are parallel.

options.text: The two computations share a prototype at the center of the square, so the threshold only changes how close an input must come to that prototype.
options.why: A single unit stores no prototype. It draws one straight line set by its weights and threshold, and here only the threshold moves.

options.text: The two computations are both rules with a simple verbal form, and any rule with a verbal form can be computed by one unit at some threshold.
options.why: Exclusive or also has a simple verbal form, and no single unit computes it. What matters is that the lines for AND and OR are parallel.

items.stem: Put a single unit into the terms of signal detection theory. What in the unit plays the part of the evidence, and what plays the part of the criterion?

options.text: The unit’s weighted sum is its evidence, and its threshold is its criterion.
options.why: Correct. The weighted sum is how much evidence the inputs supply, and the threshold is the amount of evidence at which the unit’s response changes.

options.text: The unit’s threshold is its evidence, and its weighted sum is its criterion.
options.why: This swaps the two. The threshold stays put while the weighted sum varies from input to input, so the sum is the evidence and the threshold the criterion.

options.text: The unit’s output, firing or silent, is its evidence, and its weights are its criterion.
options.why: Firing or silence is the response that follows the decision, not the evidence for it. The weights shape the evidence; the threshold is the criterion.

options.text: The unit’s weighted sum is its evidence, and the spread of that sum across trials is its criterion.
options.why: The spread of the evidence enters into sensitivity, which is measured in units of spread. The criterion is the threshold, where the line is drawn.

items.stem: A unit has weights of 2 and 1 on its two inputs and a threshold of 4. The input (2, 0) and the input (1, 2) are very different, yet each gives a weighted sum of 4. What does that tell us about where the two inputs lie?

options.text: Both lie on the unit’s decision boundary itself, since the boundary is exactly the set of inputs whose evidence sits at the criterion.
options.why: Correct. Every combination of inputs with the same weighted sum lands on the same point of the evidence axis. Those whose sum equals the threshold make up the boundary.

options.text: Both lie well inside the firing region, far from the boundary, since inputs with equal weighted sums are treated as the most typical members.
options.why: Equal sums put inputs on the same point of the evidence axis, not at the middle of a category. A sum exactly at the threshold puts them on the boundary.

options.text: They lie on opposite sides of the boundary, since they differ on both inputs and so must land in different regions of the input space.
options.why: Inputs can differ on every input and still give the same evidence. What settles the side is the weighted sum, and here the sums are equal.

options.text: Neither can be placed until the unit has been trained on both, since a single unit’s boundary is set by the inputs it has stored.
options.why: A single unit stores no inputs. Its weights and threshold already fix the line, so any input can be placed by computing its weighted sum.

items.stem: A hallway light is wired to two switches, one at each end of the hall. The light is on when exactly one switch is up, and off when both are up or both are down. Could a single unit, with the two switch positions as its inputs, fire exactly when the light is on?

options.text: No; this is exclusive or, and no setting of the unit’s weights and threshold gives one straight line with both “on” cases on one side.
options.why: Correct. The two “on” cases sit at opposite corners of the input space, and so do the two “off” cases. No single straight line divides them correctly.

options.text: Yes; with a low enough threshold the unit fires whenever either switch is up, and that is exactly when the hallway light is meant to be on.
options.why: That is OR, and OR also fires when both switches are up, when the light is off. Exclusive or excludes that case, and no single line does.

options.text: Yes; with large enough weights on the two switches, the unit’s line can be turned until it puts the “on” cases on one side of it.
options.why: Turning a line changes its angle, but no straight line at any angle puts two opposite corners on one side and the other two corners on the other.

options.text: No; a single unit can only ever compute AND, so it cannot fire to any case in which one of the two switches is down.
options.why: A single unit computes OR as well as AND, by sliding its line. What it cannot compute is exclusive or, since no single line separates the cases.

items.stem: Rats in a laboratory learn to press a lever when exactly one of two lights is on, and to leave it alone when both lights or neither light is on. What can we conclude about what is inside the rats?

options.text: Something more complex than a single neural circuit drawing a single straight line through the space of the two lights.
options.why: Correct. The task is exclusive or, which no single line can divide. An animal that learns it has something inside more complex than one circuit drawing one line.

options.text: A single neural circuit whose threshold has been set low enough that it responds whenever either of the two lights is on.
options.why: That circuit computes OR, which also responds when both lights are on. The rats leave the lever alone in that case, so OR is not what they learned.

options.text: A single neural circuit holding one stored prototype for each response, placed at the center of the cases for that response.
options.why: With exclusive or, both responses’ cases average to the same center point. One prototype per response cannot tell them apart.

options.text: Nothing about their circuits at all, since what an animal can learn tells us nothing about the procedure inside it.
options.why: The kind of problem an animal solves does constrain what is inside it. Learning exclusive or rules out one circuit drawing one straight line.

items.stem: A hummingbird drinks only from flowers whose nectar is neither too weak nor too strong, so the acceptable flowers form an island in the middle of its feature space, with unacceptable ones on every side. Which claim about modeling it with a decision-bound model is right?
