options.why: The readings are not divided among units. Each describes the whole network, and all three describe one fact.

items.stem: A network for the fruit has two hidden units, one computing OR and one computing NOT-AND, and an output unit computing AND over them. In a short paragraph, work through what the network does with each of the four combinations of the two smells, and say what the hidden layer has done that makes the last step easy.
items.answer: With neither smell present, the OR unit is silent and the NOT-AND unit fires, so the AND output is silent: no fruit. With smell A alone, or smell B alone, the OR unit fires and so does the NOT-AND unit, so the output fires: ripe fruit. With both smells present, the OR unit fires but the NOT-AND unit is silent, so the output is silent: rotting fruit. The hidden layer has re-represented the input. In the space of hidden-unit activity, the two ripe cases land on the same point, so the output needs only one straight line, AND, to separate them from the other two.
rubric: Gets neither smell right: OR silent, NOT-AND fires, output silent.
Gets either smell alone right: both hidden units fire, output fires.
Gets both smells right: OR fires, NOT-AND silent, output silent.
Says the hidden layer re-represents the input, so that a single unit or a single straight line can do the last step.

items.stem: A network with a hidden layer can compute exclusive or. Why, then, was exclusive or originally a problem for networks?

options.text: Someone had to set the hidden layer’s weights by hand, since there was no general way to train them.
options.why: Correct. The recoding a hidden layer can do was understood. What was missing was a way for training, rather than a person, to produce it.

options.text: No network had yet been built with a layer between its input and its output, so the solution could not be tried.
options.why: Early networks already had a middle layer. The perceptron had one, wired at random and never trained.

options.text: The output unit could not be trained at all, so every answer a network gave had to be fixed in advance by hand.
options.why: Output units could be trained, by a rule like the delta rule. It was the hidden units that had no general training method.

options.text: A hidden layer solves exclusive or only for two inputs, and real problems had too many inputs for it to help.
options.why: Nothing limits a hidden layer to two inputs. The obstacle was setting its weights, which had to be done by hand.

items.stem: What was true of the original perceptron’s middle layer?

options.text: It was wired at random and never trained, and learning happened only at the output.
options.why: Correct. The perceptron already had a layer between input and output. Only the connections to the output were adjusted.

options.text: It did not exist, since the perceptron connected its inputs straight to its output unit.
options.why: A common belief, but the perceptron did have a middle layer. What it lacked was any training of that layer.

options.text: It was trained by passing errors back from the output, though too slowly to be of much use.
options.why: Passing errors back is backpropagation, which came later. The perceptron’s middle layer was never trained at all.

options.text: It was trained by competition, each middle unit moving its weights toward the inputs it won.
options.why: Competition is a third way to set hidden weights. The perceptron’s middle layer was fixed at random.

items.stem: A classic analysis set out what networks without trainable hidden units cannot do. A student concludes from it that a network with a hidden layer cannot compute exclusive or. What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: The analysis concerned hidden units that cannot be trained; a hidden layer with suitably set weights does compute exclusive or.
options.why: Correct. The OR, NOT-AND, and AND network computes exclusive or with weights set by hand. The analysis was about networks without trainable hidden units, and what was missing was a general way to train a hidden layer, not the hidden layer’s power to recode the problem.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it; a hidden layer cannot compute exclusive or until its weights have been trained by passing the error back.
options.why: A hidden layer computes exclusive or as soon as its weights are right, however they were set. The hand-built OR, NOT-AND, and AND network does it with no training at all.

options.text: The analysis concerned only networks with a single input, and so it says nothing about a problem with two inputs, such as exclusive or.
options.why: The analysis was about networks without trainable hidden units, not networks with one input. Its limits bear on exclusive or, but only for networks whose hidden units cannot be trained.

options.text: The analysis concerned hidden units that can be trained; it is a hidden layer wired at random and left untrained that cannot compute exclusive or.
options.why: That reverses the analysis’s scope: it concerned networks without trainable hidden units. And a large layer wired at random is likely to contain some unit that responds to the combination exclusive or needs.

items.stem: An output unit should have fired on a training example, but stayed silent. How does a rule like the delta rule adjust that unit?

options.text: It compares the unit’s output with the correct answer and changes its weights to make the correct output more likely.
options.why: Correct. An output unit has a known correct answer, so its error can be measured and its weights adjusted to reduce it.

options.text: It strengthens whichever of the unit’s connections were most active on that example, whether the unit’s output was right or wrong.
options.why: Strengthening connections by activity alone, without regard to a correct answer, is a Hebbian change. The delta rule uses the error.

options.text: It lets the unit compete with its neighbors and moves only the winner’s weights a little toward the input.
options.why: That is competitive learning, which needs no correct answer. The delta rule compares the output with the correct one.

options.text: It leaves the unit’s weights alone and rewires the connections that feed it at random until it fires.
options.why: Random rewiring is not part of the delta rule. The rule adjusts the weights by comparing the output with the correct answer.

items.stem: A network that sorts spoken vowels gives a wrong answer. The delta rule can adjust the weights into its output units. Why can the same rule not be applied directly to its hidden units?

options.text: The rule needs each unit’s correct output, and no one knows what a hidden unit’s correct output should be.
options.why: Correct. The output has a correct answer to compare against. A hidden unit has none, which is exactly the problem training a hidden layer runs into.

options.text: Hidden units have no adjustable weights of their own, so there is nothing for the rule to change.
options.why: Hidden units do have weights, and what they stand for depends on those weights. The trouble is that there is no correct output to compare them with.

options.text: Hidden units are driven directly by the sounds, so their activity is fixed by the input and cannot be learned.
options.why: Hidden units are driven directly by neither the world nor the response. Their weights can change; the difficulty is knowing in which direction.

options.text: Hidden units fire too rarely for their output to be compared with anything, so their errors cannot be measured.
options.why: How often a hidden unit fires is not the obstacle. Even a unit that fires often has no known correct output to compare against.

items.stem: How does structural credit assignment differ from the credit assignment problem of Module 5?

options.text: Module 5’s problem is in time, which action caused a later outcome; the structural one is in space, which connections deep inside caused an output error.
options.why: Correct. The structural problem is the same question asked about position inside a network rather than about when something happened.

options.text: Module 5’s problem is in space, which connections deep inside caused an output error; the structural one is in time, which earlier action caused a later outcome.
options.why: That reverses them. Module 5’s credit assignment concerns outcomes that arrive later; the structural version concerns connections deep inside a network.

options.text: Module 5’s problem concerns rewards that arrive at once; the structural one concerns punishments that arrive only after a long and variable delay.
options.why: Neither problem is defined by reward versus punishment. One is about time, the other about where inside a network the responsible connections are.

options.text: Module 5’s problem concerns a single unit with no hidden layer; the structural one concerns whole animals choosing among actions.
options.why: That has it backward as well. Choosing among actions over time is Module 5’s problem; connections inside a network are the structural one.

items.stem: What is structural credit assignment?

options.text: Working out which connections inside a network were responsible for an error at its output.
options.why: Correct. It is credit assignment in space rather than in time: when the output is wrong, which connections deep inside were responsible.

options.text: Working out which of several earlier actions was responsible for an outcome that arrived later.
options.why: That is credit assignment in time, the version in Module 5. The structural version asks about connections inside a network.

options.text: Passing each output’s error backward through the network to compute an error for every hidden unit.
options.why: That is backpropagation, one answer to structural credit assignment. The term itself names the problem, not the answer.

options.text: Letting units compete for each input so that only the winner’s connections are credited and changed.
options.why: That is competitive learning, another answer to the problem. Structural credit assignment names the problem those answers address.

items.stem: What is the name for the problem of working out which connections inside a network were responsible for an error at its output?

options.text: Structural credit assignment.
options.why: Correct. It is Module 5’s credit assignment problem posed in space rather than in time.

options.text: Backpropagation.
options.why: Backpropagation is one answer to this problem, passing the error back to the hidden units. The problem itself is structural credit assignment.

options.text: Catastrophic interference.
options.why: Catastrophic interference is a drastic loss of old learning when new learning moves shared weights. It is not the problem of locating an error’s source.

options.text: Competitive learning.
options.why: Competitive learning is another answer to the problem, one that needs no teacher. The problem itself is structural credit assignment.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why a rule like the delta rule can train a network’s output units but not, by itself, its hidden units, and say how backpropagation gets around the difficulty.
items.answer: The delta rule compares a unit’s output with the correct answer and adjusts its weights to make the correct answer more likely. An output unit has a correct answer, so the comparison can be made. A hidden unit does not: no one knows what each hidden unit’s correct output should be. So when the output is wrong, there is the problem of working out which connections deep inside the network were responsible, which is structural credit assignment. Backpropagation answers it by computing each hidden unit’s error from the errors of the units it feeds, passed backward through the same connections the activity passed forward through, so that the delta rule’s kind of update can be applied at every layer.
rubric: Says the delta rule compares a unit’s output with a correct answer.
Says no one knows the correct output for a hidden unit.
Names or describes structural credit assignment: which connections deep inside the network were responsible for the output’s error.
Says backpropagation computes a hidden unit’s error from the errors of the units it feeds, passed backward through the same connections.

items.stem: Which list gives the three broad answers to structural credit assignment?

options.text: Pass the error back to the hidden units; leave the hidden weights fixed at random and train only the output; let the hidden units compete, with no teacher.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation, fixed random wiring with a trained output, and competitive learning differ in what the weight changes depend on and in which weights change.

options.text: Pass the error back to the hidden units; protect the weights that matter most for old learning; mix old examples back into new training.
options.why: The last two are ways engineers slow catastrophic interference. They are not answers to who sets a hidden layer’s weights.

options.text: Apply one feature detector at every position in the input; pool the detections over a small neighborhood; stack several rounds of the two.
options.why: That describes convolution and pooling, an architecture for tolerating shifts in position. It is not a list of ways to set hidden weights.

options.text: Set the hidden weights by hand for each task; copy each input to its own hidden unit; store one hidden unit for every single example the network has seen.
options.why: Setting weights by hand was the original situation the answers replaced, and the other two are fixed designs rather than ways of training a hidden layer.

items.stem: What is backpropagation?

options.text: An extension of the delta rule to networks with hidden layers, computing each hidden unit’s error from the errors of the units it feeds.
options.why: Correct. The errors are passed backward through the same connections the activity passed forward through.

options.text: A way of setting hidden weights that needs no teacher, in which units compete for each input and only the winner moves its weights toward it.
options.why: That is competitive learning. Backpropagation depends on an error measured against a target.

options.text: A way of leaving hidden weights fixed at random, in which only the connections from the hidden layer to the output are trained.
options.why: That is the perceptron’s answer, fixed random wiring with a trained output. Backpropagation changes every weight in the network.

options.text: A way of storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a pattern can reactivate the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, in which activity runs around a circuit’s own connections. Backpropagation passes errors back from outputs to hidden units.

items.stem: What is the name for an extension of the delta rule to networks with hidden layers, in which each hidden unit’s error is computed from the errors of the units it feeds, passed backward through the same connections the activity passed forward through?

options.text: Backpropagation.
options.why: Correct. It is one of the three broad answers to structural credit assignment, and it changes every weight in the network.

options.text: Competitive learning.
options.why: Competitive learning needs no teacher and no error. Only the winning unit moves its weights, toward the input.

options.text: Structural credit assignment.
options.why: Structural credit assignment is the problem backpropagation answers: which connections inside a network were responsible for an error.

options.text: Auto-association.
options.why: Auto-association stores patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells. It passes no errors back from an output.

items.stem: During backpropagation, a hidden unit is completely silent on one training example, although the output unit it feeds has a large error. On that example, what happens to the connection from the silent hidden unit to the output unit?

options.text: It does not change, because each change is proportional to the receiving unit’s error times the sending unit’s activity, which is zero.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation keeps the delta rule’s update: error at the receiving unit times activity of the sending unit. A silent sender contributed nothing, so its connection is not changed on that example.

options.text: It changes the most of any connection in the network on that example, since a silent hidden unit is the likeliest cause of a large error at the output.
options.why: A silent sending unit contributed nothing to the output on that example. Under the delta rule’s update, its connection does not change.

options.text: It changes by the full size of the output’s error, since a connection’s change depends only on the error at the receiving unit.
options.why: The error at the receiving unit is only one factor. It is multiplied by the sending unit’s activity, and here that activity is zero.

options.text: It is rewired at random, since backpropagation replaces the connections of hidden units that fail to respond.
options.why: Backpropagation never rewires anything at random. Random wiring belongs to the perceptron’s middle layer, which is set once and never changed; backpropagation adjusts weights by error times activity.

items.stem: In a network trained by backpropagation, one hidden unit feeds three output units. How is that hidden unit’s error worked out?

options.text: From the errors of the three output units, passed backward through the same connections that carried its activity forward.
options.why: Correct. Only the outputs are compared with a target. A hidden unit’s error is computed from the errors of the units it feeds.

options.text: From a comparison of its own output with a target that a teacher supplies for each hidden unit, just as for the output units.
options.why: No target is supplied for a hidden unit; no one knows what its correct output should be. Its error comes from the units it feeds.

options.text: From how often it wins the competition with the other hidden units, the frequent winners being given the least error.
options.why: Winning a competition is how competitive learning works, and it involves no error at all. Backpropagation passes errors back from the outputs.

options.text: It is never worked out, since in backpropagation only the connections from the hidden units to the outputs change.
options.why: Changing only the connections to the output is fixed random wiring with a trained output. Backpropagation changes every weight, hidden ones included.

items.stem: Two hidden units feed the same output unit through equally strong connections. For the first, a change in its input would change its output a great deal; for the second, a change in its input would barely change its output. In backpropagation, how do their shares of the output’s error compare?

options.text: The first gets the larger share, since each unit’s share is scaled by how much its output would change if its input changed.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation scales each unit’s share of the error by how much its output would change if its input changed. With equal connections to the same output unit, the unit whose output barely responds gets the smaller share.

options.text: They get equal shares, since the first and second units feed the same output unit through connections of exactly equal strength.
options.why: Equal connections would give equal shares if nothing else mattered. Backpropagation also scales each unit’s share by how much its output would change with its input.

options.text: The second gets the larger share, since a unit whose output would barely change with its input most needs adjustment.
options.why: That runs the scaling the wrong way. A unit whose output barely changes with its input is given a smaller share, not a larger one.

options.text: Neither gets a share, since backpropagation changes only the weights of the output unit that made the error.
options.why: Backpropagation passes the error back to hidden units and changes every weight in the network. Changing only output weights is the perceptron’s answer.

items.stem: How does backpropagation relate to the gradient descent of Module 5?

options.text: It is the same gradient descent, run through every layer of the network at once, hidden layers included.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation extends the delta rule, and so gradient descent, from the output to every layer at once.

options.text: It runs gradient descent at the output layer only, and leaves every hidden layer as it was wired.
options.why: Training only the output is the perceptron’s answer. Backpropagation runs gradient descent through every layer.

options.text: It replaces gradient descent with a search among random wirings, keeping whichever one works best.
options.why: Nothing in backpropagation is a random search. It is gradient descent itself, extended to the hidden layers.

options.text: It runs gradient descent on the hidden layers only, since the output layer is already trained by the delta rule.
options.why: Backpropagation includes the output layer. It is the delta rule extended through every layer at once, output and hidden layers alike.

items.stem: An engineer wants a network to learn which combinations of sensor readings signal that a bridge is unsafe, without listing those combinations in advance. If the network is trained by backpropagation, what is the method’s strength, and what does it require?

options.text: Training finds the combinations the task needs, but every output needs a target to compare against.
options.why: Correct. That is backpropagation’s strength and its cost: it finds the combinations the task needs, and every output needs a target.

options.text: Training finds clusters of readings that overlap, with no target, but they may not be the clusters that matter for safety.
options.why: That is the strength and limit of competitive learning, which needs no teacher and finds overlap rather than what the task needs.

options.text: No training of the hidden layer is needed, but it takes a great many units and no needed combination is guaranteed.
options.why: That describes fixed random wiring with a trained output. Backpropagation trains the hidden layer too.

options.text: Training finds the combinations the task needs, and its outputs need no target, since the readings alone are enough.
options.why: Backpropagation does find the needed combinations, but not from readings alone. Every output needs a target to compare against, here whether the bridge was unsafe.

items.stem: A network is given hours of recorded birdsong, with the task of predicting each next note. No one labels anything. Can backpropagation train this network, and if so, where do the targets come from?

options.text: Yes; the target for each prediction is the next note itself, as in the prediction learning of Module 5.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation needs a target for every output, but the target need not come from a teacher. The world’s next input supplies it.

options.text: No; backpropagation needs a teacher to label every example, so unlabeled recordings cannot supply any targets.
options.why: Every output needs a target, but a teacher is only one source. In prediction learning, the next input is the target.

options.text: Yes; the network’s output units compete for each note, and the winner’s response serves as the target for the rest.
options.why: Competition sets weights with no target at all, and it is a different answer. In prediction learning, the target is the next note.

options.text: No; without labels only the connections to the output can be trained, as in the perceptron’s random middle layer.
options.why: The perceptron trains only its output connections by design, not for lack of labels. Prediction supplies targets for backpropagation.

items.stem: Networks were trained on nothing but a stream of words, with the task of predicting the next word. Nothing in the input marked which words were nouns or verbs. What did their hidden layers come to do?

options.text: Group the words into nouns and verbs, and the nouns into animals, people, and inanimate objects.
options.why: Correct. Predicting the next word was enough for the hidden layers to find these groupings, although no input said which words were which.

options.text: Give each word a hidden unit of its own, with no grouping, since nothing in the input marked nouns or verbs.
options.why: The hidden layers did group the words, although nothing in the input marked them. Predicting the next word was enough.

options.text: Group the words by length and spelling, since the letters were the only thing a stream of words contained.
options.why: The groupings followed what the words were, nouns and verbs, animals and people, not how they were spelled.

options.text: Group the words by how often each one appeared, with the common words in one cluster and the rare ones in another.
options.why: The groupings these networks came to show were by kind of word, nouns and verbs, and nouns by what they named, not by how often each word appeared.

items.stem: After learning how backpropagation works, a student writes, “So this is how the cortex learns”. How does the chapter’s account of backpropagation bear on that claim?

options.text: It describes an algorithm; whether a brain could pass errors back in this way is a separate question.
options.why: Correct. The account of backpropagation is about networks. Whether brains do anything like it is a separate question, and the account settles it neither way.

options.text: It confirms the claim, since backpropagation finds the combinations a task needs, and brains must find them too.
options.why: That backpropagation works well in networks says nothing on its own about whether brains use it. That is a separate question.

options.text: It refutes the claim, since a brain has no teacher and so no source of targets for its outputs.
options.why: A target need not come from a teacher; in prediction learning it is the next input. The account does not rule brains out.

options.text: It confirms the claim for the neocortex alone, since the older cortex learns with fixed random wiring instead.
options.why: Nothing in the account of backpropagation assigns it to any part of the brain. Whether a brain could pass errors back is left as a separate question.

items.stem: An engineer builds a network whose 5,000 middle units each receive a random handful of its 20 inputs. Those connections are never changed; only the connections from the middle units to the output are trained. Which answer to who sets the hidden weights is this?

options.text: Nothing sets them: the middle layer stays as it was first wired, and only the output connections are trained.
options.why: Correct. That is the original perceptron’s answer, a large middle layer wired at random and never trained.

options.text: Backpropagation: the output’s error is passed back through the connections, so the middle units’ weights are trained too.
options.why: Backpropagation would change every weight, including those into the middle units. Here they never change.

options.text: Competitive learning: the middle units compete for each input, and each winner moves a little toward it.
options.why: In competitive learning the winner’s weights change. Here the middle layer’s weights never change at all.

options.text: Hand-setting: the engineer chose each middle unit’s handful of inputs to suit the task in advance.
options.why: The middle units’ inputs were chosen at random, not to suit the task. No one arranged which combinations they respond to.

items.stem: In a large middle layer wired at random and never trained, why is some unit likely to respond to “smell A without smell B”, though no one arranged it?

options.text: With many more middle units than inputs, each combining a random handful of inputs, such a combination is likely to turn up by chance.
options.why: Correct. No unit is built for that combination. With enough units each sampling the inputs at random, some unit is likely to land on it.

options.text: Each middle unit is trained to respond to one useful combination of inputs, and “smell A without smell B” is among the combinations trained.
options.why: The middle layer is never trained. Useful combinations turn up by chance among many random ones.

options.text: The middle units compete with one another for each input, and the winner for that input comes to respond to it over many trials.
options.why: Competition is a different answer, and it changes weights. A random middle layer never changes, yet the combination is likely there.

options.text: The inputs already include a receptor that responds to “smell A without smell B”, and the random middle layer is likely to pass it along.
options.why: No receptor responds to that combination; it has to be computed. With many random middle units, one is likely to compute it.

items.stem: What is dimensionality expansion?

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units, which makes it likelier that one straight boundary can separate the cases that matter.
options.why: Correct. A straight boundary can separate far more sets of points in a space with many dimensions than in a space with few.

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart more easily than it could tell the original inputs apart.
options.why: That is pattern separation, which is about overlap between inputs. Dimensionality expansion is about the number of units an input is spread across.

options.text: Activity in which only a small proportion of the units are strongly active for any one input, whatever the number of units.
options.why: That is sparse coding, which works well alongside expansion. Dimensionality expansion is the spreading itself, onto many more units.

options.text: Combining the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood, so that a small shift in the input no longer changes the result.
options.why: That is pooling, which builds in tolerance to small shifts. Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units.

items.stem: What is the name for spreading an input across many more units than it started with, which makes it more likely that a single straight boundary can separate the cases that matter?

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Correct. It is what a large random middle layer does, and it works best when the code is sparse.

options.text: Pattern separation.
options.why: Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, so a later stage can tell them apart. It is defined by reduced overlap, not by spreading onto more units.

options.text: Sparse coding.
options.why: Sparse coding means only a small proportion of units are strongly active at once. Expansion works best with it, but the spreading itself is dimensionality expansion.

options.text: Linear separability.
options.why: Linear separability is the property of categories that one straight boundary can divide. Dimensionality expansion is the spreading that makes it more likely.

items.stem: A robot has two touch sensors, and the cases it must sort are arranged like exclusive or, so no straight line divides them. Its engineer spreads the two readings across 500 randomly wired units and trains a single output unit on those. Why might one straight boundary now succeed?

options.text: A straight boundary can separate far more sets of points in a space with many dimensions than in a space with few.
options.why: Correct. Spread across 500 random units, the cases sit in a space of many dimensions, where a straight boundary has far more ways to divide them. Some unit is likely, though not certain, to respond to a combination the sorting needs.

options.text: In a space with many dimensions the output’s boundary can bend, which a straight boundary in two dimensions cannot do.
options.why: The output is a single unit, and its boundary is straight in any number of dimensions. What changes is how many divisions a straight boundary can make.

options.text: Spreading the readings across many units removes the noise from each reading, so the cases stop overlapping.
options.why: The exclusive-or cases do not overlap; they are arranged so that no line divides them. Expansion helps by adding dimensions, not by removing noise.

options.text: Spreading the readings across many units gives each category its own prototype, so the nearest one can be chosen.
options.why: In exclusive or the two categories share a prototype, the center of the square, and expansion does not work by storing prototypes. It adds dimensions.

items.stem: An engineer’s random expansion layer has thousands of units, but nearly all of them are active for every input. What change does the chapter’s account suggest would make the expansion work better?

options.text: Arrange for only a few units to be active for any one input, so that the code is sparse.
options.why: Correct. Dimensionality expansion works best with sparse coding, in which only a few units are active for any one input.

options.text: Arrange for every unit to be active for every input, so that no useful combination is ever missed.
options.why: Nearly every unit is active already. Expansion works best when only a few units are active for each input.

options.text: Cut the layer down to fewer units than there are inputs, so that each unit carries more of the input.
options.why: That undoes the expansion itself. The layer needs many more units than inputs, with few of them active at once.

options.text: Train the layer by backpropagation, so that every unit becomes active for the inputs that matter most.
options.why: Training the layer changes the answer from random wiring to error-driven learning, and still leaves every unit active. What helps here is sparseness.

items.stem: What is sparse coding?

options.text: Activity in which only a small proportion of neurons are strongly active at any one moment.
options.why: Correct. In an expansion layer, it means only a few units are active for any one input. It is a consequence of the energy budget, not an inefficiency.

options.text: A code in which each thing has its own unit, so that which unit is active is itself the information.
options.why: That is a localist representation. A localist code has one unit per thing; sparse coding is about what proportion of neurons is active at a time.

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units than it started with, so that a straight boundary separates more cases.
options.why: That is dimensionality expansion, which works best with sparse coding. Sparse coding is about how few units are active.

options.text: A code with very few units in total, so that each unit has to take part in representing many things.
options.why: Few units each taking part in many things is a feature of distributed codes. Sparse coding concerns the share of units active at once, not their number.

items.stem: What is the name for activity in which only a small proportion of neurons are strongly active at any one moment, a consequence of the energy budget rather than an inefficiency?

options.text: Sparse coding.
options.why: Correct. Dimensionality expansion works best with sparse coding, in which only a few units are active for any one input.

options.text: Localist representation.
options.why: A localist representation gives each thing its own unit. It is defined by one unit per thing, not by the proportion of neurons active.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units. It works best with sparse activity, but it is not the activity itself.

options.text: Pattern separation.
options.why: Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike. It is defined by reduced overlap, not by how few neurons are active.

items.stem: A company wants a device that sorts scent mixtures by combinations of chemicals that no single sensor reports. Its engineers propose a very large middle layer wired at random and never trained, with only the connections to the output trained. In a short paragraph, explain why this design might work, what kind of activity in the middle layer would help, and what its weaknesses are.
items.answer: With many more middle units than sensors, each combining a random handful of sensor readings, some units are likely to respond to the combinations that matter without anyone arranging it. Spreading the input across many more units is dimensionality expansion, and a straight boundary can separate far more sets of points in a space with many dimensions than in a space with few, so a single trained output layer may be enough. The expansion works best if the code is sparse, with only a few middle units active for any one input. The weaknesses are that it takes a great many units, and nothing guarantees that the combinations the task needs will be among the random ones.
rubric: Says random units each combine a handful of inputs, so useful combinations are likely to turn up by chance.
Names dimensionality expansion, or describes spreading the input across many more units.
Says a straight boundary can separate more sets of points in a space of many dimensions than of few.
Says the expansion works best with sparse activity, only a few units active for any one input.
Names a weakness: it needs a great many units, or there is no guarantee the needed combinations appear.

items.stem: What is the cost of backpropagation, and what is the cost of fixed random wiring with a trained output?

options.text: Backpropagation needs a target for every output; random wiring needs a great many units, with no guarantee the needed combinations appear.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation finds the needed combinations but must have targets. Random wiring needs no training of the hidden layer but may not contain what the task needs.

options.text: Backpropagation needs a great many units, with no guarantee the needed combinations appear; random wiring needs a target for every one of its outputs.
options.why: That swaps the two costs. Random wiring is the one that needs many units and offers no guarantee; backpropagation is the one that needs targets.

options.text: Backpropagation finds only how the inputs overlap, not what the task needs; random wiring needs a teacher for every hidden unit.
options.why: Finding overlap rather than what the task needs is the limit of competitive learning. Random wiring never trains its hidden units at all.

options.text: Backpropagation trains only the connections to the output; random wiring changes every weight in the network on each example.
options.why: That reverses which weights change. Backpropagation changes every weight; random wiring changes only the connections to the output.

items.stem: Each answer to who sets a hidden layer’s weights comes with cases that fit it. Which pairing of answer and case is right?

options.text: Fixed random wiring with a trained output, and the arrangement in the fruit fly’s brain.
options.why: Correct. The fly’s smell inputs are spread across many more cells by connections that look random, with learning downstream, an arrangement of the perceptron’s kind.

options.text: Competitive learning, and the next-word networks whose hidden layers grouped nouns and verbs.
options.why: The next-word networks were trained by error, with the next word as the target. Competition is paired with topographic maps.

options.text: Backpropagation, and the topographic maps that arise from experience alone.
options.why: Topographic maps arise when a competitive winner’s neighbors also move. Backpropagation is paired with the next-word and digit-reading networks.

options.text: Fixed random wiring with a trained output, and the network that read digits from zip codes.
options.why: The digit-reading network trained every weight by backpropagation. Random wiring is paired with the perceptron and the fly’s brain.

items.stem: What is competitive learning?

options.text: Learning in which units receiving the same input inhibit one another until one wins, and only the winner moves its weights toward the input.
options.why: Correct. It needs no teacher, and the winner’s step toward the input is a Hebbian one, kept in check because only the winner learns.

options.text: Learning in which each hidden unit’s error is computed from the errors of the units it feeds, passed backward through those very same connections.
options.why: That is backpropagation, which needs a target for every output. Competitive learning needs no teacher.

options.text: Learning in which a large middle layer is wired at random, and only the connections from that layer to the output are adjusted.
options.why: That is fixed random wiring with a trained output, the perceptron’s answer. In competitive learning, the winning unit’s own weights change.

options.text: Learning in which the connections among a circuit’s active cells are strengthened, so that part of a pattern can reactivate the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, used for pattern completion. Competitive learning moves only a winning unit’s weights toward the input.

items.stem: What is the name for a way of setting weights, needing no teacher, in which units receiving the same input inhibit one another until one wins, and only the winner moves its weights toward the input?

options.text: Competitive learning.
options.why: Correct. Over many inputs, each unit comes to sit at the center of a cluster of similar inputs.

options.text: Backpropagation.
options.why: Backpropagation needs a target for every output and changes every weight. The rule described needs no teacher and moves only the winner.

options.text: Auto-association.
options.why: Auto-association stores patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells. It has no competition and no single winner.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units, usually with fixed random wiring. Nothing competes and nothing moves toward the input.

items.stem: Several units all receive the same input from a microphone. For each sound, the units inhibit one another until one is left active, and then a Hebbian step moves weights a little toward the sound. What keeps that Hebbian step in check?

options.text: Only the winning unit moves its weights, and only by a small step toward each input; the other units do not change.
options.why: Correct. A Hebbian step strengthens what is active together. Limiting it to the single winner keeps it in check.

options.text: An error measured against a target pulls each unit’s weights back whenever they move too far.
options.why: No target or error is involved; competitive learning needs no teacher. The check comes from only the winner learning.

options.text: The weights into these units are fixed at random, so that only the connections to an output can change.
options.why: Fixed random weights are a different answer. Here the winner’s own weights do change, and only the winner’s.

options.text: Every unit moves toward each sound, but by an amount scaled by how much that unit’s output would change with its input.
options.why: Scaling by how much a unit’s output would change is part of backpropagation. In competition, the losing units do not move at all.

items.stem: A competitive network is shown thousands of leaf outlines, with no labels. After long training, where has each unit’s set of weights come to sit?

options.text: At the center of a cluster of similar leaf outlines, the ones that unit most often won.
options.why: Correct. Each win moves the winner a little toward the input, so over many inputs it settles at the center of a cluster of similar ones.

options.text: At the boundary between two clusters of outlines, where its response best separates the two kinds.
options.why: Competition moves winners toward inputs, not toward boundaries. Each unit ends up at a cluster’s center.

options.text: At a random position, since nothing outside the network says what any leaf outline is.
options.why: No outside signal is needed. The inputs and the competition among units are enough to move each unit to a cluster’s center.

options.text: At the average of every outline seen, the same point for every unit in the network.
options.why: If every unit sat at the same point, one would win every time. Competition spreads the units across clusters of similar outlines.

items.stem: What is a topographic map?

options.text: An arrangement in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells, so the tissue’s layout mirrors what it represents.
options.why: Correct. Competitive learning can produce one from experience alone, when the winner’s neighbors also move toward each input.

options.text: A space with one axis for each feature of an input, in which each input is a single point and inputs that are alike land close together in it.
options.why: That is a feature space, a description of inputs. A topographic map is a layout of cells in tissue.

options.text: The region of the sensory world where a stimulus changes one cell’s activity, together with the kind of stimulus that changes it.
options.why: That is a receptive field, which belongs to a single cell. A topographic map is how many cells are laid out relative to one another.

options.text: A code in which each thing is a pattern of activity across many units, and each unit takes part in representing many things.
options.why: That is a distributed representation, which says nothing about where cells sit. A topographic map concerns the layout of the cells.

items.stem: What is the name for an arrangement in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells, so that the layout of the tissue mirrors the layout of what it represents?

options.text: A topographic map.
options.why: Correct. Competitive learning produces one when the winner’s neighbors also move a little toward each input.

options.text: A feature space.
options.why: A feature space has one axis per feature and one point per input. It lays out inputs, not cells in tissue.

options.text: A receptive field.
options.why: A receptive field is the region where a stimulus changes one cell’s activity. It belongs to a single cell, not to the layout of many.

options.text: A distributed representation.
options.why: A distributed representation spreads each thing across many units. It says nothing about whether neighboring cells handle neighboring points.

items.stem: A competitive network receives input from a row of touch sensors along a robot’s finger, and pressing nearby points activates overlapping sets of sensors. During training, the winning unit’s neighbors in the network also move their weights a little toward each input. What arrangement results?

options.text: Neighboring units come to respond to nearby points on the finger, a topographic map arising from experience alone.
options.why: Correct. Because the winner’s neighbors move too, neighboring units end up responding to similar inputs, and the layout of the units mirrors the finger.

options.text: Each unit comes to respond to the whole finger about equally, since every unit moves toward every input.
options.why: Only the winner and its neighbors move on each input, not every unit. The result is units tuned to different parts of the finger, laid out in order.

options.text: Neighboring units come to respond to distant points on the finger, so that units for nearby points are spread as far apart as possible.
options.why: Moving neighbors together makes neighboring units respond to similar inputs, not dissimilar ones. The result mirrors the finger’s layout.

options.text: No orderly arrangement appears, since a topographic map has to be built in before training and cannot come from experience.
options.why: In this arrangement a topographic map arises from experience alone, once the winner’s neighbors also move toward each input.

items.stem: A competitive network is trained on recordings of calls from two frog species, one toxic to a predator and one safe to eat. The recordings differ most in loudness, which depends on how far away each frog was, not on its species. What is the risk?

options.text: The units may form clusters by loudness, since competition finds how inputs overlap, which is not always what the animal needs.
options.why: Correct. Competition finds the structure in how inputs overlap. Here that structure is distance, and the species, which matters, may go unrepresented.

options.text: The units cannot form any clusters, by loudness or by species, since competitive learning needs a label telling it which species each call came from.
options.why: Competitive learning needs no teacher or label. It will form clusters; the risk is that they follow loudness rather than species.

options.text: The units are certain to form clusters by species, since competition always finds the structure that matters for survival.
options.why: Competition finds how inputs overlap, whatever matters. When loudness dominates the overlap, the clusters may follow loudness.

options.text: The units will each respond to every call equally, since only the winner learns and so no unit wins often enough.
options.why: Only the winner learns, but over many inputs each unit wins for some calls and settles at a cluster’s center. The risk is which clusters form.

items.stem: On a single training example, which weights change under each of the three answers to who sets a hidden layer’s weights?

options.text: Error-driven learning changes every weight; random wiring changes only the hidden-to-output connections; competition changes only the winner’s.
options.why: Correct. Backpropagation reaches every layer, the perceptron’s answer touches only the output connections, and competition moves only the winning unit.

options.text: Error-driven learning changes only the hidden-to-output connections; random wiring changes every weight; competition changes only the winner’s.
options.why: That swaps the first two. Error-driven learning passes the error back through every layer, and random wiring never changes its middle layer.

options.text: Error-driven learning changes every weight; random wiring changes only the winner’s; competition changes only the hidden-to-output connections.
options.why: That swaps the last two. Random wiring trains only the output connections, and competition moves only the winning unit’s weights.

options.text: Error-driven learning changes only the winner’s weights; random wiring changes every weight; competition changes only the hidden-to-output connections.
options.why: None of the three is matched correctly. Error-driven learning changes every weight, random wiring only the output connections, and competition only the winner.

items.stem: Two networks receive the same inputs. One trains its hidden layer by backpropagation on a task; the other trains its hidden layer by competitive learning. Why might their hidden layers come to represent different things?

options.text: Backpropagation finds whatever combinations reduce the task’s error; competition finds clusters of overlapping inputs, whether or not they matter.
options.why: Correct. The two rules respond to different information: one to an error on the task, the other to nothing outside the network.

options.text: Backpropagation finds clusters of overlapping inputs, whether or not they matter to it; competition finds whatever combinations reduce the task’s error.
options.why: That swaps the two. Competition depends on nothing outside the network, so it cannot be steered by the task’s error.

options.text: Backpropagation leaves its hidden layer as it was randomly wired at the start; competition moves every hidden unit a little toward every input.
options.why: Backpropagation trains every weight, and competition moves only the winner. Neither half describes these networks.

options.text: They would not differ, since any two networks trained on the same inputs must come to represent the same combinations of those same inputs.
options.why: What a hidden layer comes to represent depends on the learning rule as well as the inputs. Different rules respond to different information.

items.stem: There are three broad answers to who sets a hidden layer’s weights. In a short paragraph, name each one, say which weights it changes, and give one cost or limit of each.
items.answer: The first is backpropagation, which passes the error at the output back to the hidden units and changes every weight in the network. It finds the combinations the task needs, but every output needs a target. The second is fixed random wiring with a trained output, as in the original perceptron: the middle layer is wired at random and never trained, and only the connections to the output change. It needs a great many units, and there is no guarantee the combinations the task needs will be among them. The third is competitive learning, in which units inhibit one another until one wins and only the winner moves its weights toward the input. It needs no teacher, but it finds how inputs overlap, which is not always the structure the animal needs.
rubric: Describes backpropagation as passing the error back and changing every weight, with a target needed for every output.
Describes fixed random wiring as training only the connections to the output.
Gives a cost of random wiring: a great many units, or no guarantee the needed combinations appear.
Describes competitive learning as changing only the winner’s weights, with no teacher.
Gives the limit of competition: it finds overlap, not necessarily what the task or the animal needs.

items.stem: What is a localist representation?

options.text: A code in which each thing has its own unit, so that which unit is active is itself the information.
options.why: Correct. It takes Module 3’s point all the way: part of a spike’s meaning lies in which cell fired it.

options.text: A code in which each thing is a pattern of activity across many units, each unit taking part in many things.
options.why: That is a distributed representation, the other broad possibility for what a hidden unit stands for.

options.text: A code in which only a small proportion of the units are strongly active at any one moment.
options.why: That is sparse coding. A localist code is defined by each thing having its own unit, not by how many units are active.

options.text: An arrangement in which neighboring units handle neighboring points in the world, mirroring its layout.
options.why: That is a topographic map, which concerns where cells sit. A localist code concerns whether each thing has a unit of its own.

items.stem: What is the name for a code in which each thing has its own unit, so that which unit is active is itself the information?

options.text: Localist representation.
options.why: Correct. Localist codes are easy to read and keep things cleanly apart.

options.text: Distributed representation.
options.why: In a distributed representation each thing is a pattern across many units, so no single unit identifies it.

options.text: Sparse coding.
options.why: Sparse coding is about what proportion of units is active at once. A code with one unit per thing is a localist representation.

options.text: Topographic map.
options.why: A topographic map is a layout in which neighboring cells handle neighboring points in the world. It says nothing about one unit per thing.

items.stem: What is a distributed representation?

options.text: A code in which each thing is a pattern of activity across many units, and each unit takes part in representing many things.
options.why: Correct. Because similar things share active units, a distributed code makes them look similar without extra work.

options.text: A code in which each thing has its own unit, so that which one unit is active is itself all of the information carried.
options.why: That is a localist representation. In a distributed code, no single unit stands for a thing.

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units than it started with, so that a straight boundary separates more cases.
options.why: That is dimensionality expansion, which is about the number of units. A distributed code is about how each thing is represented across them.

options.text: A layer of units between a network’s input and its output, whose units come to stand for various combinations of all the inputs.
options.why: That is a hidden layer. A hidden layer’s units may carry a distributed code, but the code and the layer are different things.

items.stem: What is the name for a code in which each thing is a pattern of activity across many units, and each unit takes part in representing many things?

options.text: Distributed representation.
options.why: Correct. Such codes degrade gracefully and pack many patterns into few units.

options.text: Localist representation.
options.why: A localist representation gives each thing its own unit, the opposite arrangement.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units. It names the spreading, not a code in which each unit serves many things.

options.text: Sparse coding.
options.why: Sparse coding is about how few units are active at once. The code described is defined by each unit serving many things.

items.stem: Every spike is the same size, so part of a spike’s meaning lies in which cell fired it. How does a localist code relate to that point?

options.text: It takes the point all the way: each thing has its own unit, so which unit is active becomes the whole of the information.
options.why: Correct. In a localist code, knowing which unit fired is knowing what is represented.

options.text: It sets the point aside: since spikes are all one size, a localist code carries its information in how many spikes there are.
options.why: Counting spikes is not what makes a code localist. A localist code rests on which unit is active.

options.text: It reverses the point: a localist code spreads each thing’s meaning across many cells, so no one cell matters.
options.why: Spreading each thing across many cells is a distributed code. A localist code puts each thing in its own unit.

options.text: It depends on the point being false: a localist code needs spikes of different sizes to tell its things apart.
options.why: A localist code works because the identity of the cell carries the meaning. It needs no difference in spike size.

items.stem: In one network, a sparrow and a finch are represented by patterns that share many active units, while a sparrow and a trout share few. What is learned about sparrows carries over to finches far more than to trout, with no extra mechanism added. Which property of the code explains this?

options.text: In a distributed code similar things share active units, so they look similar without any extra work.
options.why: Correct. That is one strength of distributed codes: similarity comes for free from the overlap between patterns.

options.text: In a localist code each animal has its own unit, so what is learned about one unit spreads to its neighbors.
options.why: In a localist code each animal’s unit is separate, which keeps things cleanly apart. Overlapping patterns are what carry similarity.

options.text: In a sparse code few units are active, so the sparrow and the trout share too few for learning to reach the trout.
options.why: Sparseness is about how many units are active, and it would not explain the carrying over to finches. Shared active units do.

options.text: In a topographic map the sparrow and finch units sit side by side, so learning about one spills onto the other with no extra work.
options.why: Nothing in the description places units side by side; the animals are patterns across units. Shared active units carry the similarity.

items.stem: Two networks each represent 200 words with 200 units. In the first, each word has a unit of its own; in the second, each word is a pattern across many of the 200 units. Ten units are destroyed in each network. What is the likeliest result?

options.text: The first loses about ten words outright; the second still represents every word, each a little less clearly.
options.why: Correct. In a localist code each word is its own unit, so losing a unit loses the word it stood for. A distributed code degrades gracefully: each word is spread across many units, and losing ten of 200 blurs every word a little rather than removing any.

options.text: The first still represents every word, each a little less clearly; the second loses about ten words outright.
options.why: That reverses the two codes. Losing a unit in a localist code loses its word; a distributed code degrades gracefully.

options.text: Both lose about ten words outright, since ten of the 200 units are gone from each network and each unit held one word.
options.why: Only in the first network does each unit hold one word. In the second, every unit takes part in many words.

options.text: Neither loses anything, since the remaining units in each network take over the work of the ones destroyed.
options.why: Nothing in either code moves the work of lost units to others. The second network degrades a little; the first loses words.

items.stem: Localist and distributed codes each have their own strengths. Which strength belongs to localist codes?

options.text: They are easy to read, and they keep things cleanly apart.
options.why: Correct. With one unit per thing, which unit is active can be read off directly, and different things never share units.

options.text: They make similar things look similar without any extra work.
options.why: That is a strength of distributed codes, where similar things share active units.

options.text: They degrade gracefully when some of their units are lost.
options.why: That is a strength of distributed codes, where each thing is spread across many units.

options.text: They pack many patterns into comparatively few units.
options.why: That is a strength of distributed codes. A localist code needs a unit for every thing.

items.stem: A student argues, “Distributed codes degrade gracefully and pack many patterns into few units, so brains must use distributed codes”. What does the chapter conclude about which code brains use?

options.text: Which kind brains use is still argued, whatever the strengths of each kind, and a mixture of the two is a serious option.
options.why: Correct. Each kind has strengths, and listing them does not settle what brains do. A mixture of the two is taken seriously.

options.text: Brains use distributed codes, as the student says, since graceful degradation is exactly what lost neurons would require.
options.why: The strengths are real, but strengths alone do not settle what brains do. Which code brains use is still argued.

options.text: Brains use localist codes, since a spike’s meaning lies partly in which cell fired it, and localist codes take that all the way.
options.why: That point about spikes motivates localist codes but does not settle the question. Which code brains use is still argued.

options.text: Brains use neither kind, since hidden units exist only in artificial networks and have no counterpart among neurons.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter rules brains out of either code. Which they use, or whether they use a mixture of the two, is still argued.

items.stem: A designer is choosing how a robot’s network should represent the hundreds of faces it has to recognize: one unit per face, or each face as a pattern across many units. In a few sentences, name these two broad possibilities for what a single unit stands for, give one strength of each, and say what is known about which kind brains use.
items.answer: One unit per face is a localist representation, in which which unit is active is itself the information. A pattern across many units is a distributed representation, in which each face is a pattern of activity and each unit takes part in many faces. A localist code is easy to read and keeps the faces cleanly apart. A distributed code makes similar faces look similar without extra work, degrades gracefully if units are lost, and packs many faces into few units. Which kind brains use is still argued, and a mixture of the two is a serious option.
rubric: Names one unit per face as a localist representation and the pattern across units as a distributed representation.
Gives a strength of localist codes: easy to read, or keeps things cleanly apart.
Gives a strength of distributed codes: similarity without extra work, graceful degradation, or many patterns in few units.
Says which code brains use is still argued, with a mixture a serious option, without declaring a winner.

items.stem: A hand-built hidden layer using the threshold function (a hard step) is handed to Pass the error back, and the fish learns for 1,000 encounters, with the hidden units’ sliders on the Network tab and the lines under The arithmetic on the Learning tab in view. What did the scene show?

options.text: No hidden slider moved at all, and the hidden unit’s printed slope, f′(net), and its printed Φ both read 0.000 on the encounters watched.
options.why: Correct. In backpropagation each unit’s share of the error is scaled by how much its output would change if its input changed, and a hard step’s output does not change with a small change of input. A slope of zero made the hidden unit’s Φ zero, so nothing in the hidden layer moved. Switched to the sigmoid, the hidden unit’s Φ was no longer zero and the hidden sliders began to move.

options.text: The hidden sliders crept slowly, since the slope read 0.000 but the hidden unit’s Φ still carried a small share of the output’s error.
options.why: The slope did read 0.000, but a hidden unit’s Φ is its slope times its weight to the output times the output’s Φ, so the hidden Φ read 0.000 too. Nothing reached the hidden weights.

options.text: The hidden sliders swung widely, since the step’s slope read large on every encounter, so each hidden unit took a large share of the error.
options.why: A step jumps at one point and is flat everywhere else, so its slope read 0.000, not large. With a zero slope the hidden unit’s share of the error was zero, and the sliders stayed still.

options.text: The hidden sliders moved only on the encounters the fish got wrong, when the output’s error was large enough to be passed back to them.
options.why: A large output error does not help when the slope is zero: the hidden unit’s Φ is the slope times the weight times the output’s Φ, and it read 0.000. No hidden slider moved.

items.stem: With Pass the error back and the sigmoid, the fruit is run with a single hidden unit, over three seeds. How often did the test set reach 5 percent wrong, and why?

options.text: Never, because one hidden unit draws one straight line, and no one straight line puts both ripe corners on one side.
options.why: Correct. A single hidden unit hands the output one line’s worth of information, so the network can do no better than one line. Separating the ripe corners from the other two takes at least two hidden units, each drawing its own line.

options.text: In every seed, because any hidden layer at all lets passing the error back find the combination the fruit needs.
options.why: A hidden layer helps only if it has enough units for the combination. With one unit the network is limited to a single line, which cannot hold both ripe corners.

options.text: In about two seeds in three, because whether a run succeeds depends on where its random starting weights happen to fall.
options.why: That describes two hidden units, which sometimes stick and sometimes succeed. With one, no starting point could succeed.

options.text: Never, because passing the error back cannot train a hidden layer of any size on a problem of the exclusive-or kind.
options.why: With two or more hidden units, passing the error back did solve the fruit. The trouble here was the single unit, not the rule.

items.stem: Over several seeds each, how did two hidden units and four hidden units compare on the fruit, with Pass the error back and the sigmoid?

options.text: Four reached 5 percent wrong in every seed; two reached it in some seeds, and in others settled short of it and stayed there.
options.why: Correct. Two units stuck in about one seed in three, settled where the rule could not improve. Four solved it every time: with more hidden units than the problem strictly needs, a run is far less likely to settle somewhere it cannot improve from.

options.text: Two reached 5 percent wrong in every seed; four did worse, since extra hidden units fit the noise and leave the test set further from the goal.
options.why: Overfitting is a worry when training examples are few and repeat, but the fruit stream brings new fruit at every encounter. Four units solved it every time.

options.text: Both reached 5 percent wrong in every seed, since two hidden units are all the fruit needs and any units beyond two sit idle.
options.why: Two units are enough in principle, as the hand-built network shows, but a rule starting from random weights does not always find that setting.

options.text: Neither reached 5 percent wrong reliably across seeds, since a rule that starts from random weights cannot be relied on to find any working hidden layer.
options.why: Four units found a working hidden layer in every seed. Random starting weights are a problem mainly when the units barely suffice.

items.stem: On the island, under Fixed at random, the hidden weights are drawn once and never change, and only the output unit learns. With 200 hidden units and Sparse on, after 1,000 encounters, what did the decision boundary on the feature space look like?

options.text: A ragged, roughly circular boundary around the disk of nourishing fruit, although only the output unit’s weights had changed.
options.why: Correct. No hidden weight was learned. The output unit draws one straight boundary, but in the space of the 200 random units’ activity, not in the space of the two smells. Spreading the smells across many units is dimensionality expansion, and a straight boundary can separate far more sets of points in a space with many dimensions. Drawn back onto receptors A and B, that one boundary came out as a ragged curve around the disk.

options.text: A single straight line across the feature space, since only the output unit’s weights change, and a single unit can draw only one straight line.
options.why: The output unit’s boundary is straight in the space of the random units’ activity, not in the space of the two smells. Drawn back onto receptors A and B, it bent around the disk.

options.text: A smooth, perfect circle around the disk, the same boundary that the built-in receptor Distance from the ideal strength drew there.
options.why: The built-in receptor did draw a clean circle. The random units supply only whatever combinations they happened to compute, and the boundary they gave was ragged.

options.text: A rounded triangle around the disk, since the output unit can combine only a few of the random units’ lines into the boundary it draws.
options.why: A rounded triangle is what three hidden units trained by passing the error back drew. With 200 random units the boundary was a ragged curve, not three sides.

items.stem: On the Learning tab, the arithmetic for the output unit prints Φ = a − p, with a line under it saying where the target comes from. On one encounter the fish darts to cover, and an eel lunges at the empty water where it was. On that encounter, what are a and p?

options.text: a is the outcome a moment later, an eel there, although the fish was not struck, and p is the prediction made when the smell arrived.
options.why: Correct. The line under Φ says the target is the outcome, a moment later, and that nothing inside the fish is a teacher. The outcome arrives on every encounter whatever the fish did, so an eel lunging at empty water still counts as an eel there. The world supplies the target, which is why it needs no teacher.

options.text: a is no eel, since the fish darted away and was not struck, and p is the prediction made when the smell arrived.
options.why: Not being struck is what darting bought the fish, not what the world sent. The target is whether an eel was there, and here one lunged, whatever the fish did.

options.text: a is the correct answer that the experimenter supplies, and p is the prediction made when the smell arrived.
options.why: The experimenter keeps the test sets but supplies no answers to the fish. The line under Φ says the target is the outcome, and that nothing inside the fish is a teacher.

options.text: a is the outcome a moment later, an eel there, and p is the criterion that the fish’s chemistry set when the smell arrived.
options.why: The criterion is never read by the prediction or written by learning. p is the prediction itself, the sigmoid of the evidence when the smell arrived.

items.stem: On the island, with Pass the error back, a network with three hidden units was run for up to 5,000 encounters. In a few sentences, say how close it came to 5 percent wrong, describe the boundary it drew around the disk, and explain why that is the best three hidden units can do.
items.answer: Three units usually fell short, leaving something like a fifth of the fruit wrong. The boundary was a rounded triangle around the disk. Each hidden unit draws its own straight line through the feature space, and the output combines those lines, so three units can at most cut out a three-sided region. A triangle cannot fit a disk, so some fruit near its corners or along its sides always lands on the wrong side. More units give more sides, which is why six units nearly always reached the mark, though only after thousands of encounters.
rubric: Reports how close the run came; most runs stopped short of 5 percent wrong, and a run that reached it, reported as such, also earns this element.
Describes the boundary as a (rounded) triangle around the disk.
Says each hidden unit contributes one straight line, which the output combines.
Says three lines can at most make a three-sided region, which cannot match a disk.

items.stem: Localist representation and distributed representation are two broad answers to one question about a network. What is that question?

options.text: What a single hidden unit stands for: one thing of its own, or a part in the patterns for many things.
options.why: Correct. Once a hidden layer’s weights are set, its units stand for something, and there are two broad possibilities: a unit of its own for each thing, or each thing a pattern across many units.

options.text: Which connections inside a network were responsible, when the output at the network’s end was wrong.
options.why: That is structural credit assignment, the problem backpropagation and the other answers address. Localist and distributed codes concern what a single hidden unit stands for.

options.text: What sets the weights of a hidden layer: an error passed back, wiring left at random, or competition.
options.why: Those are the three answers to who sets a hidden layer’s weights. Localist and distributed codes concern what a unit stands for, however its weights were set.

options.text: Which changes to an input should leave the network’s response to that input exactly as it was.
options.why: That is the demand of invariance, met in part by convolution and pooling. Localist and distributed codes concern what a single hidden unit stands for.

pools.title: Shared Weights: Invariance, Interference, and Small Changes
pools.covers: reading §7.2.9, §7.2.10, §7.2.11 · lecture 7.2 slides stacking_layers_for_invariance, what_shared_weights_cost, fooled_and_far_from_home

items.stem: What is convolution, in a network that recognizes images?

options.text: Applying one small feature detector, with the same weights, at every position in the input, so that a feature is found wherever it falls.
options.why: Correct. A detector for a short vertical edge, for example, is copied across the whole image, with the same weights in every copy.

options.text: Combining the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood of positions, so that a small shift in the input no longer changes the result.
options.why: That is pooling, which usually follows convolution. Convolution is the copying of one detector to every position in the input.

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units than it started with, each of those units combining a random handful of the original inputs.
options.why: That is dimensionality expansion, the random-wiring answer to who sets a hidden layer’s weights. Convolution copies one detector everywhere.

options.text: Letting units that receive the same input inhibit one another until one of them wins, so that only the winning unit moves its weights.
options.why: That is competitive learning, one way of setting weights. Convolution is about where a detector is applied, not about how its weights are set.

items.stem: What is the name for applying the same small feature detector, with the same weights, at every position in an input, so that a feature is found wherever it falls?

options.text: Convolution.
options.why: Correct. Because the detector is the same everywhere, the feature can be found at any position, and the map of where it was found moves with the input.

options.text: Pooling.
options.why: Pooling combines detections over a small neighborhood so that a small shift stops mattering. Copying one detector to every position is convolution.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units, often through random wiring. It does not copy one detector across positions.

options.text: Competitive learning.
options.why: Competitive learning is a way of setting weights with no teacher, by letting units compete. It says nothing about copying a detector across positions.

items.stem: A network finds a short vertical edge in an image. The image is then shifted a little to the right. How do convolution and pooling each respond to the shift?

options.text: Convolution’s map of where the edge was found moves right with the image; pooling over a neighborhood gives the same output again.
options.why: Correct. Convolution alone makes the response move along with the input. Pooling is the step that makes a small shift stop changing the output.

options.text: Convolution’s map of where the edge was found stays where it was; pooling then moves its own output to the right to follow the image.
options.why: That reverses the two. The feature map moves with the input, and pooling is what holds the output steady across a small shift.

options.text: Both give exactly the same output as before, since each of them was built so that a shift in position makes no difference at all.
options.why: Convolution alone does not make the response unchanged by a shift; it makes the response move along. Pooling removes small shifts, and imperfectly.

options.text: Both move their output to the right along with the image, since neither of them does anything to remove the effect of a shift.
options.why: Convolution does move with the input, but pooling combines detections across a neighborhood, so a small shift no longer changes its output.
