items.stem: A network that watches a bird feeder applies a detector for the curve of a beak at every position in each camera frame, with the same weights everywhere. A sparrow hops from the left side of the frame to the right. What happens to the map of where the beak curve was found?

options.text: The detection turns up at a new place in the map, following the beak across to the far side of the frame as it hops.
options.why: Correct. Because the same detector is applied everywhere, the beak curve is found wherever it falls, and the map of where it was found shifts with the input.

options.text: The detection drops out of the map, since the detector was trained on beaks that sat on the left side of the frame.
options.why: That would be true of a detector placed at one position only. Convolution copies the detector to every position, so the curve is found anywhere.

options.text: The detection stays at the same place in the map, since copying the detector everywhere makes its output ignore position.
options.why: Copying the detector makes the feature findable anywhere, but the map still records where it was found, so the detection moves with the beak.

options.text: The detection spreads out across the whole map, since every copy of the detector now responds a little to the sparrow.
options.why: Each copy responds to the beak curve only where the curve falls within that copy’s own small region. The result is one detection, at the new position.

items.stem: What is pooling, in a network that recognizes images?

options.text: Combining the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood, so that a small shift in the input stops mattering to the output.
options.why: Correct. Pooling usually follows convolution. Convolution makes the response move with a shift, and pooling makes a small shift stop mattering.

options.text: Applying one small feature detector, with the same weights, at every position in the input, so that a feature is found anywhere.
options.why: That is convolution. On its own it makes the response move with a shift; pooling is the step that makes a small shift stop mattering.

options.text: Keeping a single cell’s preferred response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus, such as changes in its position or its size.
options.why: That is tolerance, a property of cells in the ventral stream. Pooling is an operation in a network, which builds in tolerance to small shifts and nothing for size.

options.text: Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a stored pattern can bring back the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, proposed for the piriform cortex. Pooling combines detections over a neighborhood so that small shifts do not matter.

items.stem: What is the name for combining the detections of a feature over a small neighborhood, so that a small shift in the input no longer changes the result?

options.text: Pooling.
options.why: Correct. Pooling is what turns convolution’s moving map of detections into an output that a small shift leaves unchanged.

options.text: Convolution.
options.why: Convolution finds a feature wherever it falls, but its map moves with every shift. Combining over a neighborhood so that a small shift stops mattering is pooling.

options.text: Tolerance.
options.why: Tolerance is a cell’s keeping its response over a limited range of changes. Pooling is one operation that builds tolerance to small shifts into a network.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it. It does nothing to make a small shift in position stop mattering.

items.stem: A network that sorts photographs of leaves has several rounds of convolution and pooling stacked on one another. Its first layer responds to short edges in small parts of the image. What should we expect of the units several rounds higher?

options.text: They respond to combinations of the features below, such as edges joined into a lobe, over a wider region, with more tolerance of small shifts.
options.why: Correct. Each round responds to combinations of the features in the layer below, over a wider region of the input, and tolerates small shifts and distortions a little more.

options.text: They respond to the same short edges as the first layer, over the same small region, since every layer copies one detector across positions.
options.why: Each layer does copy its detectors across positions, but the detectors differ from layer to layer. Higher layers combine lower features over wider regions.

options.text: They respond to any leaf at any size, angle, or distance, since stacking enough rounds of convolution and pooling builds in complete invariance.
options.why: Stacking adds tolerance to small shifts and distortions, a little at a time. Convolution and pooling build in nothing for size, rotation, or viewpoint.

options.text: They respond to the whole image at once with no regard to its parts, since pooling throws away which features were present in the layer below.
options.why: Pooling gives up a little of exactly where a feature was, not whether it was there. Higher layers still respond to combinations of the features below.

items.stem: The neocognitron of 1980 and the digit-reading network of 1989 share one architecture: local detectors, weights shared across positions, and pooling. How do the two networks differ?

options.text: In who sets the weights: competition with no teacher in the earlier network, and backpropagation from labeled examples in the later one.
options.why: Correct. One architecture was built twice, with two different answers to who sets the weights. The later network kept the local, shared-weight design.

options.text: In the architecture: the earlier network shared its weights across positions, and the later network gave every position weights of its own.
options.why: Both kept the local, shared-weight design. What differed was how the weights were set, by competition in one and by backpropagation in the other.

options.text: In which weights changed: the earlier network trained only its output connections, and the later one left its middle layers wired at random.
options.why: That describes the perceptron, with its random middle layer and trained output. The digit-reading network trained every weight by backpropagation.

options.text: In what they were trained on: the earlier network learned from labeled digits, and the later one learned from unlabeled photographs of scenes.
options.why: That reverses the teacher. Competition needs no labels; the digit-reading network learned from digits whose correct labels were supplied.

items.stem: Researchers want to measure how well a new network does the job the digit-reading network did. Following the procedure used with the digit-reading network, what should they do?

options.text: Train it on several thousand handwritten digits, each labeled as one of the ten digits, and then score it on new digits it has never seen.
options.why: Correct. The digit-reading network read handwritten digits from zip codes and said which of the ten digits each one was. It learned from several thousand labeled examples and was then tested on examples it had never seen.

options.text: Train it on several thousand handwritten digits, each labeled as one of the ten digits, and then score it again on those same training digits.
options.why: A score on the training digits says little about new ones. The digit-reading network was judged on digits it had never seen.

options.text: Train it on several thousand unlabeled handwritten digits by competition among its units, and then score it on digits it has never seen.
options.why: Training by competition with no teacher was the neocognitron’s answer. The digit-reading network learned from labeled examples by backpropagation.

options.text: Train it on several thousand whole handwritten zip codes, each labeled with the town it belongs to, and then score it on new zip codes.
options.why: The digit-reading network did read digits taken from zip codes on mail, but its job was to say which of the ten digits each one was, not where a whole code belonged.

items.stem: Invariance is recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal. How can a network’s architecture, before any training, help to meet that demand?

options.text: By building into the way its units are wired some assumptions about which differences in the input do not matter for the task.
options.why: Correct. Architecture can meet part of invariance in this way. Convolution and pooling, for instance, build in the assumption that a small shift in position does not matter.

options.text: By storing a separate copy of each object as it looks from the many distances, positions, and angles at which it could appear.
options.why: Storing views is closer to an exemplar strategy, and it would need training examples to store. Architecture helps by building in which changes do not matter.

options.text: By wiring a large middle layer at random, so that among its many units some unit happens to respond to each view of each object.
options.why: Random expansion makes more divisions possible with a single straight line, but it builds in no assumption about which changes do not matter.

options.text: By making each unit respond to the whole input at once, so that a change in one part of the input would hardly alter its response.
options.why: Units that respond to everything would lose the differences that matter as well. Architecture helps by building in which particular changes do not matter.

items.stem: The bet built into a convolutional network is that a feature means the same thing wherever it appears. For which of these tasks is that bet least likely to be right?

options.text: Reading the temperature from photographs of a thermometer, where the top of the red column stands for a different temperature at each height.
options.why: Correct. Here the same feature, the top of the red column, means a different thing at each position in the image, so the bet that a feature means the same thing wherever it appears is wrong for this task.

options.text: Finding cracks in photographs of a concrete wall, where a crack is a crack whether it runs near the top or near the bottom.
options.why: A crack means the same thing anywhere in the photograph. This is a task where the convolutional bet is right, and when it is right it helps a network learn.

options.text: Reading handwritten zip-code digits from envelopes, where a 7 written a little to the left or to the right is still a 7.
options.why: This is the task of the digit-reading network, and there the bet was right: the network made fewer errors on unseen digits than a fully connected network with about as many weights.

options.text: Spotting ripe berries in photographs of a bush, where a red berry is ripe whether it hangs high or low on the branch.
options.why: A ripe berry is ripe wherever it hangs, so the feature means the same thing everywhere, and the convolutional bet helps.

items.stem: What is an inductive bias?

options.text: A tendency to find some things easier to learn than others, which is established before the learning itself begins.
options.why: Correct. It can come from an animal’s lineage or from what it has already learned, and in a convolutional network it is built into the wiring.

options.text: A tendency to fit the training examples so closely, accidents and all, that performance on new examples suffers.
options.why: That is overfitting, which happens during learning. An inductive bias is in place before learning begins, and when it is right it helps.

options.text: A tendency to categorize images by their surface texture rather than their shape, found in networks trained on photographs.
options.why: That is texture bias, a tendency in how a trained network categorizes images. An inductive bias is a tendency in what is easier to learn, in place before the learning begins.

options.text: A tendency to respond less and less to a new input the more it differs from the input that the animal was trained on.
options.why: That describes a generalization gradient, a pattern in behavior measured after training. An inductive bias is set before learning begins.

items.stem: What is the name for a tendency to find one thing easier to learn than another, established before the learning begins, whether by an animal’s lineage, by what it has already learned, or by a network’s wiring?

options.text: Inductive bias.
options.why: Correct. A convolutional network has one built into its wiring: the bet that a feature means the same thing wherever it appears.

options.text: Feature engineering.
options.why: Feature engineering is deciding, before learning, what the inputs to a learner will be. It is a choice made by an engineer, not a tendency in what is easier to learn.

options.text: Texture bias.
options.why: Texture bias is a tendency in how a trained network categorizes, by surface over shape. It is not a tendency to find one thing easier to learn than another.

options.text: Generalization gradient.
options.why: A generalization gradient is the fall-off in responding as a new input differs from a trained one. It is measured after training, not set before it.

items.stem: A fish might have a smell receptor that already responds to one particular combination of chemicals. A convolutional network shares its weights across positions. Both are inductive biases. Where does each one come from?

options.text: The fish’s comes with its lineage, and the network’s is built into the wiring of the network itself before training.
options.why: Correct. An inductive bias can be supplied by an animal’s lineage. In a convolutional network, the same kind of bet is built into the wiring.

options.text: The fish’s is built up by its training on eel smells, and the network’s comes down from earlier generations of networks.
options.why: That reverses the sources. A receptor the fish starts out with comes with its lineage, and the network’s bias is put into its wiring.

options.text: Both come from what each has already learned, since an inductive bias is always a product of some earlier training.
options.why: An inductive bias can come from earlier learning, but neither of these does. Both are in place before any learning starts.

options.text: Both come from the examples each one is trained on, since a bias only shows up once learning has shaped the weights.
options.why: An inductive bias is established before learning begins. A bias that comes from the training examples, like texture bias, is a different thing.

items.stem: The lecture describes convolution and pooling together as an inductive bias. What makes pooling, in particular, an inductive bias?

options.text: It builds into the wiring, before any training, the assumption that a small shift in where a feature appears does not matter.
options.why: Correct. An inductive bias is in place before learning begins. Pooling’s is a bet that a small change of position makes no difference to what the input is.

options.text: It picks up from the training images which features tend to appear together, and then weights those combinations more heavily afterward.
options.why: A tendency picked up from the training images is the kind of thing that produced texture bias. Pooling’s assumption is wired in before any training.

options.text: It makes the network fit its training images more closely, so that new images are judged by how much they resemble old ones.
options.why: Fitting the training images too closely is overfitting, which a well-chosen inductive bias helps to reduce. Pooling builds in that small shifts do not matter.

options.text: It assumes that a feature means something different at each position, so the network keeps a separate detector for each place.
options.why: That is the opposite of the convolutional bet. Pooling assumes that a small change in a feature’s position does not matter.

items.stem: The digit-reading network had many times more connections than adjustable weights. How is that possible?

options.text: Many connections were copies of one detector at different positions, so all of those copies used the same shared weights.
options.why: Correct. With weights shared across positions, its 64,660 connections needed only 9,760 adjustable weights.

options.text: Most of its connections were wired at random and never trained, so only the weights on connections to the output could be adjusted.
options.why: That describes the perceptron’s random middle layer. In the digit-reading network every weight was trained by backpropagation; many were simply shared.

options.text: Most of its connections were removed after training, so only the ones that mattered for reading digits were left in place.
options.why: Nothing was removed. The connections all remained, and many of them were copies that used one shared set of weights.

options.text: Most of its connections carried no weight at all, so they passed activity on from one layer to the next without change.
options.why: Every connection had a weight. The gap between connections and adjustable weights is there because so many connections shared the same weights.

items.stem: On digits it had not seen, the digit-reading network made fewer errors than a fully connected network with about as many adjustable weights. What does matching the two networks on adjustable weights, rather than on connections, let us conclude?

options.text: That the fewer errors go with the built-in local, shared-weight design, and not simply with having more weights to adjust during training.
options.why: Correct. With adjustable weights about equal, having more of them cannot be the reason. What remains is the built-in arrangement, local detectors with weights shared across positions, which is the inductive bias. When that bet is right, it helps the network learn.

options.text: That the fewer errors go with how the connections were trained, since the two networks were matched on their numbers of connections.
options.why: A fully connected network with about 9,760 weights has far fewer connections than 64,660. The comparison matches adjustable weights, not connections.

options.text: That the two networks fit their training digits equally well, so neither one can be said to be the better learner of digits.
options.why: The comparison is on digits the networks had not seen, and there the shared-weight network made fewer errors. Matching the weights is what makes that difference informative.

options.text: That sharing weights across positions helps any network on any task, since the advantage held even with the weights matched.
options.why: The comparison is on one task, digits, where the bet that a feature means the same thing wherever it appears is right. The chapter says such a bet helps when it is right for the task.

items.stem: A network built with convolution and pooling is trained only on photographs of cats seen side-on at one size, and is then tested on new photographs. To which change in a cat does its architecture alone give it some tolerance?

options.text: The cat shifted a little to the left or right in the frame, though even that is handled imperfectly.
options.why: Correct. Convolution and pooling build in tolerance to one kind of change, a shift in position, and imperfectly.

options.text: The cat much closer to the camera, so that it fills twice as much of the frame as it did in training.
options.why: That is a change in size. Convolution and pooling build in nothing for size.

options.text: The cat photographed upside down, so that every edge in the image is turned to a new orientation.
options.why: That is a rotation. Convolution and pooling build in nothing for rotation; networks mostly get it from training examples that include rotations.

options.text: The cat photographed from the front, so that the outline of its body is quite unlike the side view.
options.why: That is a change of viewpoint, and convolution and pooling build in nothing for viewpoint.

items.stem: For the small fish, an eel can appear to its left or to its right, near or far, and from the front or from the side. Which of these changes would convolution and pooling build any tolerance to?

options.text: Only the eel to the left or the right, which is a shift; near and far is a change in size, and the two angles are a change of viewpoint.
options.why: Correct. Convolution and pooling build in tolerance to a shift in position, imperfectly, and nothing for size, rotation, or viewpoint.

options.text: Only the eel near and far, since pooling over a neighborhood absorbs a change in size the same way it absorbs a small change in position.
options.why: Near and far is a change in size, and convolution and pooling build in nothing for size. The change they do cover is a shift in position.

options.text: All three of them, since enough stacked rounds of convolution and pooling build in tolerance to position, size, and viewpoint alike.
options.why: Stacking adds tolerance to small shifts and distortions a little at a time, but nothing for size or viewpoint.

options.text: Not even the eel to the left or the right, since convolution makes the response move along with the input and so removes no change.
options.why: Convolution alone does make the response move with a shift, but pooling then makes a small shift stop mattering. Together they give tolerance to shifts.

items.stem: An engineer wants a network to recognize mushroom species in photographs taken at any distance and from any angle. Following the way artificial networks mostly reach that ability, what should the engineer do?

options.text: Train it on photographs that already include those changes, often made by copying each one rescaled, rotated, or blurred.
options.why: Correct. Networks that recognize objects across changes of size and angle mostly get there through training examples that already contain those changes.

options.text: Add more rounds of convolution and pooling, since each round adds tolerance to changes of size and angle as well as of position.
options.why: Each round adds a little tolerance to small shifts and distortions, but convolution and pooling build in nothing for size or rotation.

options.text: Train it only on photographs taken at one standard distance and angle, so that its detectors are tuned to one clean view of each.
options.why: A network trained at one distance and angle has nothing to go on for others. The changes have to be in the training examples.

options.text: Give every position in the image its own detector with its own weights, so that the network can learn each view separately.
options.why: That gives up weight sharing, the bet that helped the digit-reading network, and it builds in nothing for size or angle either.

items.stem: A classmate argues: “Networks recognize objects across size and rotation because they were trained on rescaled and rotated copies of their images. So animals must recognize things across such changes in the same way”. What does the chapter say about this argument?

options.text: Whether training of that kind is enough to explain how animals manage changes of size and rotation is still a live dispute among researchers.
options.why: Correct. The first half of the argument is a fair description of networks. The step to animals is exactly what remains disputed, in either direction.

options.text: The argument is likely right, since the chapter presents varied training as the leading explanation of how animals manage such changes.
options.why: The chapter presents varied training as how artificial networks mostly get there, not as the leading account of animals. For animals the question is a live dispute.

options.text: The argument is likely wrong, since the chapter presents built-in wiring as the leading explanation of how animals manage such changes.
options.why: The chapter favors neither side for animals. Whether training of this kind is enough to explain how animals do it is left as a live dispute.

options.text: The argument is wrong, since networks get their tolerance to size and rotation from convolution and pooling, not from their training images.
options.why: Convolution and pooling build in nothing for size or rotation; networks mostly get those from varied training examples. The step to animals is what is disputed.

items.stem: A network built from convolution followed by pooling is shown a photograph of a beetle, and then the same photograph with the beetle shifted a few positions to the right. In a few sentences, explain what convolution does with the shift, what pooling adds, and which changes to the beetle this architecture would still give the network no help with.
items.answer: Convolution applies the same small detector, with the same weights, at every position, so each feature of the beetle is found wherever it falls. When the beetle shifts, the map of where each feature was found shifts with it. So convolution alone does not make the response unchanged; it makes the response move along with the input. Pooling then combines the detections over a small neighborhood, so a small shift no longer changes the pooled output. Together they give some tolerance to shifts in position, though imperfectly. They build in nothing for other changes, such as the beetle seen larger or smaller, rotated, or from another viewpoint. Networks mostly get those from training images that already include them.
rubric: Says convolution applies one detector, with the same weights, at every position, so a feature is found wherever it falls.
Says the convolution map moves with the shift rather than staying unchanged.
Says pooling combines detections over a small neighborhood, so a small shift no longer changes the output.
Names at least one change the architecture builds in nothing for: size, rotation, or viewpoint.
Keeps the tolerance to shift limited or imperfect, rather than complete.

items.stem: What is catastrophic interference?

options.text: A drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones, because the new learning moves weights that the old ones needed.
options.why: Correct. In a classic demonstration, a network that had learned the addition facts about ones began answering them as twos after a single pass through the twos.

options.text: A loss of accuracy on new examples after a network has fit its training examples so closely that it has learned even their accidents along with them.
options.why: That is overfitting, which is about doing poorly on new examples of the same kind. Catastrophic interference is old learning wiped out by newer learning.

options.text: A confident wrong answer to an input that has been changed slightly and deliberately, often in a way that a person looking at it would not notice.
options.why: That describes an adversarial example. Catastrophic interference concerns what happens to old learning when a network learns something new afterward.

options.text: A weakness in handling inputs unlike anything a network was trained on, such as numbers with many more digits than any that appeared in training.
options.why: That is weak out-of-distribution generalization. Catastrophic interference is a loss of old learning, triggered by learning in sequence.

items.stem: What is the name for a drastic loss of old learning when a network learns new patterns after old ones, because the new learning moves weights that the old patterns depended on?

options.text: Catastrophic interference.
options.why: Correct. The trigger is learning in sequence; trained on everything at once, the same network can learn it all.

options.text: Overfitting.
options.why: Overfitting is fitting the training examples so closely that new examples suffer. It is not a loss of earlier learning to later learning.

options.text: Out-of-distribution generalization.
options.why: Out-of-distribution generalization is generalizing to inputs unlike any in training. It says nothing about old learning being lost.

options.text: Pattern separation.
options.why: Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike, so a later stage can tell them apart. It is not a loss of old learning.

items.stem: A network trained to recognize the calls of ten frog species is then trained further on the calls of ten bird species. Its accuracy on the frogs drops. What is the general reason for problems of this kind?

options.text: The same units carry both sets of patterns, so learning the birds moves weights that recognizing the frogs depended on.
options.why: Correct. When the patterns a learner stores are carried by the same units, learning a new pattern moves weights that an old pattern depends on.

options.text: The network ran out of room, so the bird calls had to take over the units that had been set aside for the frogs.
options.why: With shared weights no unit is set aside for one species. Every weight takes part in many input–output pairs, and that is the source of the problem.

options.text: The frog calls were kept in their own part of the network, which faded because nothing activated it during the bird training.
options.why: Nothing in the account involves fading with disuse. The old learning is disturbed because new learning moves the very weights it depended on.

options.text: The frog training had overfit the ten frog species, so any later training was bound to expose how fragile that learning was.
options.why: Overfitting is doing poorly on new examples of the same kind. Here the frogs themselves were lost, because learning the birds moved weights the frogs depended on.

items.stem: A learner that tracks only single features is rewarded at blue round flowers, and not rewarded at blue star-shaped flowers. What happens to its weight on “blue” as the two kinds of flower keep turning up?

options.text: It is raised at each round flower and lowered at each star-shaped one, so the learner keeps undoing its own earlier learning.
options.why: Correct. A feature shared by rewarded and unrewarded objects has its weight pushed up and down in turn.

options.text: It rises steadily, since blue is present at every rewarded round flower and the learner tracks the features that come with reward.
options.why: Blue is also present at every unrewarded flower, so its weight is lowered as often as it is raised.

options.text: It falls steadily toward zero, since blue is present at the unrewarded star-shaped flowers and a feature that goes unrewarded is dropped.
options.why: Blue is lowered when it goes unrewarded, but raised again whenever it is rewarded. The weight is pushed back and forth.

options.text: It settles after the first few flowers at a value that is never changed again, whichever kind of flower turns up next.
options.why: A single-feature learner changes the weight at every flower, up for reward and down for none, so it keeps undoing its own learning.

items.stem: A learner that tracks only single features is working through a garden where some flowers are rewarded and some are not. Which change to the garden would make its problem of undoing its own learning worse?

options.text: More kinds of flower that share colors and shapes, so that more features turn up on both rewarded and unrewarded flowers.
options.why: Correct. When a feature appears on two kinds of objects, the learner keeps undoing its own learning, and the more objects share features, the worse this gets.

options.text: More kinds of flower that share no colors or shapes, so that each feature turns up on just one kind of flower in the garden.
options.why: If each feature turned up on only one kind of flower, that feature would reliably predict the outcome, and there would be nothing to undo.

options.text: Fewer flowers overall, spaced further apart, so that the learner has to travel further between one reward and the next.
options.why: Distance between flowers has nothing to do with it. The problem grows with the number of features shared between rewarded and unrewarded flowers.

options.text: Larger rewards at the rewarded flowers, so that each reward raises the weights of its features by a bigger step than before.
options.why: Larger steps up are still followed by steps down at unrewarded flowers. What makes the problem worse is more sharing of features.

items.stem: In one patch, blue round flowers and yellow star-shaped flowers carry nectar, while blue star-shaped flowers and yellow round flowers carry none. One learner tracks only single features; another can also represent combinations of features. How do they compare?

options.text: The combination learner can come to rely on “blue and round”, which is always rewarded, and the single-feature learner keeps undoing its own weights.
options.why: Correct. Each single feature here is rewarded half the time, but a combination can be reliably rewarded even when none of its parts is. Representing it stops the interference.

options.text: The single-feature learner does better, since tracking “blue” and “round” separately gives it twice as many chances to be rewarded.
options.why: Each single feature is rewarded on half its occasions and unrewarded on the rest, so its weight keeps going up and down.

options.text: The two learners do equally well, since a combination like “blue and round” carries no more than the sum of what each of its parts predicts.
options.why: If a combination were only a sum of its parts, nothing could solve this patch. Representing the combination as its own thing is what stops the interference.

options.text: Neither learner can succeed, since no learner that changes its weights with reward can use cues that are each rewarded half the time.
options.why: A learner that represents combinations can do it, because each combination is reliably rewarded even though no single feature is.

items.stem: A network trained by backpropagation answered every addition fact about “ones” correctly. It was then trained on the “twos”. After a single pass, it gave 7 for 5 + 1 and 8 for 6 + 1. What had happened?

options.text: It had begun answering ones problems as if they were twos problems, because training on the twos moved weights the ones needed.
options.why: Correct. 5 + 2 is 7, and 6 + 2 is 8. The new learning had moved the shared weights to suit the twos, and the answers to the ones moved with them.

options.text: It had begun guessing at random among nearby numbers, because training on the twos made the ones facts harder for it to tell apart.
options.why: The answers are not random. They are exactly the twos answers, which is what interference from the newer learning looks like.

options.text: It had been given wrong answers for the ones during the second training, because some twos were labeled as ones by mistake.
options.why: The training was on twos, correctly labeled. The ones answers changed because new learning moved weights the old facts depended on.

options.text: It had overfit the ones during the first training, so that any new examples at all would have produced errors on the ones.
options.why: Overfitting is doing poorly on new examples of the same kind. Here old learning was overwritten by learning a new set in sequence.

items.stem: In the classic demonstration with the ones and the twos, how did the network’s score on the ones change once it was trained on the twos?

options.text: It fell sharply after only a single pass through the twos, and it fell further still after a second pass.
options.why: Correct. From 100 percent it fell to 57 percent by the most lenient criterion after one pass, and to 30 percent after a second. That is how drastic the interference was.

options.text: It stayed close to perfect, since the ones and the twos are separate facts that are carried by separate weights.
options.why: In a network every weight takes part in many input–output pairs, so learning the twos moved weights that the ones depended on.

options.text: It fell slowly, by a percent or two with each pass, until after many passes it had come down to about half.
options.why: The fall was abrupt, not gradual: a large drop after a single pass. That abruptness is what makes the interference catastrophic.

options.text: It rose a little, since the twos share their structure with the ones and generalization carried the gain back.
options.why: Generalization is the other side of the same effect, but here the changes made for the twos overwrote the answers to the ones.

items.stem: A network that recognizes handwritten letters reads a new person’s writing well. Trained afterward on a new alphabet, it loses much of the old one. How does the chapter relate these two behaviors?

options.text: They are one effect seen from two sides: each weight serves many input–output pairs, which carries learning to new inputs and lets new learning alter old answers.
options.why: Correct. Weight sharing is why similar inputs get similar outputs without any extra work, and also why changing the weights for new pairs changes the answers to old ones.

options.text: They are two separate effects with two separate causes: generalization comes from the variety of the training letters, and interference from having too few hidden units.
options.why: The chapter traces both to one property, weights that each take part in many input–output pairs, not to the variety of the training set or the size of the network.

options.text: They trade off against each other: the better a network generalizes to new inputs, the less it will suffer from interference when it later learns something else entirely.
options.why: They go together, not against each other. The sharing that gives generalization is the same sharing that lets new learning disturb old learning.

options.text: They are both forms of overfitting: the network fits each set of training letters so closely that it cannot treat any other letters properly.
options.why: Overfitting is doing poorly on new examples after fitting the training set too closely. This network generalizes well, so overfitting is not the story.

items.stem: An engineer proposes to end interference in a letter-recognizing network by making sure that no weight takes part in more than one input–output pair. On the chapter’s account, what else would that change do?

options.text: It would also give up generalization, since that sharing is what gives similar new inputs similar outputs without any extra work.
options.why: Correct. The property that causes interference is the same one that makes the network useful. This is sharing in the sense that each weight serves many input–output pairs, not the copying of one detector across positions. Take that sharing away, and generalization goes with it.

options.text: It would make the network generalize better, since a weight that serves a single pair can be tuned exactly to that pair without disturbance.
options.why: Tuning each pair separately carries nothing over to new inputs. Generalization comes from the sharing that the change would remove.

options.text: It would leave the network much as it was otherwise, since interference comes from the order of training, not from how weights are used.
options.why: The order of training is the trigger, but the cause is weight sharing, which is also the source of generalization. Removing it changes more than interference.

options.text: It would make old learning disappear even faster, since a weight that serves a single pair is moved further by each new pair that arrives.
options.why: A weight that serves a single pair is not moved by new pairs at all. What the change gives up is generalization, not stability.

items.stem: A network must learn to name twenty birds and twenty frogs from their calls. On one schedule, the bird and frog calls are mixed together from the start. On another, all the birds come first and then all the frogs. How do the outcomes compare?

options.text: Mixed together, it can master all forty; birds first and frogs second, it loses much of the birds as it learns the frogs.
options.why: Correct. The trigger for catastrophic interference is learning in sequence. Trained on everything at once, the same network learns it all.

options.text: Mixed together, it learns neither set well, since the two sets keep pulling its weights in opposite directions at once.
options.why: Trained on all the calls at once, a network finds weights that serve both sets. The trouble comes when the sets arrive in sequence.

options.text: The two schedules end in the same place, since the network hears exactly the same calls in both and only their order differs.
options.why: The order is what matters. Learning in sequence is the trigger for catastrophic interference.

options.text: Birds first and frogs second gives the better result, since learning one set fully before the next keeps the two from mixing.
options.why: That is how it might seem, but sequence is the trigger. The network moves its weights to suit the newest set, whatever the old set needed.

items.stem: Picture every possible setting of a network’s weights as a point in a space. The settings that get all the ones facts right form one region, the settings that get all the twos facts right form another, and the two regions overlap. Why does training on the twos after the ones lose the ones?

options.text: Training on the twos moves the weights to the nearest point that suits the twos, whether or not it still lies in the ones region.
options.why: Correct. Trained in sequence, the weights leave the first region for wherever suits the newest set. Trained on both at once, they move into the overlap.

options.text: Training on the twos first returns the weights to the point where they started before any training, and then moves them into the twos region.
options.why: The weights are not reset. They move from where the ones training left them to the nearest setting that suits the twos.

options.text: Training on the twos moves the weights into the overlap, but the settings in the overlap suit neither set of facts especially well.
options.why: The overlap holds exactly the settings that get both sets right. Training on both at once ends there; training in sequence passes it by.

options.text: Training on the twos makes the ones region shrink, since each new fact that is learned takes over space the old facts were using.
options.why: The regions stay where they are; what moves is the weight setting. The ones region is left behind, not shrunk.

items.stem: When people learn a new list of associations that conflicts with an old one, how does what happens to their old list compare with what happens in a network trained the same way?

options.text: Both lose some of the old list, but people lose far less: they still recall more than half of it after mastering the new one.
options.why: Correct. In a classic study people kept more than half the old list, while the network lost all of its old list by the time it had learned about a fifth of the new one.

options.text: People lose none of the old list, since human memory keeps each list in its own separate store, while the network loses all of it.
options.why: People forget too. The difference between people and networks is in how much is lost, not in whether anything is.

options.text: Both lose about the same amount, since people and networks forget conflicting lists by the same means and at about the same rate.
options.why: People lose far less. They kept more than half the old list, while the network lost all of its old list early in the new learning.

options.text: The network loses less than people do, since it can hold far more associations at once than a person can keep in memory.
options.why: That reverses the finding. The network lost all of its old list by the time it had learned about a fifth of the new one.

items.stem: An engineer has a network that recognizes twenty kinds of fruit, and needs it to learn twenty kinds of vegetable without losing the fruit. Which approach is one that engineers use to slow the loss?

options.text: Mix photographs of the fruit back into the training, alongside the vegetables, while the vegetables are being learned.
options.why: Correct. Mixing old examples back into new training is one way engineers slow the loss. Protecting the weights that matter most for old learning is another.

options.text: Train on the vegetables for many more passes, so that the new learning has settled before the fruit can be disturbed.
options.why: More passes through the vegetables alone move the weights further toward whatever suits them. The ones score fell further after a second pass.

options.text: Train on the vegetables first, and then go back to training on the fruit alone, so that the fruit is the last thing learned.
options.why: That only reverses the sequence; now the vegetables would be lost. Learning in sequence is the trigger whichever set comes second.

options.text: Make every weight change larger, so that the vegetables are learned in as few passes as possible and the fruit is spared.
options.why: Bigger steps still move the shared weights toward whatever suits the vegetables, regardless of the fruit. Engineers instead protect important weights or mix old examples in.

items.stem: Engineers slow catastrophic interference in artificial networks by protecting the weights that matter most for old learning, or by mixing old examples back into new training. What does the chapter conclude from this about brains?

options.text: Nothing yet: how brains manage the problem is a separate question, and those two methods for fixing it do not answer it.
options.why: Correct. The two methods are fixes for artificial networks. How brains keep old learning while adding new is taken up in Module 10, and nothing here settles it.

options.text: That brains probably use the same two methods, since a learner that shares its weights would seem to need some way to protect what it learned before.
options.why: The chapter draws no such conclusion. The methods are engineers’ fixes for networks, and how brains manage is a separate question.

options.text: That brains need neither method, since people keep an old list intact when they learn a new list that conflicts with it.
options.why: People do lose some of an old list. The difference from networks is how much, and how brains limit the loss is left open here.

options.text: That brains avoid the problem because their neurons, unlike the units of a network, take part in one memory each and are never shared.
options.why: The chapter makes no claim about how brains do it. It names the question and leaves it for later.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain why generalization and catastrophic interference can be called the same effect seen from two sides, and why learning in sequence is what triggers the interference.
items.answer: In a network, every weight takes part in many different input–output pairs. That sharing is why similar inputs get similar outputs without any extra work, which is generalization. It is also why changing the weights to fit new pairs changes the answers to old ones, which is interference. So both come from one property. The interference becomes catastrophic when learning happens in sequence. Trained on one set and then another, the network moves its weights to wherever suits the newest set, regardless of where the old set needed them to be. Trained on all the facts at once, the same network learns them all.
rubric: Names the shared property: each weight takes part in many input–output pairs.
Links that sharing to generalization, with similar inputs getting similar outputs.
Links the same sharing to interference, with weight changes for new pairs changing old answers.
Says learning in sequence is the trigger, with the weights moving to suit the newest set.
Says that training on everything at once lets the same network learn it all.

items.stem: A classmate says: “Catastrophic interference proves that networks learn nothing like people, because people never lose old learning when they learn something new”. In a few sentences, say what is right and what is wrong in that claim.
items.answer: The classmate is right that the difference is real and large. In a classic study, people still recalled more than half of an old list after mastering a new one that conflicted with it, while a network lost all of its old list by the time it had learned about a fifth of the new one. But it is wrong that people never lose old learning. When people learn a new list of associations that conflicts with an old one, they lose some of the old list too. So the difference between people and networks lies in how much is lost, not in whether anything is. How brains keep most of their old learning is a separate question, and the network results do not answer it.
rubric: Says people do lose some of an old list when they learn a conflicting new one.
Says the difference between people and networks is in how much is lost.
Gives evidence of the size of the difference, such as people keeping more than half of the old list while the network lost all of it.
Does not claim that the network results explain how brains limit the loss.

items.stem: Image-recognizing networks fail in characteristic ways. Which three failures are the characteristic ones?

options.text: They can be fooled by changes a person would not notice, they lean on texture over shape, and they generalize poorly when conditions shift.
options.why: Correct. These are the three characteristic failures, and adversarial examples and texture bias are two of them with reasons attached.

options.text: They cannot learn exclusive or, they need a teacher for each weight they have, and they lose their accuracy once an image is shifted a little.
options.why: Networks with hidden layers learn exclusive or, competition needs no teacher, and convolution and pooling build in some tolerance to shifts.

options.text: They lean on shape over texture, they can be fooled by large and obvious changes but not by small ones, and they generalize well when conditions shift.
options.why: Each part is reversed. Networks lean on texture, can be fooled by changes a person would not notice, and generalize poorly when conditions shift.

options.text: They confuse objects that differ only in color, they never lose old learning, and they need far fewer examples than a child does.
options.why: None of these is among the three, and the second is false: networks can lose old learning badly when they learn in sequence.

items.stem: What is an adversarial example?

options.text: An input changed slightly and deliberately, so that a network gives a confident wrong answer, by a change that can be too slight for a person to see.
options.why: Correct. The change at each pixel can be about as small as an image file can record, and imperceptible to a person, while the network’s answer changes completely.

options.text: An input unlike anything in a network’s training examples, so that the network’s answer to it is much less reliable.
options.why: That describes an out-of-distribution input. An adversarial example is a familiar kind of input with a tiny, deliberate change.

options.text: An image whose surface texture comes from one object and whose shape comes from another, used to test what a network relies on.
options.why: Pictures like that were used to measure texture bias. An adversarial example is an input changed slightly and on purpose.

options.text: A training example that a network fits so closely, accidents included, that it then does worse on new examples.
options.why: That describes overfitting. An adversarial example is an input deliberately altered to produce a confident wrong answer.

items.stem: What is the name for an input changed slightly and deliberately, so that a network gives a confident wrong answer, by a change that can be too slight for a person to see?

options.text: Adversarial example.
options.why: Correct. The panda photograph that a network labeled “gibbon” after a carefully chosen pattern was added is a well-known case.

options.text: Texture bias.
options.why: Texture bias is a tendency to categorize by surface over shape. It is not an input altered to produce a wrong answer.

options.text: False alarm.
options.why: A false alarm is judging a target present when it is absent. An adversarial example can produce a wrong answer, but the term names the altered input.

options.text: Out-of-distribution generalization.
options.why: Out-of-distribution generalization is generalizing to inputs unlike anything in training. An adversarial example is a familiar input with a tiny, deliberate change.

items.stem: A network labeled a photograph of a panda “panda” with 57.7 percent confidence. After a carefully chosen pattern was added, it labeled the same photograph “gibbon” with 99.3 percent confidence. What makes this result striking?

options.text: The slightly altered photograph got a wrong label with far more confidence than the original photograph got its right one.
options.why: Correct. That is what makes it an adversarial example: a slight, deliberate change, and a confident wrong answer.

options.text: The network had never been trained on pandas, so any label it gave to a panda photograph was bound to be little better than a guess.
options.why: The network labeled the original photograph correctly. What is striking is the confident wrong answer after a tiny, deliberate change.

options.text: The added pattern made the panda look like a gibbon to people as well, and the network’s new label simply agreed with what they saw.
options.why: An adversarial change is slight, and can be imperceptible to people, so nothing here made the panda look like a gibbon. The striking part is that the network’s answer changed, with high confidence.

options.text: The network’s confidence fell for every label after the pattern was added, so its answers were spread evenly across many animals.
options.why: The opposite happened. The network’s confidence rose, to 99.3 percent, for one wrong label.

items.stem: A researcher changes every pixel of a photograph of an edible mushroom by the smallest step the image file can record, in a carefully chosen pattern. People shown both photographs see no difference. Can the network’s answer still change?

options.text: Yes, since a change that a person cannot perceive at all can nonetheless alter the answer that the network gives.
options.why: Correct. The change at each pixel can be about as small as an image file can record, and still change the network’s behavior.

options.text: No, since a change too small for a person to see is also too small to carry any unit in the network across its threshold.
options.why: On one explanation, tiny changes across thousands of pixels add up and can carry the weighted sum across the boundary, though no single pixel moves much.

options.text: No, since a change has to alter the mushroom’s visible shape to change the answer of a network that relies on shape.
options.why: Networks trained on standard photographs lean on texture over shape, and a change too small to see can still change their answers.

options.text: Yes, provided the network is very small, since a large network averages away a change smaller than a person can see.
options.why: Nothing about adversarial examples depends on the network being small. On one explanation, more inputs give more tiny changes to add up, not fewer.

items.stem: On one explanation of adversarial examples, how can a change too small to notice at any one pixel still change a network’s answer?

options.text: A unit sums thousands of weighted inputs, so nudging each slightly in the direction its weight favors adds up until the sum crosses the boundary.
options.why: Correct. No single pixel moves much, but every tiny change pushes the sum the same way, and the total carries the input across the boundary.

options.text: A single pixel changed by a large amount can carry the whole weighted sum across the decision boundary, while the other pixels stay exactly as they were.
options.why: On this explanation no single pixel moves much. It is the many tiny changes together that carry the sum across the boundary.

options.text: The tiny changes make the image look like a different object to the network’s first layer, whose detectors then respond to the new object’s shape.
options.why: The change alters no shape that anyone could see. The explanation turns on a weighted sum over many inputs, not on a new shape.

options.text: The tiny changes are scattered at random, and among enough random changes some are bound to push the answer over into a different category.
options.why: Direction matters on this explanation. Random noise of the same size rarely changes the answer.

items.stem: A single unit told handwritten 3s from 7s with 1.6 percent error. Yet it misclassified 99 percent of inputs nudged slightly in the direction of its own weights. Why does this result bear on the many-small-nudges explanation of adversarial examples?

options.text: The explanation predicts that even one unit computing a weighted sum should be fooled, and it was, which fits without proving it.
options.why: Correct. The single-unit result is consistent with the explanation. Whether it is the right explanation for adversarial examples is still debated.

options.text: The result proves the explanation correct, since a single unit could be fooled in no other way than by many small nudges that add up.
options.why: The result fits the explanation; it does not prove it. The researchers who first reported adversarial examples proposed a different cause.

options.text: The result counts against the explanation, since the explanation predicts that large networks with many layers are the ones fooled.
options.why: The explanation predicts the opposite: a single weighted sum over many inputs should be enough to be fooled.

options.text: The result shows that the unit was poorly trained after all, since a unit with an error rate that low should resist such tiny changes.
options.why: The unit was accurate on ordinary inputs. Nudging inputs along its own weights fooled it, which is what the explanation predicts.

items.stem: Two altered versions of one image are made, each changing every pixel by the same tiny amount. In one, each pixel moves in the direction the unit’s weight on it favors. In the other, each pixel moves up or down at random. How do the two compare?

options.text: The directed change can carry the weighted sum across the boundary; random noise of the same size rarely changes the answer.
options.why: Correct. The direction of the change is what matters. The same amount of change, made at random, rarely moves the answer.

options.text: The two are equally likely to change the answer, since what matters is the total amount of change summed across the pixels.
options.why: The total amount is the same in both, and still the directed change is the one that reliably works. Direction is what matters.

options.text: The random noise is the more likely to change the answer, since a network trained on clean images is thrown off by noisy ones.
options.why: Random noise of the same size rarely changes the answer. It is the change aimed along the weights that does.

options.text: The two are equally unlikely to change the answer, since a change this tiny at each pixel is too small to reach the boundary.
options.why: Directed changes add up across thousands of inputs and can cross the boundary, even though each one is tiny.

items.stem: A study guide states that adversarial examples are “caused by tiny nudges adding up across thousands of inputs, as researchers have established”. How does the chapter’s account differ?

options.text: It gives the many-small-nudges account as one explanation, notes that a different cause was first proposed, and calls it still debated.
options.why: Correct. The account makes the effect easy to understand, and the single-unit result fits it, but the explanation is not settled.

options.text: It rejects the many-small-nudges account, since a single unit that sums its inputs turned out to be impossible to fool by nudging them.
options.why: A single unit was fooled, on 99 percent of nudged inputs. The chapter keeps the account as one explanation, still debated.

options.text: It agrees with the study guide, adding only that the account came from the same researchers who first reported adversarial examples.
options.why: The researchers who first reported adversarial examples proposed a different cause. The account is still debated.

options.text: It traces adversarial examples instead to the training images, the same cause that it gives for texture bias in standard networks.
options.why: The training images are the source the chapter gives for texture bias. For adversarial examples, the cause is still debated.

items.stem: What is texture bias?

options.text: A tendency to categorize images by their surface texture rather than their shape, found in networks trained on standard sets of photographs.
options.why: Correct. Given a picture with a cat’s shape and an elephant’s skin, such networks mostly said “elephant”, where people say “cat”.

options.text: A tendency to categorize images by their outline rather than their surface, found in people shown pictures whose shape and texture conflict.
options.why: That is the opposite tendency, the one people show: they chose shape about 96 percent of the time.

options.text: A tendency, built into convolutional networks by their wiring, to find a feature equally well wherever in an image it happens to appear.
options.why: That is the convolutional bet, an inductive bias in the architecture. Texture bias came from the training images, not the architecture.

options.text: A tendency to give confident wrong answers to images that have been changed slightly and on purpose, in ways a person would not notice.
options.why: That describes what adversarial examples produce. Texture bias is about relying on surface texture rather than shape.

items.stem: What is the name for a tendency to categorize images by the look of their surfaces, such as fur, skin, or bark, rather than by their outline, found in networks trained on standard collections of photographs?

options.text: Texture bias.
options.why: Correct. It came from the training images: the same architecture, trained on repainted photographs, relied on shape far more often.

options.text: Inductive bias.
options.why: An inductive bias is a tendency in what is easier to learn, set up before learning begins. Texture bias is a tendency in how a trained network categorizes, and it came from the training images.

options.text: Adversarial example.
options.why: An adversarial example is an input altered slightly to produce a confident wrong answer. It is not a general tendency to rely on surfaces.

options.text: Overfitting.
options.why: Overfitting is fitting the training examples so closely that new examples suffer. Relying on surface over outline is texture bias.

items.stem: A picture has the outline of a dog, filled in with the surface texture of tree bark. What would people, and a network trained on a standard collection of photographs, most likely say it is?

options.text: People would mostly say “dog”, going by shape, while the network would more likely name something with that bark texture.
options.why: Correct. People chose shape about 96 percent of the time in such pictures; networks trained on standard photographs chose shape only 17 to 43 percent of the time.

options.text: Both would mostly say “dog”, since people and networks trained on photographs both rely on an object’s outline above all.
options.why: People rely on shape, but networks trained on standard photographs mostly go by texture. That difference is texture bias.

options.text: People would mostly go by the bark texture, while the network would more likely say “dog”, going by the outline.
options.why: That reverses the finding. People go by shape; networks trained on standard photographs mostly go by texture.

options.text: Both would mostly name something with the bark texture, since texture covers far more of the picture than the outline does.
options.why: People mostly go by shape even when texture covers the picture. Only the networks mostly went by texture.

items.stem: Researchers trained the same network architecture on two sets of photographs: a standard collection, and the same photographs repainted in the styles of different paintings, which scrambled their textures. What did the comparison show about where texture bias comes from?

options.text: From the training images rather than the architecture: on repainted photographs, the same architecture learned to go by shape far more often.
options.why: Correct. The same architecture chose shape 81 percent of the time instead of 22. Only the training images had changed.

options.text: From the architecture rather than the training images: the same architecture went by texture after training on both sets of photographs alike.
options.why: The repainted training made a large difference, which could not happen if the bias were fixed by the architecture.

options.text: From the repainting itself: training on the repainted photographs led the network to go by texture even more often than before.
options.why: The effect ran the other way. With textures scrambled, the network went by shape far more often.

options.text: From the number of photographs: the repainted set was larger, and a larger set of any kind reduces texture bias by itself.
options.why: The two sets held the same photographs, repainted. What changed was whether texture went with the category, not how many images there were.

items.stem: A team’s network sorts beetles by species, and they find that it relies on the texture of the beetles’ shells rather than their body shape. One member says a new architecture is the only possible fix. In light of the repainting result, what is the best reply?

options.text: Changing the training images so shell texture no longer goes with the label may move the network toward outline, since what it learns depends on experience.
options.why: Correct. The same architecture moved from texture toward shape when only its training images changed. What a classifier learns is not set by its build alone.

options.text: Nothing can be done about it, since every network built from convolution and pooling relies on surface texture whatever images it is trained on.
options.why: The repainting result shows otherwise: the same architecture relied on shape far more often after training on texture-scrambled images.

options.text: A new architecture is indeed the one real fix, since the repainting result showed that texture bias is wired into the architecture of these networks.
options.why: The repainting result showed the reverse. Texture bias came from the training images rather than from the architecture.

options.text: Adding many more photographs from the same collection would probably help, since texture bias tends to shrink as a training set grows larger.
options.why: More images of the same kind keep texture going with species. The repainting worked by breaking that link, not by adding more images.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain the many-small-nudges explanation of adversarial examples, why the direction of the change matters, and how firmly the explanation is established.
items.answer: A unit computes a weighted sum over its inputs, and an image has many thousands of inputs. If every input is moved a tiny amount, each in the direction its weight favors, the tiny changes add up. No single pixel moves much, but the total crosses the decision boundary. On this explanation even a single unit should be fooled, and it is: a unit that told 3s from 7s accurately misclassified almost all inputs nudged along its own weights. The direction is what matters, since random noise of the same size rarely changes the answer. But this is one explanation. The researchers who first reported adversarial examples proposed a different cause, and the matter is still debated.
rubric: Says a unit computes a weighted sum over very many inputs.
Says nudging every input slightly in the direction its weight favors makes the tiny changes add up and cross the boundary.
Says random noise of the same size rarely changes the answer, so direction matters.
Says the explanation is one account that is still debated, not an established cause.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what texture bias is, and how comparing networks trained on standard and on repainted photographs located its source. What does the result show about what a classifier learns?
items.answer: Texture bias is a tendency to categorize images by their surface texture rather than their shape. Given a picture with a cat’s shape and an elephant’s skin, people say “cat”, while networks trained on a standard collection of photographs mostly said “elephant”. When the same architecture was trained on photographs repainted in the styles of different paintings, which scrambled their textures, it chose shape far more often, 81 percent of the time instead of 22. The architecture stayed the same and only the training images changed, so the bias came from the training images, not the architecture. What a classifier learns depends on its experience, and not only on how it is built.
rubric: Defines texture bias as categorizing by surface texture rather than shape.
Describes the comparison: the same architecture, trained on standard versus texture-scrambled photographs.
States that training on the repainted photographs made the network go by shape far more often.
Concludes that the bias came from the training images rather than the architecture.
States that what a classifier learns depends on its experience, not only on how it is built.

items.stem: In the new-predator scenario, a fish trained on eels and suckers in phase 1 is scored on the pike and chub test set before it has encountered either animal. The pike lunges and the chub is harmless. How did the fish do on that test set, and why?

options.text: Wrong on nearly every item: a pike’s smell is heavy on receptor B, like a sucker’s, and a chub’s is heavy on receptor A, like an eel’s, so it stayed for pikes and fled from chubs.
options.why: Correct. On the World tab a pike’s typical smell is heavy on B, as a sucker’s is, and a chub’s is heavy on A, as an eel’s is, and the pike and chub test set came out wrong on nearly every item. Shared weights give similar inputs similar outputs without any extra work, which is generalization, and here it carried the fish the wrong way.

options.text: Wrong on nearly every item: a pike’s smell is heavy on receptor A, like a sucker’s, and a chub’s is heavy on receptor B, like an eel’s, so it stayed for pikes and fled from chubs.
options.why: The fish was wrong for this reason, resemblance to the old animal of the other kind, but the receptors are swapped. An eel’s smell is heavier on A and a sucker’s on B, while a pike’s is heavy on B and a chub’s on A.

options.text: Wrong on about half: a pike’s and a chub’s smells each fall about midway between an eel’s and a sucker’s, so the fish’s answers to them were close to guesses.
options.why: A network gives some answer to every smell, and similar inputs get similar outputs. The pike and chub smells lie far out on the old animals’ sides, and the test set came out wrong on nearly every item, not on half.

options.text: Right on nearly every item: a pike’s smell is heavy on the same receptor as an eel’s, and a chub’s on the same receptor as a sucker’s, so it fled from pikes and stayed for chubs.
options.why: That would be true if each new animal resembled the old animal of its own kind. In the scene the pike smells like a sucker and the chub like an eel, so the fish got both backward.

items.stem: In the new-predator scenario, a fish trained on eels and suckers in phase 1, and nearly all right on them, moves to phase 2, where only the pike and the chub arrive, with learning on. How did its eel and sucker test set change over the next 1,000 encounters?

options.text: It was already far worse within the first 100 encounters, and by 1,000 it was wrong on nearly every item.
options.why: Correct. The old test set collapsed fast and went past chance to nearly all wrong. Learning the pike and chub moved the shared weights to treat a smell heavy on A as harmless and one heavy on B as dangerous, the reverse of what eels and suckers need. Like the network that answered ones problems as if they were twos problems, the fish answered the old animals by the new pair’s rule.

options.text: It barely changed in the first 100 encounters, then worsened steadily, and by 1,000 it was wrong on nearly every item.
options.why: The end point is right, but the loss was not slow to start. Within the first 100 encounters the old test set was already far worse; in a network trained by backpropagation, the disturbance can be extreme.

options.text: It was already far worse within the first 100 encounters, and then it recovered to about half wrong by 1,000 as the weights settled.
options.why: The weights did not settle at a blank state. They moved to suit the new pair, which reverses the old one, so the old test set ended wrong on nearly every item, not on half.

options.text: It barely changed over the whole 1,000 encounters, since the eel and sucker learning was carried by hidden units the new pair did not use.
options.why: Every weight takes part in many input–output pairs. The new learning moved the same weights the old pair depended on, and the old test set collapsed within the first 100 encounters.

items.stem: In the downstream scenario, a fish that learns only from near eels and suckers gets the far test set about half wrong. The run is repeated with Learn from every distance switched on, so that half its encounters are far. What happened to the near and far test sets?

options.text: The far test set came out nearly all right, and the near test set stayed nearly all right as well, with no new receptor added to the fish.
options.why: Correct. Trained with near and far encounters mixed, the fish ended nearly all right on both test sets. That is how artificial networks mostly get across changes of size: by training on examples that already include those changes. Whether training of that kind is enough to explain how animals do it is a live dispute.

options.text: The far test set came out nearly all right, but the near test set lost much of its accuracy, since only half the encounters were now near.
options.why: That trade-off is what many expect, but the near test set stayed nearly all right. Half the encounters near was plenty for the near smells.

options.text: The far test set improved only to about three in four right, since faint eel and sucker smells overlap too much for any line to separate them well.
options.why: The far test set came out nearly all right. Faint smells keep the eel’s larger share of A, so a line can separate them once the fish has learned from them.

options.text: Neither test set changed much, since a fish with no hidden units draws only one line, and no single line serves near and far smells alike.
options.why: One line did serve both. With far encounters in its training, the fish’s single line came to sort faint smells as well as strong ones, and both test sets ended nearly all right.

items.stem: In the new-predator scenario, the run is repeated from the same starting weights, but with Eels and suckers stay around switched on during phase 2, so the old animals keep arriving among the pike and the chub. In a few sentences, say what happened to both test sets, including how the eel and sucker test set behaved early in phase 2, and explain why mixing the animals was enough, using what the chapter names as the trigger for catastrophic interference.
items.answer: Both test sets ended nearly all right, within a few percent of perfect. On the way, the eel and sucker line jumped up and down for the first few hundred encounters of phase 2 before it settled. The fish, the network and the rule were the same as before; only the mix of encounters changed. The trigger for catastrophic interference is learning in sequence: trained on one set and then another, the weights move to wherever suits the newest set. With both sets arriving together, a change that suited the new animals but hurt the old ones was pulled back by the old animals’ errors, so the weights settled where both were right.
rubric: Reports that both test sets ended nearly all right.
Reports that the eel and sucker line jumped up and down for the first few hundred encounters before settling.
Says nothing about the fish, the network or the rule changed, only the mix of encounters.
Names learning in sequence as the trigger.
Explains that with both sets present the weights move to a setting that suits both, not to wherever suits the newest set.

pools.title: Kinds of Failure, and What Has to Be Built In
pools.covers: reading §7.2.12, §7.2.13, §7.2.14 · lecture 7.2 slides fooled_and_far_from_home, gaps_or_something_missing, what_has_to_be_built_in

items.stem: What is overfitting?

options.text: Fitting the training examples so closely, accidents included, that performance on new examples suffers.
options.why: Correct. An overfit network does well on the examples it was trained on and poorly on new ones, because it has fit accidents that new examples do not share.

options.text: Failing to fit the training examples at all, so that performance is poor on old and new examples alike.
options.why: That is a failure to learn anything, not overfitting. An overfit network does well on its training examples; the trouble shows up only on new ones.

options.text: Giving a confident wrong answer to an input that someone has changed slightly and deliberately.
options.why: That describes an adversarial example. Overfitting is about the gap between performance on the training examples and performance on new ones.

options.text: Losing old learning drastically when new patterns are learned after old ones, because shared weights move.
options.why: That is catastrophic interference, which appears when learning happens in sequence. Overfitting is fitting the accidents of the training examples too closely.

items.stem: A network fits its training examples so closely, including the accidents in them, that its performance on new examples suffers. What is this called?

options.text: Overfitting.
options.why: Correct. A high score on the training examples is not the measure that matters, and overfitting is why.

options.text: Texture bias.
options.why: Texture bias is a tendency to categorize images by surface texture rather than shape. It comes from the training data, but it is a specific bias, not the general gap between old and new examples.

options.text: Catastrophic interference.
options.why: Catastrophic interference is a drastic loss of old learning when new patterns are learned afterward. It concerns learning in sequence, not fitting accidents.

options.text: Out-of-distribution generalization.
options.why: Out-of-distribution generalization is generalizing to inputs unlike anything in training. It names an ability that current classifiers are weak at, not the fitting of accidents.

items.stem: A network is trained to identify bird species from photographs. It labels 99.8 percent of its training photographs correctly, but only 70 percent of new photographs of the same species. What does the gap most likely show?

options.text: The network fit its training photographs closely, accidents and all, which is what overfitting means.
