options.why: Correct. A score on the training examples is not the measure that matters. Accidents of those photographs, such as a background or a quirk of lighting, are not shared by new ones.

options.text: The new photographs were adversarial examples, changed slightly and deliberately by someone.
options.why: Adversarial examples are deliberately altered inputs, and nothing here says the new photographs were altered. A high training score with a much lower score on new examples is the mark of overfitting.

options.text: The network lost its old learning, because testing it on new photographs moved its weights.
options.why: That would be catastrophic interference, which needs new learning after old. Testing a network on new photographs does not train it, so its weights do not move.

options.text: The network was trained too briefly, and more training passes over the same photographs would close the gap.
options.why: Undertraining would show up as errors on the training photographs too, and those are almost all right already. The gap is between the photographs learned from and new ones, which is the mark of overfitting.

items.stem: When an artificial classifier is built, what is its training set?

options.text: The examples the learner learns from, as distinct from any examples kept apart to evaluate it afterward.
options.why: Correct. The training set is the examples a learner learns from. A separate test set is kept apart and used only for evaluation.

options.text: The examples kept apart from training and used only afterward to evaluate how well the learner does.
options.why: That describes the test set. The training set is what the learner learns from, and it is exactly what the test set must be kept apart from.

options.text: The inputs an engineer decides on before learning begins, chosen because they carry the structure that matters.
options.why: Choosing the inputs before learning begins is feature engineering. The training set is the collection of examples the learner then learns from.

options.text: The inputs unlike anything the learner has seen, used to measure how far its performance carries.
options.why: Inputs unlike anything in training are what out-of-distribution generalization is about. The training set is the familiar material itself.

items.stem: What is the name for the examples a learner learns from?

options.text: Training set.
options.why: Correct. The training set is what a learner learns from, and a separate test set is kept apart to evaluate it.

options.text: Test set.
options.why: A test set is examples kept apart from training and used only to evaluate a learner. It is never learned from.

options.text: Prototype.
options.why: A prototype is a summary of a category, such as its average member. It is computed from examples, but it is not the set of examples itself.

options.text: Feature space.
options.why: A feature space is a space with one axis for each feature of an input, in which each input is a single point. Training examples can be placed in one, but the space is not the examples themselves.

items.stem: What is a test set?

options.text: Examples kept apart from training, never used to adjust the learner, and used only to evaluate it.
options.why: Correct. Because a network can fit its training examples and still do poorly on new ones, classifiers are scored on examples they never learned from.

options.text: The examples a learner learned from, run through it again at the end to check what it learned.
options.why: Scoring a learner on its own training examples is exactly what a test set exists to avoid, since a network can fit those examples and still do poorly on new ones.

options.text: A set of inputs unlike anything in training, gathered to measure how far a learner can extrapolate.
options.why: A test set is usually drawn from the same collection as the training set, so it holds inputs like the training examples, not unlike them.

options.text: A set of inputs changed slightly and deliberately, gathered to find out whether a network can be fooled.
options.why: Slightly and deliberately changed inputs are adversarial examples. A test set is just ordinary examples that were held back from training.

items.stem: Researchers set aside some examples, never use them in training, and use them only to evaluate the learner afterward. What are those examples called?

options.text: The test set.
options.why: Correct. A test set is kept apart from training, so a score on it shows how the learner does on examples it never learned from.

options.text: The training set.
options.why: The training set is the examples a learner learns from. The examples set aside for evaluation are the test set.

options.text: The exemplars.
options.why: Exemplars are the stored examples of a category that an exemplar model compares a new input with. They are the examples a model learned from, not ones held back.

options.text: The adversarial examples.
options.why: Adversarial examples are inputs changed slightly and deliberately so that a network gives a confident wrong answer. They are not simply held-back examples.

items.stem: A teacher builds a final exam by copying questions word for word from the practice sets the class worked through. A student who memorized the practice answers scores 98 percent. By the reasoning used for artificial classifiers, why is that score a poor measure of what the student learned?

options.text: The exam reused the very examples the student learned from, so it cannot separate fitting them from doing well on new ones.
options.why: Correct. That is why classifiers are scored on a test set kept apart from training. A score on the training examples cannot show whether the learner fit their accidents or learned something that carries over.

options.text: The exam held questions unlike anything practiced, so it measured out-of-distribution generalization instead of what was learned.
options.why: The questions were copied from the practice sets, so they were the most familiar inputs possible, not unfamiliar ones. The trouble is that they were the training examples themselves.

options.text: The exam scored the student too highly, and any score above 90 percent is evidence of overfitting, whatever questions are used.
options.why: No score is a sign of overfitting by itself. What matters is whether the examples scored were kept apart from the examples learned from.

options.text: The exam measured how readily the student answered, which is a criterion, while learning is a matter of sensitivity alone.
options.why: Criterion and sensitivity are a real distinction, from signal detection theory, but they are not the issue here. The exam fails because it reused the training examples.

items.stem: The digit-reading network made 0.14 percent errors on the 7,291 digits it was trained on, and 5.0 percent errors on 2,007 digits it had never seen. What does the difference between those two error rates show?

options.text: A network’s score on its training examples overstates how well it does on examples that were kept apart from training.
options.why: Correct. The network made many times more errors on new digits than on its training digits. That gap is why a score on the training set is not the measure that matters.

options.text: The network’s convolutional design failed, since shared weights should make every digit equally easy to read.
options.why: The digit-reading network’s design helped it, and it did better on new digits than a fully connected network with about as many weights. Shared weights reduced its errors on new digits without closing the gap to its training digits.

options.text: The new digits were out of distribution, since a test set is drawn from a different collection than the training set.
options.why: A test set is drawn from the same collection as the training set. The gap here is between examples learned from and examples held back, not between familiar and unfamiliar kinds of input.

options.text: The network suffered catastrophic interference, losing what it knew about the training digits while it read the new ones.
options.why: Reading new digits is testing, not training, so it moves no weights. Catastrophic interference needs new learning after old.

items.stem: A network is trained and tested on handwritten digits collected from forms in one country, and scores 99 percent on its test set. It is then used on digits from a country where a seven carries a crossbar and a one has a long upward stroke. Why should the test score not be taken as a guide to how it will do there?

options.text: Its test set came from the same collection as its training set, so it measured inputs like those it trained on.
options.why: Correct. Even a good test-set score is a score on inputs like the training set. Digits in an unfamiliar style lie outside that collection, where current classifiers are much weaker.

options.text: Its test score was earned on digits it had already been trained on, since a test set reuses the training examples.
options.why: A test set is kept apart and never used in training, so the score was earned on new digits. The problem is that the new digits were of the same kind as the training digits.

options.text: Its test set was too small, and more digits from the same forms would have revealed how it handles the new styles.
options.why: More digits from the same forms would still be in the familiar style. No amount of familiar material shows how a classifier does on inputs unlike anything in training.

options.text: Its test score is a measure of overfitting, and a network that scores so well on a test set has always overfit.
options.why: A high test score is evidence against overfitting, since overfitting shows up as poor performance on new examples. The limitation lies in what kind of new examples the test set held.

items.stem: What is out-of-distribution generalization?

options.text: Generalization to inputs unlike anything a learner was trained on, beyond the collection its examples came from.
options.why: Correct. It goes beyond doing well on a test set, which holds new inputs from the same collection as the training examples.

options.text: Generalization to new inputs drawn from the same collection as the training examples, as in a test set.
options.why: That is what a good test-set score shows. Out-of-distribution generalization is the harder case, inputs unlike anything in training.

options.text: The fall-off in responding to a new input as it differs more and more from the input trained on.
options.why: That is a generalization gradient, a description of how responding declines with difference. Out-of-distribution generalization is the ability to handle inputs far from training at all.

options.text: Fitting the accidents of the training examples, so that performance on any new example suffers.
options.why: That is overfitting. Out-of-distribution generalization is an ability, the one current classifiers are much weaker at than at handling familiar inputs.

items.stem: What is the name for generalizing to inputs unlike anything in a learner’s training?

options.text: Out-of-distribution generalization.
options.why: Correct. Current classifiers are much weaker at it than at handling inputs among their familiar examples.

options.text: Invariance.
options.why: Invariance is recognizing one thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as changes of viewpoint. It can fail out of distribution, but it names a different demand.

options.text: Generalization gradient.
options.why: A generalization gradient is the fall-off in responding as a new input differs more from a trained one. It describes behavior; it is not the name for generalizing far from training.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. It works from familiar patterns rather than inputs unlike anything learned.

items.stem: A network learns to tell cats from dogs from many thousands of daylight photographs of adult animals of many breeds. Which new photograph is it most likely to label correctly?

options.text: A daylight photograph of an adult cat of an unfamiliar breed that looks much like the breeds in its training.
options.why: Correct. Current classifiers interpolate well among familiar examples and extrapolate poorly beyond them. A new cat that resembles the training cats lands among familiar examples.

options.text: An infrared photograph of an adult cat taken at night by a wildlife camera, whose outline matches the cats in its training.
options.why: A matching outline does not make the input familiar. An infrared image at night is unlike anything in training, which is where current classifiers extrapolate poorly.

options.text: A child’s crayon drawing of a cat, since a drawing shows only the features shared by all breeds and none of the accidents.
options.why: A drawing is far from every daylight photograph the network learned from. Having fewer accidents does not bring an input closer to the training examples.

options.text: A blurred daylight photograph of a kitten, since blurring removes the fine detail where overfitting usually takes hold.
options.why: Blur and youth both move the input away from the training examples. Overfitting is not removed by degrading a new input.

items.stem: Why is arithmetic in early large language models a good demonstration of how current networks perform out of distribution?

options.text: The models were trained only to predict the next word in text and never taught arithmetic, so their sums show how far next-word training carries.
options.why: Correct. Nothing in their training was about arithmetic, so their answers to addition problems show how performance holds up, or fails to, as problems move away from familiar text.

options.text: The models were trained on every addition problem up to five digits, so their errors show forgetting instead of generalization.
options.why: The models were never taught arithmetic, and almost none of even the three-digit problems appeared in their training text. Their errors are not forgetting.

options.text: The models were taught the rules of carrying in addition, so their errors on long numbers show how rules fail far from training.
options.why: The models were never taught arithmetic at all. That is what makes their performance a demonstration of generalization rather than of rule-following.

options.text: The models were tested only on problems found in their training text, so their scores show how closely they fit their examples.
options.why: Almost none of the three-digit problems appeared in the training text, so the models were not just being scored on their training examples.

items.stem: Early large language models answered most three-digit addition problems correctly, although almost none of those problems appeared anywhere in their training text. How does the chapter explain this success?

options.text: Numbers of three-digit size are common in text, so each new problem sat among many familiar ones in the training text.
options.why: Correct. The success is explained by familiar neighbors, not by the models having learned arithmetic. That is also why the success did not last as the numbers grew.

options.text: The models had worked out the rules of addition from text, and applied those rules to every new problem.
options.why: If the models had learned the rules of addition, they would not have fallen to about a quarter correct with four-digit numbers. The success came from familiar neighbors.

options.text: The models carried a built-in bias toward arithmetic, placed in their wiring before training the way convolution is placed in a network.
options.why: The models were trained only to predict the next word and were never given anything for arithmetic. Their three-digit success came from familiar numbers in text.

options.text: The models had memorized each three-digit problem, since text contains the sum of almost every pair of such numbers.
options.why: Almost none of the three-digit problems appeared in the training text, so there was nothing to memorize. The numbers were familiar; the problems were not.

items.stem: Early large language models were perfect on two-digit addition, right on most three-digit problems, right about a quarter of the time with four digits, and about one time in ten with five. On the chapter’s account, what does this fall in accuracy show?

options.text: Reliability falls as the problems move further and further from the region of input that the training examples occupy.
options.why: Correct. Four- and five-digit problems sit further from familiar text, and a classifier is reliable near its training examples and much less reliable far from them.

options.text: Reliability falls as the models forget their two-digit learning, because longer problems are learned later and overwrite it.
options.why: Losing old learning to new is catastrophic interference, which needs learning in sequence. The models were never taught arithmetic at all, so there was no sequence of lessons.

options.text: Reliability falls because the models overfit their two-digit examples, leaving nothing over for longer sums.
options.why: Overfitting is fitting the accidents of training examples. Nothing suggests the two-digit successes left less for longer sums; the decline tracks distance from familiar input.

options.text: Reliability falls because each extra digit adds a step that needs a hidden layer, and the models had none to spare.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter ties the decline to a shortage of hidden layers. It explains the decline by how far longer problems lie from the familiar ones.

items.stem: A network learns to recognize chairs from thousands of photographs, all taken at about eye level. It recognizes new chairs at eye level well, but often fails on a chair photographed from directly overhead. Which description fits this failure?

options.text: The overhead view lies far from the training examples, a case of weak out-of-distribution generalization across a change of angle.
options.why: Correct. A network trained on familiar angles often fails on the same objects seen from unusual ones. The overhead view is far from the region its training examples occupy.

options.text: The overhead photograph is an adversarial example, since someone changed it slightly and deliberately to produce a confident wrong answer.
options.why: Nothing about the overhead photograph was altered deliberately or slightly. It is an ordinary photograph from an angle the training never included.

options.text: The network has texture bias, since an overhead view shows the seat’s fabric and hides the shape that people use to recognize chairs.
options.why: Texture bias is a real failure of networks trained on standard photographs, but nothing here shows the network relied on fabric. The failure tracks the unfamiliar angle.

options.text: The network has catastrophic interference, since learning the eye-level chairs wiped out what it had learned about chairs seen from above.
options.why: The network never learned chairs seen from above, so there was nothing to wipe out. It simply had no training examples near that view.

items.stem: The lecture describes classifiers that fail out of distribution as “lost far from home”. Picturing a classifier’s inputs as points in a feature space, what plays the part of home?

options.text: The region of the feature space that the classifier’s training examples occupy.
options.why: Correct. A classifier is reliable near the region its training examples occupy and much less reliable far from it, so distance from that region is what makes a classifier lost.

options.text: The region of the feature space far from the decision boundary, where the classifier’s answers are most certain.
options.why: An input can be far from the boundary and also far from every training example. A confident answer there is not a reliable one, because the classifier has nothing familiar nearby.

options.text: The prototype at the center of each category, which every new input is compared with.
options.why: Prototypes belong to one family of categorization models. Reliability in the lecture’s sense depends on nearness to the training examples, whatever the model stores.

options.text: The test set, which holds the inputs the classifier has not been trained on yet.
options.why: A test set is drawn from the same collection as the training set, so it lies at home too. Out-of-distribution inputs are the ones that lie away from it.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why a network’s score on its training set, and even its score on a test set, can both overstate how well it will do on inputs unlike anything it was trained on.
items.answer: A score on the training set can be high because the network has fit its training examples closely, accidents included, and still does poorly on new examples. That is overfitting, and it is why classifiers are scored on a separate test set, kept apart and never used in training. But a test set is drawn from the same collection of examples as the training set, so a good test score is still a score on inputs like the training examples. Current classifiers interpolate well among familiar examples and extrapolate poorly beyond them, so inputs unlike anything in training can bring much worse performance than either score suggests.
rubric: Explains that a training-set score can reflect overfitting, fitting the accidents of the training examples.
States that a test set is kept apart from training and used only to evaluate.
States that a test set is drawn from the same collection as the training set, so it measures inputs like the training examples.
Says that current classifiers are much weaker out of distribution, interpolating well and extrapolating poorly.

items.stem: Early large language models were never taught arithmetic, yet answered most three-digit addition problems correctly, and then did much worse with four and five digits. In a short paragraph, explain both the success and the decline, using the idea of a region of a feature space.
items.answer: The models were trained only to predict the next word in a huge collection of text. Almost none of the three-digit problems appeared in that text, but numbers of three-digit size are common in it, so a new three-digit problem sat among many familiar ones. The models were interpolating among familiar examples, not doing arithmetic. Four- and five-digit problems lie further from anything in the text, and accuracy fell to about a quarter and then about one time in ten. In feature-space terms, the training examples occupy a region, and a classifier is reliable near that region and much less reliable far from it.
rubric: States that the models were trained only to predict the next word and were never taught arithmetic.
Explains the three-digit success by familiar neighbors, numbers of that size being common in text, not by learned arithmetic.
Describes the decline with four and five digits as problems lying further from the training examples.
Uses the feature-space picture: reliable near the region of the training examples, much less reliable far from it.

items.stem: Not every failure of current classifiers is the same kind of failure. Which group does the chapter class as gaps in pattern recognition itself, gaps a better classifier could in principle close?

options.text: Adversarial examples, texture bias, overfitting, and failure out of distribution.
options.why: Correct. These four are gaps in pattern recognition itself. Catastrophic interference is a gap of a different kind, in the learning procedure, and the remaining failures look like marks of later capacities.

options.text: Adversarial examples, catastrophic interference, overfitting, and reasoning about causes.
options.why: Catastrophic interference lies in the learning procedure, and reasoning about causes looks like a mark of a capacity that pattern recognition alone does not supply.

options.text: Systematicity, reasoning about causes, and knowing what an object is like beyond recognizing it.
options.why: These three are the ones that look like marks of capacities pattern recognition alone does not supply. A better classifier is not expected to close them by itself.

options.text: Catastrophic interference, texture bias, systematicity, and failure out of distribution.
options.why: Texture bias and failure out of distribution belong in the group, but catastrophic interference is a gap in the learning procedure, and systematicity looks like a mark of a later capacity.

items.stem: A network learns to recognize twenty kinds of birds by their songs. It is then trained only on twenty kinds of frogs by their calls, and afterward it misnames most of the birds. How does the chapter classify a failure of this kind?

options.text: As a gap in the learning procedure, which appears when learning happens in sequence, one set after another.
options.why: Correct. This is catastrophic interference. Trained on birds and frogs together, the same network could learn both; trained on one and then the other, the new learning moves weights the old depended on.

options.text: As a gap in pattern recognition itself, of the same kind as overfitting and texture bias.
options.why: Overfitting and texture bias are gaps in pattern recognition itself. Losing the birds after learning the frogs lies in how the learning was done, in sequence.

options.text: As a mark of a later capacity, of the same kind as systematicity and reasoning about causes.
options.why: Marks of later capacities are things pattern recognition alone may not supply. The network could recognize the birds; it lost that ability through the order of its training.

options.text: As a failure out of distribution, since the bird songs became unfamiliar while the frogs were being learned.
options.why: The bird songs are the same inputs the network was trained on. They did not move away from training; the weights that handled them moved.

items.stem: Overfitting and catastrophic interference both leave a network doing badly on inputs it ought to handle. Why does the chapter sort them as different kinds of failure?

options.text: Overfitting is a gap in pattern recognition; catastrophic interference is a gap in the learning procedure, appearing with learning in sequence.
options.why: Correct. A better classifier could in principle close the gaps in pattern recognition. Catastrophic interference is about the order of learning: the same network trained on everything at once does not suffer it.

options.text: Overfitting is a mark of a capacity pattern recognition does not supply, while catastrophic interference is a gap a better classifier could close.
options.why: That reverses the sorting and misplaces both. Overfitting is a gap in pattern recognition, and catastrophic interference is a gap in the learning procedure.

options.text: Overfitting happens only in animals, while catastrophic interference happens only in artificial networks trained by backpropagation.
options.why: Overfitting is described for artificial classifiers, and people forget too when they learn conflicting lists in sequence. The difference is in the kind of gap, not in who has it.

options.text: Overfitting comes from the training data, while catastrophic interference comes from small deliberate changes made after training ends.
options.why: Small deliberate changes produce adversarial examples. Catastrophic interference comes from new learning moving weights that old learning depended on.

items.stem: A classifier correctly labels a photograph of a refrigerator. Why might knowing that the refrigerator is heavy and rigid, and what would happen if it were pushed, be a different matter?

options.text: Recognizing it is pattern recognition, but knowing what it is like and what pushing it would do may draw on something more.
options.why: Correct. Failures here look like marks of capacities that pattern recognition alone does not supply, and the chapter keeps the hedge: knowing these things may draw on something more.

options.text: Knowing the refrigerator is heavy is pattern recognition, but recognizing it in a photograph is a mark of a later capacity.
options.why: That reverses the two. Recognizing the refrigerator is the pattern recognition; knowing what it is like goes beyond its pattern.

options.text: Knowing the refrigerator is heavy needs a test set kept apart from training, while recognizing it needs only a training set.
options.why: Training and test sets are about scoring a classifier fairly. They do not separate recognizing an object from knowing what it is like.

options.text: Knowing the refrigerator is heavy is a kind of texture bias, since weight shows up in the surface texture of a photograph.
options.why: Texture bias is a tendency to categorize by surface texture rather than shape. Weight and what happens when something is pushed are not in a photograph’s texture.

items.stem: What is systematicity?

options.text: The ability to combine known parts in new ways, so that understanding one combination brings understanding of others made from the same parts.
options.why: Correct. Anyone who understands “the eel chased the fish” also understands “the fish chased the eel”. Systematicity may draw on something more than pattern recognition.

options.text: The ability to recognize one thing across changes that alter its input a great deal, such as changes of distance, position, or viewpoint.
options.why: That is invariance. Systematicity is about combining known parts in new ways, not about recognizing one thing across changes.

options.text: The ability to recover a whole stored pattern from only part of it, as when a faint or partial trace of a familiar smell brings back the whole.
options.why: That is pattern completion. Systematicity is about understanding new combinations of known parts.

options.text: The ability to sort things by a definition, with every member of a category having every one of the defining features.
options.why: Sorting by necessary and sufficient features is the classical view of categories. Systematicity is about combining parts, not about defining a category.

items.stem: What is the name for the ability to combine known parts in new ways, so that understanding one combination brings with it the understanding of others built from the same parts?

options.text: Systematicity.
options.why: Correct. Systematicity may draw on something more than pattern recognition, which is why its absence in a network looks like a mark of a later capacity.

options.text: Generalization.
options.why: Generalization is treating alike the inputs that call for the same response. Understanding a new combination of known parts is a different ability.

options.text: Distributed representation.
options.why: A distributed representation is a code in which each thing is a pattern across many units. It is a kind of code, not an ability to combine parts into new wholes.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. Systematicity builds new wholes from known parts rather than restoring old ones.

items.stem: A robot has learned to carry out the instruction “put the cup on the box”. Without any further training, it also carries out “put the box on the cup” correctly. What capacity does the second success show?

options.text: Systematicity, combining known parts in new ways.
options.why: Correct. Understanding one arrangement of the parts brings with it understanding of another made from the same parts, as with “the eel chased the fish” and “the fish chased the eel”.

options.text: Generalization, treating alike inputs that call for one response.
options.why: The two instructions call for different responses, so this is not treating them alike. The robot combined the same parts in a new way and acted on the new combination.

options.text: Invariance, recognizing one thing across large changes.
options.why: The two instructions are not one thing seen differently; they mean different things. What the robot shows is the ability to understand a new combination.

options.text: Pattern completion, recovering a whole from part of it.
options.why: Nothing here was partial. The robot received a complete new instruction built from known parts and understood it.

items.stem: Reasoning about causes, language, and the use of symbols are taken up separately in the course, not treated as further problems of pattern recognition. What is the reason for setting them apart?

options.text: Failures in them look like marks of capacities pattern recognition alone does not supply, as each may draw on something more.
options.why: Correct. Causes and planning, language, and symbols are each taken up in a later module of their own, because they may need more than recognizing patterns.

options.text: Failures in them are gaps in pattern recognition itself, which a better classifier could close without anything new being added.
options.why: Those gaps are adversarial examples, texture bias, overfitting, and failure out of distribution. Causes, language, and symbols are set apart because they may need something more.

options.text: Failures in them are gaps in the learning procedure, which appear only when the parts of a task are learned in sequence.
options.why: That describes catastrophic interference. The capacities set apart here are not about the order of learning; they may draw on something beyond pattern recognition.

options.text: Failures in them come from the input space, which pattern recognition takes as given and so cannot be asked to explain.
options.why: The input space is one of the candidates for what is built in, and it matters for pattern recognition too. It is not why causes, language, and symbols are set apart.

items.stem: A whale and a submarine are much alike in shape, size, and the ability to dive deep. They are very different in what they are made of and in how they came to exist. What argument about similarity does this pair illustrate?

options.text: Anything is similar to anything else in some respect, so similarity alone cannot say which respects matter.
options.why: Correct. This is the argument illustrated by the cloud and the white feather: alike in color and in floating, unlike in size and use. Similarity does not say which comparisons count.

options.text: Two things alike in shape are always in the same category, so shape is the respect that matters most.
options.why: The whale and the submarine are alike in shape and are plainly not the same kind of thing. The argument is that similarity alone cannot pick out which respects matter.

options.text: Similarity measured in physical units predicts generalization well, so the shared size settles the category.
options.why: Closeness in physical units is not a good predictor of how animals generalize. And the pair shows that physical likeness leaves the category unsettled.

options.text: Two things are similar only when their prototypes match, so a whale and a submarine cannot be compared at all.
options.why: Prototypes are one way of using similarity, not a condition for it. The whale and the submarine can be compared in many respects; the trouble is choosing among them.

items.stem: Some researchers argue that similarity cannot be what holds a category together. Why does that argument bear on prototype, exemplar, and nearest-neighbor models alike?

options.text: All three rest on similarity, sorting a new input by its closeness to what is stored in a feature space.
options.why: Correct. A prototype model compares with summaries, an exemplar model with every stored member, and a nearest-neighbor model with the closest few, but all three sort by similarity.

options.text: All three store a decision boundary directly, and a stored boundary is itself a measure of similarity.
options.why: Storing the boundary directly is what a decision-bound model does. Prototype, exemplar, and nearest-neighbor models store something about members and sort by similarity.

options.text: All three are definitions, and a definition lists the similar features that every member must share.
options.why: Definitions belong to the classical view, a different account of categories from these three models. All three of these models rest on similarity, not on definitions.

options.text: All three need hidden layers trained by backpropagation, and backpropagation works by computing similarity.
options.why: None of the three needs backpropagation. What they share is that each sorts by closeness in a feature space.

items.stem: On the alternative to similarity that the chapter describes, what holds a category together?

options.text: A theory, an understanding of why the category’s members have the particular features they do.
options.why: Correct. On this alternative, members belong together because of why they have their features, not just because they resemble one another. It is one alternative, and the question is still debated.

options.text: A prototype, the average member that each new input is compared with to assign its category.
options.why: A prototype is a summary used by a similarity-based model. The alternative replaces similarity with an understanding of why members have their features.

options.text: A definition, a list of features each member must have and that together guarantee membership.
options.why: A definition belongs to the classical view. The alternative described here is a theory about why members have the features they do.

options.text: A decision boundary, a single line through the feature space with every member on one side.
options.why: A decision boundary divides a feature space. The alternative to similarity is not a boundary but an understanding of why members have their features.

items.stem: In one study, children were told about a raccoon that doctors had changed to look and smell like a skunk. What did older children usually say, and what did their answer follow?

options.text: That it was still a raccoon, an answer that followed what the animal was underneath, not its looks.
options.why: Correct. Their answer followed what the animal was underneath. Knowing that goes beyond the animal’s pattern, as knowing a refrigerator is heavy does.

options.text: That it was now a skunk, an answer that followed how the animal looked and smelled after the change.
options.why: That is the answer appearance alone would give. Older children usually said the animal was still a raccoon.

options.text: That it was neither animal, an answer that followed from the change leaving it without a category.
options.why: The children did not leave the animal uncategorized. Older children usually kept it in its original category.

options.text: That it was partly each animal, an answer that followed how typical it was of the two categories.
options.why: Typicality describes how good an example a member is. The children’s answer followed what the animal was underneath, and it was still a raccoon.

items.stem: A lemon is coated and scented so that it looks, feels, and smells exactly like an orange. Inside, it still has lemon juice and lemon seeds. On the view that a category is held together by a theory, why might a person still call it a lemon?

options.text: What makes it a lemon is what it is underneath, the reason for its features, which goes beyond its outward pattern.
options.why: Correct. On the theory view, membership follows an understanding of why members have their features. Knowing what the fruit is underneath goes beyond its pattern, as with the raccoon changed to look like a skunk.

options.text: It sits closest to the lemon prototype in a feature space built from its color, its surface texture, and its smell.
options.why: In color, texture, and smell, the coated fruit now matches an orange. Closeness on those features points the wrong way; the theory view looks beneath them.

options.text: It is out of distribution for the person, who falls back on the nearest familiar category, which is the lemon.
options.why: Out-of-distribution failure is about inputs unlike anything in training, and it describes classifiers. The theory view explains the answer by what the fruit is underneath.

options.text: Its surface features carry texture bias, so the person relies on its shape, which is still the shape of a lemon.
options.why: The fruit was made to look exactly like an orange, shape included. The theory view rests the answer on what the fruit is underneath, not on any surface feature.

items.stem: How much of the work of holding a category together does similarity do, as the chapter leaves the question?

options.text: For a fish’s categories of smell it may do most of the work; for human concepts, the share is still an active debate.
options.why: Correct. The argument against similarity and the theory view are presented as one side of an open question. For a fish’s smells similarity may carry most of the load, and for human concepts the share is debated.

options.text: Very little of the work for any animal, since the argument against similarity has shown that it cannot hold a category together.
options.why: The argument is one that some researchers make, and the chapter does not treat it as settled. For a fish’s smells, similarity may carry most of the load.

options.text: All of the work for human concepts, and little for a fish’s smells, which a fish holds together by its theories about them.
options.why: That reverses the chapter’s suggestion. Similarity may carry most of the load for a fish’s smells, and for human concepts the share is debated.

options.text: Most of the work for people and fish alike, since the theory view applies to categories that can be named in words.
options.why: The chapter does not limit the theory view to named categories, and it leaves the share for human concepts open.

items.stem: Some researchers argue that current networks are missing pieces that people have. How settled is the question of whether those pieces have to be built in?

options.text: Whether they must be built in or can be learned from enough of the right experience is open, even among those researchers.
options.why: Correct. Even researchers who agree that something is missing do not agree about whether it has to be built in.

options.text: Those researchers agree that the pieces must be built in, since experience alone has never changed what a network learns.
options.why: Experience does change what a network learns: the texture-bias networks learned shape once their training images changed. And those researchers do not agree.

options.text: Those researchers agree that the pieces can be learned, since every network that changed its experience came to learn them.
options.why: One piece of evidence, the texture-bias networks, points toward learning, but another, the digit-reading network, points toward what is built in. There is no agreement.

options.text: The question of whether they must be built in has been settled in favor of building in, since the digit-reading network generalized better.
options.why: The digit-reading network is evidence on one side, not a settlement. The question remains an open dispute.

items.stem: The digit-reading network and the texture-bias networks are both offered as evidence about whether missing pieces have to be built in or can be learned. How does each bear on that question?

options.text: The digit-reading network generalized better because of what was built into it, and the texture-bias networks learned shape once their experience changed.
options.why: Correct. The two are evidence on the two sides of the dispute, and neither settles it.

options.text: The digit-reading network learned shape once its experience changed, and the texture-bias networks generalized better because of what was built into them.
options.why: That swaps the two cases. The digit-reading network’s advantage came from its built-in design, and the texture-bias networks changed with their training images.

options.text: Both show that what is built in settles everything, since each network’s architecture fixed in advance what it could come to learn.
options.why: The texture-bias networks kept their architecture and still changed from texture to shape when their training changed. The two cases point in different directions.

options.text: Both show that experience settles everything, since each network learned whatever its training examples happened to contain.
options.why: The digit-reading network did better than a fully connected network with about as many weights because of its design. The two cases point in different directions.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why texture bias and catastrophic interference are sorted as different kinds of failure, and then name and describe a failure of a third kind.
items.answer: Texture bias is a gap in pattern recognition itself, produced by the training data, and a better classifier could in principle close it. Catastrophic interference is a gap of a different kind. It lies in the learning procedure, and it appears when learning happens in sequence: the same network trained on everything at once does not suffer it. A third kind of failure looks like a mark of a capacity that pattern recognition alone does not supply. Systematicity is one: anyone who understands “the eel chased the fish” also understands “the fish chased the eel”, and that may draw on something more than recognizing patterns.
rubric: Classes texture bias as a gap in pattern recognition that a better classifier could in principle close.
Classes catastrophic interference as a gap in the learning procedure, appearing when learning happens in sequence.
Names a mark of a later capacity: knowing what an object is like, reasoning about causes, or systematicity.
Describes that third kind as something pattern recognition alone may not supply, keeping the hedge.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the argument that similarity cannot be what holds a category together, describe one alternative, and say how settled the question is.
items.answer: Prototype, exemplar, and nearest-neighbor models all rest on similarity. Some researchers argue that similarity cannot be what holds a category together, because anything is similar to anything else in some respect. A cloud and a white feather are very similar in color and in floating, and very different in size and in what they can be used for, so similarity alone cannot say which respects matter. On one alternative, a category is held together by a theory, an understanding of why its members have the features they do; older children said a raccoon changed to look like a skunk was still a raccoon. The question is not settled. For a fish’s smells similarity may carry most of the load, and for human concepts the share is still debated.
rubric: States that prototype, exemplar, and nearest-neighbor models all rest on similarity.
Gives the argument that anything is similar to anything in some respect, so similarity cannot say which respects matter, with an example.
Describes the theory alternative: an understanding of why members have the features they do.
Says the question is open, with similarity perhaps carrying most of the load for a fish’s smells and debated for human concepts.

items.stem: Whether the missing pieces of current classifiers have to be built in is a modern form of the debate between nativists and empiricists. How does each side explain a capacity?

options.text: Nativists explain it by what an animal starts out with, and empiricists by learning and experience.
options.why: Correct. The question about classifiers is the same debate, introduced in Module 2, asked of networks.

options.text: Nativists explain it by learning and experience, and empiricists by what an animal starts out with.
options.why: That reverses the two sides. Nativists appeal to what an animal starts out with, and empiricists to learning and experience.

options.text: Nativists explain it by natural selection on the species, and empiricists by the animal’s receptors.
options.why: Receptors are something an animal starts out with, so appealing to them is a nativist move. Empiricists explain a capacity by learning and experience.

options.text: Nativists explain it by the animal’s surroundings, and empiricists by the animal’s observable behavior.
options.why: Neither side is defined that way. The debate is between what an animal starts out with and what it learns from experience.

items.stem: Two researchers argue about whether a songbird’s fear of hawks is innate or learned. Following the main lesson of the nativism debate, what question would move their argument forward?

options.text: What exactly is claimed to be built in: the bird’s receptors, its wiring, its learning rule, or a detector for hawks.
options.why: Correct. The useful question is not whether a capacity is innate or learned, but what exactly is claimed to be built in, because the candidates differ enormously. Pattern recognition lets us list them precisely.

options.text: Whether the fear is innate or learned, settled once and for all by measuring how strongly adult birds react to hawks.
options.why: Asking innate or learned is the framing the nativism debate teaches us to move past. And the strength of an adult’s reaction cannot tell a ready-made detector from a learned one.

options.text: Whether the fear is useful to the bird, since useful capacities tend to be built in and less useful ones have to be learned.
options.why: Usefulness does not decide what is built in; learned capacities are useful too. The productive question is which of the candidates is being claimed.

options.text: Whether the fear varies from one bird to another, since a capacity that varies between individuals must be a learned one.
options.why: Built-in features can vary between individuals, and learned ones can be very uniform. The productive question is what exactly is claimed to be built in.

items.stem: Many flowers carry patterns that reflect ultraviolet light. Bees have receptors that respond to ultraviolet light, and the human eye does not. Two flowers differ only in their ultraviolet patterns. What follows for a person trying to learn to tell them apart by eye?

options.text: No amount of training will help, since no receptor the person has responds to the two flowers differently.
options.why: Correct. Which receptors an animal has determines which feature space it starts in and which differences it can register at all. The input space is the first way knowledge can be built in.

options.text: Enough training will help, since a hidden layer can come to stand for any difference that exists among the inputs.
options.why: A hidden layer recodes the differences its inputs carry. If no receptor responds differently to the two flowers, there is no difference in the input for it to recode.

options.text: Training will help if it is spread out over time, since learning in sequence protects old learning from new.
options.why: Learning in sequence is what causes catastrophic interference, not what prevents it. And no schedule of training can register a difference no receptor responds to.

options.text: Training will help once the person’s criterion for calling the flowers different is lowered, so weaker evidence is accepted.
options.why: Moving the criterion never changes sensitivity. With no receptor responding differently, the evidence for the two flowers is the same, wherever the criterion sits.

items.stem: A fish has receptors for each of two chemicals. Suppose it also had a receptor that responded only when the two chemicals were present together, and never to either chemical alone. Why would that matter for the fish’s later circuits?

options.text: It would make a problem easier, not only possible, handing later circuits an exclusive-or problem already solved.
options.why: Correct. With the combination already registered at the input, no hidden layer has to learn it. The input space can make a problem easier, not only possible.

options.text: It would let the fish register a difference no learning could otherwise reach, since neither chemical alone reaches any receptor.
options.why: Each chemical alone still reaches the fish’s receptors for it, so the difference was already registered, and a hidden layer could learn the combination. The combination receptor makes the problem easier rather than possible.

options.text: It would let the fish’s later circuits skip learning about those chemicals, since a built-in receptor carries the right response with it.
options.why: A receptor registers a combination; it does not say what the combination means. A detector wired to a particular response is specific content, a different candidate.

options.text: It would make the fish’s criterion more liberal, so that it fled whenever either one of the two chemicals was present.
options.why: A criterion is where the line between responses is drawn on the evidence. This receptor changes what evidence the fish has, and it responds to the pair, not to either chemical.

items.stem: A convolutional network, and a fish born with a receptor that responds to a combination of chemicals, each start out with a bet about the task ahead. How does the chapter relate the two?

options.text: Both are inductive biases, one placed in a network’s wiring, the other supplied by the lineage in what the animal starts out with.
options.why: Correct. A built-in input feature is an inductive bias from the lineage. It is the same kind of bet a convolutional network makes in its wiring, placed in a different spot.

options.text: Both are learned features, one reached by backpropagation in the network and the other by associative learning in the fish.
options.why: Both are in place before learning starts. That is what makes each an inductive bias and not a learned feature.

options.text: The network’s bet is an inductive bias, while the fish’s receptor is specific content, a detector wired for one predator.
options.why: Specific content is a detector for one particular thing, such as a predator or a caregiver. A receptor for a combination of chemicals is an input feature, and an inductive bias like convolution.

options.text: The fish’s receptor is an inductive bias, while the network’s convolution is feature engineering, a choice made about what its inputs will be.
options.why: Convolution is an assumption built into how units are wired, an architectural bias, not a choice of inputs. Both bets are inductive biases.

items.stem: Convolution and a large random expansion layer, like the one in the fruit fly’s brain, are both ways knowledge can be built in. What kind of built-in knowledge are they?

options.text: Architectural biases, assumptions about the task placed in the wiring before learning starts.
options.why: Correct. Convolution assumes a feature means the same thing wherever it appears, and a random expansion layer assumes useful combinations will turn up among many random ones.

options.text: Learning rules, which set what each weight change depends on after the system starts to learn.
options.why: A learning rule is the third candidate. Convolution and random expansion are fixed in the wiring before learning starts, which makes them architectural biases.

options.text: Input spaces, which set which differences in the world a system can register at all, before anything is learned.
options.why: The input space is set by the receptors. Convolution and random expansion operate on inputs already registered, through how the units are wired.

options.text: Specific content, detectors already wired for one particular thing in the world, such as a predator.
options.why: Specific content is a detector for one particular thing. Convolution and random expansion are general assumptions about any task, not detectors for particular things.

items.stem: Two networks receive exactly the same inputs. One is trained by backpropagation and the other by competitive learning. Why do they come to represent different things?

options.text: The two rules respond to different information, so the learning rule is itself part of what is built in.
options.why: Correct. The learning rule, what a weight change depends on, is the third way knowledge can be built in. Different rules, given the same inputs, come to represent different things.

options.text: The two networks were given different feature engineering, so their inputs carried different structure.
options.why: The inputs were exactly the same, so no difference in feature engineering is involved. The difference lies in what each rule’s weight changes depend on.

options.text: Competitive learning needs a target for every output, and it learns whatever reduces error on the task.
options.why: That describes backpropagation. Competitive learning needs no teacher; units compete, and only the winner moves its weights toward the input.

options.text: Backpropagation gives each thing its own unit, while competitive learning spreads each thing across many units.
options.why: Neither rule is defined by whether its code is localist or distributed. The two differ in the information their weight changes depend on.

items.stem: A rat links a new flavor with illness after a single pairing, even with hours between them, but hardly links a flavor with a shock at all. Which way of building knowledge in does this illustrate?

options.text: The learning rule, since the pattern shows which pairings the rat’s learning links most readily.
options.why: Correct. Animals differ in what their learning rules link most readily, and that difference is in place before the rat ever tastes the flavor.

options.text: The input space, since the pattern shows which flavors the rat’s receptors can register before it links them to anything.
options.why: The rat registers the flavor in both cases. What differs is which pairings its learning links readily, illness yes and shock hardly at all.

options.text: An architectural bias, since the pattern shows how the rat’s taste receptors are wired to each other.
options.why: Nothing here concerns how receptors are wired to one another. The asymmetry is in what the rat’s learning links.

options.text: Specific content, since the pattern shows a detector already wired for one particular food.
options.why: The rat avoids the flavor only after it has been paired with illness, so this is not a ready-made detector for one food. What is built in is a readiness to link flavor with illness.

items.stem: Newborn human babies, in their first hour, turn their eyes further to follow a pattern arranged like a face than to follow one with the same parts scrambled. Which candidate for what is built in does this bear on?

options.text: Specific content, something already wired to respond to one particular kind of thing.
options.why: Correct. The fourth candidate is specific content, such as a detector already wired for one particular predator, or caregiver. A preference for face-like patterns in the first hour bears on it.

options.text: The input space, since newborns have face receptors in the eye that adults lose.
options.why: The two patterns have the same parts, so they reach the same receptors. What differs is the arrangement, which is why this bears on specific content.

options.text: A learning rule, since the babies learned what faces look like during their first hour.
options.why: The chapter offers the first-hour result as evidence about specific content, a response to one particular arrangement of parts, not as an example of a learning rule. A learning rule is what a weight change depends on, as in the rat’s readiness to link a flavor with illness.

options.text: An architectural bias, since convolution finds a face wherever it falls in view.
options.why: Convolution is an assumption about networks, that a feature means the same thing anywhere. The newborn result is about a preference for one particular arrangement.

items.stem: With 10 input features there are 45 possible pairs, 120 possible triples, and more than a thousand possible combinations of all sizes, and a fish has many dozens of kinds of smell receptor. What does this arithmetic count against?

options.text: Building everything in, since a ready-made detector for every combination is out of the question.
options.why: Correct. That is the first of two reasons against building everything in. The number of combinations grows explosively, and which few will matter cannot be settled in advance.

options.text: Learning about combinations at all, since no learner could search through more than a thousand possibilities.
options.why: The same arithmetic is why learning is valuable: learning can arrive at the combinations a task needs without anyone listing them in advance.

options.text: Using hidden layers, since each possible combination would need a hidden unit of its own.
options.why: Hidden layers are valuable for exactly this reason. Learning in them arrives at the few combinations needed, not at every possible one.

options.text: Having receptors at all, since a receptor can respond to only one feature of a smell at a time.
options.why: Almost no one doubts that receptors are built in. The arithmetic is about detectors for combinations of what receptors register.

items.stem: A predatory fish of a kind that has never lived in a certain lake is released into it. Which minnows in the lake are more likely to end up avoiding its smell?

options.text: Minnows whose avoidance of predator smells is learned, since learning can follow a change that a detector fitted to the ancestors’ predators cannot.
options.why: Correct. That is the second reason against building everything in: when the world changes, with a new predator or a new food, a built-in detector cannot follow, and learning can. It is a claim about a changed world, not a verdict that learning beats building in everywhere.

options.text: Minnows with a built-in detector for predators, since a built-in detector responds faster than any learned one.
options.why: Speed is not what the chapter compares. A detector that fits the ancestors’ predators has no reason to respond to a predator its ancestors never encountered.

options.text: Minnows with more kinds of smell receptor, since more receptors give a detector for every combination.
options.why: More receptors make the number of possible combinations larger, not smaller. A detector for every combination is out of the question.

options.text: Minnows whose built-in predator detectors are the most finely tuned, since a sharper detector for the ancestors’ predators also catches new ones.
options.why: A detector tuned more finely to the ancestors’ predators fits that past still more closely, and does nothing for a predator the lineage never encountered. When the world changes, a built-in detector cannot follow, and learning can.

items.stem: In what sense is building in too much described as “a kind of overfitting”?

options.text: A built-in solution fits the world the lineage lived in, as an overfit network fits its training set, and fails when that world changes.
options.why: Correct. The lineage’s past plays the part of the training set. A built-in detector fits it well, and when a new predator or a new food arrives the detector cannot follow.

options.text: A built-in solution fits the animal’s own early experience so closely that its later experience can no longer change anything.
options.why: A built-in solution comes from the lineage, not from the animal’s own experience. The overfitting is to the lineage’s past.

options.text: A built-in solution adds so many detectors that the animal reacts to harmless things, raising its rate of false alarms.
options.why: False alarms are a matter of the criterion, from signal detection theory. The overfitting in question is fitting a world that may no longer exist.

options.text: A built-in solution fits its predators so closely that small deliberate changes to their smell fool it, as adversarial examples fool a network.
options.why: Adversarial examples are a different failure. The comparison with overfitting is about fitting the past, which fails when the world changes.

items.stem: The number of possible combinations of features grows explosively, and the world an animal lives in can change. Why do those two facts make hidden layers valuable?

options.text: Learning in a hidden layer can arrive at the combinations a task needs, in the world as it is now, without listing them in advance.
options.why: Correct. Hidden layers are valuable for exactly these reasons. Learning reaches only the combinations that matter, and it can follow the world as it changes.

options.text: A hidden layer holds a unit for every possible combination of features, so it is ready for any change before that change happens.
options.why: A unit for every combination is exactly what the size argument rules out. A hidden layer’s value is that learning arrives at the few combinations that are needed.

options.text: A hidden layer keeps old learning safe from new learning, so a change in the world can never disturb what was learned before.
options.why: Networks with hidden layers trained by backpropagation suffer catastrophic interference. Their value here is that learning can arrive at new combinations as the world changes.

options.text: A hidden layer is supplied by the lineage, so its combinations already match whatever the animal’s world will turn out to contain.
options.why: A lineage’s past is what a built-in solution fits, and that is the problem when the world changes. The value of a hidden layer lies in what learning puts into it.

items.stem: Natural selection, like learning, can arrive at useful combinations of features without listing them all. What difference between the two does the chapter stress?

options.text: Natural selection takes generations to accomplish what learning can do within a fraction of a single lifetime.
options.why: Correct. Both can arrive at useful combinations, but natural selection takes generations where learning needs only a fraction of a lifetime.

options.text: Learning takes generations to settle on a combination, while natural selection can do it within one lifetime.
options.why: That reverses the comparison. Learning works within a lifetime, and natural selection takes generations.

options.text: Natural selection arrives only at receptors, while learning arrives only at specific content such as face detectors.
options.why: The chapter does not divide the work this way. Its point is the difference in speed between the two processes.

options.text: Natural selection lists every useful combination in advance, while learning lists only the few that a task needs.
options.why: Neither process lists every combination; both arrive at useful ones without listing them all. The difference stressed is how long each takes.

items.stem: A student reasons that, because building everything in fails for reasons of size and change, the best design for any animal is one in which nothing is built in and everything is learned. What is wrong with that reasoning?

options.text: The reasons count against building in everything, not anything; for each domain, what is built in or learned is an empirical question.
options.why: Correct. For any given domain, whether an animal’s solution is built in, learned, or a mixture, and which would serve it better, are empirical questions. Almost no one doubts that receptors are built in.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with the reasoning, since the chapter concludes that every capacity of every animal is learned from experience alone.
options.why: The chapter does not declare either side the winner. It treats each domain as an empirical question, and it notes that receptors and some architectural biases are hardly doubted to be built in.

options.text: The two reasons count against learning, not against building in, since learning takes generations to arrive at combinations.
options.why: It is natural selection that takes generations. Learning can arrive at useful combinations in a fraction of a lifetime.

options.text: The reasoning holds only for mammals, since a built-in solution for everything has been shown to work for fish and other small animals.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter shows that building everything in works for fish; a fish’s many dozens of receptors are part of the size argument against it.

items.stem: In machine learning, what is feature engineering?

options.text: Deciding, before any learning begins, what the inputs to a learning system will be, the built-in side of the choice.
options.why: Correct. It is the machine-learning name for the built-in side of the choice between building in and learning.

options.text: Adjusting a network’s hidden weights during training so that its hidden units come to stand for useful features.
options.why: That is learning in a hidden layer, by backpropagation for example. Feature engineering is decided before learning begins.

options.text: Building into a network’s wiring the assumption that a feature means the same thing wherever it appears.
options.why: That is convolution, an architectural bias. Feature engineering is about what the inputs will be, not how the units are wired.

options.text: Copying each training image shifted, rotated, or rescaled, so that a network sees more variety in training.
options.why: That is a way of training networks across changes of size and angle, and it changes the training examples. Feature engineering decides what kind of input the learner receives.

items.stem: An engineer decides, before any learning begins, what the inputs to a learning system will be. What do machine-learning practitioners call this?

options.text: Feature engineering.
options.why: Correct. It is the built-in side of the same choice that animals face between building in and learning.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion is spreading an input across many more units than it started with. It reworks inputs inside a network rather than deciding what they will be.

options.text: Convolution.
options.why: Convolution applies the same small feature detector at every position in an input. It is an architectural bias, not a decision about what the inputs are.

options.text: Backpropagation.
options.why: Backpropagation is a learning rule that passes errors back through a network. It operates during learning, not before it.

items.stem: The networks behind AlphaGo did not learn from photographs of Go boards. They received the positions of the stones directly, along with features Go players consider important, such as how many open points surround each group of stones. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Feature engineering: even a system known for learning from experience started from inputs people chose.
options.why: Correct. People decided, before learning began, what the inputs would be, both the stone positions and the extra features players consider important.

options.text: Specific content: the networks were given a detector already wired for one particular pattern of stones.
options.why: The extra features describe positions in general, such as open points around a group, not a detector for one pattern. Choosing inputs is feature engineering.

options.text: A learning rule: what each weight change depended on was decided by people who play Go well.
options.why: A learning rule is what a weight change depends on. Here people chose what the networks would receive as input.

options.text: Out-of-distribution generalization: the networks were given inputs unlike anything in their training.
options.why: Out-of-distribution generalization concerns inputs unlike the training examples. Here the issue is what form all of the inputs took.

items.stem: A later version of AlphaGo dropped the extra features that Go players consider important, and learned from the stone positions alone. In terms of the choice between building in and learning, what changed?

options.text: Less was chosen in advance, so learning had to start further down, from the stone positions by themselves.
options.why: Correct. The extra features were removed, but the stone positions were still chosen by people. How far down learning has to reach is an open question, for machines and animals alike.

options.text: More was built in, since learning in the later version needed a new architecture in place of the dropped features.
options.why: The change was a removal of chosen inputs, which moves the starting point of learning down rather than adding to what is built in.

options.text: Nothing changed, since the stone positions were themselves photographs of the board, as before.
options.why: The networks never learned from photographs of Go boards; they received the positions of the stones directly.

options.text: Everything became learned, since the later version started from no inputs chosen by people at all.
options.why: The stone positions were still inputs chosen by people. Someone still decided which units carry the structure that matters.

items.stem: The lecture sums up feature engineering in one line: someone always decides where learning starts. How does that apply to language models?

options.text: They do not learn from images of printed text; they learn from text already cut into words and pieces of words.
options.why: Correct. Someone decided that words and pieces of words probably carry the structure that matters, and learning starts from there.

options.text: They learn from images of printed text, and someone decides which typefaces those images are allowed to contain.
options.why: Language models do not read images of printed text at all. The choice made for them is to start from text already cut into words and pieces of words.

options.text: They receive hand-chosen features, such as how many open points surround each word, as the early AlphaGo did.
options.why: Open points around a group of stones were features for Go. Language models start from text cut into words and pieces of words.

options.text: They learn from single letters, and come to group the letters into words with no word boundaries ever supplied.
options.why: Language models are given the cuts already: their text arrives divided into words and pieces of words before learning begins.

items.stem: What do the AlphaGo networks and language models suggest about the systems best known for learning from experience?

options.text: Even they start from inputs chosen by people, and how far down learning has to reach is open for them, as for animals.
options.why: Correct. In each case someone decided which units probably carry the structure that matters. How far down learning has to reach is open for machines, as it is for human and nonhuman animals.

options.text: They start from raw sensory input with nothing chosen in advance, which shows that learning can reach all the way down.
options.why: The AlphaGo networks received stone positions and language models receive text cut into words. Neither starts from raw sensory input.

options.text: They start from inputs chosen by people, which shows that learning can never reach below the level of words or stones.
options.why: The later AlphaGo dropped its extra features and still learned. How far down learning has to reach is left open, not answered in the negative.

options.text: They are built-in systems underneath, which shows that the nativists are right about machines though not about animals.
options.why: The chapter declares neither nativism nor empiricism the winner, for machines or for animals. The question of how far down learning reaches stays open.

items.stem: Researchers who disagree about nativism are often disagreeing about different items among the four candidates. Where are the live disputes?

options.text: Over how much specific content must be supplied in advance, and how much a general architecture and learning rule can extract.
options.why: Correct. Almost no one doubts that receptors are built in, and few doubt that some architectural biases are. The disputes are over specific content and what general learning can extract.

options.text: Over whether receptors are built in, and whether architectural biases such as convolution are in place before learning starts.
options.why: These are the least disputed candidates. Almost no one doubts that receptors are built in, and few doubt that some architectural biases are.

options.text: Over whether anything is built in, since the four candidates are about equally contested among researchers who study them.
options.why: The candidates are not equally contested. Receptors and some architectural biases are barely doubted; the disputes are over specific content and general learning.

options.text: Over whether learning rules exist, since what a weight change depends on has not been shown to differ between animals.
options.why: Learning rules do differ between animals: a rat links flavor with illness far more readily than with shock. The live disputes lie elsewhere.

items.stem: Wild minnows of two species both flee from the odor of pike. What would show whether either species’ reaction comes from a ready-made detector or a learned one?

options.text: Raising fish of each species that never encounter a pike, then testing whether they react the first time they smell its odor.
options.why: Correct. A ready-made detector and a learned detector can produce the same behavior, and only experiments on animals raised without the experience can tell them apart. The answer can differ by species.

options.text: Timing how fast wild fish of each species flee, to see whether a ready-made detector gives a faster escape than a learned one.
options.why: The two kinds of detector can produce the same behavior, so watching wild fish react cannot tell them apart. The test needs fish raised without the experience.

options.text: Counting each species’ kinds of smell receptor, since a species with more kinds of receptor must have learned its reaction.
options.why: The number of receptor kinds does not reveal whether a reaction was learned. Only fish raised without ever encountering a pike can show that.

options.text: Testing wild fish with pike odor mixed among other smells, since a learned detector fails whenever its odor is mixed.
options.why: Nothing suggests that learned detectors fail on mixtures. What separates the two is whether the reaction appears without any experience of pike.

items.stem: A minnow smells pike odor at the same time as chemicals released from the injured skin of another minnow. Afterward it avoids pike odor. What kind of learning is this?

options.text: Associative learning, pairing the predator’s odor with a signal that already matters to the fish.
options.why: Correct. It is associative learning of the kind described in Module 5, and it is how fish of some species come to react to a predator’s odor.

options.text: Competitive learning, with units for pike odor winning out over other smells without any teacher.
options.why: Competitive learning finds clusters in how inputs overlap, with no signal about what matters. Here the injured-skin chemicals pair the odor with danger.

options.text: Catastrophic interference, with new learning about pike overwriting what the minnow learned before.
options.why: Nothing old was lost here. The minnow added a new link between pike odor and avoidance.

options.text: A ready-made detector, switched on for the first time by the odor it was already wired to detect.
