options.why: The avoidance appeared only after the odor was paired with the injured-skin chemicals, which marks it as learned rather than ready-made.

items.stem: What evidence from the cortex bears on the question of what has to be built in?

options.text: When the input to a region of cortex is changed early in life, much of what the region comes to do follows its new input.
options.why: Correct. That bears on the same question from another direction: much of what a cortical region does is shaped by what reaches it, though not all of it.

options.text: When a region of cortex is removed early in life, a ready-made detector for its job appears in another region.
options.why: Nothing in the chapter describes ready-made detectors appearing elsewhere. The evidence is that a region’s function largely follows its input.

options.text: Every region of cortex is wired at birth for one sense, so changing its input early in life leaves its function as it was.
options.why: The opposite was found: when a region’s input is changed early in life, much of what it comes to do follows the new input.

options.text: When the input to a region of cortex is changed early in life, the region becomes interchangeable with any other region.
options.why: The evidence shows that input shapes what an area does, not that areas are interchangeable; a rewired area is not identical to the one it resembles.

items.stem: In a few sentences, give the two reasons that building everything in is not a good solution, and explain why one of them is described as a kind of overfitting.
items.answer: The first reason is size. The number of possible combinations of features grows explosively: with 10 features there are 45 pairs, 120 triples, and more than a thousand combinations of all sizes, and a fish has many dozens of kinds of smell receptor. A detector for every combination is out of the question, and which few will matter cannot be settled in advance. The second reason is change. A built-in solution fits the world the animal’s ancestors lived in, and when that world changes, with a new predator or a new food, a built-in detector cannot follow, while learning can. That is like overfitting: as an overfit network fits its training examples and does poorly on new ones, a built-in solution fits the lineage’s past and does poorly when the world changes.
rubric: Gives size as one reason: the number of combinations grows explosively, so a detector for every combination is out of the question.
Gives change as the other reason: a built-in solution fits the ancestors’ world and cannot follow a new predator or food.
Says that learning can follow a changed world where a built-in detector cannot.
Explains the overfitting comparison: fitting the lineage’s past as an overfit network fits its training examples.

items.stem: Wild fish of a newly studied species flee from the odor of a predatory crab. In a short paragraph, describe an experiment that would show whether the reaction comes from a ready-made detector or a learned one, explain why watching wild adults cannot settle the question, and say how the reaction might be learned if it is.
items.answer: A ready-made detector and a learned detector can produce the same behavior, so wild adults, which have probably encountered crabs or their odor, cannot tell them apart. The experiment is to raise fish of this species without ever encountering the crab, and test whether they react the first time they smell its odor. If they react, there is evidence of a ready-made detector; if they do not, the reaction is probably learned. If it is learned, one way is associative learning: a fish that smells the crab at the same time as chemicals released from the injured skin of another fish of its own kind comes to avoid the crab’s odor afterward. The answer could differ from one species to another, as it does among fish.
rubric: States that a ready-made and a learned detector can produce the same behavior, so wild adults cannot settle it.
Proposes raising fish without any encounter with the crab and testing their reaction on first exposure to its odor.
Describes a learned route: pairing the predator’s odor with chemicals from the injured skin of a fish of the same kind.
Notes that the answer can differ between species, keeping it hedged.

items.stem: In the lab’s small pool, a fish with eight hidden units encounters the same six eels and suckers again and again for 5,000 encounters, and then Show the test set is switched on. What did the feature space show, and what is that picture the mark of?

options.text: Six tight clusters of filled dots, a white line bending around individual clusters, and wrongly sorted hollow dots on both sides of it: overfitting.
options.why: Correct. Each resident has a smell of its own, so the encounters pile up in six clusters, and the line bends to fit those six, accidents and all. Eels and suckers the fish has never smelled then fall on the wrong side of it in both directions.

options.text: Two broad clouds of filled dots, one of eels and one of suckers, a nearly straight white line between them, and few wrongly sorted hollow dots: generalization.
options.why: Two broad clouds are what a stream of new individuals produces. In the pool the fish encountered only six individuals, so its dots formed six clusters, and the test set showed errors.

options.text: Six tight clusters of filled dots, a white line bending around them, and wrongly sorted hollow dots all on the eel side, every one a sucker the fish would flee: a criterion set too low.
options.why: A criterion set too low would slide the line and put the errors on one side, as false alarms. Here the wrongly sorted hollow dots sat on both sides, because the line had been bent around six individuals.

options.text: Six tight clusters of filled dots, with the hollow dots crowded far from all of them in the lower-left corner, on the no-eel side of the line: failure out of distribution.
options.why: Hollow dots crowded in the lower-left corner are the diluted far test set of the downstream scenario. The pool’s test set is new individuals from the same kind of water, mixed among the clusters.

items.stem: To close the gap between training and test in the small pool, three changes were tried one at a time: two hidden units instead of eight, a pool of 24 or 60 individuals, and a stream in which every encounter is a new individual. What did they show about where the trouble came from?

options.text: The smaller network left the gap about where it was, but larger pools shrank it and a stream closed it, so the small pool was the trouble.
options.why: Correct. Two hidden units, or none at all, still left a gap of about 16 or 17 points, because even one line can fit the accidents of six individuals. With 24 individuals the gap fell to about 6, at 60 to about 3, and in a stream training and test stayed within a few points.

options.text: The smaller network closed the gap while the larger pools made little difference, so having too many hidden units for so small a pool was the trouble.
options.why: A smaller network is the common remedy, which is why the lab tries it, but here it barely changed the gap. What was small was the pool.

options.text: All three closed the gap about equally well, the stream included, so any change that makes the six individuals harder to memorize removes overfitting.
options.why: The three did not work equally: the smaller network left the gap almost untouched. Only more individuals, or a new one every encounter, closed it.

options.text: None of the three closed the gap, so the trouble came from the learning rule itself, which fits whatever examples it is given.
options.why: The larger pools and the stream did close it. The rule fits its examples, but with enough different individuals the accidents of any one stop mattering.

items.stem: With Where the encounters come from set to a stream, every encounter is a new eel or sucker. In a few sentences, say what the training and test lines did with eight hidden units, including how the training line compared with where it ended in the six-fish pool, and explain why a fish in a stream cannot fit its training encounters too closely, however many hidden units it has.
items.answer: The two lines stayed within a few points of each other, with none of the gap the six-fish pool produced. The gap closed mostly from the training side: the training line no longer fell to the few percent wrong it reached in the pool, and ended near the test line instead. Overfitting is fitting the accidents of particular training examples. In a stream no individual comes back, so there are no particular individuals whose accidents could be fitted, and each training encounter is as new to the fish as a test item is. Doing well on recent training encounters therefore already means doing well on new eels and suckers.
rubric: Reports that the training and test lines stayed close together (little or no gap), with the training line ending well above the few percent wrong it reached in the pool.
Defines overfitting as fitting the accidents of particular training examples.
Says that in a stream no individual repeats, so there are no particular examples to fit.
Says each training encounter is new, like a test item, so training performance already measures performance on new examples.

items.stem: A fish with no hidden units learns only from eels and suckers close by, where every smell is strong. Its learning curve tracks a near test set and a far test set, whose smells are diluted to three tenths of their strength. What did the two lines show after the first 300 encounters, and after 2,000 more?

options.text: The near set was almost error-free by 300 and the far set about half wrong, and 2,000 more encounters left the far set where it was.
options.why: Correct. Nothing in training near the fish was as faint as the far test set, so more of the same training did not reach it. A classifier is reliable near the region its training examples occupy and much less reliable far from it, which is the weakness of out-of-distribution generalization.

options.text: Both sets were still about half wrong at 300, and 2,000 more encounters made the near set almost error-free while the far set stayed about half wrong.
options.why: The near set did not need thousands of encounters: a single line sorts strong eel and sucker smells within a few hundred. The far set’s failure was there from the start and did not move.

options.text: The near set was almost error-free by 300 and the far set about half wrong, and 2,000 more encounters slowly brought the far set close to the near set.
options.why: The far set did not improve at all. Training on strong smells taught the fish about strong smells, and the far smells lie well outside them.

options.text: The near set was almost error-free by 300 and the far set nearly all wrong, because the fish took every faint smell for an eel and fled.
options.why: The fish stayed for every faint smell, not fled. About half the far set is suckers, and staying was right for those, which leaves the far set about half wrong.

items.stem: A fish that learns only from nearby eels and suckers was given Proportion of A, a built-in receptor that responds to the share of a smell that is A, whatever its strength. In a few sentences, say what happened to the far test set with receptors A and B still connected beside it, and with them disconnected, and explain why the fish did not rely on the proportion when it had A and B as well.
items.answer: With A and B still connected, the far test set was not rescued: it stayed far worse than the near set, with many far eels taken for suckers. With A and B disconnected, the far test set came out nearly all right, though the fish had never been downstream. Near the fish, raw strength and proportion both sorted every eel from every sucker perfectly, so the rule, which only reduces errors on the encounters the fish has, had no reason to prefer the proportion. Only when A and B were removed did the proportion become the fish’s whole input space, and the one difference it could register survives dilution. A built-in feature helps only if the learner comes to depend on it.
rubric: Reports that the proportion beside A and B left the far test set poor, and that the proportion alone fixed it.
Says that near the fish, raw strength (A and B) worked just as well as the proportion on every training encounter.
Says the rule reduces error only on the encounters it gets, so nothing pushed it toward the proportion.
Says removing A and B left the proportion as the only input, which is unchanged by dilution.

items.stem: The island was solved three ways: with the built-in receptor Distance from the ideal strength, with 50 hidden units fixed at random under Sparse, and with hidden units trained by Pass the error back. Which route needed the fewest encounters and the fewest units, and what did it need in place before learning began?

options.text: The built-in receptor, which needed no hidden units and a few hundred encounters, but needed the right feature for this problem chosen in advance.
options.why: Correct. With the distance receptor the fish reached 5 percent wrong within a few hundred encounters and no hidden layer. The price is that someone had to know, before learning began, that distance from the middle is what matters.

options.text: The random hidden units, which needed few units and encounters, since unlike a built-in receptor a layer wired at random needs nothing in place before learning.
options.why: The random route needed dozens of units, and its assumption that useful combinations will turn up among many random ones is itself built in before learning.

options.text: The trained hidden units, which needed the fewest units and encounters, since passing the error back finds exactly the combinations the task needs.
options.why: Passing the error back did find the combinations, but slowly: it needed several units and thousands of encounters on the island.

options.text: All three needed about the same number of encounters and units, since the island is equally hard whichever way its features are supplied.
options.why: The routes differed a great deal. The built-in receptor was fastest by far, and the learned hidden layer was the slowest.

items.stem: A fish that learns only from nearby eels and suckers is given the built-in receptor Proportion of A alone, with receptors A and B disconnected. On the feature space, receptor A across and receptor B up, what does its decision boundary look like, and why does it also work far downstream?

options.text: A straight line running out from the lower-left corner, so a smell stays on its side however far it is diluted toward that corner.
options.why: Correct. Every smell with the same share of A lies on one straight line out from the corner where both receptors are zero, and diluting a smell slides it along that line toward the corner without changing its share. So the boundary sorts far smells as it sorts near ones, and the far test set came out nearly all right.

options.text: A circle around the near eels, so any smell far from where the eels were learned, a diluted one included, falls outside the circle.
options.why: A circle is what the distance receptor drew on the island. Far eels would fall outside a circle around near eels, and the fish would stay for them.

options.text: A straight line across the middle, parallel to the receptor B axis, so that the amount of A alone decides which side a smell falls on.
options.why: A boundary set by the amount of A is the kind that fails downstream, since dilution cuts the amount of A. The share of A is what survives dilution.

options.text: A straight line in the same place as the near-trained fish’s line, so that the boundary is unchanged and only the criterion has moved.
options.why: The near-trained fish’s line passed to one side of the far smells and missed every far eel. This fish’s boundary runs through the corner the far smells crowd toward.

pools.title: The Oldest Cortex: Separating and Completing Smells
pools.covers: reading §7.3.1, §7.3.2, §7.3.3 · lecture 7.3 slides title, the_oldest_cortex, pulling_similar_smells_apart, completing_from_part

items.stem: What is the piriform cortex?

options.text: The three-layered olfactory cortex of mammals, which receives the olfactory bulb’s output directly, without a relay in the thalamus.
options.why: Correct. In mammals the piriform cortex is the first cortex a smell reaches. It is older in form than the neocortex, and its input arrives straight from the olfactory bulb.

options.text: The six-layered sheet that makes up most of the mammalian pallium, which receives signals from the eyes, the skin, and the ears through the thalamus.
options.why: That describes the neocortex. The piriform cortex has three layers, not six, and smell reaches it without passing through a relay in the thalamus.

options.text: The first stop for signals from the nose, which gathers them before sending its own output on to the cortex for the next stage of work on a smell.
options.why: That is the olfactory bulb. The bulb sends its output to the piriform cortex, which is the cortex that receives it.

options.text: The structure in the insect brain where smell inputs are spread across many more cells, through connections that appear random, with learning at its output.
options.why: That is the mushroom body. It resembles the piriform cortex in some ways, but it belongs to an insect, and the piriform cortex belongs to a mammal.

items.stem: What is the name for the three-layered sheet in mammals that receives the olfactory bulb’s output directly, without a relay in the thalamus?

options.text: Piriform cortex.
options.why: Correct. The piriform cortex is the first cortex a smell reaches in mammals, and its input comes straight from the olfactory bulb.

options.text: Mushroom body.
options.why: The mushroom body is where smell inputs are spread across many more cells in an insect brain. The three-layered sheet in mammals is the piriform cortex.

options.text: Ventral stream.
options.why: The ventral stream is a series of visual areas running from the primary visual cortex to the inferior temporal cortex. It has nothing to do with the olfactory bulb.

options.text: Pyramidal neuron.
options.why: The pyramidal neuron is the cell the piriform cortex is built around, not the sheet itself. The sheet is the piriform cortex.

items.stem: Signals from the eyes, the ears, and the skin each reach the cortex through a relay in the thalamus. How do signals from the nose reach the cortex in a mammal?

options.text: The olfactory bulb sends its output straight to the piriform cortex, so smell reaches the cortex with no relay in the thalamus.
options.why: Correct. Smell is the exception among the senses. The olfactory bulb, the first stop for signals from the nose, sends its output directly to the piriform cortex, the first cortex a smell reaches.

options.text: The olfactory bulb sends its output to a smell relay in the thalamus, which passes it on to the piriform cortex as it would for any other sense.
options.why: That is the route the other senses take. What makes the piriform cortex unusual is that its input arrives from the olfactory bulb with no relay in the thalamus.

options.text: The nose sends its signals straight to the piriform cortex, and the olfactory bulb receives them only after the piriform cortex has worked on them.
options.why: That reverses the order. The olfactory bulb is the first stop for signals from the nose, and the piriform cortex receives the bulb’s output.

options.text: The olfactory bulb sends its output to layer 4 of the neocortex, the layer that receives the input the thalamus relays to the sensory areas.
options.why: Layer 4 is where the neocortex receives input relayed by the thalamus. A smell’s first cortex is the three-layered piriform cortex, reached without that relay.

items.stem: How does the piriform cortex differ in its layers from the neocortex?

options.text: The piriform cortex has three layers, and its form is older than that of the six-layered neocortex.
options.why: Correct. The piriform cortex is a sheet with three layers, older in form than the six-layered neocortex.

options.text: The piriform cortex has six layers, and its form is newer than that of the neocortex, which has three.
options.why: That swaps the two. The neocortex is the six-layered sheet, and the piriform cortex, with three layers, is the older form.

options.text: The piriform cortex has the same six layers as the neocortex, and differs from it only in carrying smell rather than sight.
options.why: The piriform cortex does not share the neocortex’s six layers. It has three, and it is older in form.

options.text: The piriform cortex has no layers at all, being a cluster of cells rather than a sheet like the neocortex.
options.why: The piriform cortex is a sheet, and a layered one. It has three layers where the neocortex has six.

items.stem: What is a pyramidal neuron?

options.text: The main excitatory cell of the cortex, with a roughly triangular cell body, a long apical dendrite reaching toward the surface, and shorter dendrites near the cell body.
options.why: Correct. The piriform cortex and the neocortex are both built around the pyramidal neuron. The olfactory bulb’s input lands on the far ends of its apical dendrites.

options.text: A smaller cell that sits among the excitatory cells of the cortex and damps their activity down, acting on the cell bodies of the excitatory cells on either side of it.
options.why: That describes the inhibitory cells that sit among the pyramidal neurons. The pyramidal neuron is the excitatory cell whose activity they damp.

options.text: A cell in the insect mushroom body that receives input from a few of about 50 kinds of smell input, wired at random, and responds sparsely to each odor.
options.why: That is a Kenyon cell, in a fly. The pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the mammalian cortex, recognized by its shape.

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex that responds to an edge or bar of a particular orientation anywhere within a fairly large receptive field.
options.why: That is a complex cell, defined by what it responds to. A pyramidal neuron is defined by its shape and by its place as the cortex’s main excitatory cell.

items.stem: What is the name for the main excitatory cell of the cortex, with a roughly triangular cell body, a long apical dendrite reaching toward the surface, and shorter dendrites near the cell body?

options.text: Pyramidal neuron.
options.why: Correct. The pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the piriform cortex and of the neocortex alike.

options.text: Simple cell.
options.why: A simple cell is defined by its receptive field, divided into regions where light excites it and regions where light inhibits it, not by its shape.

options.text: Complex cell.
options.why: A complex cell is defined by what it responds to, an edge of one orientation anywhere in a fairly large receptive field, not by its shape.

options.text: Piriform cortex.
options.why: The piriform cortex is the three-layered sheet built around this cell. The cell itself is the pyramidal neuron.

items.stem: A researcher follows the axons that leave the olfactory bulb to the pyramidal neurons of the piriform cortex. On which part of each pyramidal neuron does the olfactory bulb’s input land?

options.text: The far ends of the apical dendrite, the long dendrite that runs from the top of the cell toward the surface of the cortex.
options.why: Correct. The bulb’s input lands on the far ends of the apical dendrites. The lamprey’s pallium shares this arrangement, with smell arriving on the far ends of its cells’ dendrites.

options.text: The shorter dendrites that spread out near the cell body, close to the place where the cell’s own axon leaves it on its way out.
options.why: The shorter dendrites are part of the pyramidal neuron, but the olfactory bulb’s input arrives at the other end, on the tips of the long apical dendrite.

options.text: The cell body itself, the roughly triangular part of the cell from which both kinds of dendrite grow outward.
options.why: The cell body is the triangular center of the cell, and the input does not land there. The olfactory bulb’s input lands on the far ends of the apical dendrites.

options.text: The side branches of the cell’s axon, which carry signals between neighboring pyramidal neurons in the piriform cortex.
options.why: The side branches are how pyramidal neurons excite one another. They carry the cell’s output to its neighbors, not the olfactory bulb’s input to the cell.

items.stem: Researchers record from the main excitatory cells in a rat’s piriform cortex, and then from the main excitatory cells in its neocortex. What kind of cell are they most likely recording from in each?

options.text: Pyramidal neurons in both, since the pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the piriform cortex and of the neocortex alike.
options.why: Correct. The piriform cortex is built around the pyramidal neuron, which is also the main excitatory cell of the neocortex.

options.text: Pyramidal neurons in the neocortex only, since the older, three-layered piriform cortex is built around a simpler and older kind of cell.
options.why: Being older in form does not mean the piriform cortex lacks pyramidal neurons; it is built around them. It is the lamprey’s pallium whose cells lack part of the pyramidal neuron.

options.text: A different kind of cell in each, since the main excitatory cell of a cortical sheet depends on which sense supplies the sheet’s input.
options.why: Input does shape what a cortical area does. But the pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of both the piriform cortex and the neocortex, though different senses feed them.

options.text: Pyramidal neurons in the piriform cortex only, since the neocortex’s six layers are built around simple cells and complex cells instead.
options.why: Simple and complex cells are kinds of cell in the primary visual cortex, defined by how they respond rather than by their shape, so they are not an alternative to the pyramidal neuron. The pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the neocortex, as it is of the piriform cortex.

items.stem: In the piriform cortex, each pyramidal neuron’s axon leaves the area, but on the way it sends side branches to other pyramidal neurons nearby. In the terms of Module 4, what are those side branches, and what can they let a circuit do?

options.text: Recurrent connections, through which the cells excite one another, of the kind that let a circuit hold a state.
options.why: Correct. The side branches let pyramidal neurons excite their neighbors. Connections of this kind let a Module 4 circuit hold a state, and they are what the proposal that the piriform cortex completes smells relies on.

options.text: Mutual inhibition, through which the cells silence one another, of the kind that lets one unit win in a winner-take-all circuit.
options.why: The side branches excite their neighbors rather than silencing them. Damping is done by separate inhibitory cells that sit among the pyramidal neurons.

options.text: A labeled line, through which each cell’s output is routed straight to the machinery that responds to one particular smell.
options.why: A labeled line runs from one kind of sensory neuron to the machinery that acts on it, like the worm’s copper neuron. These side branches end on neighboring pyramidal neurons.

options.text: A relay, through which each cell passes the olfactory bulb’s signals on to the thalamus to be sorted before they reach the neocortex.
options.why: Smell reaches the piriform cortex without any relay in the thalamus. The side branches stay local, ending on nearby pyramidal neurons.

items.stem: Two kinds of connection inside the piriform cortex act on its pyramidal neurons. How does the effect of the side branches of the pyramidal neurons’ axons differ from the effect of the inhibitory cells?

options.text: The side branches excite neighboring pyramidal neurons, while the inhibitory cells damp the pyramidal neurons’ activity down.
options.why: Correct. Through the side branches the pyramidal neurons excite one another, and the inhibitory cells sitting among them damp that activity down.

options.text: The side branches damp neighboring pyramidal neurons down, while the inhibitory cells excite the pyramidal neurons around them.
options.why: That swaps the two. The side branches are excitatory recurrent connections, and the inhibitory cells are the ones that damp activity.

options.text: The side branches carry the olfactory bulb’s input into the piriform cortex, while the inhibitory cells carry its output away.
options.why: The olfactory bulb’s input arrives on the tips of the apical dendrites, and the output leaves along the main axon. The side branches link neighbors.

options.text: The side branches connect the piriform cortex to the thalamus, while the inhibitory cells connect it to the olfactory bulb.
options.why: No relay in the thalamus is involved. Both kinds of connection act within the piriform cortex, one exciting and one damping.

items.stem: The lamprey’s pallium is compared with the mammalian piriform cortex. Which features of the piriform plan are found in the lamprey’s pallium, and which are missing from it?

options.text: Three layers and smell arriving on the far ends of its cells’ dendrites are found, but its cells have no shorter dendrites near the cell body.
options.why: Correct. The lamprey’s pallium shares the three layers and where smell arrives, but its cells lack the shorter dendrites of a full pyramidal neuron.

options.text: The shorter dendrites near the cell body are found, but smell arrives on the cell bodies instead, and the pallium has six layers rather than three.
options.why: That reverses what is shared. The lamprey’s cells lack the shorter dendrites, while the three layers and input on the dendrite tips are what match.

options.text: The full pyramidal neuron, with both kinds of dendrite, is found, but the pallium has a single layer and receives no input from smell.
options.why: The lamprey’s pallium has three layers, and smell does reach it. It is the full pyramidal neuron that is not found there.

options.text: None of the plan is found, since a lamprey has a pallium rather than a cortex, and its smell signals never reach any layered sheet.
options.why: The lamprey does have a pallium and not a cortex, but the pallium still shares three layers and smell arriving on the far ends of its cells’ dendrites.

items.stem: Comparing the lamprey’s pallium with the piriform cortex, what can be concluded about how old the full pyramidal neuron is?

options.text: The full pyramidal neuron cannot be dated back as far as the lamprey, though parts of the piriform plan are found in the lamprey as well.
options.why: Correct. The plan is old, but not every part of it is equally old. The lamprey’s cells lack the shorter dendrites, so the full pyramidal neuron cannot be dated back that far.

options.text: The full pyramidal neuron can be dated back as far as the lamprey, since the lamprey’s pallium has the same three layers as the piriform cortex.
options.why: Sharing three layers does not carry the whole cell with it. The lamprey’s cells lack the shorter dendrites near the cell body, so the full pyramidal neuron cannot be dated that far back.

options.text: Nothing about the piriform plan can be dated back as far as the lamprey, since the lamprey has a pallium and not a piriform cortex.
options.why: The three layers and smell arriving on the far ends of the dendrites are shared with the lamprey. Only the full pyramidal neuron cannot be dated back that far.

options.text: The full pyramidal neuron must be older than the lamprey’s lineage, since the lamprey’s cells must have lost their shorter dendrites.
options.why: Loss is not what the comparison shows. The conclusion the chapter draws is a limit on dating: the full pyramidal neuron cannot be dated back as far as the lamprey.

items.stem: A rabbit at the entrance of a warren has to tell its own warren’s smell from a neighboring warren’s almost identical smell. It also has to recognize its own warren from a faint trace of that smell on the wind. Which two demands on its piriform cortex are these, in that order?

options.text: Discrimination, then generalization.
options.why: Correct. Telling apart two smells that are almost the same is discrimination. Knowing a familiar smell from a faint trace of it is generalization. The piriform cortex has been studied for both.

options.text: Generalization, then discrimination.
options.why: That swaps the two. Telling apart nearly identical smells that call for different responses is discrimination; treating a faint trace as the familiar smell is generalization.

options.text: Sensitivity, then criterion.
options.why: Sensitivity and criterion are the two quantities of signal detection theory for a single yes-or-no decision. The two demands on recognition are discrimination and generalization.

options.text: Pattern completion, then pattern separation.
options.why: These are circuit operations, and they are in the wrong order. Pattern separation carries out discrimination, and pattern completion carries out generalization.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain what comparing the lamprey’s pallium with the mammalian piriform cortex tells us about how old the piriform plan is. Say which features are shared, which are missing, and what follows.
items.answer: The lamprey’s pallium has three layers, like the piriform cortex, and smell arrives on the far ends of its cells’ dendrites, just as the olfactory bulb’s input lands on the far ends of the pyramidal neurons’ apical dendrites. But the lamprey’s cells lack the shorter dendrites that spread out near the cell body of a pyramidal neuron. So the plan is old, but not every part of it is equally old. The three layers and the input on the dendrite tips are shared with the lamprey, while the full pyramidal neuron cannot be dated back that far.
rubric: Names the three layers as shared.
Names smell arriving on the far ends of the dendrites as shared.
Names the shorter dendrites near the cell body as missing from the lamprey’s cells.
Concludes that the full pyramidal neuron cannot be dated back as far as the lamprey, though the plan as a whole is old.

items.stem: What the piriform cortex does with a smell has been measured directly. How was the measurement made?

options.text: Researchers imaged the activity of many piriform cells at once in anesthetized mice, while presenting one odor after another.
options.why: Correct. Imaging many cells at once let the researchers see which cells each odor activated, and how much two odors’ sets of cells overlapped.

options.text: Researchers built network models of the piriform circuit, and tested whether the models could recover a smell from part of it.
options.why: Network models of that kind exist, and they are the main support for pattern completion. The direct measurement was imaging in anesthetized mice.

options.text: Researchers traced the connections of a few hundred cells one at a time, and found that their combinations of inputs looked random.
options.why: Tracing that found random-looking combinations was done in the fruit fly’s mushroom body. The piriform measurement imaged activity, not connections.

options.text: Researchers recorded a single piriform cell at a time in awake mice, while training the mice to tell two similar odors apart.
options.why: The study imaged many cells at once, in anesthetized mice, while odors were presented one after another. No training was involved.

items.stem: A student predicts that any odor strong enough to smell will activate most of the cells in the piriform cortex. What did the imaging study find?

options.text: Each odor activated a small set of the cells, between about 3 and 15 percent of those imaged.
options.why: Correct. Each odor activated only a small set of the piriform cells. Sparse activity of this kind is also what the energy budget of the cortex allows.

options.text: Each odor activated most of the cells, and stronger odors activated nearly all of those imaged.
options.why: The student’s prediction was wrong. Each odor activated only a small set, between about 3 and 15 percent of the cells imaged.

options.text: Each odor activated about half of the cells, so that any two odors shared most of their active cells.
options.why: Each odor activated far fewer than half, and two odors with unrelated structures shared only 5 to 15 percent of their active cells.

options.text: Each odor activated a single cell, so that which cell fired was by itself enough to identify the odor.
options.why: Each odor activated a set of cells, and one cell could respond to two unrelated odors. No single cell stands for an odor.

items.stem: In a topographic map, neighboring cells handle neighboring points in the world. A student expects the piriform cortex to be laid out in the same way, with neighboring cells responding to similar odors. What did the imaging study find?

options.text: The active cells were scattered with no clustering, and a cell’s neighbor was as likely to respond to a quite different odor as to the same one.
options.why: Correct. There was no map in the piriform cortex. Cells that responded to the same odor were not clustered together.

options.text: The active cells were clustered, so that the cells responding to the same odor sat together and their neighbors usually responded to that odor too.
options.why: Clustering is what the student expected, and it is not what was found. The cells responding to one odor were scattered.

options.text: The active cells were arranged by chemical structure, so that neighboring cells responded to odors whose molecules were alike in their structure.
options.why: An arrangement by structure would be a map, and the piriform cortex showed none. A neighbor was as likely to respond to a quite different odor.

options.text: The active cells were arranged by the odor’s strength, with cells near the surface responding to faint odors and deeper cells to strong ones.
options.why: The study reported no arrangement of this kind. The active cells were scattered, with no clustering and no map.

items.stem: Two odors with almost the same chemical structure are presented to a mouse. How does the overlap between the two odors at the olfactory bulb compare with their overlap in the piriform cortex?

options.text: At the olfactory bulb they share more than 70 percent of their active inputs; in the piriform cortex they share only about a quarter of their active cells.
options.why: Correct. Two smells that look alike at the olfactory bulb look much less alike in the piriform cortex. That drop in overlap is pattern separation.

options.text: At the olfactory bulb they share only about a quarter of their active inputs; in the piriform cortex they come to share more than 70 percent of their active cells.
options.why: That reverses the two stages. The overlap is high at the olfactory bulb and much lower in the piriform cortex.

options.text: At both stages they share more than 70 percent, since the piriform cortex passes the olfactory bulb’s pattern on to later stages unchanged.
options.why: The piriform cortex does not pass the pattern on unchanged. The two similar odors overlapped far less there than at the olfactory bulb.

options.text: At the olfactory bulb they share more than 70 percent; in the piriform cortex they share no active cells, so similar odors are kept completely apart.
options.why: The overlap fell a long way but not to zero. The two similar odors still shared about a quarter of their active piriform cells.

items.stem: In the piriform cortex, two odors with almost the same structure shared about a quarter of their active cells, while odors with unrelated structures shared between 5 and 15 percent. What does setting those two results side by side show?

options.text: Similar odors are pulled well apart in the piriform cortex, though in those measurements they still overlapped somewhat more than unrelated odors did.
options.why: Correct. From more than 70 percent at the olfactory bulb, the similar pair falls to about a quarter, which is still above the 5 to 15 percent shared by unrelated odors. Both figures come from one way of counting a cell as active, and how much two odors overlap depends on that threshold.

options.text: Similar odors are made fully unrelated in the piriform cortex, so that they overlap no more there than odors with unrelated structures.
options.why: The similar pair’s overlap fell a long way but stayed above that of unrelated odors. They were pulled apart, not made fully unrelated.

options.text: Similar odors are drawn closer together in the piriform cortex, so that they overlap more there than they did at the olfactory bulb.
options.why: Their overlap went down, not up. At the olfactory bulb the similar pair shared more than 70 percent of active inputs.

options.text: Unrelated odors are made more alike in the piriform cortex, so that every pair of odors comes to overlap by about the same amount.
options.why: The two kinds of pair still overlapped by different amounts. The change the comparison shows is that similar odors are pulled apart.

items.stem: What is pattern separation?

options.text: Making inputs that overlap a great deal less alike than they were, so that a later stage can tell them apart.
options.why: Correct. In the piriform cortex, two similar smells that overlap heavily at the olfactory bulb overlap much less, and that change is pattern separation.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, so that a partial input gives the response the whole would.
options.why: That is pattern completion, which brings a partial input back to a whole pattern. Pattern separation pulls overlapping inputs apart.

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units, so that a single straight boundary is more likely to separate the cases.
options.why: That is dimensionality expansion. Pattern separation is defined by what happens to overlap, not by how many units carry the input.

options.text: Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a pattern can reactivate the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, the storing that makes pattern completion possible. Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike.

items.stem: What is the name for making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart?

options.text: Pattern separation.
options.why: Correct. Pattern separation has been measured in the piriform cortex, where similar smells overlap much less than they do at the olfactory bulb.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion runs the other way, recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. Making overlapping inputs less alike is pattern separation.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units than it started with. It is defined by the number of units, not by reducing overlap.

options.text: Auto-association.
options.why: Auto-association is storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells. Making overlapping inputs less alike is pattern separation.

items.stem: A deer browses two kinds of berry, one safe and one toxic, whose smells activate nearly the same inputs in its olfactory bulb. If its piriform cortex carries out pattern separation on those two smells, what happens, and why does it help the deer?

options.text: The two smells activate much less overlapping sets of piriform cells, so that the cells reading the piriform cortex’s output can tell them apart.
options.why: Correct. Pattern separation is discrimination carried out by a circuit. Smells that overlap heavily at the olfactory bulb are made less alike, so a later stage can respond to them differently.

options.text: The two smells activate one shared set of piriform cells, so that the deer learns to treat both kinds of berry as a single kind of food to eat.
options.why: Drawing two inputs together is what generalization asks for, and it would be the wrong outcome here. Pattern separation pulls overlapping inputs apart.

options.text: The olfactory bulb’s inputs for the two smells are made less alike, so that the piriform cortex receives patterns that are already separated.
options.why: In the piriform measurements, the overlap stayed high at the olfactory bulb. It was in the piriform cortex that similar smells came to overlap less.

options.text: Each smell activates its own single piriform cell, so that which cell fires is enough by itself to say which kind of berry is in front of the deer.
options.why: No single piriform cell stands for an odor. What identifies an odor is which set of cells is active.

items.stem: In the imaging study, one piriform cell responded to two odors whose chemical structures were unrelated. What does that finding imply about how the piriform cortex identifies an odor?

options.text: By which set of cells is active, since no single cell stands for any one odor.
options.why: Correct. A cell that responds to unrelated odors cannot stand for either one. The identity of an odor lies in the whole set of active cells.

options.text: By which single cell responds most strongly, since each odor has one cell that responds to it best.
options.why: That is a code with one cell per odor, and the finding rules it out. A cell responding to two unrelated odors stands for neither.

options.text: By how many cells are active, since odors with more complex structures activate larger sets of cells.
options.why: The study reported nothing linking set size to complexity. What identifies an odor is which cells are active, not how many.

options.text: By where the active cells lie, since each odor activates its own cluster of neighboring cells.
options.why: The active cells were scattered, with no clustering and no map, so location does not identify the odor.

items.stem: Responses in the piriform cortex are sparse and scattered with no map, and a single cell can respond to unrelated odors. Which wiring from the olfactory bulb has been proposed as one that would produce all of these properties?

options.text: Each piriform cell receives input from a random handful of the olfactory bulb’s outputs.
options.why: Correct. If each cell received a random handful of the bulb’s outputs, sparse and scattered responses with no map would follow, and so would cells responding to unrelated odors. The wiring itself was not observed; random wiring is a model that fits the data.

options.text: Each piriform cell receives input from the olfactory bulb’s outputs for one family of chemical structures.
options.why: Wiring by chemical family would make neighboring or individual cells track structure, which is not what was found. The proposal was a random handful.

options.text: Each piriform cell’s inputs are set by competition, so that neighboring cells come to prefer similar odors.
options.why: Competition with neighbors moving together produces a topographic map, and the piriform cortex showed no map. The proposal was random input.

options.text: Each piriform cell receives input from all of the bulb’s outputs, with inhibition settling which cells fire.
options.why: The proposal was a random handful of inputs for each cell, not every input. Inhibitory cells damp activity, but they are not the proposed explanation.

items.stem: Suppose each piriform cell in a mouse receives input from a random handful of the olfactory bulb’s outputs. What follows about how the mouse comes to treat the smell of one particular kind of seed as meaning that food is near?

options.text: What the smell means cannot be built into the piriform cortex, so it has to come from the animal’s experience with that smell.
options.why: Correct. Random wiring carries no built-in meaning. If the wiring is random, the meaning of an odor has to come from experience.

options.text: What the smell means is built into the piriform cortex before birth, since connections that are wired at random do not change afterward.
options.why: Random wiring is exactly what rules out built-in meaning. Whether the random connections themselves change is beside the point; the meaning has to be learned.

options.text: What the smell means is fixed in the olfactory bulb, since the piriform cortex passes a random sample of the bulb’s signals on unchanged.
options.why: Nothing in the account places the meaning of a smell in the olfactory bulb. With random wiring into the piriform cortex, the meaning has to come from experience.

options.text: What the smell means cannot be learned, since connections wired at random leave nothing that experience could go on to adjust.
options.why: Random wiring with a trained output is a way of learning. The input wiring is random, and what an odor means is set by experience at the output.

items.stem: Researchers proposed a wiring for the piriform cortex to explain its sparse, scattered responses. Which way of setting a hidden layer’s weights would that wiring be an instance of, in a mammal?

options.text: Fixed random wiring with a trained output, in which what a smell means has to come from experience rather than from the wiring.
options.why: Correct. Random input to the piriform cortex, with meaning learned afterward, would be the random-wiring answer to who sets a hidden layer’s weights, found in a mammal.

options.text: Error-driven learning, in which errors are passed back from the output to set every connection, the piriform cortex’s inputs included.
options.why: Passing errors back changes every weight in the network. The proposal for the piriform cortex leaves its input wiring random.

options.text: Competitive learning, in which the cell that responds most strongly to a smell moves its weights a little toward that smell.
options.why: Competition, with neighbors moving together, would produce a map, and the piriform cortex showed none. The proposal was random wiring.

options.text: Fixed wiring built in for each smell, in which nothing is trained anywhere and every response is set before birth.
options.why: Random wiring is the opposite of wiring built in for each smell. If the wiring is random, the meaning of a smell has to come from experience.

items.stem: Two research groups image the same piriform cells while presenting the same two similar odors. One group counts a cell as active if it responds even weakly; the other counts a cell only if it responds strongly. The groups report different overlaps between the two odors. What explains the difference?

options.text: How much two odors overlap depends on how strongly a cell must respond to be counted as active, so the two counting rules give different results.
options.why: Correct. That is one of the cautions attached to the piriform result. A reported overlap is relative to the threshold used to call a cell active.

options.text: One group imaged different cells by mistake, since the overlap between two odors is a fixed property that no counting rule could change.
options.why: The overlap is not a fixed property independent of measurement. Changing the threshold for counting a cell as active changes it.

options.text: One group presented the odors at different strengths, since the rule for calling a cell active has no effect on the overlap.
options.why: A threshold for counting a cell can change the overlap, and that is exactly the caution the account attaches to the measured result.

options.text: The group using the weaker threshold found the true overlap, since cells that respond weakly, rather than strongly, are the ones that identify an odor.
options.why: Neither threshold is singled out as the true one. The point is that overlap depends on the threshold, whichever is chosen.

items.stem: A classmate writes, “The imaging study showed that the piriform cortex is wired at random”. What is wrong with the sentence?

options.text: Random wiring is a model that fits the study’s data; the study observed which cells responded, not how they were connected.
options.why: Correct. The study measured responses. Random wiring was proposed to explain them, and it is a model that fits the data, not something the study observed.

options.text: Nothing is wrong with it, since scattered responses with no map could only have come from wiring that is random.
options.why: Random wiring fits the data, but fitting is not observing, and the account never says no other wiring could produce the result.

options.text: The study showed the reverse, that each piriform cell receives its input from one family of related chemical structures.
options.why: The study did not show orderly wiring either. It measured responses, and random wiring was the proposed explanation.

options.text: Random wiring was observed in the study, but only for odors with unrelated structures, and not for the similar ones.
options.why: The study observed no wiring at all, for any odors. It imaged which cells responded.

items.stem: A student argues that the piriform cortex must work like the perceptron’s middle layer, spreading the olfactory bulb’s input across many more cells than it receives from. What does the imaging study say about that claim?

options.text: Nothing either way, since the study did not count cells and so cannot say whether any expansion happens in the piriform cortex.
options.why: Correct. Expansion is a question about numbers of cells, and the study did not count them. Whether the piriform cortex expands its input is untested by it.

options.text: It supports the claim, since each odor activated only 3 to 15 percent of the cells, which is what an expansion produces.
options.why: Sparse activity is not the same thing as expansion. A small active share says nothing about whether there are more cells than inputs.

options.text: It refutes the claim, since two similar odors still shared about a quarter of their active cells in the piriform cortex.
options.why: A remaining overlap does not bear on how many cells there are. The study did not count cells, so it neither supports nor refutes expansion.

options.text: It supports the claim, since the study observed random wiring, and random wiring always comes together with an expansion.
options.why: The study did not observe the wiring, and random wiring is a model that fits its data. Expansion was not tested.

items.stem: Pattern separation and dimensionality expansion are easy to run together. How do they differ, as far as the piriform cortex is concerned?

options.text: Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike and was measured there; expansion spreads input across more cells and was not tested by the imaging study.
options.why: Correct. The imaging study measured a drop in overlap, which is pattern separation. It did not count cells, so it says nothing about expansion.

options.text: Pattern separation spreads input across more cells and was not tested by the imaging study; expansion makes overlapping inputs less alike and was measured there.
options.why: That swaps the two definitions. Pattern separation is about overlap and was measured; expansion is about the number of cells, which the study did not count.

options.text: They are one operation under two names, so the imaging study that measured pattern separation also measured expansion there.
options.why: They are different operations. One is defined by overlap and the other by the number of cells, and the study measured only overlap.

options.text: Pattern separation needs a teacher to set its weights, while expansion needs no training, so only expansion fits random wiring.
options.why: The proposed random wiring is offered as an explanation of the measured pattern separation. Neither operation is defined by needing a teacher.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how the imaging study of the piriform cortex shows pattern separation. Describe what happened to two similar odors between the olfactory bulb and the piriform cortex, and say which of the two demands on recognition this carries out.
items.answer: Two odors with almost the same chemical structure activate overlapping sets of inputs in the olfactory bulb, sharing more than 70 percent of their active inputs. In the piriform cortex, the same two odors shared only about a quarter of their active cells. So two smells that look alike at the olfactory bulb look much less alike in the piriform cortex. Making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart, is pattern separation. It is discrimination, telling apart inputs that call for different responses, carried out by a circuit.
rubric: Says the two similar odors share a large part of their active inputs at the olfactory bulb (more than 70 percent).
Says they share far fewer of their active cells in the piriform cortex (about a quarter).
Defines pattern separation as making overlapping inputs less alike, so that a later stage can tell them apart.
Identifies pattern separation as discrimination carried out by a circuit.

items.stem: Pyramidal neurons in the piriform cortex excite one another through side branches of their axons. Suppose that when a smell activates a set of these cells, the connections among them are strengthened because the cells were active together. What can happen the next time only part of that set is activated?

options.text: The strengthened connections can activate the rest of the set, so that the whole pattern is active again.
options.why: Correct. Strengthening connections between cells that are active together is Hebb’s rule from Module 5. Because the cells excite one another through these recurrent connections, part of the set can then reactivate the rest, a second job for the same connections.

options.text: The strengthened connections inhibit the rest of the set, so that only the part that was activated stays active.
options.why: The recurrent connections among pyramidal neurons are excitatory. Strengthening them makes the rest of the set easier to activate, not harder.

options.text: The partial set is treated as a new smell, and a fresh set of connections among its cells is strengthened instead.
options.why: Treating a partial input as new would lose what was stored. On this supposition, the strengthened connections fill in the rest of the stored set.

options.text: Nothing more happens, since strengthened connections take effect only when the whole set is activated at once.
options.why: Strengthened connections act whenever part of the set is active, which is what lets a partial input reactivate the whole pattern.

items.stem: What is auto-association?

options.text: Storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a stored pattern can reactivate the rest.
options.why: Correct. The patterns are stored in the connections among the very cells that carry them, which is what makes later completion from part possible.

options.text: Pairing two different things, such as a tone and food, by strengthening the connections that link their separate representations.
options.why: That is learning to pair two different things, as in Module 5. Auto-association stores a pattern in the connections among its own cells.

options.text: Learning in which units that receive the same input inhibit one another until one wins, and only the winner moves its weights.
options.why: That is competitive learning, which needs no teacher and finds clusters of inputs. Auto-association stores whole patterns in a circuit’s own connections.

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern when only part of it arrives, as when a faint trace of a smell gives the whole smell’s response.
options.why: That is pattern completion, the recovery that auto-association makes possible. Auto-association names the storing.

items.stem: What is the name for storing patterns in the connections among a circuit’s own cells, so that part of a stored pattern can reactivate the rest?

options.text: Auto-association.
options.why: Correct. Auto-association is the storing; pattern completion is the recovery it makes possible.

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Pattern completion is recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it. The storing that makes it possible is auto-association.

options.text: Competitive learning.
options.why: Competitive learning has units inhibit one another until one wins and moves its weights. It does not store whole patterns among a circuit’s own cells.

options.text: Distributed representation.
options.why: A distributed representation is a code in which each thing is a pattern across many units. Storing such patterns in a circuit’s own connections is auto-association.

items.stem: What is pattern completion?

options.text: Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it, so that a partial input produces the response the whole would.
options.why: Correct. A faint or partial version of a familiar smell can produce the response the whole smell would, if the pattern has been stored.

options.text: Making overlapping inputs less alike than they were, so that a later stage can tell those inputs apart.
options.why: That is pattern separation, which pulls overlapping inputs apart. Pattern completion brings a partial input back to a whole.

options.text: Adding an input, such as the product of two smells, so that a single straight line can separate the cases that matter.
options.why: Adding a feature can make a hard problem easy for one straight line, but that is not completion. Completion recovers a stored pattern from part of it.

options.text: Spreading an input across many more units than it started with, through wiring that is random and is never trained.
options.why: That is random expansion, as in the mushroom body. Pattern completion recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it.

items.stem: What is the name for recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it?

options.text: Pattern completion.
options.why: Correct. Pattern completion is generalization, one of the two demands of recognition, carried out by a circuit.

options.text: Pattern separation.
options.why: Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike. Recovering a whole pattern from part runs the other way, and is pattern completion.

options.text: Auto-association.
options.why: Auto-association is the storing of patterns in a circuit’s own connections. The recovery that storing makes possible is pattern completion.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion spreads an input across many more units. It stores nothing and recovers nothing.

items.stem: Recognizing a smell makes two demands: telling apart inputs that call for different responses, and treating alike inputs that call for the same one. How do the two circuit operations studied in the piriform cortex line up with those demands?

options.text: Pattern separation carries out the telling apart, and pattern completion carries out the treating alike.
options.why: Correct. Pattern separation is discrimination carried out by a circuit, and pattern completion is generalization carried out by a circuit.

options.text: Pattern completion carries out the telling apart, and pattern separation carries out the treating alike.
options.why: That swaps the two. Completion brings a partial input back to a whole, which treats it alike; separation pulls overlapping inputs apart.

options.text: Pattern separation carries out both, since making smells less alike also lets a faint trace match the whole smell.
options.why: Making smells less alike works against matching a faint trace to the whole. Treating alike is the job of pattern completion.

options.text: Pattern completion carries out both, since recovering whole patterns also keeps two similar smells from being confused.
options.why: Recovering a whole from part draws inputs together, which does nothing to keep similar smells apart. That is the job of pattern separation.

items.stem: Why was the piriform cortex proposed as a memory that could complete a smell from part of it?

options.text: Its input spreads widely across its cells, and its pyramidal neurons excite one another through recurrent connections.
options.why: Correct. The proposal rests on those two features: input that spreads widely, and cells that excite one another, which could store patterns among the circuit’s own cells and recover them from part.

options.text: Its input passes through a relay in the thalamus, which can hold a smell there until the rest of the smell has arrived.
options.why: Smell reaches the piriform cortex without any relay in the thalamus. The grounds for the proposal lie in the piriform cortex’s own connections.

options.text: Its cells are laid out in a map by odor, so that neighboring cells can fill in whichever parts of a smell are missing.
options.why: The piriform cortex has no map; its active cells are scattered. The proposal rests on widespread input and cells that excite one another.

options.text: Its cells each stand for one whole odor, so that a single active cell is enough to bring back the rest of a smell.
options.why: No single piriform cell stands for an odor. Completion is proposed to work across a whole set of mutually exciting cells.

items.stem: A dog on a walk catches only a faint whiff of its owner’s scent on the breeze, a small part of the full smell, yet it responds as it does to the owner’s full scent. If pattern completion in the dog’s piriform cortex underlies that response, what is happening there?

options.text: The faint whiff activates part of a stored set of cells, and the strengthened connections among them activate the rest of the set.
options.why: Correct. On this proposal, a partial version of a familiar smell produces the response the whole smell would, because the stored connections fill in the rest.

options.text: The faint whiff is pulled apart from the full smell, so that it activates a set of cells with little overlap with the stored one.
options.why: That is pattern separation, and it would make the whiff look like a different smell. The response described needs the whiff drawn back to the whole.

options.text: The faint whiff is relayed through the thalamus, where it is amplified until it matches the stored version of the owner’s full smell.
options.why: Smell reaches the piriform cortex without a relay in the thalamus. Completion is proposed to happen within the piriform cortex’s own connections.

options.text: The faint whiff activates the single cell that stands for the owner, which is enough by itself to produce the full response.
options.why: No single piriform cell stands for an odor. Completion works by a partial set of cells reactivating the rest of a stored set.

items.stem: A mouse at the mouth of its burrow catches only a trace of its nest’s smell, carried on a draft. What would the proposal that the piriform cortex completes patterns explain about that moment?

options.text: How a faint, partial version of the nest’s smell can be enough for the mouse to respond as it would to the whole smell.
options.why: Correct. The proposal would explain how a partial or faint version of a familiar smell produces the response the whole smell would.

options.text: How the mouse can tell its own nest’s smell apart from a neighbor’s smell that is almost the same.
options.why: Telling two nearly identical smells apart is discrimination, which pattern separation carries out. Completion concerns a faint trace of one familiar smell.

options.text: How the mouse comes to learn what the nest’s smell means, if the wiring into the piriform cortex is random.
options.why: Meaning coming from experience follows from the random-wiring proposal, not from completion. Completion explains why a trace is enough.

options.text: How the smell can reach the mouse’s piriform cortex at all, without passing through a relay in the thalamus.
options.why: The direct route from the olfactory bulb is a fact about anatomy. Completion explains what the piriform cortex might do with a partial input once it arrives.

items.stem: How does the evidence for pattern separation in the piriform cortex compare with the evidence for pattern completion there?

options.text: Pattern separation has been measured directly in mice, while pattern completion there comes mostly from models, with few direct tests in animals.
options.why: Correct. The lecture sets the two side by side as a difference in the grade of evidence: separation was measured, and completion in the piriform cortex is mostly a model result.

options.text: Pattern completion has been measured directly in mice, while pattern separation there comes mostly from models, with few direct tests in living animals.
options.why: That swaps the two. The imaging study measured separation; completion is supported mainly by network models of the piriform circuit.

options.text: Both have been measured directly in mice, in the same imaging study that presented one odor after another to many cells at once.
options.why: The imaging study measured the overlap between odors, which is separation. It did not test completion from part of a smell.

options.text: Both come only from network models, since neither operation could be measured in the piriform cortex of a living animal.
options.why: Separation was measured directly in anesthetized mice. Only completion rests mostly on models.

items.stem: A news story reports that “scientists have proved that the piriform cortex of a mouse completes smells from fragments”. How does the chapter’s account of the evidence differ?

options.text: Models built on the piriform circuit complete patterns from part, but direct tests in animals are few, so the support comes mostly from models.
options.why: Correct. Network models of the piriform circuit do store and complete patterns. In animals the direct tests are few, so the claim is a proposal with mostly model support.

options.text: The account agrees with the story, since the imaging study that measured pattern separation in mice measured pattern completion in the same animals.
options.why: The imaging study measured how much odors overlap, which is separation. It did not test completion, which rests mostly on models.

options.text: The account reverses the story, since a circuit shown to pull similar smells apart has been shown to be unable to complete them as well.
options.why: Nothing shows the piriform cortex cannot complete smells. The hippocampus, for example, is proposed to do both separation and completion.

options.text: The account limits the story to the hippocampus, since pattern completion has been tested in the piriform cortex of mice and ruled out.
options.why: Completion has not been ruled out in the piriform cortex. Direct tests there are few, and the hippocampus is named as another proposed site.

items.stem: Besides the piriform cortex, in which structure have pattern separation and pattern completion both been proposed?

options.text: The hippocampus.
options.why: Correct. The hippocampus is the other place where both operations have been proposed. Its circuits are taken up in Modules 9 and 10.

options.text: The mushroom body.
options.why: The mushroom body of insects is the clearest evidence for random wiring. It is not the other place where both operations have been proposed.

options.text: The olfactory bulb.
options.why: The olfactory bulb is the stage before the piriform cortex, where similar odors still overlap heavily. It is not the other place where both operations have been proposed.

options.text: The ventral stream.
options.why: The ventral stream re-represents images in stages toward whole objects. It is not the other place where both operations have been proposed.

items.stem: The lecture on the cortex asks us to keep track of which results were measured, which come from models, and which are inferences. Which of these claims about the piriform cortex was measured directly?

options.text: Two similar odors share far fewer active cells in the piriform cortex than they share active inputs at the olfactory bulb.
options.why: Correct. The drop in overlap between the olfactory bulb and the piriform cortex was measured by imaging many cells at once in anesthetized mice.

options.text: Each piriform cell receives its input from a random handful of the olfactory bulb’s outputs, a different handful for each cell.
options.why: Random wiring is a model that fits the measured data. The study did not observe the wiring.

options.text: The piriform cortex spreads the olfactory bulb’s input across many more cells than the number of inputs it receives.
options.why: The imaging study did not count cells, so it says nothing about whether the piriform cortex spreads its input across more cells.

options.text: The piriform cortex recovers the whole of a familiar smell when only a faint or partial version of that smell arrives.
options.why: Completion in the piriform cortex is supported mostly by network models, with few direct tests in animals.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain how the recurrent connections of the piriform cortex could let a mouse recognize its nest from a faint trace of the nest’s smell. Name the storing and the recovering, and say how strong the evidence for this is in the piriform cortex.
items.answer: The pyramidal neurons of the piriform cortex send side branches of their axons to their neighbors, so the cells excite one another. Suppose that when the nest’s smell activates a set of these cells, the connections among them are strengthened because the cells are active together. Storing a pattern in the connections among a circuit’s own cells in this way is auto-association. Later, a faint trace activates only part of the set, and the strengthened connections activate the rest, so the trace produces the response the whole smell would. Recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it is pattern completion. In the piriform cortex, though, the support comes mostly from network models, and direct tests in animals are few.
rubric: Describes the recurrent connections as pyramidal neurons exciting their neighbors.
Says connections among cells that are active together are strengthened, and names that storing auto-association.
Says a partial input activates part of the set and the strengthened connections activate the rest, and names that recovery pattern completion.
States that the evidence in the piriform cortex comes mostly from models, with few direct tests in animals.

items.stem: Claims about the piriform cortex rest on evidence of different strengths. In a short paragraph, sort these four claims by what supports each, and say why the difference matters: similar smells are pulled apart there; its wiring is random; it spreads its input across more cells than it receives from; it completes a familiar smell from part of it.
items.answer: That similar smells are pulled apart was measured directly: in the imaging study, two similar odors that shared more than 70 percent of their active inputs at the olfactory bulb shared only about a quarter of their active cells in the piriform cortex, though how much they overlap depends on how strongly a cell must respond to be counted as active. That the wiring is random is a model that fits those data; the study did not observe the wiring. Whether the input is spread across more cells was not tested by the study, because it did not count cells. And completion from part comes mostly from network models, with few direct tests in animals. The difference matters because a model that fits the data, or a possibility the study did not test, should not be reported as if it had been observed.
rubric: Identifies pattern separation as measured directly.
Identifies random wiring as a model that fits the data, not something observed.
Identifies expansion as not tested by the study, because it did not count cells.
Identifies pattern completion as supported mostly by models, with few direct tests in animals.
Says why the grades matter, for example that a model or an untested possibility should not be reported as an observation.

items.stem: A mouse at its burrow needs to tell its own nest’s smell from a neighbor’s nearly identical smell, and also to recognize its nest from a faint trace of that smell. In a short paragraph, explain why these two needs pull in opposite directions, and how two different circuit operations in the piriform cortex could serve them.
items.answer: The first need is discrimination: the two nests’ smells overlap a great deal but call for different responses, so they have to be made less alike. The second is generalization: a faint trace shares only part of the full smell but calls for the same response, so it has to be treated alike. The two push on similar inputs in opposite directions, one pulling overlapping inputs apart and the other bringing partial inputs together, so becoming more discriminating, or more general, across the board would not serve both. Pattern separation, which has been measured in the piriform cortex, makes overlapping inputs less alike and so serves discrimination. Pattern completion, proposed for the piriform cortex and supported mostly by models, recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it and so serves generalization.
rubric: Names the first need as discrimination and the second as generalization.
Explains the opposition: one demand pulls overlapping inputs apart, while the other treats partial or differing inputs alike.
Links pattern separation to discrimination, as making overlapping inputs less alike.
Links pattern completion to generalization, as recovering a whole stored pattern from part of it.
Keeps the grades of evidence apart: separation measured, completion supported mostly by models.

pools.title: Other Brains, and One Plan Across Many Areas
pools.covers: reading §7.3.4, §7.3.5 · lecture 7.3 slides a_fly_a_bird_a_fish, one_plan_many_areas, rewired_ferrets

items.stem: What is the mushroom body?

options.text: An insect brain structure that spreads smell inputs across many more cells through connections that appear random, with learning at the connections to its output neurons.
options.why: Correct. In the fruit fly, about 50 kinds of smell input reach about 2,000 Kenyon cells through combinations that look random, and the learning happens downstream, at the connections to the output neurons.

options.text: A structure in the mammalian brain, a sheet of three layers, where the olfactory bulb’s output arrives directly, without passing through a relay in the thalamus on the way.
options.why: That describes the piriform cortex of mammals. The mushroom body is in insects, and what defines it is the random spread of smell input across many Kenyon cells.

options.text: A structure in the insect brain where each kind of smell input has a dedicated cell of its own, laid out so that neighboring cells handle smells that are chemically similar.
options.why: That would be a localist code arranged as a topographic map. In the mushroom body each Kenyon cell combines a few inputs, the combinations look random, and there is no map.

options.text: A structure in the insect brain where the connections from the smell inputs are trained by passing an error back from the output neurons after each wrong response.
options.why: Passing errors back is backpropagation. The connections into the mushroom body’s Kenyon cells are never trained; learning happens only at the connections to the output neurons.
