items.stem: What is the name for a structure in the insect brain where smell inputs are spread across many more cells, through connections that appear random, with learning at the connections to its output neurons?

options.text: The mushroom body.
options.why: Correct. In the fruit fly it spreads about 50 kinds of smell input across about 2,000 Kenyon cells, and learning happens at the connections to its output neurons.

options.text: The piriform cortex.
options.why: The piriform cortex also receives smell input and has been modeled as randomly wired, but it is the three-layered olfactory cortex of mammals, not a structure in the insect brain.

options.text: The hidden layer.
options.why: A hidden layer is any layer of units between a network’s input and its output. The Kenyon cells play that part, but the insect structure itself is the mushroom body.

options.text: Dimensionality expansion.
options.why: Dimensionality expansion names what the structure does, spreading an input across many more units. The structure in the insect brain that does it is the mushroom body.

items.stem: Random wiring has been proposed both for the mouse’s piriform cortex and for the fruit fly’s mushroom body. Why does the fly give the clearer evidence?

options.text: In the fly, the connections of Kenyon cells were traced and looked random; in the mouse, random wiring is only a model that fits the measured activity.
options.why: Correct. In the piriform cortex, pattern separation was measured and random wiring is a model that fits it. In the fly, the wiring itself was traced, which is why an insect gives the clearest evidence.

options.text: In the fly, every odor activates nearly all of the Kenyon cells at once; in the mouse, only a few piriform cells respond to each odor, which hides the wiring.
options.why: Kenyon cells respond sparsely, so each odor activates only a few of them, much as in the piriform cortex. The difference in the evidence is that the fly’s wiring was traced.

options.text: In the fly, the random combinations are identical in every animal, so they can be mapped once and for all; in the mouse, they differ from one animal to the next.
options.why: That reverses the tracing result. The fly’s combinations differed from fly to fly. What makes the fly the clearer case is that its connections were traced at all.

options.text: In the fly, learning happens at the Kenyon cells’ input connections, where it can be watched directly; in the mouse, it happens only at the output connections.
options.why: The fly’s input connections are never trained; its learning happens downstream, at the connections to the output neurons. The fly is clearer because its wiring was traced.

items.stem: In the fruit fly’s mushroom body, how does the number of kinds of smell input compare with the number of Kenyon cells, and how many of those inputs does each Kenyon cell receive?

options.text: About 50 kinds of input reach about 2,000 Kenyon cells, and each Kenyon cell receives a few of the 50 kinds.
options.why: Correct. A few dozen kinds of input are spread across tens of times as many cells, each combining a few of them. That spreading is the expansion the mushroom body is known for.

options.text: About 2,000 kinds of input converge on about 50 Kenyon cells, and each Kenyon cell receives hundreds of them.
options.why: That runs the arrangement backward, compressing many inputs into few cells. The mushroom body expands about 50 kinds of input into about 2,000 cells.

options.text: About 50 kinds of input reach about 50 Kenyon cells, and each Kenyon cell receives exactly one kind of input.
options.why: A one-to-one relay would add no new combinations at all. Each Kenyon cell combines a few of the 50 inputs, and there are about 2,000 Kenyon cells.

options.text: About 50 kinds of input reach about 2,000 Kenyon cells, and each Kenyon cell receives all 50, weighted differently.
options.why: The counts are right, but each Kenyon cell receives only a few of the 50 kinds. Combining a random few is what gives each cell a different combination to respond to.

items.stem: Researchers traced which kinds of smell input reach each of 200 Kenyon cells in fruit flies. What did the tracing find?

options.text: The combinations looked random, and they were not the same from one fly to the next.
options.why: Correct. No structure appeared in which Kenyon cell received which inputs, and the combinations differed between flies. That is the clearest evidence for random wiring.

options.text: The combinations looked random, but every fly had exactly the same set of combinations.
options.why: The combinations did look random, but they were not shared between flies. Each fly’s combinations were different.

options.text: The combinations were orderly, with neighboring Kenyon cells receiving the same few inputs.
options.why: That would be a map, with neighbors alike. The tracing found no structure of that kind; the combinations looked random.

options.text: The combinations were orderly, with each Kenyon cell receiving every kind of input.
options.why: Each Kenyon cell receives only a few of the roughly 50 kinds of input, and which few looked random.

items.stem: A fruit fly catches the smell of a single odor. How many of its roughly 2,000 Kenyon cells respond?

options.text: Only a few of them, since their responses are sparse.
options.why: Correct. Kenyon cells respond sparsely, so each odor activates only a few of them. Which few depends on the random combination of inputs each cell receives.

options.text: Nearly all of them, each firing at a different strength.
options.why: That would be a dense code, with the odor carried by graded strengths across every cell. Kenyon cells respond sparsely: each odor activates only a few.

options.text: Exactly one of them, the one cell dedicated to that odor.
options.why: That is a localist code. No Kenyon cell is dedicated to one odor; each odor activates a few cells, and each cell combines a few inputs.

options.text: About half of them, with the other half held silent.
options.why: Half the cells would be far from sparse. Each odor activates only a few Kenyon cells.

items.stem: An engineer builds a smell sensor for a robot. Thirty kinds of chemical detector feed 3,000 middle units, each connected to a random four of the detectors, and those connections are never adjusted. Only the connections from the middle units to the output are trained. Which way of setting a hidden layer’s weights does the design use, and which animal structure shows it most plainly?

options.text: Fixed random wiring with a trained output, the arrangement found in the fruit fly’s mushroom body.
options.why: Correct. A large middle layer wired at random and never trained, with learning only at the output, is the mushroom body’s arrangement: about 50 inputs spread across about 2,000 cells.

options.text: Error-driven learning, in which the error at the output trains every layer, as in the digit-reading network.
options.why: Passing the error back trains every weight in the network. The robot’s middle connections are never adjusted, which is the mark of fixed random wiring.

options.text: Competitive learning, with the middle units’ starting weights set at random, as in a topographic map formed by experience.
options.why: Competition moves the winning unit’s weights toward the input. The robot’s middle connections never move, and only the output is trained.

options.text: Auto-association, with the middle units trained so that part of a pattern brings back the rest, as proposed for the piriform cortex.
options.why: Auto-association stores patterns in a circuit’s connections among its own cells. The robot has no such connections, and its middle layer is never trained.

items.stem: The connections into the fruit fly’s Kenyon cells are never trained, and learning happens only at the connections to the output neurons. Why can that arrangement still let the fly learn from its experience with odors?

options.text: With about 2,000 cells each combining a random few of about 50 inputs, some cells are likely to respond to the combinations that matter, and only the output connections need to learn to read them.
options.why: Correct. Spreading a few inputs across many randomly combining cells makes useful combinations likely without anyone arranging them, so a single trained layer at the output can do the rest.

options.text: With each Kenyon cell receiving all of the roughly 50 inputs, every cell already carries every combination the fly could need, and the output only has to read any one of the cells.
options.why: Each Kenyon cell receives only a few of the inputs. The arrangement works because many cells combine a random few, which makes the needed combinations likely, not certain.

options.text: With the output neurons passing their errors back to the Kenyon cells, the input connections are corrected after each mistake, even though they start out wired at random in every fly.
options.why: That is backpropagation, and it would train the input connections. In the mushroom body those connections are never trained.

options.text: With the Kenyon cells competing until one wins for each odor, each odor ends up with a cell of its own, and the output connections only have to learn which cell goes with which odor.
options.why: That is competitive learning, which moves the winner’s weights. The mushroom body’s input connections are never trained, and no Kenyon cell is dedicated to one odor.

items.stem: The combinations of input that Kenyon cells receive look random and differ from one fruit fly to the next. What does that imply about where, within the mushroom body, what an odor has come to mean for a fly can be stored?

options.text: Not in the connections into the Kenyon cells, which follow no plan shared between flies, but downstream, in the connections from the Kenyon cells to the output neurons.
options.why: Correct. If the input wiring is random and different in every fly, what an odor means cannot be built into it. It has to come from experience, and in the mushroom body learning happens at the connections to the output neurons.

options.text: In the connections into the Kenyon cells, since the combinations each fly inherits already pair every Kenyon cell with an odor that mattered to the fly’s ancestors.
options.why: If the combinations paired cells with meaningful odors, they would not look random or differ from fly to fly. What an odor means has to come from experience, stored downstream at the output connections.

options.text: Nowhere in the mushroom body, since randomly wired connections cannot change, so the fly must rely on fixed reflexes for every odor it meets.
options.why: The random input wiring is never trained, but the mushroom body does learn. The change happens at the connections from the Kenyon cells to the output neurons.

options.text: In which few Kenyon cells each odor activates, since a sparse response already marks out what the odor means without any connection having to change.
options.why: A sparse response does keep odors apart, but which few cells respond is set by the random wiring, which differs from fly to fly. Telling odors apart is not knowing what they mean; that is learned at the output connections.

items.stem: A fruit fly is trained so that one odor comes with sugar, and afterward it approaches that odor. On the chapter’s account of the mushroom body, where does the change that stores this happen, and what settles which connections change?

options.text: At the connections from the Kenyon cells to the output neurons, where a signal carried by dopamine settles which of those connections change.
options.why: Correct. Learning happens downstream of the randomly wired Kenyon cells, and a dopamine signal settles which output connections change. That is Module 5’s three-factor rule.

options.text: At the connections from the smell inputs to the Kenyon cells, where a signal carried by dopamine settles which of them change, so that one cell comes to stand for the odor.
options.why: Dopamine is the right signal, but the connections into the Kenyon cells are never trained, and no single cell comes to stand for an odor. The change is at the output connections.

options.text: Among the Kenyon cells themselves, where connections between cells active together are strengthened so that part of the odor brings back the rest.
options.why: That is auto-association, the proposal for the piriform cortex’s recurrent connections. In the mushroom body the change is at the output connections, under a dopamine signal.

options.text: At the connections from the Kenyon cells to the output neurons, where a connection strengthens whenever its two cells are active together, with no third signal.
options.why: The place is right, but activity at the two ends of a connection alone is Hebb’s rule. In the mushroom body a dopamine signal also settles which output connections change, which makes it the three-factor rule.

items.stem: Both the fly’s mushroom body and the proposed memory of the mouse’s piriform cortex involve connections that change with experience. How do the rules for those changes differ, as the chapter describes them?

options.text: At the mushroom body’s output, a dopamine signal settles which connections change; in the piriform proposal, Hebb’s rule strengthens connections among cells active together.
options.why: Correct. The fly’s output connections follow Module 5’s three-factor rule, with dopamine as the third factor. The piriform proposal applies Hebb’s rule to the recurrent connections among pyramidal neurons.

options.text: Both follow Hebb’s rule with no third signal; the only difference is that the fly’s changing connections run among the Kenyon cells themselves, as recurrent connections within the mushroom body.
options.why: The fly’s changes are at the connections from the Kenyon cells to the output neurons, and a dopamine signal settles them. Hebb’s rule on recurrent connections is the piriform proposal.

options.text: At the mushroom body’s output connections, an error is passed back to the Kenyon cells; in the piriform proposal, a dopamine signal settles which connections change.
options.why: Neither structure is described as passing errors back, and the dopamine signal belongs to the fly’s output connections, not to the piriform proposal.

options.text: Both follow the three-factor rule with dopamine; the difference is that it acts on the fly’s input wiring and on the recurrent connections of the mouse’s piriform cortex.
options.why: The fly’s input wiring is never trained, and the piriform proposal is described with Hebb’s rule. Dopamine settles the changes only at the fly’s output connections.

items.stem: The fly’s mushroom body and the mouse’s piriform cortex both spread smell input across many cells through connections that look random. Why is the resemblance read as convergent evolution rather than as a structure both animals inherited from a common ancestor?

options.text: The fly and mouse lineages have been separate for more than half a billion years, and the ancestor they share had nothing like either structure.
options.why: Correct. A structure the common ancestor lacked cannot have been inherited from it. So the two lineages arrived separately at a similar arrangement for a similar problem, which is convergent evolution in Module 2’s terms.

options.text: The fly’s wiring was traced while the mouse’s wiring is a model that fits the data, so the two cannot be counted as one and the same structure.
options.why: That difference is real, but it is a difference in the evidence, not in ancestry. The convergence reading rests on the common ancestor having had neither structure.

options.text: The two structures solve the same problem, and any two structures that solve the same problem count as convergent, whatever their ancestry.
options.why: Convergence is a claim about ancestry: the similar arrangement arose separately in each lineage. Doing the same job does not settle that; the family tree does.

options.text: The two structures differ in size and in the number of cells they hold, so they cannot have descended from a single structure in a shared ancestor.
options.why: Structures descended from one ancestral structure can still differ in size. The reading rests on the ancestor having had nothing like either structure.

items.stem: Two claims are made about the fly’s mushroom body: that its input wiring is random, and that its resemblance to the mouse’s piriform cortex is convergent evolution. How does the support for the two claims differ?

options.text: The random wiring was seen, by tracing the fly’s connections; the convergence reading is an inference from the family tree that neither the fly study nor the mouse study tested.
options.why: Correct. Tracing 200 Kenyon cells showed combinations that look random. That the two arrangements arose separately is inferred from which animals descend from which, and neither study tested it.

options.text: The random wiring was seen, by tracing the fly’s connections; the convergence reading was tested by comparing the genes the two structures express, which turned out to be unrelated.
options.why: The tracing half is right. Gene expression is the evidence behind the proposed layer-4 counterparts in birds and turtles; nothing of that kind is described for the fly and the mouse.

options.text: The random wiring is a model that fits the fly’s measured activity; the convergence reading was shown by tracing the connections in the fly and in the mouse and finding the same pattern.
options.why: That swaps the two animals’ evidence. The fly’s connections were traced; in the mouse, random wiring is a model that fits the measured activity. The convergence reading was tested in neither.

options.text: The random wiring and the convergence reading are both inferences from the family tree, since neither a fly’s connections nor a mouse’s could be examined directly.
options.why: The family tree is the support for the convergence reading only. The fly’s connections were examined directly: the connections of 200 Kenyon cells were traced.

items.stem: Birds and turtles have no neocortex. What does the chapter say they do have that relates to the neocortex, and on what grounds?

options.text: Cells proposed as counterparts of the neocortex’s layer-4 cells, judged from the genes those cells express.
options.why: Correct. The cells are proposed as layer-4 counterparts from the genes they express. It is a proposal, and how the bird pallium relates to the mammalian one is still disputed.

options.text: A six-layered sheet identical to the neocortex, judged from tracing that found the same connections inside it.
options.why: Birds and turtles have no neocortex, so there is no six-layered sheet to find. The proposal concerns particular cells, and it rests on the genes they express.

options.text: A mushroom body like the fruit fly’s, judged from tracing that found random combinations of input in it.
options.why: The mushroom body belongs to insects. What is proposed in birds and turtles is counterparts of layer-4 cells, from the genes those cells express.

options.text: A neocortex only three layers thick, judged from its cells’ having the triangular cell body of pyramidal neurons.
options.why: Birds and turtles have no neocortex at all, and cell shape is not the grounds given. The proposal concerns counterparts of layer-4 cells, and it rests on the genes those cells express.

items.stem: Some cells in birds have been proposed, from the genes they express, as counterparts of the neocortex’s layer-4 cells. How does the chapter leave the broader question of how the bird pallium relates to the mammalian one?

options.text: As a dispute that continues, one that the proposal based on gene expression does not settle.
options.why: Correct. The dispute described in Module 6 continues. The layer-4 proposal is one piece of evidence in it, not a resolution.

options.text: As settled: the bird pallium is a neocortex whose six layers are arranged differently.
options.why: Birds have no neocortex. How their pallium relates to the mammalian one is left open, not settled either way.

options.text: As settled: the bird pallium is unrelated to the mammalian one, and any likeness is convergent.
options.why: Convergence is the chapter’s reading of the fly and the mouse, not of birds and mammals. For the bird pallium, the dispute continues.

options.text: As open only because no one has yet compared the genes that bird cells and mammalian cells express.
options.why: The question is open, but not for want of a gene comparison: the layer-4 proposal comes from exactly that kind of comparison, and the dispute continues anyway.

items.stem: Fish have no neocortex. What does the chapter conclude about whether a fish can recognize objects?

options.text: A fish can recognize objects with no neocortex at all, though the study offered as evidence has a gap that keeps it from being clean.
options.why: Correct. The chapter says a fish can recognize objects without a neocortex, though the evidence is less clean than it sounds: in the goldfish study, the fish may have used color alone.

options.text: A fish cannot recognize objects without a neocortex, so the fish in recognition studies must have been using simpler cues.
options.why: The chapter does not tie object recognition to the neocortex. It says a fish can recognize objects without one, while noting that the evidence is less clean than it sounds.

options.text: A fish recognizes objects with a neocortex of its own, smaller than a mammal’s and with fewer layers.
options.why: A fish has no neocortex. It has a pallium, and it meets the recognition problem with other circuits.

options.text: A fish recognizes objects across rotation as cleanly as a mammal does, and the goldfish study settles it.
options.why: The chapter holds the goldfish result at arm’s length, since the two toys in that study always differed in color.

items.stem: Goldfish learned to choose a photograph of one toy animal over a photograph of another, and still chose correctly when the photographs were rotated to new orientations. Why is that result less clean evidence of object recognition than it sounds?

options.text: The two toys always differed in color, so the fish may have used color alone.
options.why: Correct. Rotating a photograph does not change its color, so a fish choosing by color would pass the rotation test without recognizing the toy at all.

options.text: The two toys always differed in size, so the fish may have used size alone.
options.why: Size is not the problem the chapter names. The trouble is color: the two toys always differed in it.

options.text: The fish have no neocortex, so whatever they did cannot count as recognizing objects.
options.why: The chapter allows that a fish can recognize objects without a neocortex. The trouble with this result is that color alone could explain it.

options.text: The fish saw the rotated photographs during training, so nothing in the test was new to them.
options.why: The rotations were to new orientations, so the test did ask for something new. The trouble is that the toys always differed in color, and color survives rotation.

items.stem: A lizard is trained to pick a photograph of a red toy car over a photograph of a blue toy boat, and it still picks the car when both photographs are turned upside down. Before concluding that the lizard recognizes the car across rotation, what should the researcher test next?

options.text: Whether the lizard still picks the car when the two toys are the same color, so that color cannot guide the choice.
options.why: Correct. That is the weakness the chapter finds in the goldfish study, where the two toys always differed in color. Removing the color difference tests whether the shape is doing the work.

options.text: Whether the lizard still picks the car when the photographs are turned through many more angles than upside down.
options.why: More rotations would not help, since a choice made by color would survive every one of them. The color difference has to be removed.

options.text: Whether the lizard still picks the car after many more training trials, so that its choices are reliable enough to trust.
options.why: The choice is already reliable. The problem is not how often the lizard is right but which cue it could be using, and color survives rotation.

options.text: Whether the lizard still picks the car after part of its pallium is damaged, so the choice can be traced to a brain region.
options.why: Locating the choice in the brain does not say what cue it rests on. A lizard choosing by color would give the same result. The color difference has to go.

items.stem: How are the pallium and the neocortex related in a mammal?

options.text: The neocortex is part of the pallium, and in mammals it makes up most of it.
options.why: Correct. The pallium is the roof of the vertebrate forebrain, and in mammals most of the pallium is neocortex.

options.text: The pallium is a small part of the neocortex, the part that smell reaches first.
options.why: The relation runs the other way: the neocortex is most of the mammalian pallium. The cortex smell reaches first is the piriform cortex.

options.text: The two are one structure, called the pallium in fish and the neocortex in mammals.
options.why: Fish and mammals both have a pallium. In mammals, most of that pallium is neocortex, and fish have no neocortex at all.

options.text: The neocortex lies outside the pallium, and the thalamus links the two together.
options.why: The thalamus relays signals to the neocortex, but the neocortex is part of the pallium, not outside it.

items.stem: Module 6 described the neocortex as a nearly uniform sheet. What correction does the chapter make to that description?

options.text: The neocortex is not one circuit copied identically from area to area, but one circuit plan repeated with variations.
options.why: Correct. The uniform-sheet description survives with that one correction. The areas share a plan, and they vary within it.

options.text: The neocortex is far from uniform, since each area is built from its own classes of cells, each suited to the area’s job.
options.why: That overcorrects. Every area has the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way. What varies is how many cells of each class there are and how strongly they connect.

options.text: The neocortex is uniform across the sensory areas, while the motor cortex follows a separate plan of its own.
options.why: The motor cortex differs mainly in having little layer 4. It follows the same plan as the other areas, with variations.

options.text: No correction is needed, since the areas are copies of one identical circuit and differ in nothing but what connects to them.
options.why: That is the picture the chapter corrects. Areas are not identical copies; they differ in how many cells of each class they have and how strongly those cells connect.

items.stem: The chapter says neocortical areas resemble one another the way hands resemble feet. What does that comparison capture?

options.text: The same kinds of parts, arranged alike, differing mainly in how many of each there are and how strongly they connect.
options.why: Correct. Every area has the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way. Like hands and feet, areas differ in how many cells of each class they have and how strongly those cells connect.

options.text: Unrelated parts that look alike because they do similar jobs, in the way a bird’s wing and an insect’s wing look alike.
options.why: That describes resemblance by convergence. Hands and feet are variations on one plan, and so are neocortical areas.

options.text: Exact copies of one another, so that any difference in what an area does has to come from what is connected to it.
options.why: Hands and feet are not copies of each other. Areas differ in how many cells of each class they have and how strongly those cells connect.

options.text: Parts built from different kinds of cells, each kind suited to the area’s own job, joined together into one sheet.
options.why: Every area has the same classes of cells. What varies is how many of each class there are and how strongly they connect.

items.stem: A town has many houses. Which way of building them best matches the chapter’s picture of how neocortical areas relate to one another?

options.text: All built from one blueprint, with rooms of different sizes in each house and wider or narrower doorways.
options.why: Correct. One plan repeated with variations: the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way, with areas differing in how many cells of each class they have and how strongly they connect.

options.text: All stamped from one mold, identical in every room, so that what goes on in each depends only on who moves in.
options.why: Identical copies whose use depends only on what arrives is the uniform-sheet picture the chapter corrects. Areas vary in cell counts and in connection strengths.

options.text: Each built to its own blueprint by a different architect, so that they share nothing but the street they stand on.
options.why: Areas do not each have their own plan. They share the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way.

options.text: Each built to a different blueprint, yet alike from the street because every one was built for the same weather.
options.why: That is resemblance from meeting similar demands with different plans, the pattern of convergence. Neocortical areas share one plan and vary within it.

items.stem: Neocortical areas share one circuit plan. Where are the biggest differences between them found?

options.text: In layer 4, the layer that receives the input arriving from the thalamus.
options.why: Correct. Layer 4 is where areas differ most, and it is the layer where input from the thalamus arrives.

options.text: In the classes of cells, since each area has some classes of its own.
options.why: Every area has the same classes of cells. The biggest differences are in layer 4.

options.text: In the number of layers, since some areas have six and others three.
options.why: Every neocortical area follows the same six-layered plan, though layer 4 is thin in some; the three-layered sheet is the piriform cortex. The biggest differences are in layer 4.

options.text: In the direction of signals, since sensory areas only send them forward.
options.why: The cortex sends feedback from each area to the one before it, as well as signals forward. The biggest differences are in layer 4, which receives the thalamus’s input.

items.stem: How does layer 4 in the auditory cortex compare with layer 4 in the motor cortex?

options.text: It is prominent in the auditory cortex, an area that receives signals from the senses, and nearly absent in the motor cortex.
options.why: Correct. Layer 4, the layer that receives input from the thalamus, is prominent in the areas that receive signals from the senses and nearly absent in the motor cortex.

options.text: It is prominent in the motor cortex and nearly absent in the auditory cortex, since the motor cortex receives more input from the thalamus than any other area.
options.why: That reverses the pattern. Layer 4 is prominent in the areas that receive signals from the senses, and the auditory cortex is one of them.

options.text: It is the same in both, since every area has the same classes of cells connected in much the same way, whatever signals the area receives.
options.why: The classes of cells and their wiring are shared, but how many cells of each class an area has varies, and layer 4 is where the variation is greatest.

options.text: It is missing from both, since only the visual cortex has a layer 4, the layer where the signals from the eyes arrive.
options.why: Layer 4 is part of the plan every neocortical area shares. It is prominent in the areas that receive signals from the senses, the auditory cortex among them, and nearly absent in the motor cortex.

items.stem: Layer 4 of the visual cortex is the layer that receives input from the thalamus. How do the excitatory synapses there that arrive from the thalamus compare in number with those that come from other cortical cells?

options.text: Those from the thalamus are fewer than a tenth of the total, and most of the rest come from other cortical cells.
options.why: Correct. Most of a cortical cell’s input comes from other cortical cells, not from outside. Even in the input layer of the visual cortex, the thalamus supplies less than a tenth of the excitatory synapses.

options.text: Those from other cortical cells are fewer than a tenth of the total, and most of the rest come from the thalamus.
options.why: That reverses the proportions. Even in the layer that receives the thalamus’s input, most excitatory synapses come from other cortical cells.

options.text: Those from the thalamus and those from other cortical cells are about equal in number, as in every other cortical area.
options.why: The shares are far from equal. Connections from the thalamus make up less than a tenth of the excitatory synapses, and the rest come mostly from cortical cells.

options.text: Those from the thalamus are most of the total in this layer, though other cortical cells supply most of the input to the layers above and below.
options.why: Layer 4 is where the thalamus’s input arrives, which makes this seem likely. But even there, connections from the thalamus make up less than a tenth of the excitatory synapses.

items.stem: Every neocortical area follows one circuit plan. Does the chapter conclude that every area therefore carries out the same computation?

options.text: It leaves the question open, and the strongest evidence on it, from rewired ferrets, shows only that input shapes what an area does.
options.why: Correct. Whether one circuit plan means one computation everywhere is still an open question. The shared plan raises the question without answering it, and the rewired ferrets show that input shapes what an area does, nothing stronger.

options.text: Yes: the rewired ferrets showed that any area can take over the computation of any other area, given the right input.
options.why: The ferrets show that input shapes what an area does. They do not show that areas are interchangeable, and the question stays open.

options.text: No: the differences in layer 4 show that each area carries out an unrelated computation of its own, whatever reaches it.
options.why: Layer 4 varies from area to area, but the chapter does not conclude from that that the computations are unrelated. The question is left open.

options.text: It leaves the question open, since the only evidence bearing on it comes from animals with no neocortex, such as birds and fish.
options.why: The question is open, but not for lack of mammalian evidence. The strongest evidence on it comes from rewired ferrets, whose auditory cortex was fed signals from the eyes.

items.stem: Whether one circuit plan means one computation everywhere is an open question. Why do the rewired ferrets count as the strongest evidence on it?

options.text: The rewiring changed what one area received without operating on the area itself, so differences in what the area came to do could be traced to its input.
options.why: Correct. The lecture describes it as an experiment that changed what an area receives. Leaving the area alone and changing its input asks how much of what an area does comes from what reaches it.

options.text: The rewiring swapped the circuits of two areas while leaving their inputs in place, so differences in what the areas came to do could be traced to the circuits.
options.why: That is the reverse design. Nothing was done to the auditory cortex itself; what changed was its input, which now came from the eyes.

options.text: The rewiring removed the auditory cortex from day-old ferrets, so the rest of the neocortex had to take over the work it would have done.
options.why: The auditory cortex was removed only at the end of the behavioral study, to check which route the lights used. The rewiring itself redirected input from the eyes.

options.text: The rewiring was done in an animal whose areas have no layer 4, so that its areas differ from one another in nothing but their input.
options.why: Ferrets are mammals, and their neocortex follows the same plan as any other. The design is strong because the input changed while the circuit did not.

items.stem: What did researchers do to ferrets a day old to produce the rewired ferrets?

options.text: They cut the auditory part of the thalamus off from its normal input; axons from the eyes grew into it, and it passed their signals on to the auditory cortex.
options.why: Correct. The auditory thalamus kept its normal connections to the auditory cortex. What changed was where its input came from: the eyes instead of the ears.

options.text: They transplanted a piece of visual cortex into the place where the auditory cortex would have been, so that sounds reached tissue that would normally handle vision.
options.why: Nothing was transplanted. The auditory cortex stayed where it was, and its input was changed by letting the eyes’ axons grow into the auditory thalamus.

options.text: They connected axons from the eyes straight to the auditory cortex, bypassing the thalamus altogether, so that visual signals arrived there without any relay.
options.why: The eyes’ axons grew into the auditory part of the thalamus, which passed their signals to the auditory cortex along its normal connections. The thalamus was not bypassed.

options.text: They cut the nerves from the eyes, so that the visual cortex was left without input and came to respond to sounds from the auditory thalamus instead.
options.why: The study changed what the auditory cortex received, not what the visual cortex received. Axons from the eyes grew into the auditory thalamus.

items.stem: As the rewired ferrets grew up, what kind of cells developed in their auditory cortex, which was now receiving signals from the eyes?

options.text: Cells that responded to edges at particular orientations, like the cells in the visual cortex.
options.why: Correct. The auditory cortex, fed by the eyes, developed cells tuned to oriented edges, the kind of cell the visual cortex normally has.

options.text: Cells that responded to particular pitches of sound, like the cells in a normal auditory cortex.
options.why: The area had stopped receiving signals from the ears. Fed by the eyes, it developed cells tuned to oriented edges.

options.text: Cells that responded to nothing, since the area could make no use of signals from the eyes.
options.why: The area did use them. It developed cells that responded to edges at particular orientations.

options.text: Cells that responded to whole objects, like the cells at the far end of the ventral stream.
options.why: Responses to whole objects belong to the inferior temporal cortex. The rewired cells responded to oriented edges, like cells in the primary visual cortex.

items.stem: How did the arrangement of the orientation-tuned cells in the rewired auditory cortex compare with their arrangement in the visual cortex?

options.text: Both formed an orientation map, but the rewired map was less orderly, with far fewer of the points where all the orientations meet.
options.why: Correct. The rewired cells were arranged in an orientation map, but a less orderly one, with about a quarter as many of the points where all the orientations meet.

options.text: Both formed an orientation map, and the rewired map was as orderly as the visual cortex’s, with as many points where all the orientations meet.
options.why: The rewired map was less orderly than the visual cortex’s, with about a quarter as many of those points.

options.text: The rewired cells formed no map at all, and were scattered with no order, much as the active cells are in the piriform cortex.
options.why: Scattered cells with no map describe the piriform cortex. The rewired cells did form an orientation map, though a less orderly one.

options.text: The rewired map was more orderly than the visual cortex’s, since it formed without the ears’ signals arriving to compete with the eyes’.
options.why: The rewired map was less orderly, not more. That is one reason the area is described as becoming more visual-like, not visual.

items.stem: Ferrets rewired on one side were trained to go to one spout for a sound and to another for a light. Then the normal visual pathway on the rewired side was cut. Why?

options.text: So that signals from one part of the visual field could reach the cortex only through the rewired route.
options.why: Correct. With the normal pathway gone, any response to a light in that part of the field had to depend on signals passing through the auditory thalamus to the auditory cortex.

options.text: So that the ferrets could no longer see at all, and would have to treat every signal they met as a sound.
options.why: The cut was on one side, for one part of the visual field, and its point was to leave the rewired route as the only way in for those lights.

options.text: So that the visual cortex would grow into the neighboring auditory cortex and take over the rewired route.
options.why: No tissue was expected to grow into another area. Cutting the normal pathway isolated the rewired route, so responses to those lights depended on it.

options.text: So that axons from the eyes would grow into the auditory part of the thalamus for the first time.
options.why: The animals were already rewired. Cutting the normal pathway came later, to leave the rewired route as the only way for those lights to reach the cortex.

items.stem: Recordings had shown that the rewired auditory cortex contained cells tuned to oriented edges. Another study then trained rewired ferrets to go to one spout for a sound and to another for a light. What could the trained ferrets reveal that the recordings could not?

options.text: Whether the animals themselves treated signals arriving through the rewired cortex as light or as sound.
options.why: Correct. The lecture puts the question this way: did the animals treat those signals as light or as sound? Cells tuned like visual cells do not say how the animal takes the signal; its choice of spout does.

options.text: Whether the rewired cells were arranged in an orientation map like the one found in the visual cortex.
options.why: The map was found by recording from the cortex. The trained ferrets answered a question about the animal, not about how its cells were arranged.

options.text: Whether axons from the eyes had in fact grown into the auditory part of the thalamus after rewiring.
options.why: Where the axons grew is a question about anatomy, answered from the tissue. The behavioral study asked how the animals treated the signals.

options.text: Whether the rewired auditory cortex still responded to sound as well as to light reaching it from the eyes.
options.why: Responses to sound could be recorded from the cells themselves. The trained ferrets showed something recordings cannot: how the animal treated what reached it.

items.stem: Rewired ferrets had learned to go to one spout for a sound and to another for a light. When lights could reach the cortex only through the rewired route, what did the three fully tested animals do?

options.text: They treated those lights as lights, going to the spout they had been trained to use for lights.
options.why: Correct. All three animals that were fully tested treated those lights as lights, not as sounds, even though the signals reached them through the auditory cortex.

options.text: They treated those lights as sounds, going to the spout they had learned to go to for a sound.
options.why: That is what we might expect if the area kept its usual job whatever reached it. The animals treated the lights as lights.

options.text: They responded at about chance, as if the lights reaching the rewired route went unnoticed.
options.why: Responses fell to about chance only later, after the auditory cortex was removed. Before that, the animals treated the lights as lights.

options.text: They ignored those lights until their auditory cortex was removed, and then treated them as lights.
options.why: The order runs the other way. They treated the lights as lights first, and removing the auditory cortex brought their responses down to about chance.

items.stem: The rewired ferrets treated lights that reached the cortex only through the rewired route as lights. When their auditory cortex was then removed, their responses fell to about chance. What does the drop to chance add?

options.text: It shows the animals had been relying on the rewired auditory cortex for those signals, not on some other route.
options.why: Correct. Once the area was gone, the animals could no longer respond to those lights above chance, so the area had been carrying them.

options.text: It shows that the rewired auditory cortex had become a visual cortex, identical to the one on the normal side.
options.why: Losing the area shows the responses ran through it. It says nothing about the area matching the visual cortex, and the area became more visual-like, not visual.

options.text: It shows that the ferrets had been guessing all along, since the rewired route never carried useful signals.
options.why: Before the removal the animals treated the lights as lights. The drop to chance came after the removal, which is why it shows the responses depended on that area.

options.text: It shows that the auditory cortex is needed for hearing, which is why the ferrets could no longer respond to the sound.
options.why: The test concerned lights reaching the rewired route. The drop to chance on those lights shows that the rewired auditory cortex was carrying them.

items.stem: A headline about the rewired ferrets reads “Any brain area can do any job”. How does the chapter’s reading of the results compare with the headline?

options.text: The results show that input shapes what a cortical area does, not that cortical areas are interchangeable.
options.why: Correct. An area that would have handled sound came to treat light as light. But the map was less orderly and sight less sharp, so the areas are not interchangeable.

options.text: The results support the headline, since the auditory cortex came to do the visual cortex’s job as well as the visual cortex does.
options.why: The rewired area did less well: its map was less orderly, and the animals saw less sharply through it. The headline claims more than the results show.

options.text: The results show nothing either way, since only three animals were fully tested in the behavioral study.
options.why: Three is a small number, and the chapter keeps that qualifier. But it still reads the results as showing that input shapes what an area does.

options.text: The results show the reverse, that each area’s job is fixed by its circuit, and that the input made no difference.
options.why: The input made a large difference: the auditory cortex developed visual-like cells and came to treat light as light.

items.stem: How did the rewired ferrets’ vision through the rewired route compare with vision through the normal visual pathway?

options.text: It was less sharp, which is part of why the area is described as becoming more visual-like, not visual.
options.why: Correct. The animals saw less sharply through the rewired route, and its map was less orderly. The area became visual-like without becoming a visual cortex.

options.text: It was just as sharp, since the rewired cells were tuned to orientation like the cells in the visual cortex.
options.why: Orientation tuning was there, but the animals saw less sharply through the rewired route. The results do not show that the ferrets saw normally.

options.text: It was absent altogether, since the ferrets treated lights reaching the rewired route as sounds.
options.why: The fully tested animals treated those lights as lights. They could see through the rewired route, though less sharply.

options.text: It was sharper, since the rewired cortex had no ear signals left to blur what came from the eyes.
options.why: Sight through the rewired route was less sharp, not sharper, and the rewired map was less orderly than the visual cortex’s.

items.stem: Suppose that, in newborn ferrets, signals from the whiskers were routed into the auditory part of the thalamus in place of its normal input. On the chapter’s reading of the rewired ferrets, what would be the most reasonable expectation?

options.text: The auditory cortex would likely come to respond in ways shaped by touch, more touch-like, but not the same as the normal touch area.
options.why: Correct. This is a prediction, not a result anyone has reported. The rewired ferrets show that input shapes what an area does: an area fed by the eyes became more visual-like, not visual. By the same reading, more touch-like, but not a touch area, is the fair expectation.

options.text: The auditory cortex would go on responding as an auditory area to the end, since what an area does is fixed by its circuit and not by its input.
options.why: The rewired ferrets argue against this. An area that would normally have handled sound came to treat light as light, because light was what reached it.

options.text: The auditory cortex would become a touch area exactly like the normal one, since the rewired ferrets showed that cortical areas are interchangeable.
options.why: The ferret results do not show that areas are interchangeable. The rewired area became more visual-like, not visual, so an exact match is more than they support.

options.text: The auditory cortex would respond to nothing at all, since signals can be relayed through the auditory thalamus only when they come from the eyes.
options.why: Nothing in the ferret results makes the eyes special. What they show is that an area’s input shapes what it does, whatever the input is.

items.stem: The fly’s mushroom body is often set beside the mouse’s piriform cortex. Which property has actually been observed in both, as the chapter describes them?

options.text: Each odor activates only a small share of the cells, so the response is sparse in both structures.
options.why: Correct. Kenyon cells respond sparsely, and in the piriform cortex each odor activated only a small set of the imaged cells. Sparse responding was observed in both.

options.text: The connections were traced in both, and in each they turned out to combine their inputs at random.
options.why: Only the fly’s connections were traced. In the piriform cortex, random wiring is a model that fits the measured activity.

options.text: Each spreads its input across many more cells than it receives from, as counted in both animals.
options.why: The fly’s expansion from about 50 inputs to about 2,000 cells is known, but the piriform study did not count cells, so expansion there was not measured.

options.text: Both descend from one structure that was present in the last common ancestor of flies and mice.
options.why: That ancestor had nothing like either structure. The resemblance is read as convergent evolution, an inference from the family tree.

items.stem: In a few sentences, describe how the fruit fly’s mushroom body is wired and where its learning happens, and explain why the fly can learn about odors even though the connections into its Kenyon cells are never trained.
items.answer: About 50 kinds of smell input feed about 2,000 Kenyon cells, and each Kenyon cell receives a few of them. The combinations look random, and the connections into the Kenyon cells are never trained. Learning happens downstream, at the connections from the Kenyon cells to the output neurons, where a dopamine signal settles which connections change, which is Module 5’s three-factor rule. The arrangement works because spreading a few inputs at random across many more cells makes it likely that some cells respond to the combinations that matter, so trained output connections can pick them out.
rubric: Describes an expansion: about 50 kinds of input spread across about 2,000 Kenyon cells, each receiving a few.
Says the combinations look random and the connections into the Kenyon cells are never trained.
Places learning at the connections from the Kenyon cells to the output neurons.
Names a dopamine signal as what settles which output connections change (the three-factor rule).
Explains that many random combinations make useful ones likely, so training the output connections is enough.

items.stem: In a few sentences, explain why the resemblance between the fly’s mushroom body and the mouse’s piriform cortex is read as convergent evolution, and say what kind of claim that reading is.
items.answer: The fly and the mouse are separated by more than half a billion years of evolution, and their last common ancestor had nothing like either the mushroom body or the piriform cortex. So the similar arrangement cannot have been inherited from that ancestor. The two lineages arrived at it separately, for a similar problem, which is convergent evolution in Module 2’s terms. That reading is an inference from the family tree of animals. Neither the fly study nor the mouse study tested it.
rubric: Says the fly and mouse lineages have been separate for more than half a billion years.
Says their last common ancestor had nothing like either structure.
Concludes that the two lineages arrived separately at a similar arrangement for a similar problem.
Labels the reading an inference from the family tree, not something either study tested.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, say what the rewired ferrets show about the neocortex and where the limits of that conclusion lie, giving the evidence for each.
items.answer: The rewired ferrets show that input shapes what a cortical area does. When signals from the eyes were routed through the auditory part of the thalamus to the auditory cortex, it developed cells tuned to edges at particular orientations, arranged in an orientation map. Animals trained to tell sounds from lights treated lights that reached the cortex only through the rewired route as lights, and their responses fell to about chance when the auditory cortex was removed. An area that would normally have handled sound came to treat light as light, because light was what reached it. But the results do not show that areas are interchangeable, or that the ferrets saw normally. The rewired map was less orderly, the animals saw less sharply through the rewired route, and the area is described as becoming more visual-like, not visual. The behavioral result also comes from the three animals that were fully tested.
rubric: States the positive conclusion: input shapes what a cortical area does.
Gives evidence for it: orientation-tuned cells or an orientation map in the auditory cortex, or lights treated as lights with a drop to chance after removal.
States that the results do not show that areas are interchangeable or that the ferrets saw normally.
Gives evidence for the limit: a less orderly map, less sharp sight, or the area becoming “more visual-like, not visual”.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain the correction the chapter makes to Module 6’s picture of the neocortex as a nearly uniform sheet. Say what stays the same from one area to the next, what varies, and where the variation is greatest.
items.answer: The neocortex is not one circuit copied identically across the sheet. It is one circuit plan, repeated with variations. Every area has the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way, so areas resemble one another the way hands resemble feet. What varies is how many cells of each class an area has and how strongly they connect. The biggest differences are in layer 4, the layer that receives input from the thalamus. Layer 4 is prominent in the areas that receive signals from the senses and nearly absent in the motor cortex.
rubric: States the correction: one circuit plan repeated with variations, not one circuit copied identically.
Says the classes of cells and the way they connect are shared across areas.
Says areas differ in how many cells of each class they have and how strongly they connect.
Places the biggest differences in layer 4, which receives input from the thalamus.
Says layer 4 is prominent in areas that receive signals from the senses and nearly absent in the motor cortex.

items.stem: On the island, under Fixed at random, the hidden weights are drawn once and never change, and only the connections to the output learn. The card for that setting names an animal whose brain is wired this way, and adds a sentence about fish. What do the card and the runs, taken together, license about real fish?

options.text: No conclusion on their wiring: the card names the fruit fly’s mushroom body as wired like this, and leaves open whether a fish’s pallium is.
options.why: Correct. In the fly, about 50 kinds of smell input reach about 2,000 Kenyon cells through connections that look random, and learning happens at the connections to the output neurons. The lab shows the arrangement can work, not that a fish has it.

options.text: No conclusion on their wiring: the card names the mouse’s piriform cortex as wired like this, and leaves open whether a fish’s pallium is.
options.why: The fish half is right, but the card names the fruit fly’s mushroom body, where the connections were traced and look random. In the mouse’s piriform cortex, random wiring is a model the data fit, not something seen.

options.text: That a fish’s pallium must be wired at random, since the lab’s fish solved the island with a hidden layer wired in just this way.
options.why: A model that works shows what an arrangement can do, not what a fish has. The card says outright that whether a fish’s pallium is wired like this is not known.

options.text: That a fish’s pallium is wired like the mouse’s piriform cortex, since random wiring was measured there and fish and mice are both vertebrates.
options.why: Random wiring in the piriform cortex is a model the data fit, not a measurement. And neither result says how a fish’s pallium is wired.

pools.title: The Visual Cortex Beside a Network
pools.covers: reading §7.3.6, §7.3.7 · lecture 7.3 slides visual_cortex_beside_a_network, two_homes, could_cortex_pass_errors_back

items.stem: What is a cell’s receptive field?

options.text: The region of the sensory world where a stimulus changes the cell’s activity, together with the kind of stimulus that does it.
options.why: Correct. A receptive field names both where a stimulus has to fall and what kind of stimulus it has to be, such as an edge at a particular orientation.

options.text: The set of other cells whose axons end on the cell, together with the strength of each of those connections to it.
options.why: That describes a cell’s inputs and their weights, which is wiring. A receptive field is defined by the stimulus in the world that changes the cell’s activity, not by which cells connect to it.

options.text: The patch of cortex around the cell, within which neighboring cells respond to stimuli similar to the ones the cell responds to.
options.why: Neighboring cells handling neighboring or similar stimuli is a topographic map, an arrangement of many cells in tissue. A receptive field belongs to one cell and is a region of the sensory world.

options.text: The range of changes to a stimulus, such as shifts in position or size, over which the cell keeps its preferred response.
options.why: That is tolerance, a cell’s keeping its response over a limited range of changes. A receptive field is where a stimulus has to fall, and what kind it has to be, to change the cell’s activity at all.

items.stem: What is the name for the region of the sensory world where a stimulus changes a cell’s activity, together with the kind of stimulus that does it?

options.text: Receptive field.
options.why: Correct. A receptive field names both where a stimulus must fall and what kind of stimulus changes the cell’s activity, such as an edge at a particular orientation.

options.text: Topographic map.
options.why: A topographic map is an arrangement of many cells, in which neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring cells. The region and kind of stimulus that drive one cell are its receptive field.

options.text: Tolerance.
options.why: Tolerance is a cell’s keeping its response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus. The region where a stimulus changes the cell’s activity at all is its receptive field.

options.text: Feature space.
options.why: A feature space is a model’s space with one axis for each feature, in which each input is a single point. It describes inputs, not the region of the sensory world that drives one cell.

items.stem: What is a simple cell?

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex whose receptive field is divided into regions where light excites it and regions where light inhibits it.
options.why: Correct. Because its field is a map of excitatory and inhibitory regions, a simple cell’s response to any pattern of light can be predicted from that map.

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex that responds to an edge or bar of the right orientation anywhere within a fairly large receptive field.
options.why: That is a complex cell. Its response depends on the orientation of an edge and hardly on where in its field the edge falls, so no map of regions predicts it.

options.text: A cell in the inferior temporal cortex that responds to a whole object and keeps that response over a limited range of changes.
options.why: That describes cells at the far end of the ventral stream, which have tolerance. A simple cell sits at the start, in the primary visual cortex, with a small field mapped into excitatory and inhibitory regions.

options.text: A unit in a network’s hidden layer, driven directly by neither the world nor the response, that comes to stand for a combination of inputs.
options.why: That is a hidden unit in an artificial neural network. A simple cell is a neuron in the primary visual cortex, defined by a receptive field split into regions where light excites and inhibits it.

items.stem: What is the name for a cell in the primary visual cortex whose response to any pattern of light can be predicted from a map of the regions of its receptive field where light excites it and where light inhibits it?

options.text: Simple cell.
options.why: Correct. The excitatory and inhibitory regions of a simple cell’s receptive field form a map, and the map predicts the cell’s response to any pattern of light.

options.text: Complex cell.
options.why: A complex cell responds to an edge of the right orientation anywhere within a larger field, so its response cannot be read off a map of excitatory and inhibitory regions.

options.text: Pyramidal neuron.
options.why: The pyramidal neuron is the main excitatory cell of the cortex, named for its triangular cell body and long apical dendrite. It is defined by its shape, not by a map of its receptive field.

options.text: Receptive field.
options.why: Every visual cell has a receptive field, the region and kind of stimulus that changes its activity. The cell whose field is mapped into excitatory and inhibitory regions is the simple cell.

items.stem: What is a complex cell?

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex that responds to an edge or bar of a particular orientation anywhere within a fairly large receptive field.
options.why: Correct. Orientation matters to a complex cell, and exact position within its field hardly does, which is why it is compared with pooling in a network.

options.text: A cell in the primary visual cortex whose receptive field is divided into regions where light excites it and regions where light inhibits it.
options.why: That is a simple cell. Its response can be predicted from a map of those regions, while a complex cell responds to the right orientation wherever in its larger field the edge falls.

options.text: A cell in the inferior temporal cortex whose activity, summed with that of a few hundred others, reports which object is in view.
options.why: A weighted sum over a few hundred IT neurons can report the object, but those cells sit at the far end of the ventral stream. A complex cell is in the primary visual cortex and responds to oriented edges.

options.text: A cell in the piriform cortex whose axon sends side branches that excite neighboring cells, so that a circuit of them can store patterns.
options.why: That describes the pyramidal neurons of the piriform cortex and their recurrent connections. A complex cell is a visual cell, defined by its response to an oriented edge anywhere within a larger field.

items.stem: What is the name for a cell in the primary visual cortex that responds to an edge or bar of the right orientation anywhere within a fairly large receptive field?

options.text: Complex cell.
options.why: Correct. A complex cell keeps its preference for an orientation across positions within its field, unlike a simple cell, whose response depends on exactly where the light falls.

options.text: Simple cell.
options.why: A simple cell is also tuned to orientation, but its field is split into regions where light excites and inhibits it, so where the edge falls matters a great deal.

options.text: Pyramidal neuron.
options.why: Pyramidal neurons are the main excitatory cells of the cortex, named for their shape. The cell defined by responding to an oriented edge anywhere in a larger field is the complex cell.

options.text: Pooling.
options.why: Pooling is the network operation a complex cell is compared with, combining detections over a small neighborhood. It is an operation in an artificial neural network, not a cell in the visual cortex.

items.stem: What is the ventral stream?

options.text: The series of visual areas running from the primary visual cortex along the underside of the brain to the inferior temporal cortex.
options.why: Correct. The ventral stream runs through V2 and V4 to IT, and at its far end cells respond to whole objects.

options.text: The route by which visual signals travel from the eyes, through a relay in the thalamus, to arrive at the primary visual cortex.
options.why: That route brings signals to V1, where the ventral stream begins. The ventral stream is the series of areas beyond V1, ending in the inferior temporal cortex.

options.text: The feedback connections that carry signals from each visual area back to the area before it, which networks lack.
options.why: The cortex does send feedback from each area to the one before it, and the networks compared with it have none. But the ventral stream is the series of areas itself, from V1 to IT.

options.text: The stack of convolution and pooling layers in a network, in which each layer covers a wider region of the image.
options.why: That describes a convolutional network, the artificial system the ventral stream is compared with. The ventral stream is a series of visual areas in the brain.

items.stem: What is the name for the series of visual areas, passing through V2 and V4, that runs from the primary visual cortex along the underside of the brain to the inferior temporal cortex?

options.text: Ventral stream.
options.why: Correct. Up the ventral stream, receptive fields grow larger, and cells at its far end, in IT, respond to whole objects.

options.text: Topographic map.
options.why: A topographic map is an arrangement within a sheet of cells, with neighboring points in the world handled by neighboring cells. The series of areas from V1 to IT is the ventral stream.

options.text: Hidden layer.
options.why: A hidden layer is a layer of units inside an artificial neural network. The ventral stream is compared with a stack of such layers, but it is a series of visual areas in the brain.

options.text: Piriform cortex.
options.why: The piriform cortex is the three-layered olfactory cortex, which receives smell signals directly from the olfactory bulb. The visual series ending in IT is the ventral stream.

items.stem: What is a visual cell’s tolerance?

options.text: Its keeping its preferred response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus, such as changes of position or size.
options.why: Correct. Tolerance is limited by definition. Cells up the ventral stream have more of it, but no single cell becomes fully invariant.

options.text: Its recognizing a thing across every change that alters its input a great deal, such as changes of distance or viewpoint.
options.why: That describes invariance, and in its strongest form. No single cell in the ventral stream becomes fully invariant; what a cell has is tolerance over a limited range.

options.text: How close its resting state sits to firing, which sets how much input it needs before it begins to respond at all.
options.why: That is excitability, the neuron’s counterpart of the criterion, which neuromodulators change. Tolerance is about how far a stimulus can change before the cell’s preferred response is lost.

options.text: The region of the visual field where a stimulus changes its activity, together with the kind of stimulus that does it.
options.why: That is the cell’s receptive field. Tolerance is the range of changes, such as shifts in position or size, over which the cell keeps its preferred response.

items.stem: What is the name for a cell’s keeping its preferred response over a limited range of changes to a stimulus, such as changes of position or size?

options.text: Tolerance.
options.why: Correct. The word “limited” is what separates tolerance from invariance. Cells up the ventral stream are tolerant, and none is fully invariant.

options.text: Invariance.
options.why: Invariance is recognizing a thing across changes that alter its input a great deal. No single cell in the ventral stream has it; a cell’s limited range is called tolerance.

options.text: Generalization.
options.why: Generalization is treating alike the inputs that call for the same response, a demand on a whole recognizer. One cell keeping its response over a limited range of changes is tolerance.

options.text: Pooling.
options.why: Pooling combines detections over a small neighborhood so that a small shift no longer changes the result, which is one way to build some tolerance. The cell’s property itself is tolerance.

items.stem: Smell signals travel from the olfactory bulb straight to the piriform cortex. By what route do visual signals reach the primary visual cortex, V1?

options.text: From the eyes through a relay in the thalamus to V1, the route that signals from senses other than smell take to the cortex.
options.why: Correct. Vision takes the usual route, through a relay in the thalamus. Smell is the unusual sense, reaching the piriform cortex with no relay in the thalamus.

options.text: From the eyes straight to V1 with no relay on the way, by the same direct kind of route that smell takes to the piriform cortex.
options.why: Smell’s direct route is the exception, not the rule. Visual signals pass through a relay in the thalamus before they reach V1.

options.text: From the eyes to the inferior temporal cortex first, which then passes the signals back down to V1 so it can handle finer detail.
options.why: IT is at the far end of the ventral stream, beyond V1, not its entry point. Signals reach V1 from the thalamus and then travel up the stream toward IT.

options.text: From the eyes through V2 and then V4, each of which passes the signals forward in turn until they finally arrive at V1.
options.why: V2 and V4 lie beyond V1 on the ventral stream, so this order is reversed. Signals reach V1 first, through a relay in the thalamus.

items.stem: Cells in the primary visual cortex, V1, of cats and other mammals come in two kinds. What do the cells of both kinds respond to, and what tells the two kinds apart?

options.text: Edges at particular orientations, and the two kinds, simple and complex, differ in their receptive fields.
options.why: Correct. V1 cells are tuned to edges at particular orientations, and simple and complex cells are told apart by their receptive fields: a field mapped into excitatory and inhibitory regions, or a larger field where the right orientation anywhere will do.

options.text: Whole objects such as faces and hands, and the two kinds differ in how many different objects each one prefers.
options.why: Cells that respond to whole objects are found at the far end of the ventral stream, in IT. In V1, the cells respond to edges at particular orientations.

options.text: Single points of light, and the two kinds differ in whether light at that point excites them or inhibits them.
options.why: A simple cell’s field does have regions where light excites it and regions where light inhibits it, but within one cell. The cells respond to oriented edges, and the two kinds are simple and complex.

options.text: Edges at any orientation, and the two kinds differ in whether they lie in the left half of V1 or the right half.
options.why: Each cell responds to edges at a particular orientation, not at any orientation. And the two kinds, simple and complex, are told apart by their receptive fields, not by where they lie.

items.stem: Mapping a cell in the primary visual cortex, researchers find a narrow vertical strip of its receptive field where a spot of light excites the cell, with strips on either side where a spot of light inhibits it. What kind of cell is it, and what does the map make possible?

options.text: A simple cell, whose response to a new pattern of light, such as a tilted bar, can be predicted from the map of its regions.
options.why: Correct. A receptive field split into regions where light excites and regions where light inhibits is what makes a cell simple, and the map predicts its response to any pattern.

options.text: A complex cell, whose response to a vertical bar would be the same wherever in its large receptive field the bar happened to fall.
options.why: A complex cell responds to an oriented edge anywhere within a larger field, so where the light falls hardly matters. Separate excitatory and inhibitory strips mark a simple cell.

options.text: A simple cell, whose response to a new pattern cannot be predicted, because only single spots of light were used to make its map.
options.why: The point of a simple cell is the reverse: its response to any pattern can be predicted from the map of where light excites it and where light inhibits it.

options.text: A complex cell, built from simple cells, whose map shows which of the simple cells feed it and at which positions in the field.
options.why: Building complex cells from simple cells is a tentative proposal, and a map of where light excites and inhibits says nothing about wiring. Such a map describes a simple cell.

items.stem: A cell in the primary visual cortex fires to a bar of light tilted at 45 degrees whether the bar falls toward one side, in the middle, or toward the other side of its fairly large receptive field. It barely fires to a vertical bar in any of those places. What kind of cell is it?

options.text: A complex cell, which responds to an edge or bar of the right orientation anywhere within a larger receptive field.
options.why: Correct. Orientation matters to this cell and exact position within its field does not, which is what defines a complex cell.

options.text: A simple cell, whose receptive field is divided into regions where light excites the cell and regions where light inhibits it.
options.why: A simple cell is tuned to orientation too, but its response depends on exactly where the light falls relative to its excitatory and inhibitory regions.

options.text: A cell in IT, which responds to a whole object and keeps its response over wider changes in the object’s position and size.
options.why: IT cells respond to whole objects, not single bars, and they lie at the far end of the ventral stream. The cell described is in V1 and tuned to an orientation.

options.text: A fully invariant cell, which keeps its response to a stimulus across every change of position, size, and orientation.
options.why: This cell stops responding when the orientation changes, so it does not keep its response across every change. And no single cell in the ventral stream becomes fully invariant.

items.stem: A complex cell could be built by combining the outputs of several simple cells that prefer the same orientation at slightly different positions. What standing does that idea have?

options.text: A suggestion about how a complex cell might be built, put forward from the start as “obviously tentative”.
options.why: Correct. The arrangement is the one built into the neocognitron and described in networks as convolution followed by pooling, but in the visual cortex it remains a proposal, hedged from the start.

options.text: An established wiring fact, since tracing the connections of complex cells showed each one receiving input from such simple cells.
options.why: Tracing connections cell by cell is what was done for the fly’s Kenyon cells, not for complex cells. In V1, complex-from-simple is a proposal, put forward as “obviously tentative”.

options.text: A conclusion from models, since networks built on the arrangement recognize objects well, which shows the cortex is wired that way.
options.why: A network that works shows that an arrangement could do the job, not that the cortex uses it. The idea about complex cells is a tentative proposal.

options.text: A rejected idea, since complex cells were later found to take all of their input straight from the thalamus, with no simple cells involved.
options.why: The proposal has not been rejected, and complex cells are not described as taking all their input from the thalamus; most of a cortical cell’s input comes from other cortical cells. It stands as a tentative suggestion about how a complex cell might be built.

items.stem: Suppose complex cells are built as proposed, from simple cells that prefer the same orientation at slightly different positions. Which network operations would the two kinds of cell correspond to?

options.text: Simple cells to convolution, detecting a feature at each position, and complex cells to pooling, which ignores exactly where.
options.why: Correct. Each simple cell detects an oriented edge at one position, as one copy of a convolution detector does, and the complex cell combines them so the exact position no longer matters.

options.text: Simple cells to pooling, combining detections over a neighborhood, and complex cells to convolution, applying one detector everywhere.
options.why: The pairing is reversed. The cells that detect a feature at each position are the simple cells, and the cell that combines them and ignores where is the complex cell.

options.text: Simple cells to the input layer, which receives the image, and complex cells to the output, a weighted sum that reports the object.
options.why: In the comparison, the weighted sum that reports the object sits at the top of the ventral stream, over IT, not in V1. Simple and complex cells correspond to convolution and pooling.

options.text: Simple cells to a randomly wired middle layer that is never trained, and complex cells to the output connections that are trained.
options.why: Random wiring with a trained output is the mushroom body’s arrangement. The proposal for V1 pairs simple cells with convolution and complex cells with pooling.

items.stem: An engineer building a system to spot cracks in photographs of bridges copies one small detector for a thin diagonal line to every position in the image.
