options.why: That is a prototype model, one of the psychologists’ algorithms, and with one prototype per category it can only sort linearly separable categories. Re-representation pulls apart and brings together.

options.text: It passes each input on unchanged to a final stage, where one curved boundary does all of the sorting at once, with no recoding.
options.why: Passing the input on unchanged is the opposite of re-representing it. The point of the recoding is that the final step can be a single straight line.

items.stem: A penguin parent returning to a crowded colony has to pick out its own chick’s call. The chick’s call varies from one call to the next, and some neighbors’ chicks sound much like it. In the chapter’s terms, what must the stages between the parent’s ears and its response do with these calls?

options.text: Bring its own chick’s varied calls together and pull the neighbors’ similar calls apart, until one straight line separates them.
options.why: Correct. That is re-representation: different-sounding calls from one chick are brought together, and similar calls from other chicks are pulled apart, until one line will do.

options.text: Pull every call apart from every other one, so that no two calls, not even two calls from its own chick, are ever treated alike.
options.why: That meets only the demand to tell apart. A parent that did only this would treat each of its own chick’s calls as a new thing.

options.text: Bring similar-sounding calls together, so that its own chick and the neighbors’ chicks that sound like it are treated as one.
options.why: That meets only the demand to treat alike, and it would lump the neighbors’ chicks in with its own. Both demands have to be met at once.

options.text: Pass the raw sounds unchanged to a single unit, and lower that unit’s criterion until every call from its own chick is caught.
options.why: Lowering the criterion catches more of the chick’s calls but also more of the neighbors’, since it trades misses for false alarms. Only a better representation pulls the calls apart.

items.stem: A mouse needs to tell the smell of its own nest from the smell of a neighbor’s nest, which is almost the same. What does its piriform cortex do with two smells like these?

options.text: It pulls the two smells apart, so that the cells reading its output can tell them apart.
options.why: Correct. Two odors that share more than 70 percent of their active inputs at the bulb share only about a quarter of their active cells in the piriform cortex. That is pattern separation.

options.text: It brings the two smells together, so that both produce the response the familiar nest smell would.
options.why: Bringing a partial or faint smell back to the whole familiar pattern is pattern completion, which is mostly a model result there. For two similar smells, what was measured is separation.

options.text: It passes the two smells through a relay in the thalamus, which sharpens the difference between them.
options.why: Smell is the one sense that reaches the cortex without a relay in the thalamus. The bulb sends its output straight to the piriform cortex, which pulls the two smells apart.

options.text: It maps the two smells onto neighboring cells, so that similar smells sit side by side in an odor map.
options.why: The active piriform cells were scattered, with no clustering and no map. A cell’s neighbor was as likely to respond to a quite different odor as to the same one.

items.stem: In rewired ferrets, signals from the eyes were routed into the auditory cortex from the first day of life. What does this case add to the chapter’s answer that the neocortex re-represents whatever reaches it?

options.text: An area that would normally have handled sound came to treat light as light, because light was what reached it.
options.why: Correct. The same kind of cortex worked on a new kind of input when that input arrived. Input shapes what an area does, which is what an operation applied to whatever reaches it would predict.

options.text: Any area of the neocortex can take over any other area’s job, since auditory and visual cortex proved interchangeable.
options.why: The ferrets do not show that areas are interchangeable. The rewired map was less orderly, and the researchers describe the area as more visual-like, not visual.

options.text: The rewired ferrets saw as sharply through auditory cortex as through visual cortex, with an equally orderly map.
options.why: The rewired animals saw less sharply through that route, and their orientation map was less orderly, with about a quarter as many points where all orientations meet.

options.text: Auditory cortex holds a visual map from birth, which stays hidden until light signals from the eyes arrive and switch it on.
options.why: The orientation map developed as the animals grew up with visual input. The result is that input shapes what an area does, not that a hidden map was waiting.

items.stem: A person sees a cup near and far, to the left and to the right. By the chapter’s account, what do the stages of the ventral stream do with these many different images?

options.text: They turn the cup at many positions and sizes into a pattern that a weighted sum over a few hundred cells can report.
options.why: Correct. Up the stream, receptive fields grow and cells keep their preferences over wider changes, until a weighted sum over a few hundred IT neurons can report which object is in view.

options.text: They pass the images up to a single cell in IT that is fully invariant, so that it fires for the cup at every position and size.
options.why: No single cell becomes fully invariant. Cells in IT are tolerant, keeping their response over a limited range of changes, and the report comes from a weighted sum over a few hundred of them.

options.text: They store every image of the cup in V1, so that each new image can be matched against the stored examples of cups.
options.why: Storing every example is an exemplar model, an algorithm from psychology. The ventral stream re-represents the image in stages rather than storing every view.

options.text: They send each image straight from the thalamus to IT, where a cell for cups has been wired in since birth.
options.why: Visual signals reach V1 first and then pass through V2 and V4 to IT. The stages re-represent the image along the way, and nothing says a cup cell is wired in.

items.stem: A fish, a fly, a mouse, and a network all recognize things by pattern. What does the chapter say they share, and what does it say differs?

options.text: They share the problem of telling apart and treating alike from inputs never twice the same, and differ in the machinery that handles it.
options.why: Correct. The problem is the same for all four. Each handles it with different machinery: other circuits in the fish, a different nervous system in the fly, cortex in the mouse, and units on a computer in a network.

options.text: They share the machinery, one circuit plan repeated with variations, and they differ in the problems that their different inputs pose.
options.why: One circuit plan repeated with variations describes the mammalian neocortex, not a fish, a fly, and a network. The four share the problem, not the machinery.

options.text: They share a learning rule that passes errors back through every layer, and they differ only in how many units each one has.
options.why: There is no direct evidence for or against backpropagation in the cortex, and the fly’s expansion layer is never trained. What the four share is the problem.

options.text: They share a random expansion layer with a trained output, and they differ only in which of the senses feeds that layer.
options.why: Random expansion is the fly’s arrangement, and random wiring is only a model for the piriform cortex. The four share the problem and differ in machinery.

items.stem: In the chapter’s terms, the computational level can hold steady while the implementation is rebuilt beneath it. Which observation from the chapter best illustrates that?

options.text: A fly’s mushroom body and a mouse’s piriform cortex both handle similar smells, in structures their last common ancestor had nothing like.
options.why: Correct. The problem of sorting smells is the same, and the tissue that handles it arose separately in two lineages. Reading the resemblance as convergent evolution is an inference from the family tree, not something either study tested.

options.text: The neocortex is one circuit plan repeated with variations, so every area has the same classes of cells, connected in much the same way.
options.why: That is roughly the reverse pattern: one implementation repeated across areas that receive different inputs. Whether one plan means one computation everywhere is still open.

options.text: A hungry worm and a fed worm run the same circuit with different chemistry, so the same input can lead to different responses.
options.why: That is a criterion moved by neuromodulators, with the same wiring in both worms. The implementation stays put; it is not rebuilt beneath a steady problem.

options.text: Two odors that share more than 70 percent of their active inputs at the bulb share only about a quarter of their active cells in the piriform cortex.
options.why: That is pattern separation, measured in one structure. It shows what one implementation does with its input, and sets no second, different implementation against the same problem.

items.stem: Suppose researchers find that an octopus tells a crab from a rock by the pattern of activity across many receptors on its arms, from inputs that are never twice the same. Using the chapter’s lesson about levels, what can be said in advance about how the octopus does it?

options.text: It faces the same computational problem as a fish, a fly, or a mouse, though its machinery may turn out quite unlike any of theirs.
options.why: Correct. The problem does not fix the tissue. A fish, a fly, a mouse, and a network share the problem and differ in machinery, so an octopus could too.

options.text: It will turn out to have a pallium or something descended from one, since fish and mice both recognize with structures of that kind.
options.why: A fly recognizes smells with a mushroom body and no pallium at all. The computational level can hold steady while the implementation is rebuilt.

options.text: It will turn out to have a layered cortex like the mouse’s, since only a sheet of repeated circuits can re-represent its input.
options.why: The fly’s mushroom body re-represents smells with no cortex at all. Knowing the problem does not tell us which machinery handles it.

options.text: It is not recognizing patterns in the chapter’s sense, since an animal with no cortex has no means of telling inputs apart.
options.why: A fish and a fly recognize patterns with no neocortex. Lacking a cortex does not rule out handling the problem with other machinery.

items.stem: A fox recognizes a shape in the long grass as a hare. Which question does that recognition, by itself, leave unanswered?

options.text: What would happen if the fox pounced on the hare from where it now stands.
options.why: Correct. Recognizing a pattern tells an animal what a thing is. It does not, by itself, say what would happen if the animal acted on it, or why the thing is there.

options.text: Whether the shape in the grass is a hare at all, rather than a clump of earth.
options.why: Telling a hare from a clump of earth is exactly what recognition supplies: what the thing is.

options.text: Whether this hare, seen from the side, is the same kind of thing as hares seen from the front.
options.why: Treating one thing alike across viewpoints is invariance, part of the recognition problem itself. Recognition does answer it, imperfectly.

options.text: Whether the smell drifting from the grass belongs with hare smells the fox has smelled before.
options.why: Treating a new smell like familiar ones is generalization, one of the two demands of recognition. It is not among what recognition leaves out.

items.stem: Recognition tells an animal what a thing is. What does the chapter conclude about questions such as why the thing is there, what would happen if the animal acted on it, or how the parts of a thought combine?

options.text: They take more than recognizing a pattern does, and they return in later modules of the course.
options.why: Correct. Recognition alone does not answer them. The chapter marks them as needing more than recognition, and leaves them for later.

options.text: They are answered by recognition as well, once enough layers have re-represented the input.
options.why: More layers give a better recognizer, which still tells an animal only what a thing is. Why it is there, and what acting on it would do, take more than recognition.

options.text: They are answered by pattern completion, which fills in the rest of a situation from the part that was recognized.
options.why: Pattern completion recovers a whole stored pattern from part of it, which is still recognizing what a thing is. Why it is there, or what acting on it would do, takes more than recognition.

options.text: They are answered by the criterion, which sets what an animal does about whatever it recognizes.
options.why: The criterion sets where a yes-or-no line is drawn for one decision. It does not say why a thing is there or what acting on it would bring about.

items.stem: Which of these questions does the chapter’s account of recognition leave aside, rather than try to answer?

options.text: How the receptors in the nose turn odor chemicals into the activity that reaches the olfactory bulb.
options.why: Correct. The account takes its inputs as given: a smell already turned into activity in the olfactory bulb, an image already relayed through the thalamus. How the senses produce those signals is a separate question.

options.text: How two smells that overlap heavily at the bulb come to share far fewer active cells in the piriform cortex.
options.why: That is pattern separation, measured in the piriform cortex and explained, as a model that fits the data, by random wiring. It sits inside the account, which starts from the bulb’s output.

options.text: How a weighted sum over a few hundred cells in IT can report which object is in view.
options.why: That readout is the account’s own endpoint: a single straight line at the top of stages that have re-represented the image. The account starts from the image already relayed through the thalamus.

options.text: Why an auditory cortex fed by the eyes came to have cells tuned to edges at particular orientations.
options.why: The rewired ferrets are part of the account, and its answer is that input shapes what a cortical area does. What the account leaves aside is how the senses produce their signals in the first place.

items.stem: The chapter treats recognizing objects and recognizing words as specializations of the pattern recognition problem. What does calling them specializations commit it to?

options.text: Each still has to tell apart and treat alike from varied inputs, and each adds demands of its own on top of that.
options.why: Correct. Objects and words inherit the whole problem. On top of it, an object has a three-dimensional shape to recover from flat images, and a word is a pattern whose meaning is set by a language.

options.text: Each is a separate problem with its own kind of machinery, sharing nothing with how a mouse tells two smells apart.
options.why: Objects and words do bring their own demands, but a specialization keeps the general problem rather than replacing it. Telling apart and treating alike still have to be done.

options.text: Each is the general problem exactly, so the account of recognition already covers objects and words in full.
options.why: If nothing were added they would not need separate treatment. Each adds demands of its own, such as recovering a three-dimensional shape or a meaning set by a language.

options.text: Each is an easier case of the general problem, since objects and words fall into fixed categories with clear edges.
options.why: Categories have graded structure, with typical and atypical members, and objects and words are no exception. Specializing the problem adds demands; it does not remove them.

items.stem: A flat disc seen face-on and a ball can cast the same round outline on the eye. Which demand does this case illustrate?

options.text: A three-dimensional shape has to be recovered from the flat images it casts, since different shapes can cast the same one.
options.why: Correct. The outline alone does not say which shape cast it. Recovering the shape from flat images is a demand that recognizing objects adds to the general problem.

options.text: A pattern’s meaning has to be supplied by a language, since the same pattern can mean different things to different readers.
options.why: That is the demand that recognizing words adds: a word is a pattern whose meaning is set by a language. The disc and the ball are objects, and what the case shows is a shape to be recovered from flat images.

options.text: Overlapping inputs that call for different responses have to be pulled apart, so that a single line can sort them.
options.why: Pattern separation makes overlapping inputs less alike. Here the trouble is that the flat outline does not carry the shape at all, so the shape has to be recovered.

options.text: A criterion has to be set by what each kind of error costs, so that the more damaging mistake is the rarer one.
options.why: Setting a criterion decides where a yes-or-no line falls on evidence that already distinguishes the cases. Here the outline does not distinguish them; the shape has to be recovered.

items.stem: The written pattern “gift” means a present in English and poison in German. Which demand does this case illustrate?

options.text: A pattern’s meaning has to be supplied by a language, since the same pattern can mean different things in different languages.
options.why: Correct. The letters are the same in both cases. What they mean depends on which language they are read in: a word is a pattern whose meaning is set by a language. That is a demand recognizing words adds to the general problem.

options.text: A three-dimensional shape has to be recovered from the flat images it casts, since different shapes can cast the same one.
options.why: That is the demand recognizing objects adds. The “gift” case is about a word, whose meaning is set by a language.

options.text: Similar inputs that call for different responses have to be pulled apart before a line can sort them.
options.why: The two inputs here are not similar but identical, so no recoding of the pattern can pull them apart. What decides the meaning is the language.

options.text: A pattern has to be recognized across changes in size and position, such as large print and small print.
options.why: Recognizing a word in large and small print is invariance, part of the shared problem. The case shows meaning being set by a language.

items.stem: The chapter’s account of recognition starts from an image already relayed through the thalamus and a smell already turned into activity in the olfactory bulb. What becomes of the question of how the senses produce those signals?

options.text: It is left to a separate account of the senses, which is taken up together with recognizing objects.
options.why: Correct. The inputs were taken as given. Objects, and the senses that deliver their images, are taken up later, together, rather than inside the account of recognition.

options.text: It is answered inside the account of recognition, since the piriform cortex is where a smell is first turned into activity.
options.why: The olfactory bulb is the first stop for signals from the nose, and the piriform cortex receives its output. How the bulb’s signals are produced is a question about the senses.

options.text: It is set aside as unimportant, since what a cortical area does comes from its circuit plan and not from the senses that feed it.
options.why: The rewired ferrets showed that input shapes what a cortical area does, so input matters a great deal. The question is deferred, not dismissed.

options.text: It is answered by labeled lines, since each receptor already stands for one particular thing in the world.
options.why: A labeled line is one way of recognizing, like the worm’s copper detector, and most things have no detector of their own. How the senses produce their signals is deferred to a separate account.

items.stem: In a short paragraph, explain what it means to say that the computational level can hold steady while the implementation is rebuilt beneath it. Use two of the chapter’s cases.
items.answer: The computational level is the problem being solved. In this chapter it is the same for every case: tell apart what calls for different responses, and treat alike what comes from the same thing, from inputs that are never twice the same. The implementation is the physical machinery, and it differs from case to case. A mouse’s piriform cortex pulls similar smells apart with sparsely active cells in a three-layered cortex. A fly faces the same problem with a mushroom body, in a different nervous system altogether, built by an expansion onto randomly wired cells. The problem holds steady across the two while the tissue that handles it is rebuilt, so knowing the problem does not tell us which machinery will handle it.
rubric: Identifies the computational level as the problem: telling apart and treating alike from inputs never twice the same.
Identifies the implementation as the physical machinery that handles the problem.
Describes two of the chapter’s cases correctly (for example the fish’s pallium, the fly’s mushroom body, the mouse’s piriform cortex, the ventral stream, or a network).
States that the two cases share the problem but differ in machinery.
Draws the consequence that the problem does not fix which machinery handles it.

items.stem: On the island, with 200 hidden units fixed at random, Sparse is switched on and the run repeated. A line under the network’s drawing reports, for the smell now, how many of the 200 hidden units are active. What did Sparse change?

options.text: Far fewer of the 200 units were active than the hundred or so without it, and the test set held or improved, since few of many units active lets one line draw many more divisions.
options.why: Correct. Without Sparse about half the units were active; with it, far fewer. The test set came out nearly all right. When only a few of many units are active for each input, many more ways of dividing the inputs can be drawn with a single straight line, so one trained layer can do the work.

options.text: More of the 200 units were active than the hundred or so without it, and the test set improved, because more active units give the output unit more evidence to add up for each smell.
options.why: That reverses the count: Sparse cut the number of active units well below the hundred or so active without it. The gain comes from few units being active, not many.

options.text: Far fewer of the 200 units were active than the hundred or so without it, and the test set got worse, because silencing most of the units throws away information the output unit needed.
options.why: The count did fall, but fewer active units did not cost accuracy here; the test set held or improved. A code with few of many units active makes more divisions drawable with one straight line.

options.text: Far fewer of the 200 units were active than the hundred or so without it, and the hidden weights began to change, because under Sparse the active units’ weights are trained.
options.why: Under Fixed at random the hidden weights are drawn once and never move, with Sparse on or off; only the output unit learns. What changed was how many units each smell made active.

items.stem: A classmate argues that recognizing by pattern needs a neocortex, so an animal without one can only respond to what its labeled lines detect. How do the fish and the fly bear on that argument?

options.text: Both count against it: the fish meets the problem with a pallium, the fly with a mushroom body in a different nervous system altogether.
options.why: Correct. Neither animal has a neocortex, and both face the problem of telling apart and treating alike. The fish meets it with other circuits, and the fly with a structure in an insect’s brain, whose last common ancestor with the mouse had nothing like either the mushroom body or the piriform cortex.

options.text: Only the fish counts against it, since a fish’s pallium is a neocortex in all but name, while the fly’s mushroom body is no cortex at all.
options.why: A fish has a pallium and no neocortex, and the chapter keeps the two apart. The fish faces the problem with other circuits, and the fly counts against the argument too, with a different nervous system altogether.

options.text: Neither counts against it, since the fish’s pallium and the fly’s mushroom body each work as a set of labeled lines, one cell for each thing.
options.why: In the mushroom body each smell activates a few of about 2,000 Kenyon cells, each combining inputs at random, so no single cell stands for a smell. That is a pattern across many cells, not a labeled line.

options.text: Both count against it, because the fly’s mushroom body is inherited from the same ancestral structure as the mouse’s piriform cortex.
options.why: The fly and the mouse are separated by more than half a billion years, and their last common ancestor had nothing like either structure. The fly meets the problem with a different nervous system altogether, not with an inherited one.
